hazards.name: Large asteroid impact (≥1 km near-Earth asteroid)
hazards.one_line: A kilometre-class stony or iron near-Earth asteroid strikes Earth, lofting enough fine dust and soot into the stratosphere to suppress photosynthesis and destroy one or more global growing seasons.
hazards.mechanism: A ≥1 km asteroid arriving at ~20 km/s deposits 10^4–10^6 Mt of kinetic energy in seconds; the crater excavates and vaporises target rock, and the rising plume injects micrometre-scale silicate dust into the stratosphere, while thermal radiation from re-entering ejecta ignites wildfires that add soot. The blast, tsunami and thermal pulse kill regionally — hundreds of kilometres — and are not the global mechanism. The global mechanism is optical: Senel et al. (2023) show that fine silicate dust in the ~0.8–8.0 μm range has an atmospheric lifetime of order 15 years and, for the Chicxulub loading, drove global-average surface temperature down by as much as 15 °C and shut photosynthesis down for almost two years. Sub-Chicxulub impacts scale this down but the qualitative chain is the same: reduced photosynthetically active radiation plus surface cooling plus shortened frost-free season equals simultaneous harvest failure across the northern-hemisphere breadbaskets. Xia et al. (2022) calibrate the human end of that chain for stratospheric soot: injections above 5 Tg already cause mass food shortages that livestock and fisheries cannot offset, and a 150 Tg injection leaves more than 5 billion people without enough calories. People die of famine, in the second and third years, in countries that were never near the crater.

annual_probability.event_definition: impact on Earth by a near-Earth asteroid of diameter ≥1 km — the long-run background rate from the telescopic size-frequency distribution and collision probability, NOT adjusted for the fact that ~95% of this population is already catalogued and known to be clear for the next century
annual_probability.trend: The background arrival rate is flat on any human timescale. The rate of an UNWARNED ≥1 km impact is falling steeply and is now roughly 20x below the background rate: ~95% of ≥1 km NEOs are catalogued (NASEM 2023 decadal, Ch.18) and JPL Sentry currently lists only two objects at Palermo scale ≥ −2 — Bennu (0.49 km, cumulative impact probability 5.7e-4) and 29075 (1950 DA, 1.3 km, 3.77e-4) — neither of which threatens Earth this century. For the 140 m class the trend is also downward but far less advanced: 11,584 NEAs with H<22.0 are catalogued out of an estimated ~25,000, and NEO Surveyor (launch no earlier than 2027) is intended to close that gap.

severity_tiers.label: Regional catastrophe, no sustained impact winter
severity_tiers.description: A 1–1.5 km body, or an ocean strike, or a strike on sparsely populated land. Crater, tsunami and thermal pulse devastate a region; stratospheric dust loading stays below the threshold for multi-season global crop failure. NRC (2010) conservatively places the global-catastrophe threshold at 1.5 km diameter, so most of the ≥1 km distribution sits below it.

severity_tiers.label: Impact winter with global harvest failure
severity_tiers.description: A 1.5–5 km body. Dust plus wildfire soot in the stratosphere for years; photosynthetically active radiation and growing-season length both cut across the whole northern hemisphere. Deaths are overwhelmingly from famine in years 2–4, not from the impact. Death fraction anchored on Xia et al. (2022), where a 150 Tg stratospheric soot injection leaves >5 billion of ~8 billion people short of calories; a few-kilometre impact plausibly sits an order of magnitude below that loading.

severity_tiers.label: Chicxulub-class
severity_tiers.description: A ≥5 km body. Senel et al. (2023) parameters apply directly: ~15 year dust lifetime, up to 15 °C global cooling, ~2 years of effectively no photosynthesis. Agriculture is impossible for several consecutive years anywhere on Earth. Survival depends on stored food, fisheries, and non-photosynthetic (resilient) food production, none of which currently exists at scale.

severity_tiers.label: Terminal
severity_tiers.description: The residual case in which no self-sustaining human population persists through the winter and the subsequent centuries. Note that mammals, birds and crocodilians survived Chicxulub; humanity is far more capable than a Cretaceous mammal but also far more dependent on a functioning grain system. This tier is an author-estimate residual, not a measured quantity.

key_parameters.label: Survey completeness for NEAs ≥1 km
key_parameters.effect: Completeness does not change the arrival rate; it converts unwarned impacts into warned ones. Unwarned rate = (1−c) x 1.7e-6/yr. At c=0.95 that is 8.5e-8/yr. Because the catalogued fraction is additionally known to be clear for the next century (Sentry: no ≥1 km object with Palermo ≥ −2 before ~2880), the effective century risk from ≥1 km asteroids is roughly 20x below the geological rate.

key_parameters.label: Survey completeness for NEAs ≥140 m
key_parameters.effect: Derived live: 11,584 NEAs with H<22.0 in the JPL SBDB against an estimated ~25,000 (NASEM 2023). Unwarned ≥140 m rate = (1−c) x 1/20,000 yr (NASEM 2019 interval). c=0.46 gives 2.7e-5/yr; the congressional c=0.90 gives 5.0e-6/yr — a 5.4x reduction in the surprise rate for the regionally devastating size class.

key_parameters.label: Warning time from detection to impact
key_parameters.effect: Required deflection Δv to shift the impact point by one Earth radius ≈ 6371 km / (t x 3.156e7 s): 0.020 m/s at t=10 yr, 0.0040 m/s at t=50 yr. Required Δv ∝ 1/t, so deflectable mass at fixed impulse ∝ t and deflectable diameter ∝ t^(1/3). NRC (2010) places the kinetic-impactor regime at 'years to decades of warning time'; below roughly 5 years no impactor can be designed, built, launched and cruised, and only nuclear options remain.

key_parameters.label: Kinetic-impactor momentum enhancement factor β
key_parameters.effect: Δv delivered = β x m_spacecraft x v_impact / M_target. DART measured β = 3.61 (+0.19/−0.25, 1σ) assuming ρ = 2400 kg/m³, with the plausible range 2.2–4.9 across ρ = 1500–3300 kg/m³ (Daly et al. 2023). Because β is measured to be ~3.6 rather than the naive 1.0, the required impactor mass for a given deflection is ~3.6x smaller than pre-DART planning assumed. β is a target-property, not a spacecraft property: a monolithic or highly porous body could return β near 1, which would triple the launch mass required.

key_parameters.label: Launch-ready deflection spacecraft held in reserve
key_parameters.effect: NRC (2010): with 40 years of warning, roughly ten 10-tonne kinetic impactors could divert a body up to about 0.75 km diameter. Target mass ∝ D³, so deflectable diameter scales as (N x m x β x t)^(1/3): going from 1 to 10 impactors buys ~2.2x in diameter, not 10x. The current value is 0 — no deflection hardware exists on the shelf, so any real response starts with a multi-year build.

cascades_into: global-famine: the actual kill mechanism of every tier above the regional one is multi-year simultaneous harvest failure, not blast
nuclear-war: an unwarned airburst over or near a nuclear-armed state, or the collapse of food trade during an impact winter, both raise conflict probability
infrastructure-collapse: a food system holding a few months of grain stocks cannot absorb the loss of one or more consecutive global growing seasons

hazards.uncertainty_notes: WEAKEST POINTS, in order. (1) The severity tiers are the soft part of this entry. The three probabilities I report are of different kinds and must not be conflated: the EVENT rate (~1.7e-6/yr for ≥1 km) is well constrained by the telescopic size-frequency distribution and the cratering record and is probably good to a factor of ~1.5; the CONDITIONAL death fractions are author-estimates anchored on a soot-to-famine curve (Xia et al. 2022) that was built for nuclear war, not for impacts, and the mapping from impactor diameter to stratospheric dust and soot loading in Tg is exactly the step I could not find a published, quantitative, sub-Chicxulub curve for. A serious critic should attack the 0.30 deaths_fraction in the impact-winter tier first; it is a judgement, not a measurement. (2) The p_given_event split between tiers is derived by interpolating the size-frequency distribution between two retrieved anchors (1 km every ~520,000 yr, 10 km every ~100 Myr, implying P(≥10 km | ≥1 km) ≈ 0.005) with an assumed D^-2.5 slope; the slope is not itself cited here. (3) The terminal tier (p = 0.002 given a ≥1 km event, i.e. ~3.4e-9/yr) is a pure author-estimate. Ord's The Precipice (2020, Table 6.1) is widely reported as giving ~1 in 1,000,000 per century for asteroid/comet existential catastrophe — I could NOT retrieve the table itself this session, only secondary summaries, so I have deliberately excluded it from the citation list. My figure implies ~3.4e-7 per century for terminal outcomes from ≥1 km asteroids, i.e. about 3x below the reported Ord number; that is agreement within the noise of this kind of estimate, but I am not treating it as corroboration. (4) The two completeness figures for ≥1 km disagree slightly: dividing the live catalogue (867 with H<17.75) by Harris & D'Abramo's population estimate of 920 gives 94%, matching the decadal survey's '~95 percent', but the H<17.75 to 1 km conversion assumes an albedo of 0.14 and dark objects are systematically under-counted. Real completeness for ≥1 km is probably a few percent lower than the headline. (5) The 46% completeness I compute for ≥140 m divides a live H<22.0 count by a population estimate from a different source and a different epoch; the sources I retrieved that state completeness directly say 'about one third' (2019 and 2021 vintage) and one modelling paper says ~38%. 46% is the most current number but is the least cleanly sourced of the completeness figures. (6) NEO Surveyor is currently no earlier than September 2027 per NASA reporting; I did not fetch a NASA mission page confirming this and have not used it as a cited figure.

hazards.name: Long-period comet impact
hazards.one_line: A comet nucleus from the Oort cloud, discovered only months to a couple of years before arrival, strikes Earth at roughly twice the speed of an asteroid — the residual impact risk that no survey can retire in advance.
hazards.mechanism: A long-period comet spends essentially all of its orbit beyond detection range and becomes visible only on the inbound leg, typically inside a few AU. Comet Siding Spring, the standard case study, was discovered on 3 January 2013 and reached Mars on 22 October 2014 — 22 months of warning, and that was for a close approach, not a collision with a body being tracked toward Earth. If such an object is on an Earth-impacting trajectory the physical outcome is the asteroid impact-winter chain but harder: meteor-stream proxies give a median comet encounter velocity of 39.5 km/s against ~20 km/s for asteroids, so an equal-mass comet delivers ~3.9x the kinetic energy, and Nuth et al. put a typical comet impact at 50–100x the energy of a typical asteroid impact. More energy at higher altitude means more fine silicate dust and vaporised material injected higher into the stratosphere, where the ~15-year dust lifetime measured for Chicxulub applies. The kill mechanism is identical to the asteroid case — years of suppressed photosynthetically active radiation, cooling, growing-season loss and famine — but the response window is measured in months, and the NRC found that long-period-comet intercept trajectories typically permit only a ~0.5 tonne payload, which is 'sufficient for a nuclear package but rather small for a kinetic impactor'. DART-style deflection is therefore essentially inapplicable to this hazard.

annual_probability.event_definition: impact on Earth by a long-period comet nucleus of diameter ≥1 km (orbital period >200 years, i.e. dynamically new or near-new Oort-cloud objects)
annual_probability.trend: Flat to very slightly falling. Unlike asteroids, this rate cannot be retired by surveying: the population is not resident in the inner solar system and cannot be catalogued in advance. Wide-field surveys (Rubin/LSST, NEO Surveyor's comet sensitivity) will push the typical detection distance outward and so lengthen warning time from months toward a few years, which reduces the CONSEQUENCE-weighted risk without changing the arrival rate at all. This is the irreducible residual: as asteroid completeness rises toward 90–95%+, long-period comets become a progressively larger share of the remaining unwarned impact risk.

severity_tiers.label: Ocean or regional strike, limited global winter
severity_tiers.description: A ~1 km nucleus, low-density and volatile-rich, disrupting high in the atmosphere or striking deep ocean. Devastating tsunami and regional destruction; stratospheric dust loading stays below the multi-season global-crop-failure threshold. Less likely than for an asteroid of the same diameter because of the ~4x energy multiplier from the higher encounter velocity.

severity_tiers.label: Impact winter with global harvest failure
severity_tiers.description: The modal outcome for a ≥1 km comet. Energy comparable to a 1.5–3 km asteroid because of the 39.5 km/s median velocity. Years of dust- and soot-suppressed photosynthesis; simultaneous failure of the northern-hemisphere grain harvest. Worse than the asteroid equivalent in expectation because warning time is months, so no evacuation, no strategic grain build-up and no deflection are realistically possible.

severity_tiers.label: Chicxulub-class
severity_tiers.description: A ≥5 km nucleus. Full Senel et al. parameters: ~15-year dust lifetime, up to 15 °C cooling, ~2 years without effective photosynthesis. Total agricultural shutdown. Weighted slightly higher than the asteroid case because the comet size-frequency distribution extends to large nuclei and the velocity multiplier moves smaller bodies into this severity band.

severity_tiers.label: Terminal
severity_tiers.description: No self-sustaining human population persists. Author-estimate residual, set slightly above the asteroid case purely because the deflection option is absent and the warning is too short for any preparatory response.

key_parameters.label: Warning time from discovery to impact
key_parameters.effect: The single dominant knob. Below ~24 months no bespoke interceptor can be designed, built and flown, so the response set collapses to whatever hardware already exists. Required deflection Δv to move the impact point by one Earth radius ≈ 6371 km / t: at t = 22 months (5.8e7 s) that is 0.11 m/s, more than 5x the Δv needed at 10 years' warning, applied to a body that is typically larger and always faster. Above ~36–48 months a standing-launch-vehicle nuclear standoff mission becomes conceivable; below ~6 months only evacuation and food stockpiling remain.

key_parameters.label: Payload deliverable onto a long-period-comet intercept trajectory
key_parameters.effect: NRC (2010): LPC intercepts 'typically permit delivery of only 0.5-ton payloads — sufficient for a nuclear package but rather small for a kinetic impactor'. Kinetic Δv = β·m·v_rel/M: 0.5 t at 50 km/s relative with β = 3.6 gives ~9e7 kg·m/s, which on a 1 km comet of mass ~5e11 kg is only ~1.8e-4 m/s — roughly 600x short of the 0.11 m/s needed at 22 months' warning. Nuclear standoff yields 10^2–10^3 times more impulse per kilogram and is the only physically viable option in this regime.

key_parameters.label: Long-period comet share of total impact risk
key_parameters.effect: Scales this hazard's contribution linearly. The published range is genuinely wide and the two ends mean different things: NRC (2010) and the 2023 decadal both say comets are 'on the order of <1 percent' / '~1 percent' of the total NEO impact RISK, while Nuth et al. (2018) argue comets are '100 times less likely' to strike but represent 'about half of the destructive threat' because each impact carries 50–100x the energy. The two are reconcilable — they agree on the rate ratio (~1/100) and disagree on how to weight energy — but a simulator must pick one convention and state it.

key_parameters.label: Comet encounter velocity
key_parameters.effect: Kinetic energy ∝ v². At the meteor-stream median of 39.5 km/s a comet delivers 3.9x the energy of an equal-mass asteroid at 20 km/s; at the 71 km/s retrograde extreme, 12.6x. Since stratospheric dust and soot loading rises roughly with delivered energy, and the death fraction rises with loading (Xia et al.: 5 Tg soot already causes mass food shortage, 150 Tg kills >5 billion), velocity moves a comet up the severity ladder by roughly one diameter octave relative to an asteroid.

key_parameters.label: Nuclear-capable interceptor held launch-ready
key_parameters.unit: binary (0 = none, 1 = ready to launch on demand)
key_parameters.effect: A step function, not a continuum. NRC (2010): long-period comets 'would require a spacecraft that is ready to launch when the decision is made to act'. At 0 (the current value) the deflectable fraction of the long-period-comet hazard is approximately zero regardless of every other knob, because the build time exceeds the warning time. At 1, the deflectable fraction becomes roughly the fraction of LPC impacts with warning time above the mission's flight time — perhaps 0.3–0.6 for a 22-month median warning, an author-estimate. This knob, not survey completeness, is the only one that retires any of this hazard.

cascades_into: large-asteroid-impact: shares the identical impact-winter severity ladder and the identical famine kill-chain; a simulator should apply one dust-to-mortality curve to both
global-famine: the terminal pathway for every tier above the regional one
nuclear-war: the only feasible short-warning response requires nuclear devices held ready for launch, which itself has arms-control and misattribution consequences

hazards.uncertainty_notes: WEAKEST POINTS, in order. (1) The annual probability is the weakest number in this entire packet. It is not measured; it is constructed by taking the ≥1 km asteroid rate (~1.7e-6/yr, well sourced) and multiplying by a rate ratio of ~1/100 that comes from two independent statements — the NRC/decadal '<1 percent of total risk' and Nuth et al.'s '100 times less likely' — which happen to agree numerically but are not the same quantity: one is a RISK share, the other a RATE ratio. If the NRC's <1% is risk-weighted (i.e. already includes the energy multiplier), then the true rate ratio is nearer 1/300 to 1/1000 and my best estimate is high by up to an order of magnitude. I have widened low/high to 5e-9–1e-7 to cover this, but a critic should attack this construction first. There is no direct observational determination of the long-period-comet Earth-impact rate in anything I retrieved — the observed sample of LPC Earth impacts is zero. (2) The NRC/decadal figure (~1%) and Nuth et al. (~50% of destructive threat) genuinely disagree about how large this hazard is, by a factor of ~50. I have exposed that as a tunable knob rather than silently picking one. A model that adopts Nuth's convention should expect this hazard's expected-mortality contribution to approach that of asteroids despite the far lower rate. (3) The severity tier probabilities are author-estimates. There is no published comet-specific size-frequency distribution in what I retrieved, so the split across tiers is inferred from the asteroid distribution shifted upward by the velocity-energy factor (39.5 vs 20 km/s → 3.9x energy → roughly one size-class shift). That inference is mine, not a citation. (4) The '22 months' warning figure is a single case study (Siding Spring, a Mars close approach, not an Earth impactor), used by Nuth et al. as their exemplar. It is not a distribution. Real warning times for an impacting LPC could plausibly range from a few weeks to several years depending on nucleus size, activity onset distance, and survey cadence; treating 22 months as a median is an assumption. (5) The 0.3–0.6 'deflectable fraction with a standing interceptor' quoted in the interceptor knob is an author-estimate with no source; it should be treated as a placeholder for a proper mission-design study. (6) I could not retrieve Ord's The Precipice Table 6.1 or the 2023 Existential Risk Persuasion Tournament report at source this session (the XPT working paper exceeded the fetch size limit and the Precipice table exists only as an image in the sources I could reach), so no expert-elicitation figure is cited in this packet. Secondary reporting puts Ord's asteroid/comet existential estimate at ~1 in 1,000,000 per century and the XPT's non-anthropogenic extinction estimate at ~0.004% by 2100 with experts and superforecasters in near-agreement; I have deliberately NOT dressed either as a citation, and a follow-up pass should retrieve both at source.

hazards.name: Mainline anthropogenic warming (chronic damage)
hazards.one_line: Continued greenhouse-gas forcing warms the planet by roughly 1.4–4.4 °C by 2100 depending on emissions pathway, killing people chronically through heat, food-system stress and conflict rather than in a single event.
hazards.mechanism: Radiative forcing from accumulated CO2 and other greenhouse gases raises global mean surface temperature; AR6 assesses 1.09 °C of warming already realised over 2011–2020 relative to 1850–1900. The warming does not kill directly at the global scale — it shifts the distribution of heat, drought, flood and growing-season conditions. The dominant proximate killers are (a) direct heat mortality in hot, poor, low-adaptive-capacity regions, which Carleton et al. quantify at an additional 85 deaths per 100,000 per year by 2100 under RCP8.5 after netting adaptation benefits against adaptation costs, and (b) food-price and food-availability shocks when major breadbaskets fail in the same year. Gaupp et al. show the annual probability of simultaneous climate risk across all major breadbaskets already rose between 1967–1990 and 1991–2012 (wheat 0.3% to 1.2%). Kornhuber et al. show that the jet-stream meander states that drive synchronous Northern-Hemisphere harvest failures are systematically under-reproduced by bias-adjusted crop and climate models, so the modelled tail of simultaneous failure is too thin. Mass death in this hazard is famine and heat, mediated by markets and governments, not drowning or storms.

annual_probability.event_definition: The chronic hazard is ACTIVE in any given year — i.e. anthropogenic warming continues to accumulate and impose damage. This is not a stochastic event: AR6 assesses human influence on warming as unequivocal and 2011–2020 as 1.09 °C above 1850–1900. In a simulator the SSP knob must set the MAGNITUDE of damage, not the probability of occurrence.
annual_probability.trend: Severity rising, probability flat at ~1. Under SSP2-4.5 (best estimate 2.7 °C by 2081–2100) damage roughly doubles per ~0.6 °C of additional warming in the 2.7–4.4 °C band, inferred from the two Carleton mortality points. Probability of the hazard being active cannot rise above 1.

severity_tiers.label: Paris-consistent (~1.8 °C)
severity_tiers.description: SSP1-2.6 pathway; 1.8 °C best estimate (very likely 1.3–2.4 °C) by 2081–2100. Coral reefs are lost and regional impacts are severe, but global excess mortality stays an order of magnitude below the high-emissions case. Deaths fraction is a 10-year cumulative excess-mortality figure near 2100, extrapolated below Carleton's RCP4.5 point.

severity_tiers.label: Current-policy (~2.7 °C)
severity_tiers.description: SSP2-4.5 pathway; 2.7 °C best estimate (very likely 2.1–3.5 °C) by 2081–2100. Carleton et al. put RCP4.5 full mortality risk about 84% below the RCP8.5 figure, i.e. roughly 14 additional deaths per 100,000 per year by 2100; over ten years that is ~0.14% of population. Several Armstrong McKay tipping thresholds are exceeded on the way, which is why this hazard cascades into the tail entry.

severity_tiers.label: High emissions (~3.6–4.4 °C)
severity_tiers.description: SSP3-7.0 to SSP5-8.5; 3.6 °C (2.8–4.6) to 4.4 °C (3.3–5.7) by 2081–2100. Carleton et al.: an additional 85 deaths per 100,000 annually by 2100 under RCP8.5 including adaptation costs, i.e. ~0.85% of population over a decade. This is a mortality-only figure; it excludes famine, conflict and displacement deaths.

severity_tiers.label: High emissions with food-system failure
severity_tiers.description: High-end warming coinciding with repeated multi-breadbasket failure and the conflict/displacement channel that Carleton's mortality-only estimate excludes. Author-estimate: the excess over the pure-heat figure is not published as a single number. Severe regional state failure, no global industrial collapse.

key_parameters.label: Emissions pathway (SSP end-of-century forcing)
key_parameters.effect: Maps directly to AR6 Table SPM.1 warming for 2081–2100 relative to 1850–1900: SSP1-1.9 → 1.4 °C (1.0–1.8); SSP1-2.6 → 1.8 °C (1.3–2.4); SSP2-4.5 → 2.7 °C (2.1–3.5); SSP3-7.0 → 3.6 °C (2.8–4.6); SSP5-8.5 → 4.4 °C (3.3–5.7). Use piecewise-linear interpolation in forcing; the mapping is close to linear over 1.9–8.5 W/m2 (~0.45 °C per W/m2).

key_parameters.label: Equilibrium climate sensitivity
key_parameters.effect: AR6 best estimate 3 °C, likely range 2.5–4 °C, very likely 2–5 °C. 2100 warming scales approximately linearly with ECS for a fixed pathway: at the very likely bounds, SSP2-4.5's 2.7 °C central becomes roughly its 2.1–3.5 °C very likely range. Combined with the convex mortality response, moving ECS from 3.0 to 5.0 on SSP2-4.5 raises end-century heat mortality by roughly a factor of 4–6.

key_parameters.label: Realised warming in 2081–2100
key_parameters.effect: Heat-mortality driver. Two retrieved anchor points (Carleton et al.): ~14 additional deaths per 100,000/yr at RCP4.5 (≈2.7 °C) and 85 at RCP8.5 (≈4.4 °C). That is a factor of ~6 over 1.7 °C, i.e. a doubling roughly every 0.65 °C — use m(T) = 14 * 2^((T-2.7)/0.65) deaths per 100,000 per year, valid only inside 2–4.5 °C.

key_parameters.label: Annual probability of simultaneous climate risk in ALL major breadbaskets (wheat)
key_parameters.effect: Gaupp et al. measure this rising from 0.3% (1967–1990) to 1.2% (1991–2012) for wheat, 0.8% to 1.1% for maize, 1.7% to 2% for soybean. Treat as the trigger rate for a global food-price shock. Kornhuber et al. find the jet-meander mechanism that drives synchronous failure is under-reproduced in bias-adjusted models, so the upper end of the knob's range is not an absurd setting.

citations.claim: AR6 assessed 2081–2100 warming relative to 1850–1900 for each SSP, and the assessed equilibrium climate sensitivity.
citations.authors: IPCC AR6 Working Group I (figures retrieved via Carbon Brief's reproduction of Table SPM.1; ipcc.ch returned HTTP 403 to direct fetches this session)
citations.venue: Carbon Brief, In-depth Q&A: The IPCC's sixth assessment report on climate science (reproducing IPCC AR6 WGI Table SPM.1)

citations.claim: AR6 equilibrium climate sensitivity and observed warming.
citations.authors: IPCC AR6 Working Group I, Summary for Policymakers (retrieved via Carbon Brief's SPM comparison article)
citations.venue: Carbon Brief, 'IPCC: How the AR6 WG1 summary for policymakers compares to its predecessor'
citations.exact_figure: ECS: 'likely range is given as 2.5C to 4C, which also provides a best estimate of 3C'; very likely range 2 °C (high confidence) to 5 °C (medium confidence). Observed warming: 'AR6 finds that 2011-20 was 1.09C warmer than 1850-1900.' Human-caused warming 1850–1900 to 2010–19: 1.07 °C (range 0.8–1.3 °C).

citations.claim: Globally comprehensive, adaptation-adjusted mortality cost of warming.
citations.authors: Carleton T, Jina A, Delgado M, Greenstone M, Houser T, Hsiang S, Hultgren A, Kopp RE, McCusker KE, Nath I, Rising J, Rode A, Seo HK, Viaene A, Yuan J, Zhang AT

Mortality partial social cost of carbon $36.6/ton (high emissions) and $17.1/ton (moderate), 2% discount rate.

citations.claim: The annual probability of simultaneous breadbasket failure has already risen measurably.
citations.authors: Gaupp F, Hall J, Hochrainer-Stigler S, Dadson S
citations.venue: Nature Climate Change 10: 54–57 (figures retrieved via ClimateChangePost's summary)

citations.claim: Crop and climate models systematically underestimate the synchronous-failure mechanism, so the modelled famine tail is too thin.
citations.authors: Kornhuber K, Lesk C, Schleussner CF, Jägermeyr J, Pfleiderer P, Horton RM
citations.venue: Nature Communications 14: 3528 (abstract retrieved via Europe PMC)
citations.exact_figure: 'we find an increased likelihood of concurrent low yields during summers featuring meandering jets in observations and models. While climate models accurately simulate atmospheric patterns, associated surface weather anomalies and negative effects on crop responses are mostly underestimated in bias-adjusted simulations.' No single quantitative multiplier is given in the abstract.

cascades_into: tipping-cascade-high-sensitivity-tail: every tenth of a degree of mainline warming raises the probability that Armstrong McKay thresholds are crossed, and several central thresholds (~1.5 °C) sit BELOW the SSP2-4.5 best estimate of 2.7 °C

conflict-and-war: Kemp et al. name conflict as one of four proximate mass-mortality channels, and project 2 billion people living above 29 °C mean annual temperature by 2070 in politically fragile regions containing two nuclear powers
systemic-food-system-failure: multi-breadbasket failure is the actual famine mechanism, and its annual probability is already measurably rising
hazards.uncertainty_notes: Three weaknesses a serious critic would attack. (1) The IPCC figures were NOT retrieved from ipcc.ch — every direct fetch of the AR6 SPM PDF and HTML returned HTTP 403 this session — so Table SPM.1, the ECS ranges and the 1.09 °C observed-warming figure come from Carbon Brief's reproduction of them. They match my prior knowledge of AR6 exactly, but the chain of custody is one hop longer than ideal and a reviewer should re-verify against IPCC_AR6_WGI_SPM.pdf. I could not retrieve the very likely range on the 1.09 °C figure at all. (2) The mortality figures are heat-mortality only. Carleton et al. explicitly value temperature-driven mortality net of adaptation; they do NOT include famine, conflict, displacement, vector-borne disease, or sea-level-rise deaths. Using their 85/100,000/yr as the total death rate at 4.4 °C is therefore a LOWER bound, and my fourth severity tier's 0.04 deaths fraction is an author-estimate with no published anchor. (3) The exponential fit m(T) = 14 * 2^((T-2.7)/0.65) is my own two-point interpolation between Carleton's RCP4.5 and RCP8.5 results; the underlying paper does not publish that functional form, and it should not be extrapolated below 2 °C or above 4.5 °C. Also note the honest shape: this hazard has probability ~1 and severity that is large in absolute deaths but small as a fraction of world population within any decade. It is a near-certain major harm, not a plausible extinction cause; a simulator that treats it as a Poisson event with a small rate has the shape wrong.

hazards.name: Tipping cascade / high-sensitivity climate tail
hazards.one_line: The badly-studied upper tail in which high climate sensitivity, a strong carbon-cycle feedback, or a cascade of crossed tipping elements pushes warming past 3 °C and breaks food systems and habitability over large regions.
hazards.mechanism: Armstrong McKay et al. identify sixteen tipping elements whose central thresholds cluster low: Greenland Ice Sheet ~1.5 °C, West Antarctic Ice Sheet ~1.5 °C, tropical coral reefs ~1.5 °C, widespread abrupt permafrost thaw ~1.5 °C, Labrador–Irminger Sea convection ~1.5–2 °C. Crossing them commits multi-metre sea-level rise over centuries and, in the permafrost case, amplifies permafrost carbon emissions by roughly 50%, which feeds back into warming. Higher up sit Amazon dieback (~3.5 °C) and AMOC shutdown (central ~4 °C, range 1–8 °C); an AMOC collapse would cool north-west Europe abruptly while disrupting monsoons that feed billions. The kill chain is not the ice or the current: it is agriculture. Kemp et al. name famine and undernutrition, extreme weather, conflict, and vector-borne disease as the Four Horsemen, and project that areas with annual mean temperature above 29 °C — home to about 30 million people today — will hold about 2 billion by 2070 under SSP3-7.0, overlapping two nuclear powers and seven maximum-containment laboratories. Wet-bulb limits set the outer bound on habitability: Vecellio et al.'s empirical critical limit of 30.55 ± 0.98 °C in humid conditions is well below Sherwood & Huber's theoretical 35 °C, so uninhabitable-by-heat conditions arrive at lower warming than the classic figure implies. Extinction, as opposed to catastrophe, is not a mechanism anyone has demonstrated; it would require the food system to fail globally and permanently, which no retrieved study models.

annual_probability.event_definition: Onset, in a given year during the 21st century, of the 'extreme climate change' regime as Kemp et al. define it — mean global surface temperature rise of 3 °C or more above preindustrial by 2100 — TOGETHER with the crossing of three or more core tipping elements. Best estimate corresponds to about 14% over the century; the range spans about 3% to 40% per century.
annual_probability.trend: Rising through mid-century then pathway-dependent. Under SSP2-4.5's 2.7 °C best estimate the low-threshold elements (~1.5 °C) are crossed regardless; the >3 °C condition is what the emissions and sensitivity knobs control. Under SSP1-2.6 (1.8 °C) the >3 °C condition is very unlikely and this hazard's rate falls by roughly an order of magnitude.

severity_tiers.label: Cascade without decimation
severity_tiers.description: Several core elements cross. Multi-metre sea-level rise is committed but plays out over centuries; coral fisheries collapse; permafrost feedback adds warming. Adaptation and trade absorb the food shocks. Large regional harm, large economic loss, no global mass-mortality event within a decade.

severity_tiers.label: Global decimation (Kemp et al. threshold)
severity_tiers.description: Kemp et al.'s 'Global Decimation Risk': loss of 10% or more of global population and severe disruption of global critical systems such as food, within a given timeframe. Mechanism is repeated multi-breadbasket failure plus conflict and displacement in the 29 °C-plus belt, not the tipping events themselves.

severity_tiers.label: Global catastrophe (Kemp et al. GCR threshold)
severity_tiers.description: Kemp et al.'s 'Global Catastrophic Risk': loss of 25% of the global population and severe disruption of global critical systems. Requires the climate shock to compound with war, financial and state collapse — the 'catastrophe convergence' the Climate Endgame paper argues is under-studied. Industrial capacity survives but is set back for generations.

severity_tiers.label: Terminal
severity_tiers.description: Humanity does not recover. No retrieved study demonstrates a mechanism by which climate change alone does this; Sherwood & Huber's 11–12 °C figure (majority of the currently-distributed human population in regions exceeding the 35 °C wet-bulb limit) is the nearest thing to a physical route, and it requires warming far above any SSP best estimate. The number here is anchored on Ord's elicited 1-in-1,000-per-century existential estimate divided by this hazard's per-century rate.

key_parameters.label: Emissions pathway (SSP end-of-century forcing)
key_parameters.effect: Sets 2081–2100 warming per AR6 Table SPM.1 (1.4 / 1.8 / 2.7 / 3.6 / 4.4 °C for SSP1-1.9 / 1-2.6 / 2-4.5 / 3-7.0 / 5-8.5). Count how many Armstrong McKay central thresholds that warming exceeds: at 1.8 °C roughly five (coral, Greenland, WAIS, abrupt permafrost thaw, Labrador–Irminger convection); at 2.7 °C add boreal dieback, mountain glaciers, Barents sea ice, Sahel greening; at 4.4 °C add East Antarctic subglacial basins (~3 °C), Amazon (~3.5 °C), Yedoma permafrost (~3–4 °C) and AMOC (~4 °C central).

key_parameters.label: Equilibrium climate sensitivity
key_parameters.effect: AR6: best estimate 3 °C, likely 2.5–4 °C, very likely 2–5 °C. This is the single knob that most cleanly generates the tail: holding SSP2-4.5 fixed, ECS = 5 pushes 2100 warming toward the top of the 2.1–3.5 °C very likely band and crosses the >3 °C 'extreme climate change' condition, whereas ECS = 2 keeps it near 2.1 °C. Warming scales approximately linearly in ECS; the number of crossed tipping thresholds is a step function of the resulting warming.

key_parameters.label: Tipping threshold offset (shifts all Armstrong McKay central thresholds)
key_parameters.effect: Adds a uniform offset to every central threshold. At offset 0 the paper's own uncertainty ranges are wide — Greenland 1–3 °C on a ~1.5 °C central, AMOC 1–8 °C on a ~4 °C central — so an offset of about ±1.5 °C spans most of the published spread for the ice sheets and about ±3 °C would be needed to span the AMOC range. Negative offsets bring Amazon dieback (~3.5 °C) and East Antarctic basins (~3 °C) inside the SSP2-4.5 best estimate; +1.5 °C leaves only tropical coral (~1.5 °C, range 1–2 °C) crossed at 2.7 °C.

key_parameters.label: Human wet-bulb survivability limit
key_parameters.effect: Sets when a region becomes physically uninhabitable to unaided humans. At 35 °C (Sherwood & Huber's theoretical value) the limit is first exceeded at about 7 °C of global-mean warming and covers the majority of the current human distribution at 11–12 °C. Vecellio et al. measured 30.55 ± 0.98 °C empirically in humid conditions and lower still in hot-dry conditions, so the real limit sits ~4.5 °C below the theoretical one — but NO retrieved source gives the corresponding shifted global-warming threshold, so the mapping from this knob to warming must be flagged as unmeasured rather than fitted.

key_parameters.label: Annual hazard of AMOC collapse onset
key_parameters.effect: Deliberately set between two contested poles. IPCC AR6 assesses a full 21st-century collapse as unlikely; Ditlevsen & Ditlevsen's data-driven estimator gives a central tipping year of 2057 with a 95% confidence interval of 2025–2095, which if spread over that window is roughly 1.4%/yr; van Westen et al. find a physics-based early-warning indicator suggesting the present-day AMOC is on route to tipping, without dating it. 0.3%/yr (~20%/century) is my compromise, not a published figure. Raising this knob should raise the decimation tier's weight via European agricultural collapse and monsoon disruption, not the terminal tier.

citations.claim: Tipping element central thresholds, ranges and timescales.
citations.authors: Armstrong McKay DI, Staal A, Abrams JF, Winkelmann R, Sakschewski B, Loriani S, Fetzer I, Cornell SE, Rockström J, Lenton TM (threshold table retrieved from the lead author's own paper explainer at climatetippingpoints.info; the Science table itself is paywalled)
citations.venue: Science 377(6611): eabn7950 (bibliographic record confirmed via Europe PMC)
citations.exact_figure: Global core elements, central threshold (range), timescale: Greenland Ice Sheet ~1.5 °C (1–3 °C), hundreds–thousands of years, 7+ m SLR; West Antarctic Ice Sheet ~1.5 °C (1–3 °C), hundreds–thousands of years, 3–4 m SLR; East Antarctic subglacial basins ~3 °C (2–6 °C), centuries–millennia, 10+ m SLR; AMOC ~3–5 °C (1–8 °C), decades–centuries; Labrador–Irminger Sea convection ~1.5–2 °C (1–3 °C), decades; tropical coral reefs ~1.5 °C (1–2 °C), ~1 decade; Amazon rainforest ~3.5 °C (2–5 °C), decades–centuries; southern boreal forest dieback ~2 °C (1–3 °C); widespread abrupt permafrost thaw ~1.5 °C (1–3 °C), decades, amplifies permafrost emissions ~50%. Regional: mountain glaciers ~2 °C (1–4 °C); Barents sea ice ~2 °C (1–3 °C); northern boreal expansion ~2–3 °C (1–4 °C); Yedoma permafrost collapse ~3–4 °C (2–5 °C), releases 0.2–0.4 °C of feedback warming; Arctic winter sea ice ~5 °C+ (3–8 °C); Sahel greening ~2–3 °C (1–4 °C). Abstract: current warming at ~1.1 °C already approaches certain tipping ranges; multiple tipping points could activate between 1.5–2 °C.

citations.authors: Kemp L, Xu C, Depledge J, Ebi KL, Gibbins G, Kohler TA, Rockström J, Scheffer M, Schellnhuber HJ, Steffen W, Lenton TM

citations.claim: Theoretical wet-bulb habitability limit and the warming required to breach it.
citations.authors: Sherwood SC, Huber M
citations.venue: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences 107: 9552–9555 (abstract retrieved verbatim via Europe PMC)

Any exceedence of 35 degrees C for extended periods should induce hyperthermia in humans and other mammals... While this never happens now, it would begin to occur with global-mean warming of about 7 degrees C, calling the habitability of some regions into question. With 11-12 degrees C warming, such regions would spread to encompass the majority of the human population as currently distributed.'

citations.claim: Empirical revision of the 35 °C wet-bulb threshold downward.
citations.authors: Vecellio DJ, Wolf ST, Cottle RM, Kenney WL
citations.venue: Journal of Applied Physiology 132(2): 340–345 (abstract retrieved verbatim via Europe PMC)

citations.claim: Expert elicitation anchor for the EXISTENTIAL (not catastrophic) tail.
citations.authors: Ord T
citations.venue: The Precipice (Bloomsbury), Table 6.1; restated by the author on tobyord.com
citations.exact_figure: 'I gave my best guess probabilities for the existential risk over the next 100 years in each of these areas. These were 1 in 1,000 for Climate and for Nuclear, 1 in 30 for Pandemics and 1 in 10 for Unaligned AI.' In the same piece Ord says his climate risk estimate has since decreased, without giving a revised number.

cascades_into: mainline-warming-damage: the permafrost feedback (widespread abrupt thaw amplifies permafrost emissions ~50%; Yedoma collapse releases 0.2–0.4 °C of warming) raises realised warming for a fixed emissions pathway, so the tail feeds back into the mainline damage function
conflict-and-war: Kemp et al. note the 29 °C-plus belt in 2070 overlaps two nuclear powers, and name conflict as one of the Four Horsemen
engineered-pandemic: Kemp et al. note seven maximum-containment laboratories fall inside the projected extreme-heat zone by 2070, a state-fragility-meets-biosafety coupling
systemic-food-system-failure: multi-breadbasket failure is the proximate kill mechanism for both the decimation and catastrophe tiers
hazards.uncertainty_notes: This is the weakest entry in the packet and should be labelled as such in any UI. (1) The annual probability is an AUTHOR-ESTIMATE with no published anchor. No retrieved source gives a probability for a multi-element tipping cascade. I could not obtain climate-specific numbers from the 2023 Existential Risk Persuasion Tournament: the report PDF exceeded the fetch size limit, the Forecasting Research Institute landing page and the EA Forum sequence contain no climate row, and my WebSearch budget was exhausted before I could reach the per-domain table. So the only elicitation anchor here is Ord's 1-in-1,000-per-century existential figure, from which I back out p(terminal | tail) = 0.005. A critic who thinks Ord's figure is too high or too low moves my terminal tier proportionally, and they would be right to. (2) The tipping thresholds are from the lead author's own explainer, not from the Science paper's Table 1 directly (paywalled). The explainer's AMOC figure reads '~3–5 °C central, 1–8 °C range'; I have seen the paper cited elsewhere as a 4.0 °C best estimate with a 1.4–8.0 °C range, and a reviewer should check Table 1 before compiling. (3) Armstrong McKay's thresholds carry LOW confidence in the paper itself for most elements — a critic would attack any simulator that treats them as sharp step functions, which is exactly why the tipping_threshold_offset knob exists. (4) The AMOC hazard rate of 0.3%/yr is mine, not anyone's: IPCC AR6 says a full 21st-century collapse is unlikely, Ditlevsen & Ditlevsen imply roughly 1.4%/yr, and their result is genuinely contested — the estimator is a highly idealised stochastic differential equation fitted to a sea-surface-temperature fingerprint proxy, the direct AMOC observational record only starts in 2004, and the authors themselves say 'we don't have an explanation for the outcome we observe'. A 2025 Author Correction moved the tipping-time estimate by 8 years, which is itself a signal of how sensitive the result is. (5) The wet_bulb_limit knob's mapping to global warming is UNMEASURED: Sherwood & Huber's 7 °C figure is for the 35 °C limit, and no retrieved source gives the equivalent warming for Vecellio's 30.6 °C limit. Do not fit a curve there. (6) Most important for honesty in both directions: the terminal tier is small on purpose. Kemp et al.'s whole argument is that this tail is UNDER-STUDIED, not that it is probable — they call it 'dangerously underexplored', which is a claim about our ignorance, not a probability. Nothing retrieved this session demonstrates a physical mechanism by which climate change alone permanently ends humanity below roughly 11–12 °C of warming, which is above every SSP best estimate including SSP5-8.5's 4.4 °C.

hazards.name: Deliberate release of an engineered pandemic pathogen
hazards.one_line: A state programme or small group deliberately releases a pathogen modified to be more transmissible, more lethal, or harder to counter than anything circulating naturally.
hazards.mechanism: A deliberately released respiratory-transmissible pathogen spreads through travel networks faster than surveillance detects it; the defining feature versus a natural pandemic is that the attacker chooses the trait combination (transmissibility, incubation period, case fatality, countermeasure evasion) rather than accepting the trade-offs evolution imposes, and can seed many locations simultaneously rather than at one index point. Direct infection deaths are only the first term. The larger term is the collapse of the systems that keep eight billion people alive: healthcare workers are among the first infected and hospitals fail as staffing collapses; ports, freight, refineries and fertiliser plants stop when absenteeism passes a threshold, and food-exporting countries impose export bans. Historically famine, untreated ordinary illness, and loss of clean water kill more than the epidemic agent itself in a collapse. Extinction from any single agent is not the expected path even in the worst tiers — pockets of survivors are geographically isolated and infection eventually burns out — so a terminal outcome requires either multiple simultaneous agents (Esvelt's 'many pandemic viruses across travel hubs' scenario) or a permanent loss of the industrial base that prevents recovery. This is why Ord's ~3% existential figure is far below his implied probability that such an event occurs at all.

annual_probability.event_definition: deliberate release of a genetically engineered pathogen that kills more than 1% of the world's human population within a five-year window
annual_probability.trend: Rising. The number of actors able to attempt this is increasing as gene synthesis costs fall and AI biodesign tools diffuse; Esvelt (2022) argues that within roughly a decade tens of thousands of individuals will hold the necessary information, versus a handful of state programmes historically. Countervailing downward pressure comes from synthesis screening (IGSC ~80% coverage), the 2024 US OSTP screening framework, and the AI-screening patches deployed after Wittmann et al. (2025). Net direction is up on capability diffusion, ambiguous on defence — Ord's own 2023 revisit calls the pandemic story 'mixed'.

severity_tiers.label: Severe global pandemic
severity_tiers.description: Comparable to or worse than 1918: mass mortality concentrated in a 1-3 year window, health systems overwhelmed, but supply chains, states and industrial capacity survive largely intact.

severity_tiers.label: Catastrophic pandemic
severity_tiers.description: Countermeasure-evading agent; sustained excess mortality plus a global depression, food-export bans and regional famine. Several states fail; global institutions do not.

severity_tiers.label: Civilisational collapse
severity_tiers.description: Deaths concentrated in the working-age population and in technical specialists; loss of the division of labour that sustains fuel, fertiliser, pharmaceutical and semiconductor production. Most deaths are from famine and untreated ordinary disease, not the pathogen. Recovery happens, but from a pre-industrial or early-industrial base.

severity_tiers.label: Unrecoverable / terminal
severity_tiers.description: Either a simultaneous multi-agent release with no safe refuge, or a collapse deep enough that the surviving population never rebuilds industrial civilisation. Ord's 1-in-30-per-century figure is an estimate of this outcome class, not of the event as defined above.

key_parameters.label: Gene-synthesis screening coverage fraction
key_parameters.unit: fraction of global commercial synthesis capacity screened
key_parameters.effect: Acts as a leaky filter on one chokepoint. If a fraction f of capacity screens orders and screening catches a fraction d of flagged sequences, the residual accessible fraction is (1-f) + f*(1-d); at f=0.80 and perfect detection the residual is 0.20. Treat the hazard rate as roughly proportional to that residual for actors who must buy synthesis rather than build capability in-house — so raising f from 0.80 to 0.99 cuts the synthesis-dependent branch by ~20x, while benchtop synthesisers outside the screened market set a floor that f cannot reduce. The Wittmann et al. (2025) result shows d is not 1: current tools left hundreds of AI-redesigned sequences unflagged before patching, so coverage and detection must be modelled as two separate multipliers.

key_parameters.label: Number of actors with the capability to attempt
key_parameters.effect: The attempt rate is close to linear in this count for a fixed per-actor intent probability: rate ≈ N * p_intent * p_technical_success. This is the dominant term in the model. Esvelt (2022) projects N rising into the tens of thousands within a decade, i.e. a ~3-order-of-magnitude increase, and this is the single knob most capable of moving the annual probability by orders of magnitude. Note that p_technical_success falls sharply as N grows, because the marginal actor is far less competent than the Soviet state programme — Aum Shinrikyo held a chemistry PhD staff, a nine-figure budget and a dedicated facility and still produced zero anthrax casualties in 1993.

key_parameters.label: Detection latency
key_parameters.unit: days from first human case to public-health detection
key_parameters.effect: For an agent with reproduction number R and generation interval g, the seeded case count at detection grows as R^(t/g); every extra generation-interval of latency multiplies the outbreak size at intervention by R. At R=2 and g=5 days, cutting latency from 21 to 7 days reduces cases at detection by ~2^2.8 ≈ 7x, which is the difference between a containable cluster and an established pandemic. The 7-1-7 target sets 7 days as the goal; in the five-country implementation study only 54% of 41 outbreaks met it and only about one in four met all three targets, so a realistic current-world default is 7-21 days, not 7.

key_parameters.label: Number of BSL-4 laboratories
key_parameters.unit: laboratories in operation, under construction or planned
key_parameters.effect: A weak driver for the deliberate-release hazard and a strong one for the accidental branch (see hazard 'laboratory-accident-enhanced-pathogen'). Its relevance here is via the trained-personnel pool and the diffusion of tacit knowledge: attempt rate scales sublinearly, roughly as sqrt(N_labs), and the governance quality matters more than the count — of the 27 countries hosting BSL-4 labs, 12 scored high on biosecurity, 9 medium and 6 low in Global BioLabs 2023.

key_parameters.label: Countries with legislated dual-use research oversight
key_parameters.effect: An inverse multiplier on the probability that a hazardous capability is created and published in the open literature in the first place, which is upstream of both the deliberate and accidental branches. The GHS Index 2021 found this to be the indicator on which the fewest countries have any capacity — 94% of countries lacked oversight measures. Model as a multiplier of roughly (1 - 0.5*C/195) on the rate at which new pandemic-capable information enters the public domain; the effect saturates because the small number of countries with the largest life-science sectors dominates.

hazards.uncertainty_notes: Three distinct quantities must not be conflated and are separated above: (a) probability the release EVENT occurs at the >=1%-mortality threshold (my 5e-4 to 1.4e-3 per year, taken directly from the XPT medians spread over 2022-2100); (b) probability of a catastrophic outcome given the event (the tier distribution); (c) probability of permanent human extinction (annual rate = 8e-4 x 0.005 = 4e-6/yr, i.e. ~0.04% per century). THAT LAST NUMBER IS THE WEAKEST POINT AND IT DISAGREES WITH ORD BY ~80x. Ord's Table 6.1 gives 1 in 30 per century (~3.3%) for the existential outcome specifically; my parameterisation sits between the XPT superforecaster median (0.01%/century) and the XPT domain-expert median (1%/century), and below all of them. A serious critic will attack this from either direction: Ord's defenders will say my p(terminal | catastrophic event) of 0.005 is an unargued guess that ignores multi-agent simultaneous release, which is precisely Esvelt's scenario and the one that breaks the 'survivors are geographically isolated' argument; XPT superforecasters will say even 4e-6/yr is two orders of magnitude too high given that no pathogen in recorded history, including the Black Death and 1918, came near extinction. Do not treat the modelled extinction rate as a consensus figure; it is a derived quantity of a tier decomposition I chose, and the tier probabilities themselves are author-estimates with no published elicitation behind them. Ord's reasoning for 1-in-30 is NOT reproduced here: I could not retrieve the text of Chapter 5 of The Precipice this session, only his headline number via a secondary tabulation (Risk Frontiers) and his own restatement of the number on tobyord.com. Anyone compiling this into a model should read the primary chapter before attributing reasoning to him. Two further retrieval caveats: (1) WebFetch was blocked by a safety classifier partway through this session, so the Esvelt GCSP paper, the XPT PDF, the Global BioLabs 2023 PDF, the Lancet 7-1-7 paper, the RAND report, the Science 2025 paper's numeric results, and the IGSC/NTI/OSTP pages were retrieved as live WebSearch result summaries quoting those sources, not as full texts — the figures are quoted as the summaries stated them and should be spot-checked against the primary documents. The Wittmann et al. counts (76,080 sequences, 72 proteins of concern) came through secondary reporting of the Science paper; the author list, journal and 2 October 2025 date were confirmed on the Microsoft Research publication page directly. The Lancet 7-1-7 first author was not verified. (2) I could not retrieve a primary per-base DNA synthesis cost series this session; search results offered figures ($0.0009/base in 2024, $0.07/base 'currently', ~21%/yr decline) with unclear or non-authoritative provenance, so I have DELIBERATELY OMITTED a cost-per-base parameter rather than dress a poorly-sourced number as a citation. Esvelt's absolute construct costs (US$1,500 / ~US$2,000) are the only synthesis-cost figures here with a clear published source. Finally, the actor-count parameter's current value of 30 is an author-estimate anchored only on the 27 countries hosting BSL-4 labs; no published count of 'actors with capability' exists, and the true value depends entirely on where the capability threshold is drawn.

hazards.name: Accidental release of an enhanced or high-consequence pathogen from a research facility
hazards.one_line: A pathogen made more dangerous for research purposes, or a high-consequence agent held for study, escapes containment and seeds a human outbreak.
hazards.mechanism: An infected worker, a containment failure or a filtration fault carries a pathogen out of a laboratory; the released organism then behaves exactly as a natural outbreak except that its properties were selected in the laboratory rather than by natural selection. The 1979 Sverdlovsk release demonstrates the physical chain concretely: an aerosol escaped a military microbiology facility, the plume followed the prevailing wind, and casualties fell in a narrow downwind zone. Anthrax is not transmissible person to person, so Sverdlovsk terminated after one generation; the catastrophic branch requires a respiratory-transmissible agent, where the released organism seeds a chain of human transmission that ordinary outbreak response must then race. Deaths in the small tiers are direct infection deaths. In the large tiers, the killing mechanism converges with the deliberate-release hazard: healthcare collapse, then interruption of food, fuel and pharmaceutical supply chains, then famine and untreated ordinary illness. The distinguishing risk-structure feature versus deliberate release is that accident probability scales with the volume of research activity, so it is directly governed by a countable and regulable quantity — laboratories and their oversight regimes — whereas deliberate release scales with intent, which is not countable.

annual_probability.event_definition: accidental release from a high-containment or enhanced-pathogen research facility that seeds a human outbreak of 50 or more cases
annual_probability.trend: Rising with laboratory count. Global BioLabs 2023 counted 69 BSL-4 labs in operation, under construction or planned across 27 countries, and reported that the construction boom has not been matched by strengthened biorisk oversight, with most planned labs in countries scoring relatively low on governance and stability.

severity_tiers.label: Contained local outbreak
severity_tiers.description: The release infects workers and the immediate downwind or contact population and is stopped within one or two transmission generations, as at Sverdlovsk in 1979.

severity_tiers.label: Regional epidemic
severity_tiers.description: A transmissible agent establishes sustained human-to-human chains and is contained only after national-scale response, at the cost of tens of thousands of lives.

severity_tiers.label: Global pandemic
severity_tiers.description: Containment fails; the agent becomes globally endemic or sweeps the world before countermeasures are deployed. Mortality is comparable to a severe natural pandemic.

severity_tiers.label: Catastrophic pandemic
severity_tiers.description: An agent enhanced for both transmissibility and lethality escapes and is not contained; mass mortality plus supply-chain and healthcare collapse. This is the outcome class the 2011-12 H5N1 controversy was actually about.

key_parameters.label: Number of BSL-4 laboratories
key_parameters.unit: laboratories in operation, under construction or planned
key_parameters.effect: The accident rate is close to linear in facility-years: rate = N_labs * p_escape_per_lab_year. With 69 facilities and a best-estimate hazard of 0.02/yr for a seeded outbreak, the implied per-lab-year escape probability is ~3e-4, which should be treated as the tunable primitive rather than the aggregate. Doubling the lab count doubles the rate unless per-lab safety improves proportionally, which Global BioLabs 2023 found it has not. Note that BSL-3 and BSL-3+ facilities, which are far more numerous, host much of the work on transmissible respiratory pathogens, so N_labs at BSL-4 alone understates the exposed base.

key_parameters.label: Fraction of host countries with high biosecurity oversight
key_parameters.unit: fraction of BSL-4-hosting countries scoring high
key_parameters.effect: Global BioLabs 2023 scored 12 of 27 BSL-4-hosting countries high on biosecurity, 9 medium and 6 low, giving 12/27 = 0.444. Model per-lab-year escape probability as scaling roughly inversely with this: p_escape ~ p_base * (2 - Q), so moving Q from 0.44 to 0.90 roughly halves the accident rate. This is the single cheapest intervention in the model because it does not require reducing the amount of research done.

key_parameters.label: Detection latency
key_parameters.unit: days from first human case to public-health detection
key_parameters.effect: Controls the split between the contained and uncontained tiers rather than the event rate. Because an accidental release starts from a single seeding point (unlike a deliberate multi-hub release), latency is far more decisive here: at R=2 and a 5-day generation interval, detection at 7 days finds ~2-4 cases and detection at 28 days finds ~30-60, which straddles the practical limit of contact-tracing containment. Shift probability mass from the 'Contained local outbreak' tier to the 'Regional epidemic' and 'Global pandemic' tiers as latency rises past ~14 days.

key_parameters.label: Volume of enhanced-potential-pandemic-pathogen research
key_parameters.effect: Multiplies the fraction of accidents involving an agent capable of the catastrophic tiers. Sverdlovsk-class accidents with a non-transmissible agent cannot produce the top two tiers at all; only work on transmissible agents can. Set the conditional probabilities of the 'Global pandemic' and 'Catastrophic pandemic' tiers proportional to this index. EO 14292 (May 2025) is a direct downward intervention on this knob for US federally funded and, prospectively, non-federally-funded work.

cascades_into: engineered-pandemic-deliberate-release: a demonstrated accidental escape publicises both the feasibility and the failure modes, and published enhancement results lower the information barrier for deliberate actors — this is precisely the information-hazard argument made against publishing the 2011-12 H5N1 work
hazards.uncertainty_notes: THE ANNUAL PROBABILITY HERE IS AN AUTHOR-ESTIMATE AND IS THE WEAKEST NUMBER IN THIS PACKET. I retrieved exactly one documented accidental release with quantified human casualties this session (Sverdlovsk 1979). The well-known published per-lab-year escape estimates — Lipsitch and Inglesby's analysis accompanying the 2014 US gain-of-function funding pause, and Klotz's laboratory-acquired-infection frequency work — I was NOT able to retrieve this session (the WebSearch budget was exhausted and WebFetch was blocked by a safety classifier), so I have not cited them and have not used their numbers. My 0.02/yr central value is a judgement built from one verified event plus the widely reported but unverified-this-session cluster of laboratory-associated outbreaks (1978 Birmingham smallpox, the 2003-04 SARS laboratory escapes); a reviewer should replace it with a properly sourced per-lab-year figure before the model is used for anything decision-relevant. The derived per-lab-year escape probability of ~3e-4 is therefore also unsourced. Two further weaknesses. First, the denominator is wrong in a known direction: I have scaled on BSL-4 labs because that is the number Global BioLabs counts, but work on transmissible respiratory pathogens largely occurs at BSL-3/BSL-3+, which is far more numerous and much less well enumerated, so the model understates the exposed base and correspondingly overstates the per-lab hazard. Second, the top two severity tiers are extrapolations with no empirical anchor whatsoever: no accidental release in history has produced a global pandemic with agreed attribution, and the one candidate event that is publicly contested (SARS-CoV-2 origins) I deliberately excluded because its attribution is unresolved and including a contested case would smuggle a disputed prior into the tier weights. A critic will reasonably say that excluding it biases the top tiers low. On the H5N1 citation: note the important qualifier that the airborne-transmissible ferret virus was reported as not lethal by the airborne route, so the experiments are evidence about the information hazard and about transmissibility enhancement, NOT evidence that a transmissible-and-lethal agent was produced; conflating those two is the standard error in commentary on this episode.

hazards.name: Large-scale state biological weapons programme use
hazards.one_line: A state with an industrial-scale biological weapons programme uses it in conflict, at the production scale historically demonstrated by the Soviet Union.
hazards.mechanism: State programmes differ from non-state attempts by orders of magnitude in three respects that all bear directly on the death toll: production scale, delivery engineering, and the ability to select and characterise agents against defined military requirements. The Soviet programme is the only case with reliable public figures on scale, and it establishes that the industrial capability existed at the level of hundreds of tons of formulated agent and tens of thousands of staff. Use in conflict kills initially through mass exposure of a target population; the catastrophic branch arises only if a transmissible agent is used, at which point the attacker loses control of the outcome and the agent returns through the same travel networks. From there the mechanism is identical to the other two hazards: healthcare collapse, then breakdown of the food, fuel and pharmaceutical supply chains, then famine. A state programme is also the only actor class plausibly able to mount a simultaneous multi-agent release, which is the scenario in which the geographic-isolation argument against extinction fails. Note the counterweight the historical record provides: the Soviet programme was never used, and its most significant human toll was a domestic accident.

annual_probability.event_definition: deliberate state use of biological weapons in armed conflict causing 100,000 or more deaths
annual_probability.trend: Unclear. The BWC entered into force in 1975 and the Soviet programme was dismantled after 1992, so declared state programmes have fallen; against that, Ord's 2023 revisit notes nuclear risk is up, and the same great-power tensions that drive it would drive any renewed programme. I could not retrieve the current US State Department arms control compliance assessment this session, so the number of states currently assessed as having offensive programmes is UNKNOWN in this packet.

severity_tiers.label: Theatre-scale use
severity_tiers.description: Use against military formations or a limited civilian target set with a non-transmissible agent. Deaths in the hundreds of thousands; effects geographically bounded.

severity_tiers.label: Escalated multi-theatre use
severity_tiers.description: Retaliation and escalation; multiple states employ biological or mixed CBRN weapons. Regional economies and health systems collapse; global trade disrupted.

severity_tiers.label: Strategic exchange with transmissible agents
severity_tiers.description: Transmissible agents released at strategic scale escape the intended target set and become global. This is the tier where the Soviet-programme production scale matters: a state can release enough, in enough places, that no country is a refuge.

severity_tiers.label: Unrecoverable
severity_tiers.description: Simultaneous multi-agent strategic release combined with concurrent nuclear or infrastructure destruction; the surviving population never rebuilds industrial civilisation.

key_parameters.label: Number of states with an offensive biological weapons programme
key_parameters.effect: The use rate scales linearly in this count for a fixed per-state-per-year probability of use: rate = N_states * p_use. This is the primary knob for the hazard, and it is also the one on which my current value is least well grounded — see uncertainty notes. Historically the count peaked in the Cold War and the single largest programme (the Soviet Union's) was unilaterally dismantled after 1992, demonstrating that this knob is movable downward by treaty and regime change, unlike the actor count in the deliberate-release hazard.

key_parameters.label: Formulated agent stockpile a programme can hold
key_parameters.effect: Sets the ceiling on the initial exposed population and therefore on the theatre-scale tier. Alibek's testimony establishes the historical maximum at 'hundreds of tons' of anthrax formulation with a capacity of 'many hundreds of tons of various agents annually'. Initial deaths in the theatre-scale tier scale roughly linearly with tonnage for a non-transmissible agent; for a transmissible agent tonnage matters far less than the number of independent seeding locations, because after the first few generations transmission rather than the initial dose dominates. Current value set to 0 because no state acknowledges an offensive stockpile.

key_parameters.label: Detection and attribution latency
key_parameters.unit: days from release to detection and attribution
key_parameters.effect: Has a dual and partly opposing effect here. Short latency improves containment of a transmissible agent (as in the other hazards), but fast ATTRIBUTION also accelerates retaliation and therefore raises the probability of the escalated tiers. Model containment benefit as monotone decreasing in latency and escalation probability as decreasing in attribution latency, and do not collapse the two into one knob — a simulator that uses a single latency parameter here will produce a spuriously monotone policy conclusion.

key_parameters.label: Strength of BWC verification
key_parameters.unit: index, 0 = no verification protocol (current), 1 = intrusive verification
key_parameters.effect: The Biological Weapons Convention has no verification protocol, which is why the Soviet violation remained one of the best-guarded secrets of the USSR until defector testimony in the 1990s. Model as reducing both the probability that a state maintains an undeclared programme and the number of programme-years that go undetected: N_states_effective ~ N_states * (1 - 0.6*V). The effect is bounded well below total because verification of dual-use biological facilities is intrinsically harder than for fissile material.
