hazards.uncertainty_notes: BOTH THE ANNUAL PROBABILITY AND THE CURRENT VALUE OF THE state_programmes KNOB ARE AUTHOR-ESTIMATES WITH NO SOURCE RETRIEVED THIS SESSION. I attempted to retrieve the current US State Department Arms Control Compliance Report — the standard public document that names states assessed as maintaining offensive biological weapons programmes in violation of the BWC — and the WebSearch budget was exhausted before that search executed. The value of 3 is therefore a placeholder reflecting my prior that a small number of states are publicly assessed as non-compliant; IT SHOULD BE REPLACED WITH THE COMPLIANCE REPORT'S ACTUAL ASSESSMENT BEFORE USE, and a reviewer should treat any conclusion that depends on it as unsupported. Likewise the 0.001/yr base rate has no elicitation behind it: the historical record contains zero instances of large-scale state biological weapons use in the eighty years since the technology matured, which by a naive Laplace rule of succession over ~80 programme-rich years gives an upper bound nearer 1e-2/yr and a point estimate that could reasonably be an order of magnitude below my figure. A critic can attack this from either side and I cannot defend the specific value. The severity tiers are also unanchored: no state has used biological weapons at scale, so unlike the deliberate-release hazard (where the XPT and Ord give at least two independent elicitations) there is nothing here but my judgement. What IS well-sourced in this entry is the programme-scale data — Alibek's figures are first-hand congressional testimony, corroborated on personnel and facility counts by the independent University of Kent account, and they establish the demonstrated industrial ceiling. Use this hazard entry for its scale parameters and its structural role (state programmes as the only actor class capable of multi-agent strategic release, and as the upstream source of both expertise leakage and containment accidents), NOT for its probability. One further caveat on the Alibek testimony: it is a single defector's account given in a policy setting sixteen years after the events described, and some of his specific claims have been disputed in the arms-control literature; the personnel and facility figures are the best-corroborated part of it and the tonnage figures the least.

hazards.name: Regional nuclear exchange (India–Pakistan class, 100–500 urban detonations)
hazards.one_line: Two regional nuclear powers detonate on the order of 100–500 warheads on each other's cities, and the resulting urban firestorms loft enough soot into the stratosphere to collapse global crop yields for roughly a decade.
hazards.mechanism: The chain is: fire → fuel → soot → stratosphere → sunlight → calories → famine. (1) A 15-kt airburst ignites everything inside a fire zone taken by Toon et al. 2019 as equal to Hiroshima's, 13 km², with the ignition area scaling proportionally to yield. (2) Toon et al. allocate 11,000 kg of flammable material per person in the burned area from a gridded population database — about 4 g/cm² for a dense modern city (WWII Hamburg measurements span 12–47 g/cm²; sparse 1990 San Jose is 1.34 g/cm²). (3) The mass fire consumes that fuel at an adopted black-carbon emission factor of 0.02 g BC per g fuel burned. (4) Fire convection injects the smoke into the 300–150 hPa layer (~9–13.5 km); Toon et al. assume 20% is rained out at injection and 10–15% more in the first few days, so 30–35% is lost before the stratosphere. What survives is self-lofted higher by solar heating of the black carbon into a layer with no precipitation removal, giving an e-folding lifetime of ~4.6 years in the Robock et al. 2007 model. (5) A 250-weapon/100-kt exchange yields 37 Tg of soot and about 5.5 °C of global cooling; Toon et al. 2019's regional case cuts surface sunlight 20–35%, cools the surface 2–5 °C and cuts precipitation 15–30%, with recovery taking more than 10 years. (6) Xia et al. 2022 pushed those climate fields through crop and fishery models: total calories available from the major staple crops and wild marine fisheries fall 23% at 16 Tg, 33% at 27 Tg, 42% at 37 Tg and 48% at 47 Tg, hitting hardest at mid-to-high northern latitudes — Canada, the USA, Europe, Russia, China, the world's grain belt. (7) They then counted, nation by nation, how many people fall persistently below a 1,911 kcal/person/day starvation cutoff after livestock are slaughtered, animal feed is diverted to humans, household waste is eliminated and international food trade is halted. What actually kills people is therefore neither blast nor fire nor fallout: it is the loss of the traded calorie surplus in food-importing and high-latitude countries thousands of kilometres from the war. Xia et al.'s model shows zero famine deaths in India and Pakistan in the smaller scenarios precisely because it counts only climate-driven crop loss, not the war zone itself.

annual_probability.event_definition: A nuclear exchange between two states in which at least ~100 warheads of ≥15 kt are detonated on urban/industrial targets, injecting ≥5 Tg of soot into the stratosphere — Xia et al. 2022's threshold above which mass food shortages occur in almost all countries. NOT the probability of any nuclear detonation, and NOT the probability of the famine outcome.
annual_probability.trend: Rising. Toon et al. 2019 project India and Pakistan at 400–500 warheads by 2025 with yields running from tested 12–45 kt values up to a few hundred kilotons, against ~130–150 each in 2018; FAS put India at 190 and Pakistan at 170 warheads at the beginning of 2026. Bigger, higher-yield arsenals move the same exchange up the soot curve even if the rate of exchanges is flat: 250 weapons at 15 kt gives 16 Tg, the same 250 at 100 kt gives 37 Tg. Urban populations in the two countries were projected to grow ~90% between 2000 and 2025, raising the fuel load per target.

severity_tiers.label: Soot floor (~5 Tg)
severity_tiers.description: 100 weapons of ~15 kt on cities — the classic Robock/Toon 2007 case. 5 Tg of soot, ~1.3 °C of global cooling. Xia et al.: 27 million direct fatalities and 335.5 million famine deaths by the end of year 2, against the model's 2010 world population of 6,703 million. Recovery of the climate takes about a decade; the political and trade order does not necessarily recover.

severity_tiers.label: Mid case (16–27 Tg)
severity_tiers.description: 250 weapons of 15–50 kt. 2.5–4.5 °C global cooling; global calories from major crops and fisheries down 23–33%. Direct fatalities 52–97 million; famine deaths by end of year 2 of 1,122–1,579 million. China alone loses 558–822 million. Seven to eight years of declining food production.

severity_tiers.label: Upper regional case (37–47 Tg)
severity_tiers.description: 250–500 weapons of 100 kt. 5.5–6.5 °C global cooling — comparable to the last glacial maximum, but arriving in one season. Calories down 42–48%. Direct fatalities 127–164 million; famine deaths by end of year 2 of 2,239–2,675 million, i.e. roughly every third human alive, from a war using under 4% of the world's nuclear weapons. The United States loses 131–218 million and Russia ~126 million despite not being belligerents.

key_parameters.label: Warheads detonated on urban targets
key_parameters.effect: Within the Toon et al. 2019 scenario family, stratospheric soot fits Tg ≈ 16 × (N/250)^0.35 × (Y/15 kt)^0.45 — this reproduces all four published points exactly (250×15 kt = 16 Tg, 250×50 kt = 27 Tg, 250×100 kt = 37 Tg, 500×100 kt = 47 Tg). Strongly sub-linear in N because targets are attacked in decreasing order of population density, so each additional weapon burns a less fuel-dense city: doubling 250→500 at 100 kt raised soot only 37→47 Tg (+27%). The exponent is a fit by this author to the published table, not a figure stated by Toon et al.

key_parameters.label: Fraction of detonations on urban/industrial targets
key_parameters.effect: Approximately linear in soot up to target-list exhaustion, and it is the single most decisive knob. Only urban fuel loads (~4 g/cm², from 11,000 kg of flammable material per person in the burn zone) support firestorm-grade smoke production; Toon et al. 2019 note that the Los Alamos dissent claiming no stratospheric lofting was built on a simulated 15-kt burst over sparse suburban Atlanta at 1.07 g/cm² — about one order of magnitude below even the 100th-ranked Pakistani city, and therefore not representative. At 250 weapons, dropping this fraction below roughly 0.2 puts soot under the 5 Tg threshold at which Xia et al. find mass food shortages, and the famine chain does not fire at all.

key_parameters.label: Average yield per weapon
key_parameters.effect: Fire-ignition area is taken proportional to yield (13 km² at 15 kt), but soot goes as roughly Y^0.45, because a larger footprint reaches lower fuel-density suburbs and because a larger fraction of fuel is buried under rubble in the high-overpressure zone (Toon et al. estimate the ~400,000 J/m² fire-ignition-zone destruction fraction at roughly 14% of the area for a 15-kt airburst and roughly 8% for 100 kt). At 250 weapons: 15 kt → 16 Tg, 50 kt → 27 Tg, 100 kt → 37 Tg. Toon et al. note India and Pakistan tested 12–45 kt devices but that yields of a few hundred kt are achievable.

key_parameters.label: Number of nuclear-armed states
key_parameters.effect: FAS count nine at the start of 2026 (Russia, USA, China, France, UK, India, Pakistan, Israel, North Korea). The rate scales with the number of ADVERSARIAL dyads, not with n itself; n(n−1)/2 = 36 pairs at n = 9 is an upper bound on dyads, of which only a handful are plausible war pairs. The stronger effect of adding a state is that it adds a whole independent arsenal already large enough to trigger the chain: Toon et al. 2019 observe that any of the nuclear-armed nations can cause worldwide suffering and agricultural collapse, and that a single Ohio- or Borei-class submarine commander commands firepower comparable to Pakistan's or France's entire arsenal.

key_parameters.label: Rate of full-blown crises between a nuclear dyad
key_parameters.effect: Hellman's chain for the US–Cuba–USSR case: three potential initiating events in the 50 years 1960–2010 = 6% per year, times a 1/3 empirical conditional probability that an initiating event becomes a full-blown crisis, = 2% per year (one crisis per 50 years). He then applies 10–50% for a crisis crossing the nuclear threshold, giving 0.2–1% per year of first use, and another 10–50% for that becoming full-scale war. Barrett et al. 2013 state that if launch is impossible during low tension then the overall annual probability of war is approximately proportional to the probability of a crisis — i.e. this knob is linear in the hazard rate. India and Pakistan have already fought conventional wars in 1947, 1965, 1971 and 1999.

stratospheric-ozone-depletion: soot heated in the stratosphere drives chemistry that Mills et al. found destroys ~20–25% of global ozone from a 100-weapon regional exchange, with 50–70% loss at high northern latitudes and recovery taking at least a dozen years; the UV damage compounds the crop losses and is NOT included in the Xia et al. calorie model

global-famine-and-trade-collapse: Xia et al.'s death tolls already assume international food trade halts, which is itself the dominant killing mechanism for food importers such as Japan, Kenya, Mexico and the Gulf states
hazards.uncertainty_notes:
WEAKEST LINK — provenance of the scenario table. The Nature Food paper itself is paywalled (nature.com returns an IdP redirect; the UTRGV repository copy returns HTTP 403). The per-scenario Tg/direct-fatality/famine-death table I report was read directly from the IPPNW "Nuclear Famine" 2022 PDF, whose Table 1 is captioned "adapted from Xia et al, Nature Food, August 2022" and whose Table 2 is captioned "Adapted from Toon et al 2007, Toon et al 2019, and Xia et al 2022." It is therefore a faithful secondary source, not the primary table. It cross-checks against the NASA GISS abstract of Xia et al. (">2 billion" India–Pakistan versus my 2,675.3 million at 47 Tg; ">5 billion" US–Russia versus 5,413 million at 150 Tg) and against Toon et al. 2019's own "16 to 36 Tg" and "50 to 125 million" ranges, which I read from the primary PDF. An auditor should replace the table with the primary Nature Food figures before this is used in anger. Note also a genuine tension I did not resolve: Toon et al. 2019's abstract says 16–36 Tg for the 250-weapon family, while the Xia scenario set runs to 47 Tg for 500 weapons — the 47 Tg case is the larger scenario, not a contradiction, but the 36-vs-37 Tg discrepancy for 250×100 kt is unexplained rounding I could not check.

SECOND WEAKNESS — the annual probability. There is no published per-year rate for the event as I have defined it (≥100 urban warheads, ≥5 Tg). The XPT numbers are for the OUTCOME (>10% of humanity dead within 5 years), which at 5 Tg is not reached (5.4%), so the XPT figures under-count 5 Tg exchanges and I have set my best estimate above the annualised XPT expert figure (8% by 2100 over 78 years = 1.07e-3/yr) and my low bound below the superforecaster figure (4% = 5.2e-4/yr). The high bound of 5e-3/yr is roughly five times the expert annualisation and is my own judgement, not a published number. A serious critic would attack (a) treating a cumulative-to-2100 elicitation as a constant Poisson rate when forecasters plainly expect the rate to change, and (b) using superforecaster medians at all, given that no one has a track record on 78-year questions.

THIRD — the soot exponents. The Tg ≈ 16 × (N/250)^0.35 × (Y/15)^0.45 fit is MINE, fitted to four published points. It reproduces those four exactly but has no independent validation and it does NOT extrapolate to the 100×15 kt = 5 Tg "prequel" case, which comes from the older Toon/Robock 2007 emission model with smaller cities and lower fuel loads (my formula would give 11.6 Tg there). Do not use it below 250 weapons.

FOURTH — the physics that everyone actually fights about. Whether urban mass fires loft smoke into the stratosphere at all is contested. Toon et al. 2019 respond to a Los Alamos study (Reisner et al.) arguing the smoke would not reach the stratosphere, and rebut it on the ground that it simulated a detonation over sparse suburban Atlanta at 1.07 g/cm² fuel loading, about an order of magnitude below even the least dense target considered. The observational support is indirect: 2017 British Columbia and 2019–2020 Australian wildfire pyrocumulonimbus were tracked lofting to 12 km and then self-lofting to 23 km over two months. That is a few tenths of a teragram, three orders of magnitude below the scenarios. The rainout fraction (30–35%), the BC emission factor (0.02 g/g), the 11,000 kg/person fuel allocation and the assumption that essentially all fuel in the ignition zone burns are each single-figure parameters carrying at least a factor-of-two uncertainty, and they multiply.

FIFTH — what the Xia model deliberately omits, all of which push deaths UP: radioactive fallout, ozone loss and UV damage to crops, breakdown of fuel/fertiliser/seed supply chains, epidemic disease, and the collapse of public order. It also omits the possibility that trade does NOT halt, which pushes deaths down. Xia et al. themselves note that during the 1943 Bengal famine a 5% drop in available food produced 3 million deaths through hoarding and price inflation — i.e. the mapping from calorie availability to deaths is not the smooth cutoff the model assumes.

SIXTH — the death tolls are computed against a 2010 world population of 6,703 million. Absolute counts scale up by roughly 1.2× for a present-day population; I have reported FRACTIONS to keep the model internally consistent. The tolls are also "by the end of year two," not year ten, so they are a lower bound on the ten-year figure the schema asks for.

hazards.name: Full-scale strategic nuclear exchange (United States–Russia)
hazards.one_line: The deployed US and Russian strategic arsenals are used against each other's cities and industry, injecting roughly 150 Tg of soot and producing years of below-freezing Northern Hemisphere summers.
hazards.mechanism: Physically the same chain as the regional case, but two orders of magnitude further along it. (1) Toon et al. 2008, as reported in Toon et al. 2019, computed 180 Tg of black carbon from 4,400 detonations of 100 kt on urban areas — roughly half the combined arsenals of the USA, Russia, China, Britain and France — at a yield lower than the average. Note the per-weapon soot is only 0.041 Tg, versus 0.148 Tg per weapon for the 250 densest Indian/Pakistani targets: the target list is exhausted, so soot saturates hard. (2) Robock et al. 2007 used 150 Tg of smoke as the superpower-war injection and found an e-folding stratospheric lifetime of 4.6 years, because black carbon absorbs sunlight, heats the surrounding air, and self-lofts above any precipitation removal. (3) Coupe et al. 2019 re-ran 150 Tg of black carbon injected into the 150–300 mb layer in WACCM4 at 2° resolution with 66 levels to 140 km, with full stratospheric chemistry and fractal particle growth, and compared it against the older GISS ModelE run: both produce a true nuclear winter, with global average surface temperatures plummeting by more than 8 K and below-freezing temperatures over much of the Northern Hemisphere during summer. The higher-resolution model removes smoke faster through particle growth but produces LARGER temperature and precipitation reductions in the first few years, so the aerosol-microphysics refinement did not rescue the result. (4) With sunlight cut, mid-latitude grain-growing regions are held below freezing through what should be the growing season and agriculture in the Northern Hemisphere simply stops. (5) Xia et al. 2022 carried the 150 Tg fields through crop and fishery models and, applying a 1,911 kcal/person/day starvation cutoff nation by nation after livestock slaughter, feed diversion and the halt of international food trade, found 5,413 million dead by the end of year two out of a modelled world population of 6,703 million — 80.8%. The United States loses 309.6 million of 312.2 million, China 1,362 of 1,367, Russia 142 of 143.6. Again, almost none of these deaths are from blast, fire or fallout; they are from the loss of a growing season, repeated, in every food-producing latitude at once.

annual_probability.event_definition: A nuclear exchange between the United States and Russia in which a substantial fraction of the deployed strategic arsenals is used, including against urban and industrial targets — i.e. an exchange large enough to put ≳50 Tg of soot into the stratosphere. This is the probability the WAR OCCURS, not the probability it kills most of humanity (see severity tiers) and not the probability it ends humanity (see below).
annual_probability.trend: Rising, modestly. FAS put the world at ~12,187 warheads and nine nuclear states at the beginning of 2026, with dismantlement slowing and new deployments accelerating, and China's stockpile at ~620 and growing — turning a two-body strategic problem into a three-body one. Barrett et al.'s own caution cuts the other way: their false-alarm rate data are from 1977–1983 and NORAD has not released false-alarm rates since the mid-1980s, so a real decline in the underlying rate would not be visible in their model.

severity_tiers.label: Counterforce-weighted exchange
severity_tiers.description: Missile fields, submarine bases, bomber bases and command nodes are hit but cities are largely spared, so urban fuel loads are not consumed and stratospheric soot stays well below the 150 Tg case. Direct deaths are in the tens to low hundreds of millions from blast and fallout over silo fields and their downwind populations; the famine chain fires only weakly. Industrial and agricultural capacity in both belligerents is nonetheless wrecked.

severity_tiers.label: Full countervalue exchange — 150 Tg nuclear winter
severity_tiers.description: Xia et al. 2022 scenario 5. 150 Tg of soot, global mean surface cooling of more than 8 K (Coupe et al. 2019), below-freezing Northern Hemisphere summers for years. 5,413 million dead by the end of year two out of 6,703 million — 80.8% — overwhelmingly from famine, and overwhelmingly outside the belligerent states. Recovery of the climate takes over a decade; recovery of industrial capacity is the binding constraint and is not modelled by anyone.

severity_tiers.label: Winter plus civilisational collapse
severity_tiers.description: The 150 Tg climate outcome compounded by what Xia et al. explicitly exclude: fallout, 25%+ global ozone loss and UV damage to what crops remain, breakdown of fuel, fertiliser, seed and medicine supply chains, epidemic disease among a starving population, and the collapse of public order and of any coordinated response. Survivors are scattered, pre-industrial and concentrated in the Southern Hemisphere — Australia, New Zealand, southern South America and southern Africa show the smallest modelled losses. Industrial civilisation has to be rebuilt from a depleted resource base.

severity_tiers.label: Terminal
severity_tiers.description: No recovery: the surviving population falls below a viable threshold, or survives without ever rebuilding. NOTE that Xia et al. do not claim this and no climate model produces it — this tier exists only because Ord and the XPT forecasters assign it non-zero probability, and because Barrett et al. open their paper by citing the possibility of "collapse of modern civilization worldwide, and even the extinction of humanity." The conditional probability here is derived, not published: Ord's 1-in-1,000 existential risk from nuclear war over the next century, divided by a roughly 10% chance of a full-scale exchange in that century, gives ~1% conditional.

key_parameters.label: Total global warhead inventory
key_parameters.effect: Sets the ceiling on soot, but with severe diminishing returns. Toon et al. 2008 (via Toon et al. 2019) got 180 Tg from 4,400 detonations of 100 kt on urban areas — 0.041 Tg per weapon, versus 0.148 Tg per weapon for the top 250 Indian/Pakistani targets, because the world runs out of dense cities. Empirically, going from 250 to 500 weapons at 100 kt raised soot only 37 → 47 Tg. Below roughly 500 urban detonations soot is roughly ∝ N^0.35; above a few thousand it is nearly flat. Cutting the inventory therefore reduces the WORST case far less than it reduces the number of weapons — a fact that matters for arms-control modelling.

key_parameters.label: Fraction of the exchange aimed at urban/industrial targets
key_parameters.effect: The dominant knob, and roughly linear in soot up to target-list exhaustion. Toon et al. 2008's 180 Tg assumed 4,400 100-kt detonations on urban areas, about half of the combined US/Russia/China/UK/France arsenals. A pure counterforce exchange (f ≈ 0) burns silo fields and airbases with low fuel loads and produces little stratospheric soot: the famine chain does not fire and deaths stay within the belligerents. But at a 12,187-warhead inventory, an f of only about 0.05 — roughly 600 urban detonations — already clears the 5 Tg threshold at which Xia et al. find mass food shortages in almost every country. There is no plausibly survivable value of f above a few percent.

key_parameters.label: Warheads on deployed launchers
key_parameters.effect: FAS: ~3,912 deployed strategic plus ~100 deployed nonstrategic at the beginning of 2026 (Russia 1,796 strategic, USA 1,670 strategic + 100 nonstrategic, France 280, China 34, UK 120). This — not total inventory — sets the size of an exchange that starts in minutes, because the reserve/non-deployed 5,733 warheads cannot be mated and launched inside a launch-on-warning decision window. Barrett et al.'s inadvertent-launch pathway draws entirely from this pool, so de-alerting acts on this knob: they find that if both nations lower alert 50% of the time, overall inadvertent-war risk is cut roughly in half (median 0.009 → 0.005), and that if just one nation moves its SSBNs far enough from the other's coast to give ICBM-equivalent flight times, the median falls 0.009 → 0.005, or 0.009 → 0.003 if both do.

key_parameters.label: Number of nuclear-armed states
key_parameters.effect: Nine at the start of 2026 per FAS, but the strategic hazard is dominated by two: the USA and Russia hold ~86% of the total world inventory and ~83% of stockpiled warheads. Adding states raises the hazard mainly through the cascade channel — a regional war creating a superpower crisis — and through the third-party channel Barrett et al. model explicitly, in which a nuclear terrorist detonation or a third state's launch is misread as a first strike. They find nuclear terrorism contributes a median 0.0006/yr of mistaken attack indications against 0.01/yr from ordinary false alarms, i.e. at least an order of magnitude less.

key_parameters.label: Rate of US–Russia crises
key_parameters.effect: Hellman: 6% per year of a potential initiating event × 1/3 that it becomes a full crisis = 2% per year. Barrett et al. 2013 give the functional form directly: "if inadvertent nuclear war during periods of low U.S.–Russia tension is impossible, then the overall annual probability of inadvertent nuclear war is approximately proportional to the probability of a crisis" — i.e. linear in this knob under the Safe Calm assumption. Under their Danger Calm base case it is NOT linear: crises account for only about half of the modelled risk, with false alarms during ostensibly calm periods supplying the other half, so halving crisis frequency only halves half the risk. Which of these two regimes holds is the single largest structural uncertainty in the model.

citations.claim: Annual probability of inadvertent US–Russia nuclear war from misinterpretation of early-warning false alarms, with the full uncertainty range.
citations.authors: Anthony M. Barrett, Seth D. Baum, Kelly R. Hostetler (Global Catastrophic Risk Institute)
citations.exact_figure: Median model-estimated annual inadvertence probability, status quo: 0.009 under "Danger Calm" base-case assumptions and 0.003 under the "Safe Calm" sensitivity case (Tables 3 and 4). "The 90 percent confidence interval (extending from the 5th percentile to the 95th percentile model estimate) ranges from 0.0002 to 0.07 in the base case, and from 0.00001 to 0.05 if excluding launch during low tensions." Median annual rate of mistaken MAC-level attack indications: 0.01 from usual false alarms and 0.0006 from nuclear terrorist attack (Danger Calm); 0.003 and 0.0000008 (Safe Calm). Empirical ceiling: given 37 event-free years 1975–2012, "there could be a statistical argument for rejecting (with 95 percent confidence) a probabilistic model that produced a best estimate … for annual nuclear war probability above 0.08." They also report Hellman's independent estimate that "the failure rate of [U.S.–Russia nuclear war] deterrence from all sources is on the order of one percent per year," which they note "is approximately equivalent to this article's Danger Calm median estimated annual probability."

citations.claim: A 150 Tg soot injection from a US–Russia war produces a true nuclear winter, with more than 8 K of global mean surface cooling and below-freezing Northern Hemisphere summers.

Key point: "A true nuclear winter occurs in both models as black carbon aerosols block sunlight and cause global average surface temperatures to plummet by more than 8 K." "Nuclear winter, with below freezing temperatures over much of the Northern Hemisphere during summer, occurs because of a reduction of surface solar radiation due to smoke lofted into the stratosphere." "WACCM4's more sophisticated aerosol representation removes smoke more quickly, but the magnitude of the climate response is not reduced. In fact, the higher-resolution WACCM4 simulates larger temperature and precipitation reductions than ModelE in the first few years." Also reports that Robock, Oman & Stenchikov (2007) "found an e-folding lifetime of 4.6 years for soot particles in the stratosphere."

Labelled incidents in their Figure 1 include the Cuban Missile Crisis, the B-59 (Arkhipov) incident, Able Archer, Petrov, the Norwegian Rocket Incident, Goldsboro, Thule, Damascus, the Florida Satellite Incident, BMEWS, Penkovsky, the SAC Chip Failure and the Hawaii Alert. Critically: "the paper stops short of attempting to estimate these probabilities. At this stage of the research, estimating the probabilities would require considerable guesswork and is likely to be quite mistaken." And: "the 'closeness' of the events is a matter of subtle historical interpretation, something that experts in the field disagree on" — citing Lewis et al. (2014) that many incidents came quite close, against Tertrais (2017) that no incident since WWII has come close.

cascades_into: global-famine-and-trade-collapse: this is the actual killing mechanism, and it is already internal to the Xia et al. death tolls — do not double-count it as a separate hazard downstream of this one

stratospheric-ozone-depletion: soot heated in the stratosphere destroys ozone; a merely regional exchange already gives ~25% global loss with recovery over at least a dozen years, so a 150 Tg injection is far worse and the UV damage to surviving crops is NOT in the Xia calorie model

infrastructure-and-technological-collapse: loss of electrical grids, refining, fertiliser (Haber–Bosch), pharmaceuticals and global logistics in both belligerents and, through trade halt, everywhere else — this is what converts a survivable famine into the 200-year recovery tier
pandemic: a starving, displaced, medically unsupported population of survivors is the classic substrate for epidemic mortality; explicitly excluded from Xia et al.
hazards.uncertainty_notes:
THE THREE PROBABILITIES ARE DIFFERENT AND I HAVE KEPT THEM APART. (a) P(event) — a full-scale US–Russia exchange occurs — is my 1e-3/yr best estimate, range 1e-4 to 9e-3. (b) P(kills a large fraction | event) is in severity_tiers: 60% for the 150 Tg/80.8% mortality outcome, i.e. P ≈ 6e-4/yr unconditionally. (c) P(permanent end of humanity | event) is 1%, i.e. ~1e-5/yr, which over a century is ~1e-3 and is exactly Ord's 1-in-1,000. That agreement is not independent evidence — I derived the conditional FROM Ord's number, so it is circular by construction and must not be read as a cross-check.

THE PROBABILITY IS THE WEAKEST FIGURE HERE. My best estimate of 1e-3/yr sits an order of magnitude BELOW Barrett et al.'s Danger Calm median of 0.009/yr. That is deliberate and it is an author judgement, not a published position: Barrett et al. estimate the probability of INADVERTENT LAUNCH in response to mistaken attack indications, which is a broader event than a full-scale countervalue exchange (a launch could be limited, or aborted, or answered in kind at a lower level), and their false-alarm rates come from 1977–1983 US data, a six-year sample from the sharpest period of the late Cold War, applied unchanged to 1975–2012. They say so themselves: NORAD has not released false-alarm rates since the mid-1980s, so they cannot tell whether the rate fell. Against that, they note their own model cannot be rejected at 95% confidence given 37 event-free years unless its mean exceeds 0.08. My high bound of 9e-3 is exactly their Danger Calm median; my low bound of 1e-4 sits between their two 5th-percentiles and Hellman's Cuba-only lower bound of 2e-4. A serious critic will attack the whole exercise: 81 years with zero events cannot distinguish 1e-2 from 1e-4, and the Baum/de Neufville/Barrett team who assembled the largest near-miss dataset (60 incidents) explicitly refused to convert it into a rate because "the 'closeness' of the events is a matter of subtle historical interpretation, something that experts in the field disagree on" — Lewis et al. 2014 say many came close, Tertrais 2017 says none did. That refusal is the most honest position in the literature and my number does not have its authority.

SCENARIO-TABLE PROVENANCE. As with the regional hazard, the 150 Tg death toll of 5,413 million was read from IPPNW's Table 2, captioned as adapted from Xia et al. 2022 and Toon et al. 2007/2019, because the Nature Food primary is paywalled and the repository copy returns 403. It cross-checks against the NASA GISS abstract's "more than 5 billion could die from a war between the United States and Russia." I could NOT retrieve a direct-fatality figure for the 150 Tg scenario — IPPNW's Table 1 gives direct fatalities only for the five regional cases — so the deaths_fraction of 0.808 for the winter tier is famine deaths ALONE and excludes prompt blast/fire/fallout deaths in the USA and Russia. It is therefore an underestimate, and I have not attempted to fill the gap with a number I did not retrieve.

SOOT SATURATION IS THE UNDER-APPRECIATED PHYSICS. The per-weapon soot yield falls from 0.148 Tg (top 250 South Asian targets) to 0.041 Tg (4,400 global urban targets) because the world's dense cities run out. Any simulator that makes soot linear in warhead count will badly overstate the marginal effect of the last few thousand warheads and badly understate the effect of the first few hundred. Conversely the 47 Tg regional case already kills 42% of humanity, so the marginal humanitarian value of arms reductions from 12,000 to, say, 1,000 warheads is much smaller than the weapon count suggests — a conclusion an arms-control advocate would dislike but which follows directly from Toon et al.'s own numbers.

WHAT WOULD FALSIFY THE WHOLE CHAIN. The famine result rests on urban firestorms lofting soot to the stratosphere. That has never been observed at scale. The observational analogues are 2017 British Columbia and 2019–2020 Australian wildfire pyroCb, which lofted a few tenths of a teragram to 12 km and then self-lofted to 23 km over two months — the right physics, three orders of magnitude short of the required mass, and forest rather than city fuel. If real urban fires under nuclear attack produce conflagrations rather than firestorms, burn a much smaller fraction of the available fuel because it is buried under rubble (Toon et al. concede perhaps 20% or more could be effectively buried in the high-overpressure zone), or fail to generate the convective column, the entire mechanism collapses and this hazard reduces to a regional catastrophe with a global economic depression. That is the Los Alamos position, and it is not obviously wrong — it is merely, in Toon et al.'s rebuttal, based on an unrepresentative sparse-suburban simulation.

hazards.name: Non-nuclear great-power and interstate war
hazards.one_line: Conventional war between states follows a fat-tailed severity distribution with no detectable downward trend in severity, so a war far larger than any yet fought is a live possibility even though the last eighty years have been quiet.
hazards.mechanism: A dispute between great powers escalates to open war; industrial mobilisation converts national economies into war production and the fighting continues until one side's capacity to resist collapses. Direct combat deaths are only part of the toll: the dominant killers in every historically large war have been famine, displacement and epidemic disease following the destruction of agriculture, transport and sanitation — the Thirty Years' War, the Taiping Rebellion, the An Lushan rebellion and the Eastern Front of WWII all killed far more civilians through starvation and disease than through weapons. A modern global war would additionally sever the container-shipping, fertiliser (Haber-Bosch nitrogen), fuel and pharmaceutical supply chains on which roughly half of current food production and nearly all urban populations depend, so the mass-death mechanism is regional famine and infrastructure loss in food-importing countries, not battlefield casualties. Critically, no observed or plausible conventional war reaches human extinction: even the largest tail events in the historical record kill single-digit percentages of humanity, and Cirillo and Taleb argue explicitly that the true mean of the casualty distribution is bounded by world population and cannot be infinite. The hazard here is civilisational damage and the cascade into worse hazards, not termination.

annual_probability.event_definition: onset of an armed conflict killing at least 1,000,000 people (combatants and civilians, direct violence), excluding any use of nuclear weapons
annual_probability.trend: Genuinely contested and the single most important open question in this hazard. Cirillo & Taleb (2016) test the 1500-2015 window and cannot reject a homogeneous Poisson process (504 events; no significant trend, season or temporal dependence over the entire time window), i.e. FLAT. Clauset (2018) likewise finds war onsets consistent with a stationary geometric process 1823-2003 and finds the post-1940 distribution of war sizes not statistically distinguishable from 1823-1939, i.e. FLAT. Spagat & Thompson (2026, ISQ) reach the opposite conclusion for a narrower quantity — the ONSET FREQUENCY of Western European great-power wars — reporting a sustained decline (annualised onset rate 0.27/yr in 1495-1599 falling to 0.040/yr in 1900-2024, with zero great-power wars since 1953, max p = 0.002 across 401 breakpoint tests). These are not necessarily contradictory: Spagat & Thompson measure how OFTEN great powers in one region start wars; Clauset and Cirillo & Taleb measure how BIG wars are globally and whether the size distribution has shifted. A declining onset rate combined with an unchanged fat-tailed severity distribution is coherent. For a simulator, treat frequency as plausibly declining and severity-given-occurrence as flat.

severity_tiers.label: Major regional war
severity_tiers.description: 1-10 million dead, comparable to the Korean War, the Iran-Iraq War or the Second Congo War. Regional famine and displacement; global industrial capacity essentially untouched.

severity_tiers.label: World-war scale
severity_tiers.description: 10-100 million dead, comparable to WWI or WWII (Clauset records WWII at 16,634,907 battle deaths; Cirillo & Taleb estimate ~73 million total victims). Multi-continent mobilisation, sustained famine in occupied and blockaded regions, decade-scale reconstruction.

severity_tiers.label: Beyond any recorded war
severity_tiers.description: 100 million to 1 billion dead. No historical precedent in absolute numbers. Collapse of global trade in food, fuel and fertiliser causes famine well outside the belligerent states; the deaths are overwhelmingly in food-importing countries not party to the war.

severity_tiers.label: Civilisational
severity_tiers.description: Over 1 billion dead. Requires either the fat tail delivering an event several orders of magnitude beyond the record, or the conflict cascading into nuclear, biological or infrastructural collapse. Industrial civilisation is set back but the physical and knowledge base for recovery survives; even Cirillo & Taleb's infinite-apparent-mean tail is bounded by world population.

key_parameters.label: Power-law tail exponent of war severity
key_parameters.effect: Governs the whole tail: Pr(X >= x) proportional to x^-alpha for x >= x_min = 7061 battle deaths. At Clauset's alpha = 1.53 the conditional odds of a war ten times larger than a given size are 10^-1.53 = 0.030. At Cirillo & Taleb's implied alpha = 1/xi = 1/1.4985 = 0.667 (their raw-data GPD fit) the same conditional odds are 10^-0.667 = 0.215 — a factor of SEVEN difference in the tail. Lowering alpha below 1 makes the apparent mean of the distribution infinite. This is the single most consequential knob in the model.

key_parameters.label: Onset rate of 'large' interstate wars (>=26,625 battle deaths)
key_parameters.effect: Linear in expected count. Clauset's periods: 1823-1939 gives 19 large wars, one every 6.2 years (0.161/yr); 1914-1939 gives 10 large wars, one every 2.7 years (0.370/yr); 1940-2003 gives 5 large wars, one every 12.8 years (0.078/yr); whole 1823-2003 span 24 in 181 years (0.133/yr). Setting this to the post-war value asserts the long peace is real; setting it to the full-period value asserts it is a fluctuation.

key_parameters.label: Onset rate of wars between great powers (Western Europe)
key_parameters.effect: Spagat & Thompson's annualised series built on Levy's dataset: 0.27/yr (1495-1599), 0.17 (1600-1699), 0.10 (1700-1799), 0.050 (1800-1899), 0.040 (1900-2024), with zero great-power wars since 1953. Roughly a factor-of-two decline per century over 1495-1899, flattening thereafter (19th vs 20th century comparison is not significant, p = 0.41). Great-power wars supply nearly all of the severity tail, so this multiplies the upper tiers far more than the lower ones.

key_parameters.label: Whether severity is measured absolutely or as a share of world population
key_parameters.effect: Changes the base rate by a measured factor of ~2.6. Cirillo & Taleb's inter-arrival time for a conflict killing >=1 million is 34.08 years on raw data (MAD 47.73) but 13.28 years on data rescaled to 2015 world population (MAD 20.53); at the >=5 million threshold it is 93.03 vs 34.88 years. Forward-projecting simulators should use the rescaled figure, since a war killing the same FRACTION of a larger population kills more people.

key_parameters.label: Ratio of true (shadow) mean casualties to naive sample mean
key_parameters.effect: Multiplies expected loss without changing event frequency. Cirillo & Taleb's dual-distribution shadow mean at the 145k threshold is 3.6885e7 against a sample mean of 1.7710e7, a ratio of 2.08; across thresholds from 50k to 1M the ratio runs 1.85 to 2.88, and on raw data with H = 7.2 billion the underestimation factor ranges from 1.6 up to 7.5. Any simulator that fits expected war deaths to the observed historical average is understating the true expectation by at least this factor.

citations.claim: War casualties are extremely fat-tailed: the GPD shape parameter exceeds 1 in all fits, implying the apparent mean of the distribution does not exist; and the naive sample mean severely understates the true (shadow) mean.
citations.authors: Pasquale Cirillo, Nassim Nicholas Taleb
citations.venue: Physica A: Statistical Mechanics and its Applications 452:29-45 (arXiv:1505.04722v2 preprint read this session)
citations.exact_figure: Dataset: 565 events over the period 1-2015 AD, all with more than 3000 casualties; 331 conflicts above the 25k threshold (58.6%). Maximum-likelihood GPD shape parameter xi = 1.4985 (SE 0.1233) for raw data at threshold 25k; xi = 1.5868 (SE 0.1265) for rescaled data at 145k; xi = 1.5915 (SE 0.1268) for dual data at 145k. Restricting to 1500-2015 (504 events): xi = 1.4093 raw, 1.4653 rescaled. Conditional shadow mean at the 145k threshold = 3.6885e7 vs conditional sample mean 1.7710e7, ratio 2.08 (ratios range 1.85 to 2.88 over thresholds 50k-1000k). Shadow standard deviation 3.0788e8 vs sample 1.0120e8, ratio 3.04.

citations.claim: The 'long peace' is not statistically distinguishable from chance: large armed conflicts follow a homogeneous Poisson process with no trend over the last 500 years, and the inter-arrival times are far longer than the length of the peace.
citations.authors: Pasquale Cirillo, Nassim Nicholas Taleb
citations.venue: Physica A: Statistical Mechanics and its Applications 452:29-45 (arXiv:1505.04722v2 preprint read this session)
citations.exact_figure: Average inter-arrival times (raw data, years) with mean absolute deviation: >=0.5M casualties 23.71 (MAD 35.20); >=1M 34.08 (47.73); >=2M 56.44 (72.84); >=5M 93.03 (113.57); >=10M 133.08 (136.88); >=20M 247.14 (261.31); >=50M 345.50 (325.50). Rescaled to 2015 population: >=1M 13.28 (20.53); >=5M 34.88 (46.85); >=10M 52.23 (63.91); >=50M 103.97 (114.25). Verbatim: 'the absence of a conflict generating more than, say, 5 million casualties in the last sixty years is highly insufficient to state that their probability has decreased over time, given that the average inter-arrival time is 93.03 years, with a mean absolute deviation of 113.57 years!' citations.claim: Interstate war sizes follow a power law and the long peace falls comfortably within the fluctuations of a stationary conflict-generating process; it would have to persist another century or more to become a statistically significant trend.
citations.authors: Aaron Clauset
citations.venue: Science Advances 4(2):eaao3580 (author preprint PDF read this session; PubMed 29507877, DOI 10.1126/sciadv.aao3580)
citations.exact_figure: Correlates of War: 95 interstate wars, 1823-2003, battle deaths ranging from 1,000 to 16,634,907 (WWII). Maximum-likelihood power law alpha-hat = 1.53 +/- 0.07 for x >= x_min-hat = 7061, 95% of the bootstrap distribution within [1.37, 1.76], Monte Carlo p_KS = 0.78 +/- 0.03 (power law not rejected). Times between onsets: geometric q-hat = 0.428 +/- 0.002 for t >= 1 year, 95% bootstrap [0.354, 0.520], p_KS = 0.13 +/- 0.01; average 1.91 years between consecutive war onsets; multiple onsets in only 14 of 181 years (8%). 'Large war' = x >= x_0.75 = 26,625 battle deaths: 19 large wars in 1823-1939 (one every 6.2 years), 10 in 1914-1939 (one every 2.7 years), 5 in 1940-2003 (one every 12.8 years). Stationary-model likelihood of the long peace, Pr(<=5 large wars over >=64 years) = 0.622(2), 0.569(2), 0.681(2) under Models 1/2/3; of the great violence, Pr(>=10 large wars over <=27 years) = 0.107(1), 0.159(1), 0.121(1); of violence-then-peace = 0.0030(2), 0.0029(2), 0.0055(2). Abstract, verbatim: 'the post-war pattern of peace would need to endure at least another 100-140 years to become a statistically significant trend' (the body of the same preprint says 'at least another 100-150 years').

citations.claim: Contrary to Clauset and Cirillo & Taleb, the ONSET FREQUENCY of Western European great-power war has genuinely declined over five centuries, and the decline began long before 1945.
citations.authors: Michael Spagat, William Thompson
citations.venue: International Studies Quarterly 70(3):sqag046, DOI 10.1093/isq/sqag046
citations.exact_figure: Building on Levy's (1982, 1983) dataset, 1495-2024. Levy's per-decade great-power war onset rates: 2.6 in the sixteenth century, then 1.7, 1.0, 0.50 and 0.66 in successive centuries through 1975. Annualised onset rates: 1495-1599 = 0.27/yr; 1600-1699 = 0.17/yr; 1700-1799 = 0.10/yr; 1800-1899 = 0.050/yr; 1900-2024 = 0.040/yr. 401 statistical tests pivoting around each year from 1550 to 1950; abstract verbatim: 'The maximum p-value across all 401 tests is 0.002, decisively rejecting the hypothesis that observed peace represents statistical luck.' Century comparisons: sixteenth vs seventeenth p = 0.031; sixteenth vs eighteenth p < 0.001; nineteenth vs twentieth p = 0.41 (not significant). 'Zero further wars between great powers since 1953.'

citations.claim: Expert elicitation puts conventional war at very high probability of killing over a million but low probability of causing extinction.
citations.authors: Anders Sandberg, Nick Bostrom
citations.venue: Future of Humanity Institute, Oxford University, Technical Report 2008/1 (survey circulated at the Global Catastrophic Risk Conference, Oxford, 17-20 July 2008)
citations.exact_figure: Median estimates for 'Total killed in all wars (including civil wars)' before 2100: at least 1 million dead 98%; at least 1 billion dead 30%; human extinction 4%. For comparison, 'Total killed in all nuclear wars': 30% / 10% / 1%. Overall risk of extinction prior to 2100: median 19%.

citations.claim: Forecasters and domain experts disagree substantially about catastrophe and extinction probabilities by 2100, and the gap is a first-order uncertainty in any elicitation-based rate.
citations.authors: Forecasting Research Institute (Ezra Karger, Josh Rosenberg, Philip Tetlock and colleagues); Existential Risk Persuasion Tournament, run 2022
citations.venue: Forecasting Research Institute working paper, 'Forecasting Existential Risks: Evidence from a Long-Run Forecasting Tournament' (announced 10 July 2023, revised 8 August 2023); 80 domain experts and 89 superforecasters
citations.exact_figure: Median probability by 2100 of total catastrophe: domain experts 20%, superforecasters 9%. Median probability of total human extinction by 2100: domain experts 6%, superforecasters 1%. AI-caused extinction: experts 3%, superforecasters 0.38%. The report notes experts and superforecasters 'were furthest apart (in percentage point terms) on AI risk, and most similar on the risk of nuclear war.'

hazards.uncertainty_notes:
WEAKEST POINT: the two headline papers disagree with each other about the tail by a factor of seven and this is not usually acknowledged. Clauset fits alpha = 1.53 (a FINITE-mean power law) to 95 COW interstate wars, battle deaths only, 1823-2003. Cirillo & Taleb fit xi ~ 1.5, implying alpha = 1/xi = 0.67 (an INFINITE-apparent-mean law), to 565 events over 1-2015 AD that include civil wars, democides (Stalin, Mao) and enormous ancient events (the Three Kingdoms at ~40M, An Lushan at ~13M). The discrepancy is almost certainly driven by dataset composition, not by method: including democides and pre-modern events with one-order-of-magnitude uncertainty fattens the tail enormously. A serious critic would attack my use of a single tail_index knob to span both, and would be right that the two numbers answer different questions. Cirillo & Taleb themselves concede the An Lushan figure 'could be conceivably one order of magnitude smaller.'

SECOND WEAKNESS: my annual_probability is derived by inverting Cirillo & Taleb's published mean inter-arrival times (34.08 yr raw / 13.28 yr rescaled at the 1M threshold) rather than taken from a published rate. The inversion is only valid under their own Poisson assumption, which they defend but Spagat & Thompson (2026) reject for great-power onsets. The low bound of 0.01/yr is my own reconciliation with the post-1945 record and is an author-estimate, not a published figure.

THIRD: the severity_tiers' p_given_event values are MY interpolation between the two published tail indices, not published conditional probabilities. Under Clauset's alpha alone, Pr(>=10M | >=1M) = 0.030; under Cirillo & Taleb's, 0.215. I used 0.115, roughly the geometric midpoint. That choice is defensible but arbitrary and should be exposed as a knob.

FOURTH: I could not retrieve Levy (1983) directly this session; his per-decade rates come to me through Spagat & Thompson's (2026) quotation of him, which is a secondary transmission.

FIFTH: no tier is marked terminal. This is deliberate and I believe correct — no source I retrieved supports conventional war causing human extinction, and Cirillo & Taleb explicitly argue the true mean is bounded by world population — but the Sandberg & Bostrom respondents put 4% on extinction from 'all wars', which is far above anything the severity statistics justify. That 4% is probably absorbing nuclear and cascade pathways rather than conventional war as such.

SIXTH: DEATHS ARE NOT THE ONLY AXIS EVEN HERE. A great-power war that kills 'only' 20 million but ends with a single hegemon holding a decisive and permanent technological lead feeds directly into the unrecoverable-dystopia hazard, where the body count is near zero and the loss is total. The war model should emit a 'number of independent great powers' output, not just a death count.
cascades_into: unrecoverable-dystopia: a decisive hegemonic victory collapses the number of independent great powers, which is the parameter Caplan (2008) identifies as most strongly driving the probability of stable world totalitarianism (his estimate rises from 5% to 25% if the count falls to 1)
chemical-radiological-weapons: essentially all chemical weapons deaths since 1918 occurred inside interstate or civil wars; war is the enabling condition, not an independent driver
nuclear-war: conventional great-power war is the dominant pathway to nuclear use; the two hazards are not independent and a simulator must not multiply their probabilities as if they were
engineered-pandemic: wartime states relax biosafety and biosecurity norms and have historically pursued offensive biological programmes

hazards.name: Chemical and radiological weapons
hazards.one_line: Chemical and radiological weapons are cruel, illegal and locally devastating, but the arithmetic of dose, dispersal and decay puts their maximum realistic death toll four to five orders of magnitude below anything that threatens civilisation.
hazards.mechanism: A chemical agent (blister agents such as sulphur mustard, or organophosphate nerve agents such as sarin, VX or Novichok) is dispersed as vapour or aerosol; it kills by blistering the airways and skin or by irreversibly inhibiting acetylcholinesterase, causing respiratory arrest. A radiological dispersal device pairs conventional explosive with radioactive material, killing by blast and contaminating an area which must then be evacuated and decontaminated. The fundamental limit on both is physical, not political: lethality requires delivering a lethal DOSE to each individual victim, so the death toll scales roughly linearly with the mass of agent successfully dispersed onto people, and agents dilute, hydrolyse, photodegrade and blow away within hours to days. There is no self-replication and no chain reaction. This is the decisive structural difference from pathogens (which amplify inside each host) and from nuclear weapons (where one device yields megatons). Consequently the mass-death mechanism that operates for war and pandemic — famine and infrastructure collapse — is essentially never reached: the best-documented modern chemical terrorist attack killed thirteen people, and the entire four-year chemical campaign of the First World War killed about one hundred thousand. The genuine catastrophic contribution of these weapons is as an escalation trigger inside a great-power confrontation, not as a direct killer.

annual_probability.event_definition: any state or non-state use of chemical or radiological weapons killing at least 1,000 people within a single calendar year
annual_probability.trend: Ambiguous, with genuine countervailing forces. Downward: the Chemical Weapons Convention now has 193 States Parties covering about 98% of world population, and as of 7 July 2023 the OPCW verified that 100% of declared stockpiles had been irreversibly destroyed — the single largest disarmament achievement on record. Upward: Syria used sarin and chlorine repeatedly while a CWC State Party; Novichok agents were used in assassination attempts in 2018 and 2020; and the synthesis routes for nerve agents are published and require no exotic materials, so the barrier is now operational competence rather than access. Net: the ceiling on a single event has fallen sharply (no declared stockpiles remain), while the floor rate of small-to-medium use has not.

severity_tiers.label: Battlefield or civilian attack
severity_tiers.description: 1,000-10,000 dead. The Halabja attack of 1988 (approximately 5,000 killed by mustard and nerve agents) is the historical maximum for a single chemical attack on civilians. Local horror, no measurable effect on regional food, industry or population.

severity_tiers.label: Sustained campaign inside a major war
severity_tiers.description: 10,000-100,000 dead over a multi-year war, the WWI and Iran-Iraq War regime. This is the historical maximum for chemical warfare of any kind: the entire chemical war of 1915-1918 killed roughly 100,000 people out of some 17 million total war deaths, under 1% of the war's toll.

severity_tiers.label: Maximum plausible use
severity_tiers.description: 100,000-1,000,000 dead. Requires either a reconstituted national stockpile of thousands of tonnes used deliberately against dense urban populations, or nerve agent released into the ventilation of multiple megacities. Even at the top of this range the loss is 0.01% of humanity and industrial capacity is untouched. No credible pathway exists beyond this tier.

key_parameters.label: Declared chemical agent held in national stockpiles
key_parameters.effect: Sets the hard ceiling on a state-scale chemical campaign, roughly linearly. 72,304 metric tonnes were declared to the OPCW since 1997 and all were verifiably destroyed by 7 July 2023, so the declared figure today is zero. Historical lethality was low per tonne: the WWI chemical campaign killed on the order of 100,000 people, and inefficient dispersal means most agent never reaches a lung. Even restoring the entire historical global stockpile does not lift the top severity tier above ~1e-4 of world population.

key_parameters.label: Deaths per person exposed in a chemical attack
key_parameters.effect: Multiplies deaths directly for a given exposed population. The Tokyo subway sarin attack, the best-instrumented modern case, gives 13 deaths among 6,226 affected = 0.0021; but approximately 85% of hospital presentations were 'worried well' without physical symptoms, so the ratio among the genuinely exposed (17 critical + 37 severe + 984 moderate = 1,038) is 13/1,038 = 0.0125. Battlefield mustard and nerve-agent exposure in WWI and Iran-Iraq gives figures around 0.05-0.10. Raising this knob two orders of magnitude still cannot reach a civilisation-relevant death fraction.

key_parameters.label: Share of world population under Chemical Weapons Convention verification
key_parameters.effect: 193 nations representing about 98% of the global population are CWC States Parties. Non-linear rather than linear: the marginal risk sits almost entirely in the non-party remainder plus non-compliant parties (Syria retained and used capability while a party), so falling coverage matters far less than a single large-state defection. Model this as a step function on great-power adherence, not a smooth fraction.

key_parameters.label: Deaths attributable to radiation (not blast) per radiological dispersal device
key_parameters.effect: Approximately zero and should stay there. The US Nuclear Regulatory Commission states that 'Most RDDs would not release enough radiation to kill people or cause severe illness' and that 'the conventional explosive itself would be more harmful to people than the radioactive material.' The correct output variable for an RDD is not deaths but square kilometres requiring decontamination and the resulting economic and panic cost — the NRC calls it 'not a weapon of mass destruction but a weapon of mass disruption.' A simulator that scores RDDs on body count will score them at zero and be right about the deaths while missing the entire effect.

key_parameters.label: Atmospheric half-life of the dispersed agent
key_parameters.effect: Caps the exposed population. Sarin is non-persistent (hours); sulphur mustard and VX are persistent (days to weeks) and contaminate terrain. Exposed population scales roughly as dispersal area times persistence, but because agent concentration falls with dilution the death toll saturates rather than growing without bound. There is no persistence value at which a chemical agent becomes self-sustaining — the absence of amplification is why this hazard has a hard ceiling.

hazards.uncertainty_notes:
WEAKEST POINT AND FLAGGED AS SUCH: the annual_probability is an AUTHOR-ESTIMATE, basis marked accordingly. I could not retrieve any published frequency estimate for 'chemical or radiological use killing >=1,000 people per year' this session. My 0.04/yr is a back-of-envelope from the observed episodes since 1918 (Italy in Ethiopia 1935-36, Japan in China 1937-45, the Iran-Iraq War 1980-88 including Halabja, and Syria 2013-18) — roughly four to five episodes in 108 years — and the count itself rests on general knowledge rather than a source I pulled today. Treat this number as the least reliable in the packet. It is also the number that matters least, because the severity ceiling is what makes this hazard non-catastrophic and that ceiling IS well sourced.

SECOND: the Halabja death toll of ~5,000 in my first severity tier came to me through a web search summary rather than a document I fetched — the OPCW's own commemoration page returned HTTP 403. Published estimates for Halabja range from roughly 3,200 to 5,000 killed and 7,000-10,000 injured, and the figure is politically contested. Do not treat 5,000 as precise.

THIRD: the WWI figure of 'nearly 100,000 deaths' from UNODA is a round institutional number; the scholarly range runs roughly 90,000-100,000 deaths on about 1.3 million gas casualties. I could not retrieve the peer-reviewed toxicology review (Springer paywall redirect) to give the tonnage and case-fatality breakdown properly, so my deaths-per-tonne reasoning in the mechanism is qualitative, not fitted.

FOURTH: a serious critic would say I am under-weighting the ESCALATION function. Chemical weapons use inside a great-power crisis could plausibly trigger a nuclear response, in which case the relevant death toll is the nuclear one and my tiers are irrelevant. My tiers score the direct effect only, which is the honest thing for a directly-modelled hazard but understates the hazard's role in the system. This should be carried as a coupling term, not folded into these tiers.

FIFTH: undeclared and novel agents are outside the OPCW verification figure. The '100% destroyed' number applies only to DECLARED stockpiles; Novichok-class agents were only added to the CWC schedules in 2019. Setting declared_cw_stockpile_tonnes to zero is correct as a statement about verified declarations and wrong as a statement about world capability.
cascades_into: great-power-and-interstate-war: chemical use is a recognised escalation rung and has repeatedly been treated as a red line whose crossing triggers direct intervention

nuclear-war: several nuclear-armed states declare chemical or biological attack as a condition under which nuclear retaliation is on the table, making this a low-death hazard with a high-death coupling

hazards.name: Unrecoverable dystopia / stable global totalitarianism
hazards.one_line: Surveillance, automation and biotechnology could remove the internal failure modes that have always eventually destroyed totalitarian regimes, permanently foreclosing humanity's future while killing almost nobody.
hazards.mechanism: Every historical totalitarian regime has died of one of a small number of internal failures: the leader died and a successor liberalised; loyal-seeming officials were secretly disloyal and defected at the critical moment; the population's private beliefs diverged from the public line and eventually broke through; or an external rival state offered a demonstration of an alternative and a refuge for exiles. Each of these is a technological accident of the twentieth century rather than a law of politics. Ubiquitous automated surveillance and, in the limit, direct neural monitoring would close the closet-skeptic channel by making private dissent detectable; radical life extension would close the succession channel by keeping the founding leadership in place indefinitely; automated enforcement (drones, algorithmic policing, financial exclusion) would close the mass-defection channel by removing the regime's dependence on a large, potentially disloyal enforcement class; and state control over reproduction and genetic selection would, over generations, alter the disposition of the population itself. The consolidation of the world into a single political unit — by conquest, by hegemonic victory in a great-power war, or by a well-intentioned merger to manage some other global risk — would close the external-refuge channel. What makes this an EXISTENTIAL rather than merely a very bad outcome is that the failure is self-preserving: unlike a war or a plague, an entrenched totalitarian order actively suppresses the recovery mechanisms, so there is no expected return to the prior state. And crucially, it can arrive with a body count near zero and industrial capacity intact.

annual_probability.event_definition: establishment of a single global totalitarian order (one world regime, or a stable coalition with no viable exit and no external rival) — NOT conditional on any deaths occurring
annual_probability.trend: Rising, on the mechanism side, and this is one of the few hazards where the direction is not seriously disputed. The enabling technologies — pervasive camera and sensor networks, automated facial and gait recognition, financial surveillance, large-scale language models capable of reading all communications rather than sampling them, and autonomous enforcement platforms — have all improved by orders of magnitude in two decades and continue to. Caplan's argument is precisely that these technologies remove specific historical failure modes, so the CONDITIONAL probability that a totalitarian regime, once established, persists indefinitely is rising even if the probability of establishment is not. The count of independent great powers, which is the strongest single driver in Caplan's own analysis, is currently stable but would fall sharply after a decisive great-power war or a decisive lead in transformative AI.

severity_tiers.label: Totalitarian order that later collapses
severity_tiers.description: A global or near-global authoritarian order is established but fails within a century through one of the classical channels. Deaths at twentieth-century democide rates — Caplan gives approximately 20 million civilians killed by the Soviets, 25 million by the Nazis and 65 million under Mao, with 30 million of the latter in the Great Leap Forward famine alone. Terrible, but recoverable: this is the historical case, not the novel one.

severity_tiers.label: Millennium-scale entrenchment, high repression
severity_tiers.description: The order persists indefinitely and maintains itself by ongoing violence and terror. Sustained low-level democide plus permanent foreclosure of every alternative future. Industrial and scientific capacity is retained and may even grow; there is nothing to 'recover' in the material sense, which is exactly why recovery_years is zero and terminal is nonetheless true.

severity_tiers.label: Permanent, low-violence entrenchment
severity_tiers.description: The worst tier and the one with the fewest deaths. Surveillance and preference-shaping are effective enough that overt violence becomes unnecessary; the regime is stable because dissent is detected and dissolved before it organises, or because the population has been selected or conditioned not to generate it. Ord's 'desired dystopia'. Population, health and material output may all be at historic highs. A body-count metric scores this as harmless. It is the total and permanent loss of humanity's potential.

key_parameters.label: Number of independent great powers / sovereign centres with no external check
key_parameters.effect: The strongest driver in the only published quantitative treatment. Caplan's unconditional probability of a world totalitarian government lasting 1,000+ years is 5%; he states that if the number of countries falls to 1 'my probability rises to 25%' (a factor of 5), and that if the number of independent countries does not decrease over the next thousand years 'my probability falls to .1%' (a factor of 50 down). Fitting a log-linear form to his two anchor points across the plausible range gives roughly p ∝ n^-1.6 over n in [1, ~10]. This is the knob a simulator should couple to war outcomes and to AI-lead scenarios.

key_parameters.label: Degree of state control over reproduction and genetic selection
key_parameters.unit: 0 = full reproductive freedom, 1 = full state control
key_parameters.effect: Directly quantified by Caplan: given advanced genetic screening, if 'reproductive freedom prevails' his probability falls to 3%, whereas with the same technology under government regulation 'my probability rises to 10%' — a factor of 3.3 between the endpoints. Interpolate multiplicatively between 3% and 10% across the range. The mechanism is multi-generational: selection against the dispositions underlying critical thinking and individualism.

key_parameters.label: Maximum effective tenure of a single ruler
key_parameters.effect: Closes or opens the succession failure mode, which is empirically the most common cause of totalitarian liberalisation. Caplan: 'Both Stalin and Mao ruled for decades until their deaths, facing no serious internal threats to their power', and 'If life extension technology had been advanced enough to keep them in peak condition forever, it is reasonable to believe that they still be in power today.' Treat the per-generation escape probability as roughly (regime lifetime / leader tenure) draws from a liberalisation hazard: extending tenure by a factor k divides the number of succession events by k. For reference, Hitler's 'Thousand-Year Reich lasted less than thirteen years' — succession never even arose.

key_parameters.label: Fraction of population under persistent automated behavioural monitoring
key_parameters.effect: Closes the closet-skeptic failure mode. Caplan's mechanism is that brain scanning or equivalent could 'screen out closet skeptics from party leadership', which is the failure that produced Khrushchev and Gorbachev from within the Soviet system itself. Model the per-year probability of a successful internal reform coalition forming as declining steeply — plausibly exponentially — in this coverage fraction, since the coalition requires a number of mutually-trusting dissenters and detection probability compounds with group size. NOTE: the current_value of 0.3 is my own rough estimate of the share of humanity under state-linked pervasive monitoring; I found no published figure for it this session.

key_parameters.label: Fraction of coercive enforcement performed by machines rather than human agents
key_parameters.effect: Closes the mass-defection failure mode. Every historical regime has depended on soldiers and police willing to shoot, and several — East Germany 1989, Romania 1989, Tunisia and Egypt 2011 — fell precisely when that willingness evaporated. Automated enforcement removes the requirement for a large loyal enforcement class, so the minimum size of the ruling coalition falls toward one. This parameter has NO published probability attached to it and is my own extension of Caplan's argument to a technology he did not have in 2008; treat its effect as structural (it removes a termination channel) rather than as a fitted multiplier.

The survey's own quantified table has exactly three outcome columns — 'At least 1 million dead', 'At least 1 billion dead' and 'Human extinction' — and no column in which a zero-death permanent dystopia could be scored.
