hazards.uncertainty_notes:
Frequency: the three estimates span a factor of 2.4 (0.83 to 2.0 per millennium) and are not independent - Newhall's 'closer to 2 per millennium' is an incompleteness-corrected reading of the same Holocene record that Rougier's 1200-yr figure is derived from. The single most attackable step in this entry is the event definition: Lin et al.'s 1.60/millennium counts SULFUR-FORCING events exceeding Tambora, not VEI-7 eruptions, and these sets differ in both directions. Laki 1783 is the archetypal false negative - a VEI 4 fissure eruption that released ~120 Mt SO2 - while a sulfur-poor VEI 7 would be a false positive. I have deliberately defined the hazard by forcing rather than by VEI because forcing is what drives the famine, but a critic could reasonably object that the resulting rate is then not 'the VEI-7 rate' and should not be labelled as such.

Severity: much weaker than frequency. Tambora's -1.9 +/- 0.2 degC is a global LAND anomaly for 1816 (Wilson et al. 2023); the commonly quoted 0.4-0.7 degC is the global land-plus-ocean mean, and quoting the land number as a global mean is a common and serious error - the simulator must not conflate them. Tambora's global death toll is poorly constrained: direct deaths are of order 10^5, but 1816-1817 famine mortality and the subsequent cholera pandemic are contested and much larger, and Newhall et al. quote Guillet et al. and Campbell cautioning that some post-Samalas famines started before the eruption and cannot all be attributed to it. All deaths_fraction values in the severity tiers are AUTHOR ESTIMATES: no published figure exists for the fraction of a 2026 world population killed by a VEI-7, and the tier probabilities are my own partition of a space with one modern data point in it.

The evacuation_lead_days parameter is the weakest quantified knob. Newhall et al. give the qualitative facts (hours-to-days final runup; never millions evacuated for months) but no survival-versus-lead-time curve exists; the saturating form I give is an author construction.

What I could NOT verify this session: the full text of Cassidy & Mani 2022 (Nature 608:469-471) is paywalled, so the widely circulated '1 in 6 chance of a magnitude-7 eruption this century' is sourced here to Wilson et al. 2023, who state it in that exact form, rather than to Cassidy & Mani. The Cabaniss et al. 2018 GRL figures are quoted from a ScienceDaily summary, not the paper. Both are flagged in the citations above.

hazards.name: VEI-8 / Magnitude-8 supereruption (Toba class)
hazards.one_line: A magnitude-8 eruption injects hundreds of teragrams of sulfur into the stratosphere, producing a volcanic winter of several kelvin lasting years to a decade and a simultaneous, global failure of agriculture.
hazards.mechanism: A magnitude-8 eruption discharges of order 10^15 kg (about 1000 Gt) of magma - Toba's Youngest Toba Tuff is estimated at more than 2800-5300 km3 dense rock equivalent, forming a 3500 km2 caldera. Proximal effects are total but geographically bounded: pyroclastic flows sterilise an area hundreds of kilometres across, and centimetre-to-metre ash blankets cover subcontinental areas. The global mechanism is again sulfate. Ice-core sulfur-isotope work puts the stratospheric loading of the Toba candidate horizons at 72-233 Tg S, two to four times the 1257 Samalas eruption and roughly 7-23 times Pinatubo. That veil cools the surface by several kelvin, cuts precipitation, collapses the monsoons and shortens or eliminates growing seasons across the mid-latitudes for years. Nobody dies of the eruption itself outside the proximal zone; they die of famine, of the collapse of grain trade and of the conflict that follows, over the two to ten years the veil persists. Ozone destruction of up to 60% after large caldera-forming eruptions, recovering over one to two decades, adds a UV stress on top of the cold. Crucially, the one M8 in the human record did NOT produce a demographic collapse: archaeological sites in India, Sumatra and South Africa show occupation continuing across the 74 ka ash, and no genomic bottleneck coincides with that date.

annual_probability.event_definition: A magnitude-8 explosive eruption anywhere on Earth, defined by Rougier et al. as at least 1000 Gt (10^15 kg) of erupted mass. Best estimate is the reciprocal of their 17 ka return period; low and high are the reciprocals of the upper and lower ends of their 95% credible interval (48 ka and 5.2 ka). Note that the folk figure of 1 in 50,000 yr (2e-5 /yr) sits at the extreme LOW end of this interval, and that an independent ice-core estimate - Lin et al.'s 0.07 eruptions per millennium with climate forcing at or above Taupo Oruanui, i.e. 7e-5 /yr - lands almost exactly on the best estimate.
annual_probability.trend: Flat over the coming century. No anthropogenic mechanism alters magma supply on that timescale, and Lin et al. find the large-eruption frequency constant across 60-9 ka. One weak upward mechanism is worth recording but not applying: Lin et al. observe a marked rise in large Northern Hemisphere eruptions during the deglacial period 16-9 ka and attribute it to isostatic unloading of the NH ice sheets, so sustained large-scale ice loss is a plausible long-run forcing of volcanism - but the implied lag is millennial and the effect on this century's M8 rate is negligible. What does change is exposure: a globally integrated, low-inventory, mid-latitude-dependent food system is more vulnerable to a multi-year cold shock than the subsistence agriculture of any previous century, even as total stored calories and technical adaptive capacity are far greater.

severity_tiers.label: Attenuated - aerosol microphysics limits the forcing
severity_tiers.description: The eruption is extratropical, sulfur-poor, or - most importantly - the injection is so large that aerosol microphysics blunts it: bigger droplets scatter less per unit mass and sediment faster, so forcing scales far below linearly with sulfur mass. This is the Timmreck et al. reading of Toba, and it is what the archaeological record of 74 ka actually supports. Global cooling of 1-2 K for 2-5 years; proximal deaths in the millions to tens of millions; multi-year famine in import-dependent regions; severe but survivable damage to global agriculture and trade.

severity_tiers.label: Volcanic winter
severity_tiers.description: Tropical vent, high sulfur yield. Global cooling of 3-5 K sustained for 5-10 years with decadal ocean and sea-ice feedbacks; monsoon failure across Asia and Africa; three or more consecutive near-total harvest failures in the mid-latitude breadbaskets. Grain export bans become universal; the ~10^9 people who depend on imported staples are the first to die, followed by urban populations everywhere as distribution fails. Industrial capacity survives in fragments; global institutions do not.

severity_tiers.label: Decade without a summer
severity_tiers.description: Upper end of the plausible forcing range: 5-8 K global cooling persisting a decade or more, at or beyond the top of what any modern civilisation has faced. Conventional outdoor agriculture fails across all mid- and high-latitude land for several consecutive years. Deaths are overwhelmingly from famine and the wars fought over the remaining food; survival concentrates in low-latitude coastal and island regions with fisheries access, and wherever resilient-food production (seaweed, methane single-cell protein, cellulosic sugar, greenhouses) has been pre-positioned. Industrial civilisation is set back generations but the species persists.

severity_tiers.label: Terminal
severity_tiers.description: Humanity does not recover. This requires the cold shock to be compounded - by nuclear exchange over remaining food-producing land, by the permanent loss of the accessible fossil and mineral base needed to re-industrialise, or by a residual population too small and too scattered to sustain a technological society. Note that this tier is NOT supported by the 74 ka record, where a genuine M8 failed to bottleneck a hunter-gatherer humanity of far fewer people with far less technology; it is included because modern civilisation has failure modes that hunter-gatherers did not.

key_parameters.label: Stratospheric sulfur loading
key_parameters.effect: The master knob, and the one where the literature disagrees by a factor of ~5. Crick et al. 2021 put the Toba candidate horizons at 154 (T1), 233 (T2) and 72 (T3) Tg S, against 59.4 Tg S for Samalas 1257. Naive linear scaling from Pinatubo - assuming Toba's stratospheric loading was 33 to 900 times Pinatubo's aerosol - yields global mean cooling of 7 K to 19 K (Jones et al. 2005; Robock et al. 2009, as reported by Newhall et al. 2018). But Newhall et al. immediately caution that larger injections produce larger aerosol droplets, less effective at reflecting per unit mass and faster to fall, so that Timmreck et al. 2010 'inferred that climate effects of Toba would have been far less than the size of the eruption might suggest'. For a simulator, use a strongly sublinear form such as dT = 0.5 K * (S / 10 Tg S)^0.4 (which returns ~2.4 K at 233 Tg S) as the central case and expose the exponent as a tunable in [0.33, 1.0]; the exponent, not the sulfur mass, is where the real uncertainty lives.

key_parameters.label: Sulfur-to-cooling scaling exponent
key_parameters.effect: Explicitly exposes the single largest disagreement in supereruption science. At exponent 1.0 (linear, no microphysical saturation) a 233 Tg S Toba gives ~12 K of global cooling and the outcome is near-terminal. At exponent 0.33 it gives ~1.5 K and the outcome is a bad decade. The empirical arbiter - that humans and other mammals show no 74 ka bottleneck, and that eastern African and South African records show continuity across the ash - argues for the low end. Any simulator that hard-codes a linear scaling will systematically overstate this hazard.

key_parameters.label: Vent latitude
key_parameters.effect: Same physics as for VEI-7 but with more at stake. Tropical injections (Toba at 2.7 degN, Yellowstone would NOT qualify at 44.4 degN) are carried into both hemispheres by the Brewer-Dobson circulation with e-folding lifetimes of ~1 yr; extratropical injections stay in one hemisphere with e-folding lifetimes of 3-5 months. Multiply integrated global forcing by ~1.0 for |lat| < 25 deg and ~0.3-0.5 for |lat| > 45 deg. This matters enormously for candidate selection: the popularly feared Yellowstone system is at a latitude that substantially blunts its global reach relative to an equatorial equivalent.

key_parameters.label: Duration of significant radiative forcing
key_parameters.effect: Sets how many consecutive harvests fail, which is what converts a shock into a famine. Zielinski et al. 1996 inferred an elevated sulfate signal of ~6 yr for the Toba horizon and suggested as much as 200 yr of cooler temperatures; Timmreck et al. argue for much less. Ocean and sea-ice coupling extends surface cooling well beyond aerosol residence - Newhall et al.'s Table 2 lists 'centennial cooling' via reduced heat flow to the Arctic Ocean with a 10-100 yr duration. Famine deaths should scale super-linearly with the number of consecutive failed harvests once stored grain (order 3-6 months of world consumption) is exhausted.

key_parameters.label: Pre-positioned resilient-food capacity
key_parameters.unit: fraction of global caloric need deployable within 12 months
key_parameters.effect: The only knob under human control, and the entire policy content of the ALLFED framing. Pham et al. show that nutritionally adequate diets built on resilient foods (seaweed, microbial and single-cell protein, cellulosic sugar, greenhouses) are feasible with existing technology given preparation, with residual chronic risks in vitamins D, E and K. Current deployable capacity is effectively negligible (the value given is an author estimate, not a measured figure). Model famine deaths as scaling with the caloric deficit remaining after this fraction is met; moving it from ~0 to ~0.3 plausibly removes most of the deaths_fraction in the middle severity tiers, which makes it by far the highest-leverage intervention in this hazard.

citations.claim: The modern revision of the supereruption return period: magnitude-8 eruptions recur far more often than the folk figure of once per 50,000 years.
citations.authors: Jonathan Rougier, R. Stephen J. Sparks, Katharine V. Cashman, Sarah K. Brown
citations.venue: Earth and Planetary Science Letters, 482, 621-629, doi:10.1016/j.epsl.2017.11.015
citations.exact_figure: "Our estimate for the return period of 'super-eruptions' (1000Gt, or M8) is 17ka (95% CI: 5.2ka, 48ka), which is substantially shorter than previous estimates, indicating that volcanoes pose a larger risk to human civilisation than previously thought." The relationship is derived empirically from the LaMEVE database for eruptions of at least 300 Mt erupted mass (M4.5), and differs from prior work "mainly in our conservative treatment of magnitude-rounding and under-recording".

citations.claim: Stratospheric sulfur loading of the Toba eruption candidates measured directly from polar ice-core sulfur isotopes.
citations.authors: Laura Crick, Andrea Burke, William Hutchison, Mika Kohno, Kathryn A. Moore, Joel Savarino, Emily A. Doyle, Sue Mahony, Sepp Kipfstuhl, James W. B. Rae, Robert C. J. Steele, R. Stephen J. Sparks, Eric W. Wolff

The candidates fall on the transition into Greenland Stadial 20, suggesting "Toba was not the trigger for the large Northern Hemisphere cooling".

citations.claim: The physical scale of the Toba eruption and the contested status of both its climate impact and the genetic-bottleneck claim.
citations.authors: Benoit Caron, Giulia Del Manzo, Benoit Villemant, Annachiara Bartolini, Eva Moreno, Anne Le Friant, Franck Bassinot, Francois Baudin, Adriana Alves
citations.exact_figure: Toba "emitted magma volume is estimated > 2800-5300 km3 (dense rock equivalent)"; the Young Toba Tuff is "classically dated around 74 ka BP"; it formed "the largest known Quaternary caldera (3500 km2)". The authors state the huge ash and SO2 emissions "are likely to have triggered a volcanic winter" but that the impacts "are hotly debated", and propose that a series of large-volume eruptions over several thousand years "may have had a more persistent climate impact than a single short-lived cataclysmic event".

citations.claim: The factor-of-five disagreement over Toba's climate impact, the VEI-8 return-period ballpark from the geological literature, and the ozone-destruction side-effect.
citations.authors: Chris Newhall, Stephen Self, Alan Robock
citations.venue: Geosphere (Geological Society of America), v. 14, no. 2, doi:10.1130/GES01513.1
citations.exact_figure: "Jones et al. (2005) and Robock et al. (2009) simulated the climate response to the Toba eruption, assuming that the stratospheric loading was a multiple of the 1991 Pinatubo eruption from 33 to 900 times the amount of aerosols, and calculated large climate responses with global average cooling of 7 K to 19 K." Immediately followed by: "Following this reasoning, Timmreck et al. (2010) inferred that climate effects of Toba would have been far less than the size of the eruption might suggest." On VEI-8 recurrence: Taupo 26.5 ka, Toba ca. 74-72 ka, Yellowstone ca. 640 ka - "Such events have global return times of tens to hundreds of thousands of years." On ozone: as much as 60% loss after large caldera-forming eruptions, "gradually recovering over 1-2 decades". On the Toba sulfate signal: an "increase in sulfate for ~6 yr, inferred by Zielinski et al. (1996) to be the Toba signal", with Zielinski inferring "as much as 200 yr of cooler temperatures".

citations.claim: The Toba genetic-bottleneck hypothesis is not supported by current genomic or archaeological evidence; the real bottleneck signal in the human genome is elsewhere in time.
citations.authors: John Hawks (Vilas-Borghesi Distinguished Achievement Professor of Anthropology, University of Wisconsin-Madison) - expert commentary, not peer-reviewed, summarising the peer-reviewed literature
citations.venue: johnhawks.net (expert blog; cites Henn et al. 2012, Lippold et al. 2014, Karmin et al. 2015, Malaspinas et al. 2016, Li & Durbin 2011, Kidd et al. 2012)
citations.exact_figure: "Numerous genetic analyses have not detected a bottleneck that coincides with the Toba eruption." The bottleneck signal that does exist is dated to ~50 ka and attributed to an out-of-Africa founder effect (Lippold et al. 2014; Karmin et al. 2015; Malaspinas et al. 2016), with a separate earlier population reduction at ~150-130 ka (Li & Durbin 2011; Kidd et al. 2012). Anatomically modern human populations "were always relatively low, started to decline around 150 ka, and continued to decrease until ~30 ka".

citations.claim: The framing of a supereruption as an abrupt sunlight reduction scenario, and the feasibility of resilient foods as the mitigation lever.
citations.authors: Anna Pham, Juan B. Garcia Martinez, Vojtech Brynych, Ratheka Stormbjorne, Joshua M. Pearce, David C. Denkenberger
citations.exact_figure: ASRS defined as: "A sudden catastrophic event causes an immense amount of aerosol material of sulfates or black carbon (soot) to be projected and entrapped in the stratosphere for several years." Causes listed as volcanic winter from a large eruption, an exceptionally large asteroid or comet impact, and nuclear winter. Effects last "several years at a minimum", with the response divided into three periods each "expected to last between 3 and 9 months". Their finding: nutritionally adequate resilient-food diets are achievable with existing technology given preparation, with residual chronic deficiency risks in vitamins D, E and K.

citations.claim: Toby Ord's existential-risk estimate for supervolcanic eruption, reported at second hand.
citations.authors: Mike Cassidy and Lara Mani (EA Forum post 'On the assessment of volcanic eruptions as global catastrophic or existential risks'), reporting figures from Toby Ord, The Precipice (2020), Table 6.1
citations.venue: EA Forum (secondary source; I could not retrieve the text of The Precipice itself this session)
citations.exact_figure: They report Ord's estimate of "1 in 10,000 chance this century" for existential risk from volcanic eruptions, and his claim that volcanic existential risk is "100 times that of asteroids and comets combined". They also reproduce Rougier et al.'s figure as "17,000 (95% CI: 5,200, 48,000)" years, note an ice-core-based M8 recurrence of "15,000" years, and conclude that the "combined probability of an eruption of magnitude 7 and above occurring is ~1 in 6 this century". They explicitly state they offer no new existential-risk probability of their own.

cascades_into: abrupt-sunlight-reduction-famine: this is the canonical natural ASRS and shares its entire downstream model with nuclear winter

nuclear-war: Newhall et al. record that analogies between giant eruptions and nuclear war have been drawn since Rampino et al. 1988, and competition for the remaining food-producing land under a multi-year veil is the plausible trigger
great-power-conflict: grain export bans and mass migration under a decade-long cold shock
ozone-depletion-and-uv-stress: up to 60% ozone loss after large caldera-forming eruptions, recovering over 1-2 decades

pandemic: cold, malnutrition, displacement and crowding are the classic conditions for epidemic mortality - Newhall et al. note that reduced crop yields, famine and cold made populations more vulnerable to the Black Death, without claiming direct causation
infrastructure-and-supply-chain-collapse: subcontinental ash fall plus multi-year loss of agricultural output
hazards.uncertainty_notes:
WARNING ASYMMETRY (applies to both volcanic entries and should be modelled explicitly). The warning we would get and the warning we could act on are different things. Long-lead: silicic caldera systems are expected to inflate for a very long time before a catastrophic eruption - Cabaniss, Gregg & Grosfils 2018 expect 'tens to hundreds of meters of uplift' over 'hundreds to thousands of years' of rejuvenation, far larger than any unrest observed today. Short-lead: that long signal does not resolve into a date. Newhall et al. 2018 report that at Rabaul, Campi Flegrei and Pinatubo, 'despite prolonged early unrest, the final runup to eruption was just hours to days', that 'an eruption was imminent did not become clear until hours to days before those eruptions', and that 'most unrest at calderas dies out rather than culminates in eruption' - so the base rate of false alarms is high and the cost of acting on them is enormous. And there is no prevention: no proposed intervention on a magma chamber of this size has any empirical support. The honest model is therefore decades of ambiguous warning, days of unambiguous warning, and zero mitigation of the event itself - which makes pre-positioned resilience (food, not evacuation) the only lever with real expected value.

FREQUENCY. The Rougier 17 ka figure rests on very few M8 events in LaMEVE and its 95% CI spans nearly an order of magnitude (5.2-48 ka). A serious critic would say the under-recording correction is doing all the work: moving the return period from ~50 ka to 17 ka is a modelling choice about how fast the geological record degrades with age, not a new observation. The independent ice-core corroboration (Lin et al., 0.07 per millennium) is reassuring but is itself based on n = 3 events in a 51 kyr window, and it measures sulfur forcing rather than erupted mass - the two are only loosely coupled. Two weak estimates agreeing is weaker evidence than it looks.

SEVERITY - THE WEAKEST PART OF THIS ENTRY BY FAR. There is exactly one M8 in the human record and the modelled climate impact spans a factor of about eight: 7-19 K under naive linear scaling from Pinatubo (Jones et al. 2005; Robock et al. 2009) versus 'far less than the size of the eruption might suggest' once aerosol microphysics is included (Timmreck et al. 2010). Both are reported in Newhall et al. 2018 without adjudication. That is why I have exposed the scaling exponent as an explicit parameter rather than burying a choice inside a fixed cooling figure - a simulator that hard-codes the linear form will overstate this hazard by an order of magnitude in deaths.

The empirical arbiter cuts toward the low end: Toba did not bottleneck humanity. Occupation continues across the 74 ka ash in India, Sumatra and South Africa, and no genomic bottleneck coincides with that date - the bottleneck signal in the human genome is at ~50 ka and is an out-of-Africa founder effect. Anyone using the 'Toba nearly killed us all' framing is using a claim that the field has largely abandoned. The honest counter-argument is that this is not reassuring in the way it first appears: 74 ka hunter-gatherers were mobile, low-density, locally self-provisioning and tropical, whereas a modern population of eight billion depends on a small number of mid-latitude breadbaskets, a few months of stored grain, and a globally integrated distribution system - exactly the configuration a multi-year mid-latitude cold shock breaks. The past under-states the modern risk on the vulnerability axis while over-stating it on the forcing axis.

ALL deaths_fraction AND p_given_event VALUES IN THE SEVERITY TIERS ARE AUTHOR ESTIMATES. No published study gives the fraction of a 2026 world population killed by an M8. The terminal tier's p_given_event of 0.015 is anchored on Ord's reported ~1 in 10,000 per century existential estimate divided by this entry's ~0.6% per century M8 rate; I obtained Ord's figures from a secondary source (an EA Forum post by Cassidy & Mani) because I could not retrieve the text of The Precipice this session, and the figure should be treated as an expert's subjective prior, not a derived result. The recovery_years value of 100000 in the terminal tier is a sentinel meaning 'never', not an estimate.

I could not retrieve any Existential Risk Persuasion Tournament figure specific to supervolcanoes, and no such number is reported here. I also could not retrieve the full text of Cassidy & Mani 2022 (Nature 608:469-471) or Rougier et al. 2018 itself - the Rougier abstract quoted above is verbatim from the University of Bristol's institutional record, and the M7 return period of 1200 yr is quoted from Lohmann & Svensson 2022 citing Rougier, not from Rougier directly.

hazards.name: Thinness of the global grain buffer (stocks-to-use)
hazards.one_line: The world holds roughly four months of cereal consumption in store, and most of it sits inside a few countries that will not release it, so a production shock becomes scarcity within one season.
hazards.mechanism: Global cereal stocks are a buffer between a production flow and a consumption flow. When the buffer is large relative to annual utilization, a bad harvest is absorbed by drawdown and prices move modestly; when it is small, the shortfall must be rationed by price in real time. Price rationing does not kill people in rich countries — it kills net food importers whose households already spend 40-70% of income on food, and it kills them through purchased-calorie collapse, not through absence of physical grain. The buffer also sets a hard deadline on every mitigation: nothing that takes longer than the buffer to deploy can prevent the first famine year. The headline stocks-to-use ratio overstates the real buffer, because the great majority of world stocks are held by countries that treat them as national strategic reserves and do not export them under stress.

annual_probability.event_definition: world cereal ending stocks-to-use ratio at or below 20 percent in a given marketing year — the level at which the 2007/08 price crisis occurred
annual_probability.trend: Headline ratio is currently rising and near a multi-year high (31.6% forecast for 2026/27, down slightly from 31.9% the previous season), so the probability of a sub-20% year is falling in the near term. The tradable fraction of that buffer is falling, however: the US share of world reserves has gone from up to 40% in the 1980s to just above 5%, while China now holds the majority of world stocks of all three main cereals. The effective buffer available to net-importing countries has therefore deteriorated even as the global number improved.

severity_tiers.label: Price spike without a production shock
severity_tiers.description: Thin stocks alone produce a speculative and precautionary price spike of the 2007-08 or 2010-11 kind. Hundreds of millions of people are pushed into food insecurity; excess mortality is concentrated in the poorest importing countries and is largely invisible in national statistics.

severity_tiers.label: Thin buffer coincides with a multi-breadbasket failure
severity_tiers.description: A simultaneous 8-12% shortfall in global cereal output (correlated drought or heat across two or more of the major export regions) lands on a buffer of under 75 days. Export restrictions follow, importers cannot cover, and famine appears in import-dependent regions within one to two seasons.

severity_tiers.label: Thin buffer coincides with an abrupt sunlight reduction or infrastructure loss
severity_tiers.description: The buffer is the only thing standing between a 40-90% production collapse and immediate global famine. With under 75 days of stock and no resilient-food capacity built, mass starvation begins in the first year rather than the second.

key_parameters.label: World cereal stocks-to-use ratio
key_parameters.effect: Days of global buffer = 3.65 x ratio. At 31.6% the world holds about 115 days of cereal consumption; at the 2007/08 value of 19.2% it held about 70 days. THIS IS A MULTIPLIER ON OTHER HAZARDS: for any hazard that suppresses production for T_shock days (nuclear winter, supervolcano, impact winter, multi-breadbasket failure, Haber-Bosch loss), the famine-exposed interval is max(0, T_shock - buffer_days), so scale that hazard's deaths_fraction by max(0, T_shock - 3.65*ratio) / T_shock. For a 5-year sunlight shock the buffer changes almost nothing (115/1825 = 6%); for a 6-month logistics or fertilizer shock it can be the difference between zero deaths and mass famine.

key_parameters.label: Fraction of world grain stocks actually available to the world market
key_parameters.effect: China holds 69% of the corn, 60% of the rice and 51% of the wheat stored worldwide and does not release these to the world market under stress; the US share of global reserves fell from up to 40% in the 1980s to just above 5%. The buffer that a net-importing country can actually buy is stocks x this fraction, so the effective import-side buffer today is roughly 0.35 x 115 = 40 days, not 115. MULTIPLIER USE: apply the stocks_to_use effect above using (3.65 * ratio * tradable_fraction) as buffer_days when computing deaths in net-importing regions, and the full buffer only for stockholding countries. Moving this knob to 0.9 (a genuine internationally callable reserve) roughly triples the importer buffer and is the cheapest single intervention in this packet.

key_parameters.label: Total global food stores including pipeline inventory
key_parameters.effect: Roughly 6 months of food stocks exist for the global population when pipeline and non-cereal inventory are included. THIS IS THE DEADLINE PARAMETER FOR EVERY MITIGATION IN THIS PACKET: any resilient food, fertilizer substitute or grid restoration that reaches scale in M months leaves max(0, M - this_value) months of unfed gap. Raising it to 18 months would bring the slower resilient-food routes (methane single-cell protein, quoted at 'a few years' to global protein sufficiency) inside the window; lowering it to 2 months makes even the fastest published route (seaweed at 9-14 months) arrive too late.

cascades_into: grain-export-ban-cascade: a buffer under ~75 days is the observed trigger condition for precautionary export restrictions, which then remove more supply from the market than the harvest shortfall did
resilient-food-deployment-failure: the buffer sets the deadline that every resilient-food ramp must beat, so a thin buffer directly converts a slow ramp into famine deaths
synthetic-nitrogen-dependence: fertilizer interruption shows up as a yield shortfall one to two seasons later, and the buffer is what decides whether that shortfall is a price event or a famine
hazards.uncertainty_notes: The annual probability is an author frequency count over roughly 35 years of FAO tracking (approximately 3-5 marketing years at or under 20%), not a published hazard rate; nobody publishes a probability distribution over future stocks-to-use ratios, and the ratio is strongly autocorrelated, so treating years as independent draws overstates the effective sample size. The severity tiers are entirely author estimates of a COMPOUND state (thin buffer AND a production shock) and no published source attributes a deaths_fraction to buffer thinness alone — a serious critic would attack the tier-3 figure hardest, since the deaths there properly belong to the sunlight-reduction hazard and this packet is only claiming the buffer changes their timing and magnitude. The tradable_stock_fraction of 0.35 is an author-derived arithmetic combination of two separately cited figures (China's share of world stocks, and China's near-zero export behaviour); it is not itself a published quantity, and a critic could reasonably argue that China's stocks would in fact be partially released, or that Indian and Russian stocks are more accessible than assumed. The 'days of consumption' framing is also flattering: real buffers are not fungible across grains, geographies or qualities, so 115 physical days is an upper bound on 115 useful days.

hazards.name: Grain export concentration and the export-ban cascade
hazards.one_line: Staple grain exports come from a handful of countries, and when prices spike those countries ban exports, which raises prices further and triggers more bans.
hazards.mechanism: Most countries do not feed themselves; they buy the marginal calorie from a very small set of exporters. When a price spike begins, each exporting government faces a domestic political incentive to restrict exports and a negligible cost from doing so, so it restricts. Each restriction removes supply from the world market and pushes the price up further, which strengthens the same incentive in the next exporter — a positive feedback with no equilibrating force until either the harvest recovers or importers stop bidding. The importing country then faces not an expensive market but an absent one: there is no counterparty at any price. Deaths come from famine and from the civil conflict that food-price spikes reliably ignite in import-dependent low-income states, not from any physical destruction of grain. Because the network has grown both more connected and more homogeneous, a shock now propagates further than it did in the 1990s.

annual_probability.event_definition: onset of a new multi-country staple-food export-restriction episode in which the restricting countries account for at least 10 percent of globally traded food calories
annual_probability.trend: Rising. Puma et al. document a food trade network that between 1992 and 2009 doubled its number of wheat and rice trade connections while 83-85 percent of countries remained at low or marginal self-sufficiency — more paths for a shock to travel and fewer places that can absorb one. Four qualifying episodes have occurred in roughly 20 years (2007-08, 2010-11, 2020, 2022), and the 2022 episode was the largest on record by number of measures.

severity_tiers.label: Price spike and food riots
severity_tiers.description: Restrictions add 20-50 percent to staple prices for one to two seasons. Food riots in a dozen or more import-dependent countries; governments fall; excess mortality is small and mostly unattributed.

severity_tiers.label: Import-dependent famine
severity_tiers.description: Restrictions coincide with a genuine harvest shortfall. Least-developed importers — some of which take over 96 percent of their wheat imports from a single supplier — cannot source at any price. Localized famine in the Sahel, Horn of Africa, Yemen, and parts of South and Southeast Asia.

severity_tiers.label: Trade shutdown during a global production shock
severity_tiers.description: An abrupt sunlight reduction or global infrastructure loss triggers near-total withdrawal of exporters from the market. Every country is thrown onto its own production. Puma's finding that 83-85 percent of countries have low or marginal self-sufficiency becomes the mortality distribution directly.

key_parameters.label: Share of globally traded food calories under export restriction
key_parameters.effect: At the 2022 peak this reached roughly 0.17 of traded calories (bans ~12.4%, licensing ~4.6%). MULTIPLIER USE: this knob does not itself kill anyone — it multiplies the import price faced by every net-importing country during any other hazard. The empirical anchors are that Indian and Vietnamese rice restrictions plus importer panic buying moved world rice prices 117-149 percent in Q1 2008, and USDA attributed roughly a 20 percent wheat price rise to restrictions. A defensible simulator form is import_price_multiplier = 1 / (1 - k*share) with k ~ 3 calibrated to the 2008 rice episode; the deaths_fraction of any production-shock hazard should then be scaled in net-importing regions by that price multiplier's effect on purchasing power. The functional form is author-constructed; only the two price anchors are published.

key_parameters.label: Share of countries with low or marginal food self-sufficiency
key_parameters.effect: Puma et al. find 85 percent of countries at low or marginal self-sufficiency across their study period, and 83 percent for 2005-2009. MULTIPLIER USE: this is the fraction of the world's states for which a trade shutdown converts directly into a domestic production constraint. In a simulator, use it as the population weight that receives the full deaths_fraction of a trade-shutdown tier while the self-sufficient remainder receives only its own production shortfall. Driving it to 0.4 (through regional reserves, diversified sourcing and domestic production floors) roughly halves the population exposed to any export-ban cascade.

key_parameters.label: Share of world wheat trade held by the top 17 exporters
key_parameters.effect: In 2008, 6 of the top 17 wheat exporters — who between them account for 90 percent of total wheat trade — imposed some degree of trade restriction, and 4 of the top 9 rice exporters did so. MULTIPLIER USE: the number of independent decisions needed to shut the world market is small and the correlation between those decisions is high, so the probability that a given fraction of trade is withdrawn is far higher than an independent-actor model predicts. In a simulator, model exporter decisions as correlated Bernoulli draws with correlation rising in the price spike rather than independently; the practical effect is to fatten the tail of the traded_calorie_share_restricted distribution by roughly an order of magnitude at the extremes.

key_parameters.label: Wheat trade links relative to 1992
key_parameters.effect: The number of global wheat and rice trade connections doubled between 1992-1996 and 2005-2009, with trade flows up 42 and 90 percent respectively. NOTE THE SIGN IS NOT OBVIOUS: more links diversify sourcing in normal conditions but, per Buldyrev et al., increased coupling between interdependent networks makes the coupled system collapse discontinuously rather than gracefully. Puma et al. explicitly conclude the system shows 'an accelerating sensitivity' to harmful stressors. Treat this knob as reducing the probability of a small shock propagating while increasing the severity of a large one — a variance-increasing, not mean-reducing, parameter.

hazards.uncertainty_notes: PROVENANCE WARNING: the IFPRI figures (16 countries, 17 percent of traded calories, 12.4 percent via bans, 4.6 percent via licensing, 32 countries and 77 restrictions across 2022) were obtained this session through a web-search result summary of the IFPRI blog page; a direct fetch of that URL returned empty content and I could not confirm the wording against the page itself. Treat those numbers as one step removed. The 117-149 percent rice price move and the USDA's ~20 percent wheat attribution likewise came from search summaries of secondary sources (ODI and USITC reports) that I did not retrieve directly, and I have therefore not listed them as citations — they appear only inside a parameter effect field as calibration anchors and should be re-verified before being compiled into a model. The annual probability is an author frequency count of four episodes in about twenty years; a critic would note that the episode definition is mine, that the four episodes are not independent (2010-11 was partly a rehearsal of 2007-08 in the same institutional setting), and that a 20-year window straddling two unusual decades is a poor base rate. The severity tiers are author estimates; no published source assigns a deaths_fraction to export restrictions separately from the harvest shortfall they accompany, and disentangling the two is the central unsolved empirical problem in this literature.

hazards.name: Dependence of the food supply on Haber-Bosch synthetic nitrogen
hazards.one_line: About half of humanity is fed on nitrogen fixed industrially from natural gas, applied fresh every season by a few hundred plants with no stockpile behind them.
hazards.mechanism: Crops remove nitrogen from soil every harvest, and industrial ammonia synthesis is what puts it back at current yields. Around 100 Tg of Haber-Bosch nitrogen goes into global agriculture each year at an energy cost of at least 32 MJ per kg of nitrogen fixed, roughly one percent of global primary energy, and roughly 80 percent of all manufactured nitrogen goes into fertilizer. There is no meaningful buffer: fertilizer is applied within months of being made, and soil organic nitrogen cannot carry current yields for more than a season or two. If ammonia output stops, yields of the four staples fall by 35-48 percent within one to two growing seasons, and the deaths are famine deaths concentrated in dense, import-dependent, high-yield-dependent regions — not deaths from the interruption itself. The dependency is doubly fragile because it runs on pipeline natural gas, which is itself dependent on the electricity grid.

annual_probability.event_definition: a sustained reduction of at least 50 percent in global Haber-Bosch ammonia output for at least twelve consecutive months
annual_probability.trend: Roughly flat to slightly rising in the near term. The 2021-22 European gas price shock curtailed a large share of EU ammonia capacity without moving global output much, which shows the tail is real but also that capacity is geographically diversified (notably coal-based Chinese production). The dominant consideration is that this event is almost always a CONSEQUENCE of another hazard — infrastructure loss, great-power war, an extreme energy shock — rather than a standalone failure, so its rate is largely inherited.

severity_tiers.label: Regional fertilizer famine
severity_tiers.description: One major producing or importing region loses fertilizer supply for one to two seasons. Yields there fall by a third or more; the region becomes a large net importer at exactly the moment world stocks are being drawn down.

severity_tiers.label: Global staple yield collapse
severity_tiers.description: Global loss of industrial fertilizer, alongside the pesticide, irrigation and mechanization inputs that usually fail with it. Modelled yield reductions with no industrial inputs are -35% rice, -37% wheat, -41% soybeans, -48% corn. Global calorie supply falls by roughly 40 percent while the population that those calories currently feed remains the same.

severity_tiers.label: Fertilizer loss compounding a sunlight reduction or full infrastructure loss
severity_tiers.description: Industrial nitrogen and sunlight both fail. The 40 percent input-driven yield loss stacks multiplicatively on the up-to-90 percent sunlight-driven loss in the worst year of a severe nuclear winter. Nothing recognizable as industrial agriculture survives the first three years.

key_parameters.label: Share of world population fed by Haber-Bosch nitrogen
key_parameters.effect: Erisman et al. estimate 44 percent for 2000 and 48 percent for 2008; a later estimate puts it at about half for 2019. MULTIPLIER USE — AND THE MOST COMMON MISUSE IN THIS LITERATURE: this is an UPPER BOUND on the deaths_fraction of a total Haber-Bosch loss, not the deaths_fraction itself, because manure, legume rotation, soil mineralisation, dietary shift away from meat, and redistribution all partially substitute. In a simulator, apply an extra famine term of (haber_bosch_population_share x fraction_of_ammonia_capacity_lost x substitution_shortfall) on top of any hazard that also disables industry — global catastrophic infrastructure loss, HEMP, extreme geomagnetic storm, extreme pandemic, severe sunlight reduction — with substitution_shortfall in the range 0.3-0.7 rather than 1.0.

key_parameters.label: Staple crop yield reduction with no industrial inputs
key_parameters.effect: Modelled reductions in a global catastrophic infrastructure loss scenario with no synthetic fertilizer, pesticides, irrigation or mechanization are -35% for rice, -41% for soybeans, -48% for corn and -37% for wheat; 40 is the unweighted mean. MULTIPLIER USE: this is a straight multiplicative factor on global calorie production, to be COMPOSED WITH, not substituted for, any sunlight-driven yield loss. For a combined nuclear-winter-plus-infrastructure-loss scenario, calories_remaining = (1 - sunlight_loss) x (1 - this_value/100), which for a severe winter's 90 percent sunlight-driven loss and a 40 percent input-driven loss leaves 6 percent of normal production.

key_parameters.label: Global nitrogen-use efficiency of cereals
key_parameters.effect: Global nitrogen-use efficiency of cereals decreased from about 80 percent in 1960 to about 30 percent in 2000, and of 100 Tg N applied to agriculture in 2005 only 17 Tg N was actually consumed by humans in crop, dairy and meat products. MULTIPLIER USE: this is the largest published lever on this hazard. Because the fraction of the population supported by synthetic N scales roughly with (N applied x efficiency), recovering efficiency toward its 1960 value would let the same food output be produced from proportionally less fixed nitrogen, cutting haber_bosch_population_share — and hence the extra famine term this hazard contributes to every industry-disabling hazard — by up to a factor of 2. It is also the only knob here that is purely agronomic and can be moved without any new technology.

key_parameters.label: Energy required per kg of nitrogen fixed
key_parameters.effect: Haber-Bosch consumes an energy supply equivalent to at least 32 MJ per kg N fixed, about 1 percent of global primary energy. MULTIPLIER USE: this is the coupling coefficient between energy hazards and food hazards. Any hazard that cuts global primary energy availability by a fraction f cuts ammonia output by at least f (in practice more, because fertilizer is an early casualty of energy rationing), which then propagates into the yield loss above with a one-to-two-season lag. In a simulator, wire energy_shortfall -> ammonia_shortfall -> yield_loss with a 1.5 year delay rather than treating food and energy hazards as independent.

interdependent-infrastructure-cascade: ammonia synthesis runs on pipeline natural gas, which runs on electrically driven compressor stations, so the grid hazard is upstream of this one
