hazards.uncertainty_notes: The annual probability is explicitly an AUTHOR ESTIMATE. I found no published frequency estimate for a sustained global ammonia-output collapse, and I have not dressed one up: the figure is a judgment anchored on the observation that the 2021-22 European gas crisis curtailed a large regional share without approaching a 50 percent global cut. The weakest link in the whole hazard is the step from '48 percent of humanity is fed by Haber-Bosch nitrogen' to any deaths_fraction. Erisman's 48 percent is a counterfactual nitrogen-balance accounting figure — it says how much of current food production is attributable to synthetic N under stated assumptions (including that other improvements would have accounted for a 20 percent productivity increase between 1950 and 2000), not that 48 percent of people die if it stops. Smil's independent estimate of 40 percent for 2000 differs from Erisman's 44 percent for the same year, which is a fair indication of the method's precision. A serious critic would attack three things: (1) that the substitution_shortfall factor of 0.3-0.7 in the first parameter is entirely mine and unsupported by any published study I retrieved; (2) that the Moersdorf yield figures are modelled, not observed, and come from an ALLFED-affiliated group whose institutional interest is in the fragility being real; (3) that I read those figures out of a non-peer-reviewed ALLFED preprint quoting the peer-reviewed paper rather than out of the peer-reviewed paper itself, because the Wiley page returned HTTP 403 this session.

hazards.name: Interdependent infrastructure cascade and the black-start trap
hazards.one_line: The electricity grid, the gas network and the communications network each require the other two to function, so a large enough failure in any one of them does not stop there.
hazards.mechanism: Critical infrastructures are coupled physically (gas turbines need pipeline pressure; pipeline compressors need grid power), cyber-physically (grid control needs SCADA telemetry; SCADA needs powered communications), geographically (co-located rights of way), and logically. Buldyrev et al. show that this coupling changes the qualitative behaviour of the system rather than merely degrading it: interdependent networks fragment through a discontinuous, first-order transition at a much higher connectivity than a single network needs, and a broader degree distribution — hub-heavy, like every real infrastructure — makes them MORE fragile to random failure rather than less. The concrete trap is black start: 60 percent of the black-start resources registered with NERC are gas turbines, wind and solar contribute zero, nuclear plants cannot black-start at all under NRC rules, and a cold coal unit cannot be synchronized for more than 48 hours. Deaths do not come from the loss of light; they come from the loss of water pumping, refrigeration of medicines and food, hospital function, fuel distribution, and — beyond a few weeks — the fertilizer and food chain.

annual_probability.event_definition: a North American blackout of at least 186,000 MW of load — the size Hines, Apt and Talukdar compute as the 100-year event from NERC data for 1984-2006
annual_probability.trend: Not improving. Hines et al. find the frequency of large blackouts in the United States has not decreased over time even after controlling for demand and population growth, and they find strong statistical support for a power-law relationship between blackout size and frequency, meaning the tail does not thin. Two trends push in opposite directions: rising inverter-based generation removes rotational inertia and contributes zero registered black-start capability, while grid-scale batteries have now been demonstrated as black-start sources (a 33 MW / 20 MWh lithium-ion system starting a 44 MW combined-cycle plant).

severity_tiers.label: Days-scale blackout restored by black start
severity_tiers.description: A cascading outage takes down a large fraction of an interconnection; black-start units and cranking paths work as planned and bulk service returns within one to three days. Deaths from heat, cold, medical device failure and traffic; economic loss dominates.

severity_tiers.label: Weeks-scale outage with gas and water failure
severity_tiers.description: Black start is delayed because gas compressor stations lost power, gas-fired black-start units cannot get fuel, and coal units are past their 48-hour cold-start window. Municipal water pumping and sewage treatment fail after their few days of on-site reserve. Disease and dehydration mortality begins; the fuel distribution network stops because pumps are electric.

severity_tiers.label: Months-scale continental grid loss
severity_tiers.description: Extra-high-voltage transformers are physically damaged — geomagnetic storm, HEMP, coordinated physical or cyber attack — and replacement lead times run to months or years. Industrial agriculture, ammonia synthesis, refrigeration, water and medical infrastructure all stop across a continent for a growing season or more.

key_parameters.label: Share of NERC-registered black-start resources that are gas turbines
key_parameters.effect: NERC-registered black-start units are 60 percent gas turbines, 37 percent hydropower, 1 percent each fossil, combined cycle and diesel, and 0 percent wind and solar; nuclear units cannot serve as black-start resources at all. Gas turbines need pipeline pressure and pipeline compressor stations need grid power — a closed loop that must be broken from outside. MULTIPLIER USE: this parameter sets the restoration time T, and T is what turns a blackout into a catastrophe. Restoration time enters every downstream hazard roughly linearly beyond the ~3-day municipal water and fuel reserve: multiply the deaths_fraction of water-borne disease, medical failure and cold-chain loss by max(0, T_days - 3)/T_days. Reducing this knob (by shifting toward hydro, batteries and diesel, which need no external fuel network) is the direct lever on T.

key_parameters.label: Mean degree below which two interdependent networks collapse
key_parameters.effect: Buldyrev et al.: "For two interdependent Erdos-Renyi (ER) networks, we find that the critical average degree below which both networks collapse is <k_c>=2.445, compared to <k_c>=1 for a single ER network." MULTIPLIER USE: this is the correction factor for every single-network robustness estimate in a model. An analysis that treats the grid, the telecoms network and the gas network as independent understates the fragmentation threshold by roughly this factor of 2.45, and gets the ORDER of the transition wrong — coupled systems fail discontinuously, so there is no graceful-degradation regime to plan against. Note also the sign reversal Buldyrev report: "for interdependent networks, the broader the distribution is, the more vulnerable the networks become to random failure", which inverts the standard scale-free-networks-are-robust intuition for exactly the hub-heavy topologies real infrastructure has.

key_parameters.label: Size of the 100-year North American blackout
key_parameters.effect: Hines, Apt and Talukdar, following natural-disaster planning procedure applied to NERC 1984-2006 data: "the size of the 100-year blackout, which for North America is 186,000 MW." MULTIPLIER USE: the power-law size-frequency relation means P(size > S) falls only algebraically, so the probability of an event ten times larger than the design basis is roughly 100 times, not 10^10 times, less likely. In a simulator, sample blackout size from a power law with exponent near -2 rather than a thin-tailed distribution; the practical effect is that the correlated, multi-region blackouts that break black start are two to three orders of magnitude more likely than a Gaussian or exponential model implies.

key_parameters.label: Time to restore bulk electricity service after a total interconnection collapse
key_parameters.effect: MULTIPLIER USE — this is the master coupling variable between the grid hazard and every other hazard in the packet. Below ~3 days, municipal water reserves, hospital diesel and fuel-station backup absorb the outage and deaths are near zero. Between 3 and 30 days, water, sewage, cold chain and medicine fail and deaths scale roughly linearly with T. Beyond ~90 days the outage begins to consume a growing season through loss of irrigation, ammonia synthesis and mechanization, at which point the synthetic-nitrogen hazard's -40 percent yield term applies and deaths become famine deaths, which are two to three orders of magnitude larger than the direct outage deaths. Anchors: cold-start coal units are not available for more than 48 hours; nuclear units were offline for several days after the 14 August 2003 blackout.

citations.claim: Interdependent networks collapse at a much higher connectivity than single networks, and broader degree distributions make them worse
citations.authors: Sergey V. Buldyrev, Roni Parshani, Gerald Paul, H. Eugene Stanley, Shlomo Havlin
citations.exact_figure: "For two interdependent Erdos-Renyi (ER) networks, we find that the critical average degree below which both networks collapse is <k_c>=2.445, compared to <k_c>=1 for a single ER network." And: "While for a single network a broader degree distribution of the network nodes results in higher robustness to random failure, for interdependent networks, the broader the distribution is, the more vulnerable the networks become to random failure."

citations.claim: Blackout size-frequency power law, no decline in large-blackout frequency, and the 100-year event size
citations.authors: Paul Hines, Jay Apt, Sarosh Talukdar
citations.venue: Energy Policy (Carnegie Mellon Electricity Industry Center Working Paper CEIC 09-01)
citations.exact_figure: "Using data from the North American Electric Reliability Council (NERC) for 1984-2006, we find several notable trends. We find that the frequency of large blackouts in the United States has not decreased over time... and that there is strong statistical support for the previously observed power-law statistical relationship between blackout size and frequency... we use the observed statistical trends to calculate the size of the 100-year blackout, which for North America is 186,000 MW." A 'large blackout' is defined as one causing "service disruptions to at least 50,000 customers or 300 MW of demand."

citations.claim: Composition of North American black-start resources and the fuel-network dependency
citations.authors: James G. O'Brien, Michael Cassiadoro, Tamara Becejac, Gerald B. Sheble, James Follum, Urmila Agrawal, Eric Andersen, Md Touhiduzzaman, Jeffery Dagle
citations.venue: Pacific Northwest National Laboratory, PNNL-32773 (prepared for the U.S. Department of Energy), April 2022
citations.exact_figure: Table 3, Blackstart units registered with NERC: Hydropower turbine generators 37%, Gas turbines 60%, Fossil 1%, Combined cycle 1%, Diesel 1%, Wind & solar 0%. Also: "NRC regulations prevent the operation of the power plant without two separate power sources being available for station service. As such, a nuclear power plant cannot be used in any blackstart capability (PJM 2019)." Coal start-up: "cold start - not available to be synchronized to the grid for more than 48 hours". And: "In the case of the August 14, 2003 blackout, multiple nuclear power facilities were offline for several days following the event."

citations.claim: Taxonomy of critical infrastructure interdependency (physical, cyber, geographic, logical) and of failure propagation (cascading, escalating, common-cause)
citations.authors: Steven M. Rinaldi, James P. Peerenboom, Terrence K. Kelly
citations.venue: IEEE Control Systems Magazine 21(6), 11-25, DOI 10.1109/37.969131
citations.exact_figure: NO NUMERICAL FIGURE IS TAKEN FROM THIS PAPER. It is cited only for its four-class taxonomy of interdependency (physical, cyber, geographic, logical) and its distinction between cascading, escalating and common-cause failures, as reported in the secondary literature retrieved this session; the full text was not obtainable.

cascades_into: synthetic-nitrogen-dependence: gas compressor stations are electrically driven, so a long outage stops ammonia synthesis and applies the -40 percent yield term one to two seasons later

jit-logistics-and-settlement-spof: settlement systems, port cranes, refrigerated containers and fuel pumps all stop with the grid, so a grid failure of more than a few days is automatically a logistics failure
grain-reserve-buffer-thinness: refrigerated and milled stocks spoil without power, so a long outage destroys part of the buffer rather than merely blocking access to it
hazards.uncertainty_notes: The 0.01 per year figure is the Hines et al. 100-year North American blackout SIZE threshold reinterpreted as a rate, which is legitimate for the size but says nothing about DURATION — and duration is what actually drives mortality. I could not find a published probability for a months-scale continental grid loss, so the tier-3 conditional probability of 0.03 is an author estimate. It is also a North American rate applied to a global hazard: European, Indian and Chinese grid statistics were not retrieved this session and the black-start composition figures are specifically NERC-registered units, so extrapolating the 60 percent gas figure worldwide is unjustified. The PNNL report itself notes a FERC-NERC finding that 'grid operators currently have sufficient blackstart resources' and that additional unregistered units exist — I have not modelled that mitigating factor and a critic would rightly say the 60 percent figure overstates the trap. Rinaldi et al. 2001 is cited bibliographically only: I could not retrieve the paper this session (the IEEE full text is paywalled and the two open PDFs I fetched did not yield extractable text), and I have deliberately attached no number to it rather than reconstruct one from memory. The National Grid restoration planning assumptions (24 hours to 60 percent of national demand, 5-7 days to full restoration, up to 14 days worst case) that circulate widely could not be verified: the National Grid Black Start Strategy PDF returned HTTP 404, so I have set restoration_days from the PNNL coal cold-start and 2003-blackout anchors instead and marked it accordingly.

hazards.name: Just-in-time logistics and single points of failure in timing, shipping and settlement
hazards.one_line: Modern production holds days of inventory and runs on a small number of shared timing, shipping and settlement utilities, so a short interruption in one place becomes a shortage everywhere.
hazards.mechanism: Half a century of inventory optimization has converted buffer stock into working capital, which means the physical slack that used to absorb disruptions no longer exists anywhere in the chain. The same optimization has concentrated function: a handful of container ports, a handful of chip fabs, one satellite timing signal that most of the world's telecommunications, electricity and financial timestamping depend on, and a small number of settlement utilities through which most cross-border value passes. Failure therefore propagates by starvation rather than by damage — a plant with no parts stops as completely as a plant that burned down, and it stops within days rather than months. The mortality mechanism is indirect: interrupted medical supply, interrupted fuel, interrupted fertilizer and interrupted food distribution, arriving fastest in low-income importing countries with the least domestic substitution capacity. 2020-22 was the observed demonstration of the mechanism at a severity well below the tail.

annual_probability.event_definition: a global supply-chain disruption reducing world merchandise trade volume by at least 5 percent for at least three consecutive months
annual_probability.trend: Rising slightly. Post-2022 reshoring and inventory rebuilding have added some slack, but concentration in semiconductors, container shipping and settlement has not meaningfully reduced, and GPS jamming and spoofing incidents have increased. The strongest argument against a rising trend is that the 2020-22 experience produced real, if modest, corporate buffer-stock rebuilding.

severity_tiers.label: Shortage and inflation without famine
severity_tiers.description: A 2021-22-style disruption: goods shortages, freight rate spikes, inflation, and production stoppages in the industries with the thinnest inventories. Deaths are indirect and small — deferred medical care, delayed medicine shipments.

severity_tiers.label: Medicine, fuel and fertilizer chain break in importing countries
severity_tiers.description: Disruption long or deep enough that low-income net importers lose access to pharmaceuticals, refined fuel and fertilizer for one or more seasons. Excess mortality from treatable disease, from loss of cold-chain vaccines, and from the following season's yield shortfall.

severity_tiers.label: Simultaneous logistics, timing and settlement failure during another shock
severity_tiers.description: Timing (GNSS), settlement and physical logistics fail together — plausibly through a grid or cyber event — while a production shock is already underway. Trade cannot be priced, financed or moved. Every net-importing country is thrown onto domestic production with no way to buy the difference.

key_parameters.label: Median inventory held by manufacturers of critical components
key_parameters.effect: MULTIPLIER USE: inventory_days is the delay before a supply interruption becomes a production stoppage, and it therefore sets the minimum duration a disruption must reach to matter at all. Multiply the deaths_fraction of any trade- or transport-interrupting hazard by max(0, T_disruption_days - inventory_days) / T_disruption_days. At 5 days of inventory essentially every disruption longer than a week propagates fully; at 60 days most propagate not at all. THE CURRENT VALUE IS AN AUTHOR ESTIMATE, NOT A VERIFIED FIGURE — see uncertainty_notes.

key_parameters.label: Economic cost of a GPS outage
key_parameters.effect: "a GPS outage could potentially have an economic impact of $1 billion a day", rising to "as high as $45 billion" for a 30-day outage during planting season. MULTIPLIER USE: GNSS is a shared dependency of electricity grid timestamping, telecommunications synchronization, financial transaction timestamping, maritime navigation (with, per the study, no current backup) and precision agriculture. In a simulator, wire a GNSS failure as a simultaneous partial degradation of the grid, telecoms, shipping and agriculture nodes rather than as an independent hazard; this is the cleanest published example of a common-cause dependency in the Rinaldi sense, and it converts what would be four uncorrelated failures into one correlated one.

key_parameters.label: Share of global FX turnover settled through the single largest settlement utility
key_parameters.effect: CLS settles over 50 percent of global FX transactions, roughly USD 1.5 trillion daily, and provides multilateral netting that shrinks participants' funding requirements by an average of 96 percent. MULTIPLIER USE: the netting efficiency is exactly what makes an outage catastrophic — participants hold liquidity for the netted amount, not the gross, so a settlement interruption creates an instantaneous gross funding demand roughly 25 times the normal netted flow. In a simulator, treat a settlement outage as multiplying the effective liquidity requirement of the banking node by 1/(1-0.96) for its duration, and as a hard gate on cross-border food, fuel and medicine purchases — which is how it becomes a mortality parameter rather than merely a financial one.

key_parameters.label: Share of countries dependent on imports for staple calories
key_parameters.effect: 83-85 percent of countries have low or marginal food self-sufficiency. MULTIPLIER USE: this is the population weight that receives the full logistics-failure deaths_fraction; the self-sufficient remainder receives only the domestic-production component. It is the same knob as in the export-ban hazard and MUST be shared between them in a simulator rather than applied twice, or the model will double-count the same exposed population.

citations.claim: Economic dependency on GPS and the cost of an outage
citations.authors: RTI International for the U.S. National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST), as reported by the U.S. Office of Space Commerce
citations.venue: NIST / U.S. Department of Commerce, Office of Space Commerce
citations.exact_figure: "Though uncommon, a GPS outage could potentially have an economic impact of $1 billion a day." "If a 30-day outage occurred during critical planting seasons for farmers, the impact could be as high as $45 billion." "GPS generated $1.4 trillion in U.S. economic benefits since the system became available in the 1980s." Released 6 June 2019. A 30-day maritime outage was put at almost $10 billion "because there is currently no backup for GPS".

citations.claim: Concentration of FX settlement and the scale of netting
citations.authors: CLS Group
citations.venue: CLS Group, "Settlement Risk in the Global FX Market: How Much Remains?"
citations.exact_figure: CLS settles over 50% of global FX transactions, roughly USD 1.5 trillion daily; multilateral netting shrinks participants' funding requirements by an average of 96%; CLSSettlement covers 18 eligible currencies linked to their RTGS systems.

citations.claim: Complex supply chains as a source of systemic vulnerability in a global catastrophe, and the COVID demonstration
citations.authors: Juan B. García Martínez, Jeffray Behr, Joshua M. Pearce, David C. Denkenberger
citations.venue: ALLFED preprint, EarthArXiv (version 08/2024), "Resilient foods for preventing global famine"
citations.exact_figure: "It also depends on complex supply chains supported by a massive global infrastructure, which brings key benefits but also increases systemic vulnerability, such that a disruption in a given point could affect the entire system (Maynard 2015)." And: "The COVID-19 pandemic highlighted the fragility of food systems and the insufficient preparedness of global governments to handle the shocks to the food system and supply chains that would occur during a global catastrophe."

citations.claim: Import dependence of the country population exposed to a logistics failure
citations.authors: Michael J Puma, Satyajit Bose, So Young Chon, Benjamin I Cook
citations.venue: Environmental Research Letters 10(2) 024007
citations.exact_figure: "85% of countries have low or marginal food self-sufficiency"; "83% of countries for 2005-2009"

cascades_into: grain-export-ban-cascade: shipping, insurance and payment friction acts as a de facto export restriction even where no policy restriction exists

interdependent-infrastructure-cascade: GNSS is a common-cause dependency of grid timestamping, telecoms synchronization and settlement, so a timing failure is a correlated multi-network failure rather than an independent one
synthetic-nitrogen-dependence: fertilizer is bulky, seasonal and traded, and is among the first commodities to be crowded out of constrained freight capacity
hazards.uncertainty_notes: PROVENANCE WARNING, and the most important caveat in this hazard: the widely quoted figure that median semiconductor inventory fell from 40 days in 2019 to under 5 days in 2021 comes from the U.S. Department of Commerce's semiconductor supply-chain Request for Information results (January 2022). I attempted to fetch commerce.gov directly this session and received HTTP 403, so I could NOT verify it against the primary document; the inventory_days parameter's current value is therefore recorded as an author estimate anchored on that unverified figure and must be re-checked before compilation. The same applies, more weakly, to the CLS figures: the CLS PDF URL was returned by search with these figures but was not fetched directly, so the 50 percent share, USD 1.5 trillion daily and 96 percent netting reduction should be re-verified against the CLS document or a BIS Triennial Survey. The annual probability rests on n=2 clear historical episodes (2008-09 and 2020) in about 35 years, which is far too small a sample to support the stated range; I have widened the range accordingly but a critic would correctly say this is closer to an author estimate than an observed frequency. The GPS figure is a US-economy, economic-cost figure with no published mapping to mortality; the mapping in the effect field is mine. Finally, the tier-3 deaths_fraction of 0.08 is entirely an author estimate — no published work I retrieved assigns mortality to a combined logistics-timing-settlement failure.

hazards.name: Absence of deployed resilient-food capacity (the resilience knob, inverted)
hazards.one_line: Published resilient-food routes could in principle feed everyone through a sunlight collapse, but essentially none of them are built, so the capacity available on day one today is close to zero.
hazards.mechanism: This hazard is the resilience side of the packet stated as a hazard, because that is the form in which it multiplies. If sunlight or industrial agriculture fails, humanity has roughly six months of food stores and then needs a calorie source that does not depend on sunlit farmland. Several published routes exist on paper — seaweed, lignocellulosic sugar from repurposed paper mills and biorefineries, single-cell protein from methane, synthetic fats from paraffins, greenhouses, leaf protein concentrate, crop relocation — and the modelled totals are large enough to matter. The failure mode is not that the science is wrong; it is that none of it has been built, so the ramp starts at zero on the day it is needed, and the ramp must beat the six-month stock clock. Deaths are therefore famine deaths that occur in the gap between the stocks running out and the ramp reaching scale, and the size of that gap is entirely a function of pre-built capacity and pre-existing plans.

annual_probability.event_definition: a global catastrophic food shock (abrupt sunlight reduction or global catastrophic infrastructure loss) beginning in a year in which deployed resilient-food capacity remains below 1 percent of global calorie demand — that is, in today's state of preparation
annual_probability.trend: Falling very slowly. National preparedness reports for an abrupt sunlight reduction scenario now exist for Argentina and New Zealand, and the UN Secretary-General's 2021 Common Agenda called for managing existential risks, but no country has built pilot capacity. The conditional probability of being unprepared given a shock is therefore still close to 1, and this rate is essentially inherited from the underlying shock hazards rather than being independent.

severity_tiers.label: Shock met with full resilient-food deployment
severity_tiers.description: Rationing, redirection of crops away from livestock and biofuel, crop relocation, greenhouses and novel foods are all deployed on a pre-existing plan. The one worked national case study — Argentina under a 150 Tg soot abrupt sunlight reduction — moves from about 32 million people fed under rationing alone to about 305 million with the full ladder of interventions, against a national population of about 46 million.

severity_tiers.label: Partial deployment: trade holds, crops relocated, no novel foods
severity_tiers.description: International trade and coordination survive; crops are relocated to newly suitable latitudes and food is redirected from animal feed and biofuel to humans, but no industrial resilient-food capacity exists to build on. Substantial but incomplete famine.

severity_tiers.label: No deployment and trade collapse
severity_tiers.description: The shock arrives with zero pre-built capacity, and the export-ban and logistics cascades in this packet fire simultaneously, so even the interventions that would work in principle cannot be coordinated or financed. Stocks run out at six months and nothing replaces them.

key_parameters.label: Share of global calorie demand covered by pre-built resilient-food capacity
key_parameters.effect: THE MASTER MULTIPLIER OF THIS ENTIRE PACKET, and the one the user should expose first. Multiply the deaths_fraction of every sunlight-reduction hazard (nuclear winter, supervolcano, impact winter) and every infrastructure-loss hazard by (1 - min(1, deployed_fraction + ramp_achievable_within_stock_window)). At the current value of approximately zero this multiplier is 1 and the entire resilient-food literature buys nothing on day one — its value is purely optional, contingent on a ramp that has not been started. This is the honest reading of the ALLFED corpus: it is an argument that abrupt sunlight reduction is SURVIVABLE, not an argument that it will be survived.

key_parameters.label: Time to scale seaweed production to 45 percent of global food demand
key_parameters.effect: Modelled on Gracilaria tikvahiae forced by nuclear-winter climate simulations: growth actually INCREASES after a nuclear war because more ocean nutrients become available, allowing scale-up to "an equivalent of 45% of the global human food demand (spread among food, animal feed, and biofuels) in around 9-14 months, while only using a small fraction of the global ocean area" — enough to substitute 15 percent of human food, 10 percent of animal feed and 50 percent of global biofuel production. MULTIPLIER USE: with total_food_store_months = 6, a ramp of M months leaves max(0, M-6) months of unfed gap, so scale the sunlight-hazard deaths_fraction by roughly max(0, M-6)/M. At M=11 that leaves a ~45 percent residual; at M=6 it goes to zero. Pre-building even a small seed capacity is what moves M downward, which is why this and the deployed_fraction knob are coupled.

key_parameters.label: Global caloric requirement coverable by lignocellulosic sugar
key_parameters.effect: "converting the entire global production of roundwood and agricultural residues to sugars could produce an amount of calories equivalent to the entire global population's caloric requirement, at an estimated cost of $0.43-0.91 to provide a person's daily caloric requirement", obtained through rapid repurposing of paper mills and second-generation biorefineries. MULTIPLIER USE: this sets the CEILING on how far the deployed_fraction knob can be pushed, and the cost figure sets what it takes to get there. A simulator should treat this as a capacity ceiling of 1.0 reachable only with pre-existing repurposing plans; without them the repurposing itself takes an industrial mobilization that a global-catastrophic-infrastructure-loss scenario has by definition destroyed.

key_parameters.label: Global caloric requirement coverable by methane single-cell protein
key_parameters.effect: "Converting the entire global production of natural gas to food through single cell protein results in nearly 3 times the caloric requirement of the global population, or 9-15 times the protein requirement, with models indicating that fulfilling the global protein requirement using this technology could be done in a few years - at an estimated cost of $1.65-2.81 to provide a person's daily caloric requirement." MULTIPLIER USE: note the timescale mismatch that makes this knob nearly inert today — 'a few years' is far beyond the six-month stock window, so this route reduces deaths only in the second and third year of a multi-year sunlight reduction, not in the first. In a simulator it should reduce the TAIL of a nuclear-winter mortality curve, not its peak. It also fails entirely under infrastructure loss, since it needs a functioning gas industry and fermentation plant.

key_parameters.label: Global food stores available to bridge to any resilient food
key_parameters.effect: "there are only enough food stocks to feed the global population for around 6 months." MULTIPLIER USE: this is the gate that every ramp above must beat, and it is shared with the grain-reserve hazard — a simulator must use one value for both, not two. Any resilient food with a ramp longer than this contributes nothing to first-year mortality no matter how large its ultimate capacity. Raising it (through a strategic global reserve) and lowering ramp times are exact substitutes for one another in the model; raising it is by far the cheaper of the two today.

citations.claim: Resilient food capacities, costs, scale-up times, and the size of the global food buffer
citations.authors: Juan B. García Martínez, Jeffray Behr, Joshua M. Pearce, David C. Denkenberger
citations.venue: ALLFED preprint, EarthArXiv (version 08/2024), "Resilient foods for preventing global famine: a review of food supply interventions for global catastrophic food shocks including nuclear winter and infrastructure collapse"
citations.exact_figure: "converting the entire global production of roundwood and agricultural residues to sugars could produce an amount of calories equivalent to the entire global population's caloric requirement, at an estimated cost of $0.43-0.91 to provide a person's daily caloric requirement (Throup et al. 2022). Converting the entire global production of natural gas to food through single cell protein results in nearly 3 times the caloric requirement of the global population, or 9 - 15 times the protein requirement, with models indicating that fulfilling the global protein requirement using this technology could be done in a few years - at an estimated cost of $1.65-2.81 to provide a person's daily caloric requirement (Garcia Martinez et al. 2022). Paraffins derived from oil could be converted into synthetic fats to produce 8-17% of the global caloric requirements at an estimated cost of $0.74-2.71..." Also: "there are only enough food stocks to feed the global population for around 6 months (Denkenberger and Pearce 2014)"; "Models simulating plausible nuclear winter scenarios with varying degrees of severity estimate a loss of up to ~90% of global staple crop production in the worst year of the catastrophe (Xia et al. 2022)"; and Vitamin C is "already produced industrially at 140,000 tonnes/year, and lysine at 2.2 million tonnes/year". Figure 10 shows Argentina under a 150 Tg abrupt sunlight reduction going from about 32 million people fed under rationing to about 305 million with full intervention, against a population line at about 46 million.

citations.claim: Seaweed scale-up rate and fraction of global food demand after nuclear war
citations.authors: Florian Ulrich Jehn and colleagues (ALLFED)
citations.venue: Earth's Future 12(3), e2023EF003710 (AGU)
citations.exact_figure: "The simulated growth is high enough to allow a scale up to an equivalent of 45% of the global human food demand (spread among food, animal feed, and biofuels) in around 9-14 months, while only using a small fraction of the global ocean area" — enough to substitute 15% of human food, 10% of animal feed and 50% of global biofuel production; modelled with an empirical model of Gracilaria tikvahiae forced by nuclear winter climate simulations, in which seaweed growth increases after nuclear war because more ocean nutrients become available.

citations.claim: The size of the food buffer the resilient-food ramp must beat
citations.authors: FAO Markets and Trade Division (Cereal Supply and Demand Brief)
citations.venue: Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations
citations.exact_figure: World cereal stocks forecast at 947.2 million tonnes against world cereal utilization of 2 965 million tonnes in 2026/27, a stocks-to-use ratio of 31.6 percent — approximately 115 days of cereal consumption (brief dated 04/09/2026)

citations.claim: Concentration of the reserves that would actually be available to bridge to a resilient-food ramp
citations.authors: Adin Richards
citations.venue: Institute for Progress (IFP)
citations.exact_figure: China "currently possesses 69% of the corn, 60% of the rice, and 51% of the wheat stored worldwide"; the U.S. share of global reserves "declined from up to 40% in the 1980s to just above 5% today"

cascades_into: grain-reserve-buffer-thinness: the buffer and the ramp are the two halves of a single inequality, and the hazard is real only when ramp_months exceeds buffer_months
grain-export-ban-cascade: every resilient-food scale-up in this literature assumes maintained international trade and coordination, so an export-ban cascade removes most of the modelled benefit

synthetic-nitrogen-dependence: the industrial routes (lignocellulosic sugar, methane single-cell protein, synthetic fats) all fail in exactly the infrastructure-loss scenario in which fertilizer also fails, so the two hazards are strongly positively correlated rather than mutually offsetting
hazards.uncertainty_notes: THE SINGLE BIGGEST WEAKNESS IN THIS PACKET, and the one a serious critic should attack first: almost the entire resilient-food literature is produced by one small institutionally-interested group (ALLFED and its co-authors — Denkenberger, Pearce, Garcia Martinez, Jehn, Throup, Rivers), it is not independently replicated, and the key review I read is explicitly labelled 'a non-peer reviewed preprint submitted to EarthArXiv'. No published resilient-food analysis I found reports a terminal outcome, which is itself suspicious given the authorship concentration; I have set terminal=false on every tier to report the literature faithfully rather than to assert it. The scale-up figures are order-of-magnitude technical potentials, not deployment forecasts: they assume functioning industry, functioning international trade, functioning finance and rapid political coordination, all four of which are precisely what fails in a global catastrophic infrastructure loss scenario. The seaweed figures were obtained this session through a web-search result summary of the Earth's Future paper rather than a direct fetch of the article, so the 45 percent and 9-14 month numbers should be re-verified against the paper before compilation. The Argentina numbers are read off a bar chart in the review, so they are approximate to within perhaps 10 percent. The tier probabilities and deaths_fractions are ALL author estimates — no source assigns a probability to 'the world does or does not deploy resilient foods'. Finally, this hazard's annual probability is not a real independent rate: it is the rate of the underlying sunlight-reduction and infrastructure-loss shocks multiplied by a conditional probability of unpreparedness that is currently close to 1, so a simulator should implement it as a conditional modifier on those hazards rather than as a separate draw, or it will double-count.

hazards.name: Natural pandemic (zoonotic emergence of a novel human pathogen)
hazards.one_line: A pathogen crosses from an animal reservoir into humans, spreads globally, and kills a large fraction of the population before immunity, behaviour change and countermeasures halt it.
hazards.mechanism: A pathogen circulating in a wild or livestock reservoir acquires the capacity for sustained human-to-human transmission at a contact interface (bushmeat handling, live-animal markets, agricultural intensification at a forest edge). Jones et al. 2008 found 60.3% of 335 emerging-infectious-disease events 1940-2004 were zoonoses, of which 71.8% originated in wildlife. Unlike most global catastrophic risks, the proximate killer here is usually the pathogen itself rather than famine: in 1918 death came from primary viral pneumonia and secondary bacterial pneumonia within days of onset. The famine and infrastructure channel only dominates in the deep tail, where simultaneous absenteeism across food, power, water-treatment and logistics workforces, plus panic-driven trade and border closure, kill more than the infection does. The event terminates not because the pathogen is defeated but because susceptibles run out: transmission is throttled by depletion of the most-exposed and most-susceptible strata long before the population-average attack rate approaches 100%, which is the single most important reason a natural pandemic is a mass-casualty risk and not an extinction risk.

annual_probability.event_definition: Onset in a given year of a novel epidemic with intensity greater than or equal to that of the 1918-1920 'Spanish influenza', which Marani et al. quantify as i = 5.7 per mil per year (deaths / [global population x epidemic duration]). Historically this corresponds to roughly 20-100 million deaths over ~2-3 years. NOTE: this is probability (a) — that the EVENT occurs. It is NOT the probability of mass casualties given the event, and emphatically not the probability of extinction; see severity_tiers and uncertainty_notes.
annual_probability.trend: Rising. Marani et al. state that 'a tripling of the rate of disease emergence, an increase consistent with the recorded recent changes, implies an approximate tripling of the probability of extreme epidemics ... bringing, possibly over decadal time scales, the mean recurrence interval of a Spanish flu-like event down to 292 y (95% CI 243 to 360 y)' — i.e. annual probability rising from 1.14e-3 to ~3.4e-3. Independently, Meadows et al. 2023 measure high-consequence zoonotic spillover EVENTS increasing at 4.98%/yr (95% CI 3.22-6.76) and reported DEATHS at 8.7%/yr (95% CI 4.06-13.62) over 1963-2019, projecting 4x the spillover events and 12x the deaths in 2050 relative to 2020. Drivers: land-use change at forest margins, wildlife trade, and livestock density (livestock are now ~60% of mammalian biomass, Bar-On et al. 2018). Countervailing: genomic surveillance, mRNA platform speed and NPIs are not in the 1600-1945 fitting window and are not captured by the stationary intensity distribution.

severity_tiers.label: 1918-class
severity_tiers.description: A pandemic of roughly the 1918 influenza's realised intensity. Marani et al. adopt 32 million deaths as 'an accredited estimate' against a 1918 world population of 1.8 billion (~1.8%); the published range spans Spreeuwenberg et al. 2018 at 17.4 million (~0.97% of world population) to Johnson & Mueller's 50-100 million (2.7-5.4% per Our World in Data). Health systems are overwhelmed regionally; global industrial capacity is essentially unaffected within a year.

severity_tiers.label: Great-Dying-class regional annihilation
severity_tiers.description: A pathogen encounters one or more large immunologically naive or otherwise highly susceptible populations and kills a very large fraction of them while leaving the rest of the world near-intact. The historical exemplar is the post-1492 Americas: Koch et al. 2019 find European epidemics removed 90% (IQR 87-92%) of an indigenous population they reconstruct at 60.5 million (IQR 44.8-78.2 million) — roughly 54 million deaths, about 10% of the global population of the time, and enough to abandon 55.8 Mha of farmland and lower atmospheric CO2 by ~3.5 ppm. Note this required no prior exposure PLUS warfare and enslavement; even so, the residual 10% survived and the species was never in question.

severity_tiers.label: Civilization-stressing pandemic
severity_tiers.description: Attack rate and case fatality high enough, and duration long enough, that the proximate infectious mortality is compounded by failure of food distribution, power and water treatment. No historically observed event reaches this tier; it lies roughly 1-1.5 orders of magnitude beyond the Marani dataset's most intense observation and requires simultaneous high lethality and high transmissibility (see uncertainty_notes on the virulence-transmission trade-off). Industrial capacity is lost in some regions and rebuilt from surviving ones.

severity_tiers.label: Terminal
severity_tiers.description: Human extinction, or an unrecoverable collapse from which industrial civilisation never returns. Derived, not observed: Ord's Table 6.1 puts naturally arising pandemics at 1 in 10,000 existential catastrophe per century (~1e-6/yr); dividing by the 1.14e-3/yr event rate gives ~9e-4 conditional. This is ~333x lower than his engineered-pandemic estimate of 1 in 30 per century, and it sits about 10x below the 'likely' natural-extinction ceiling of 1 in 87,000 per year that Snyder-Beattie et al. 2019 derive from the survival of Homo sapiens for 200,000 years. A naive simulator that extrapolates the fat power-law tail without a susceptibility-heterogeneity term will land 50-500x above this figure.

key_parameters.label: Rate of novel-pathogen emergence, relative to present
key_parameters.effect: This is Marani et al.'s own explicit knob and the cleanest lever in the packet. The MEVD probability of an extreme epidemic scales close to linearly with it: at x1 the mean recurrence interval of a 1918-intensity event is 879 y (95% CI 730-1081); the paper computes that x3 gives 292 y (95% CI 243-360), i.e. T ~ 879/m and P_annual ~ 1.14e-3 x m. Lifetime probability follows P_life = 1 - (1 - m/T0)^100.

key_parameters.label: Annual growth in high-consequence zoonotic spillover events
key_parameters.effect: Measured by Meadows et al. 2023 over 75 spillover events in 24 countries, 1963-2019 (17,232 deaths), for filoviruses, SARS-CoV-1, Machupo and Nipah, excluding COVID-19 and influenza. Compounding: events(t) = events(2020) x (1+r)^(t-2020), giving 4x events by 2050 at r=4.98%. Deaths grow faster, at 8.7%/yr (95% CI 4.06-13.62), giving 12x deaths by 2050 — i.e. severity per event is rising too, not just count. This is the empirical driver that feeds emergence_rate_multiplier.

key_parameters.label: Power-law exponent of the epidemic-intensity tail
key_parameters.effect: Marani et al. fit a generalized Pareto distribution with shape xi = 1.40, scale sigma = 0.0113 per mil/yr and location mu = 0.001 per mil/yr, giving alpha = -0.71 for i > 3e-2 per mil/yr. Exceedance probability H(i) ~ i^alpha, so a 10x more intense epidemic is only 10^0.71 = 5.1x less likely. |alpha| < 1 means the distribution is fat-tailed and has no characteristic scale — this is the paper's central claim. WARNING for the simulator: extrapolating this relation naively to i = 250 per mil/yr (50% of humanity in 2 years) gives (250/5.7)^-0.71 = 0.068, hence ~7.8e-5/yr, and to i = 500 per mil/yr gives ~4.8e-5/yr. That is a ~0.5%-per-century extinction rate, which is ~50x Ord's figure and ~4x above Snyder-Beattie's 'likely' anthropic ceiling. Cap the tail or add a heterogeneity term.

key_parameters.label: Livestock share of total mammalian biomass
key_parameters.effect: Bar-On et al. 2018 give livestock ~0.1 Gt C, humans ~0.06 Gt C, wild mammals ~0.007 Gt C — livestock are ~60% of mammalian biomass and outweigh wild mammals ~14:1; domesticated poultry (~0.005 Gt C) outweigh wild birds (~0.002 Gt C) ~3:1. This is the amplification-host reservoir: it sets how large a bridging population sits between wildlife and humans. NO published dose-response function links this fraction to spillover rate, so treat it as a monotone driver of emergence_rate_multiplier with an assumed exponent, not as a calibrated coefficient.

key_parameters.label: Factor by which NPIs reduce deaths below the unconstrained counterfactual
key_parameters.effect: Marani et al. observe COVID-19 progressing at 2.5 million deaths/yr = 0.33 per mil/yr, whose MEVD recurrence is 129 y (95% CI 120-140). They then apply a factor of 8 from modelling of unconstrained spread, obtaining an unmitigated intensity of 2.63 per mil/yr with recurrence 523 y (95% CI 450-622) and a lifetime probability P_Life = 1 - (1 - 1/523)^100 = 0.17, rising to 0.44 under a tripled emergence rate. Direction matters: raising this knob makes the counterfactual event MORE intense and therefore RARER on the intensity axis, while raising realised deaths if NPIs fail.

Also: 'The fitted GPD is characterized by a power-law exponent alpha = -0.71 approximately for i > 3 x 10^-2 per mil/year'; shape xi = 1.40, scale sigma = 0.0113 per mil/yr, location mu = 0.001 per mil/yr, P(i <= mu) = 0.62; dataset 1600-1945, 395 events, 182 with known occurrence, duration and deaths. COVID-19: unmitigated intensity 2.63 per mil/yr, 'an average recurrence time of 523 y (95% CI 450 to 622 y)', 'P_Life = 1 - (1 - 1/523)^100 = 0.17', tripled: 0.44.

All three are superseded by the 2023 correction, which states the code 'erroneously computed the number of epidemics in one year by summing the number of events in two subsequent years ... resulting in an inflated number of events/year and, as a consequence, in larger probabilities of occurrence and lower mean recurrence intervals.'

citations.claim: Columbian-exchange die-off: the largest pathogen-driven population collapse in the record, and its limits.
citations.authors: Alexander Koch, Chris Brierley, Mark M. Maslin, Simon L. Lewis
citations.venue: Quaternary Science Reviews 207:13-36, doi:10.1016/j.quascirev.2018.12.004

European epidemics removed 90% (IQR 87-92%) of the indigenous population over the next century. This resulted in secondary succession of 55.8 Mha (IQR 39.0-78.4 Mha) of abandoned land, sequestering 7.4 Pg C (IQR 4.9-10.8 Pg C), equivalent to a decline in atmospheric CO2 of 3.5 ppm (IQR 2.3-5.1 ppm CO2).'

citations.claim: Spatial heterogeneity of mortality even in the most lethal pandemic in European history — the empirical core of the anti-extinction argument.
citations.authors: Adam Izdebski, Piotr Guzowski, Radoslaw Poniat, et al. (55 authors)
citations.exact_figure: 'We collected pollen data on landscape change from 261 radiocarbon-dated coring sites (lakes and wetlands) located across 19 modern-day European countries ... to evaluate whether the changes we see in the landscape at the time of the Black Death agree with the hypothesis that a large portion of the population, upwards of half, died within a few years in the 21 historical regions we studied. While we can confirm that the Black Death had a devastating impact in some regions, we found that it had negligible or no impact in others.' Sharp agricultural decline in Scandinavia, France, western Germany, Greece and central Italy; 'continuity and uninterrupted agricultural growth in central and eastern Europe, and several regions of western Europe, particularly in Ireland and Iberia'.

citations.claim: Upper bound on the annual probability of human extinction from all natural causes — the hardest constraint on the terminal tier.
citations.authors: Andrew E. Snyder-Beattie, Toby Ord, Michael B. Bonsall
citations.exact_figure: 'Using only the information that Homo sapiens has existed at least 200,000 years, we conclude that the probability that humanity goes extinct from natural causes in any given year is almost guaranteed to be less than one in 14,000, and likely to be less than one in 87,000. Using the longer track record of survival for our entire genus Homo produces even tighter bounds, with an annual probability of natural extinction likely below one in 870,000.' The authors add: 'No similar guarantee can be made for risks that our ancestors did not face, such as anthropogenic climate change or nuclear/biological warfare.'

citations.claim: Expert-elicitation split between natural and engineered pandemic existential risk.
citations.authors: Toby Ord, The Precipice (2020), Table 6.1 — retrieved this session via a third-party reproduction of the table, not from the book itself
citations.venue: Bloomsbury (book); table reproduced in a post on the Effective Altruism Forum

Ord states these give 'the right order of magnitude' and may be off by a factor of 3 either way.

citations.claim: 1918 influenza death toll as a fraction of world population, across the competing estimates.

citations.venue: American Journal of Epidemiology 187(12):2561-2567

The authors conclude that 'simulations of total number of deaths being greater than 25 million are not realistic based on the underlying mortality rates'. This revises Johnson & Mueller's (2002) 50-100 million downward.

citations.claim: Denominator for the 1918 death fraction and the spread across published estimates.

citations.exact_figure: 335 EID events analysed, 1940-2004. 'EID events are dominated by zoonoses (60.3% of EIDs): the majority of these (71.8%) originate in wildlife ... and are increasing significantly over time.' 54.3% of events were caused by bacteria or rickettsia. Emergence is 'driven largely by socio-economic, environmental and ecological factors'.
