citations.claim: Why an extremely lethal AND extremely transmissible pathogen is evolutionarily disfavoured — and why the constraint is weaker than usually asserted.
citations.authors: Miguel A. Acevedo, Forrest P. Dilleuth, Andrew J. Flick, Matthew J. Faldyn, Bret D. Elderd
citations.exact_figure: Meta-analysis of 29 empirical studies, selected after reviewing over 6000 published papers, testing the four core trade-off relationships. 'We found strong support for an increasing relationship between replication and virulence, and replication and transmission. Yet, it is still uncertain if these relationships generally decelerate due to high within-study variability. There was insufficient data to quantitatively test the other two core relationships predicted by the theory. Overall, the results suggest that the current empirical evidence provides partial support for the trade-off hypothesis, but more work remains to be done.' Mechanism: 'increasing within-host replication rate increases mortality rates, which ultimately translates into a shorter infectious period at the population level, resulting in a deceleration in transmission rate.'

citations.claim: Black Death mortality as a fraction of Europe's population — the high-end scholarly estimate.
citations.authors: Ole J. Benedictow (2021 estimate, as reported by Medievalists.net), with earlier estimates from Philip Ziegler (1969) and John Aberth
citations.venue: Medievalists.net, reporting Benedictow, The Complete History of the Black Death (2021)
citations.exact_figure: Benedictow (2021): a 65% mortality rate across Europe; 'roughly 52 million died by or in connection with the Black Death' from a pre-plague European population of approximately 80 million. Ziegler (1969): England 34-45% mortality, 'one European in three died' as plausible but unprovable. Aberth: approximately half. Contrast with Izdebski et al. 2022, whose 261-site pollen record finds negligible impact in several of 21 regions.

hazards.uncertainty_notes:
THE CORRECTION TRAP. Marani et al. issued a correction in March 2023 (PNAS 120(12):e2302169120): their code 'erroneously computed the number of epidemics in one year by summing the number of events in two subsequent years', inflating events/year. The famous headline numbers — '2% per year for a COVID-like pandemic', '0.3-1.9% per year for a 1918-like event', '400-year mean recurrence', '38% lifetime probability' — are the WITHDRAWN pre-correction values, and they still dominate secondary coverage and at least one search engine's summary of the correction itself, which reported the direction backwards. The post-correction values used here (0.11-0.89%, 879 y, P_Life = 0.17) are taken from the republished PDF, downloaded 18 October 2023, which is internally consistent (Fig. 2A shows 1918 at p ~ 0.55%). Two residual worries: (i) I could not retrieve the correction notice's own text — pnas.org, PubMed and Europe PMC all refused — so the direction is established by triangulation between the corrected PDF and the August 2021 press release rather than by reading the correction; (ii) the Significance statement in the corrected PDF still reads 'probability of experiencing it in one's lifetime currently about 38%' while the Discussion of the same PDF computes 0.17. I believe the Significance box was not re-typeset. Do not use 38%.

WHERE A NAIVE SIMULATOR GETS THIS WRONG. The Marani GPD has |alpha| = 0.71 < 1, i.e. no characteristic scale. Extrapolating it to extinction intensities is arithmetically trivial and badly wrong. My own calculation (author-estimate, NOT Marani's — they never extrapolate this far and explicitly restrict the MEVD to intensities above the location parameter): an event killing 50% of humanity in two years is i = 250 per mil/yr, giving (250/5.7)^-0.71 = 0.068 and ~7.8e-5/yr; 100% gives ~4.8e-5/yr, i.e. ~0.5% per century. That is ~50x Ord's 1-in-10,000-per-century and ~4x above Snyder-Beattie's 'likely' natural-extinction ceiling of 1 in 87,000 per year, though still under their near-certain 1-in-14,000 bound. Three physical reasons the extrapolation fails: (1) HETEROGENEITY OF SUSCEPTIBILITY AND EXPOSURE. Transmission burns through high-contact, high-susceptibility strata first, so the effective herd-immunity threshold falls well below the homogeneous-mixing 1 - 1/R0. Izdebski et al.'s 261-site pollen record shows this at continental scale for the deadliest pandemic on record: devastating in Scandinavia, France, western Germany, Greece and central Italy; negligible in Ireland, Iberia and much of central and eastern Europe. Even Koch et al.'s Great Dying — 90% (IQR 87-92%) of an entire hemisphere's naive population, compounded by warfare and enslavement — left 10% alive. (2) ISOLATED POPULATIONS. Extinction requires reaching every human group, including uncontacted peoples, remote island and Arctic communities, submarine crews and research stations. I found no published quantification of this residual in this session, so it is asserted qualitatively and should be flagged for a modeller who wants a number. (3) BEHAVIOURAL RESPONSE SCALES WITH MORTALITY and is entirely absent from a stationary intensity distribution fitted to 1600-1945.

LETHAL *AND* TRANSMISSIBLE. The virulence-transmission trade-off (Anderson & May 1982) predicts an intermediate optimum: faster within-host replication raises transmission but shortens the infectious period. Acevedo et al.'s meta-analysis (29 studies from >6000 screened) finds strong support for replication->virulence and replication->transmission, but says it 'is still uncertain if these relationships generally decelerate', and had insufficient data for the other two core relationships — i.e. the trade-off is real but only 'partial' support, and it is a soft constraint, not a ceiling. It weakens or vanishes where transmission is pre-symptomatic (SARS-CoV-2), environmental/durable (smallpox, anthrax), vector-borne (the vector, not the host, does the moving), or where the human is a dead-end host and virulence is under no selection at all in humans (rabies ~100% CFR, Nipah, H5N1). So 'disfavoured but not impossible' is the correct framing: 1918 itself combined ~R0 of 2 with a case fatality far above seasonal flu. I wanted to quote WHO's cumulative H5N1 human case and death counts as the standing example of extreme lethality without transmissibility, but every WHO and CDC URL I tried returned 404 or empty; I have therefore NOT reported an H5N1 case-fatality figure rather than recall one from memory.

OTHER GAPS. (a) The Marani dataset stops at 1945 for the intensity fit, deliberately excluding the antibiotic/vaccine era; a critic would argue the resulting distribution overstates modern risk for bacterial agents and understates it for a fast respiratory virus in an air-travel network. (b) The Black Death 'fraction of Europe' figure is genuinely contested — Benedictow's 65% / 52 million of 80 million versus Ziegler's one-in-three versus Izdebski's regionally-null findings — and my Benedictow citation is a reputable secondary reporting his 2021 book, not the book. (c) The severity-tier conditional probabilities are author-estimates constrained at the top by Ord and Snyder-Beattie and at the bottom by the 1918/Great-Dying record; the two middle tiers have no direct empirical anchor. (d) I could not retrieve the 2023 Existential Risk Persuasion Tournament report — the PDF at forecastingresearch.org exceeds the fetch size limit — so no superforecaster-versus-domain-expert split on natural-pathogen catastrophe or extinction is included, and its absence should be treated as a real hole in the elicitation basis. (e) Chytridiomycosis in amphibians is the standard counterexample that a pathogen CAN drive species extinct at scale; I did not retrieve Scheele et al. 2019 this session and so state no figure for it.
cascades_into: antimicrobial-resistance: an influenza-type pandemic drives mass empirical antibiotic use for secondary bacterial pneumonia, accelerating resistance selection
systemic-supply-chain-failure: simultaneous absenteeism across food, power, water treatment and logistics, plus panic-driven export bans
conflict: state fragility, contested borders and scapegoating under mass mortality
engineered-pandemic: a natural pandemic supplies the published sequence, the demonstrated fitness landscape and the political incentive for deliberate misuse

hazards.name: Antimicrobial resistance (slow-burn erosion of the antibiotic era)
hazards.one_line: Bacteria accumulate resistance faster than new antimicrobials arrive, so ordinary infections and the routine surgery that depends on prophylaxis become progressively lethal again.
hazards.mechanism: Antimicrobial use in humans and in agriculture selects for resistant lineages; horizontal gene transfer spreads resistance determinants across species and continents faster than vertical evolution alone would. The proximate killer is not exotic: it is ordinary bacterial infection reverting to its pre-1940 case fatality. GRAM found lower respiratory infections alone accounted for more than 1.5 million deaths associated with resistance in 2019, the single most burdensome syndrome, with bloodstream and intra-abdominal infections next. Six organisms — E. coli, S. aureus, K. pneumoniae, S. pneumoniae, A. baumannii, P. aeruginosa — carry most of the burden. The second, larger channel is indirect and does not appear in the death counts at all: caesarean section, gut surgery, joint replacement, transplantation and cytotoxic chemotherapy are all safe only because perioperative prophylaxis works, so their risk-benefit inverts as resistance rises. Unlike a pandemic this hazard has no onset date and no peak; it is a monotone drift with a rising floor, which is why it must be modelled as a certainty with a magnitude rather than as an event with a probability.

annual_probability.event_definition: A calendar year in which bacterial AMR is the DIRECT cause of at least 1 million deaths worldwide. This is already the observed state and has been since at least 1990 (GRAM: 1.06 million in 1990, 1.27 million in 2019, 1.14 million in 2021), so the event probability is 1.0 by construction. This is deliberate: AMR is a slow-burn hazard and the probability field carries no information for it. All of the modelling content sits in severity_tiers and key_parameters. Do NOT read this 1.0 as 'AMR is a certain catastrophe' — it means 'AMR is a certain ongoing burden whose magnitude is the uncertain quantity'.
annual_probability.trend: Rising in aggregate but sharply divergent by age. GRAM 2024 finds deaths directly due to AMR among children under five FELL by ~50% between 1990 and 2021 (vaccination, water and sanitation, and paediatric infection control), while deaths among people aged 70 or older ROSE by more than 80% (population ageing, more invasive procedures, more hospital exposure). Forecast: 1.91 million direct deaths annually by 2050, a ~67.5% increase on 2021, with 8.22 million associated. The threshold question for a simulator is whether the O'Neill 10-million-per-year trajectory or the GRAM 1.91-million trajectory is right; they differ by a factor of five and were produced by scenario modelling versus systematic burden estimation respectively.

severity_tiers.label: Current burden (observed)
severity_tiers.description: The 2021 GRAM estimate: 1.14 million deaths directly attributable to bacterial AMR and 4.71 million associated, per year. Over a decade against a world population of ~8.0 billion, associated deaths are ~47 million, or ~0.59%. No loss of industrial capacity; the cost is chronic and absorbed. MRSA alone caused more than 100,000 attributable deaths in 2019.

severity_tiers.label: GRAM 2050 trajectory
severity_tiers.description: The GBD-based forecast: 1.91 million direct and 8.22 million associated deaths per year by 2050; cumulatively more than 39 million direct and 169 million associated deaths between 2025 and 2050. Against a projected ~9.7 billion, a decade at that rate is ~0.85% of world population. Burden concentrates in the over-70s and in low- and middle-income countries. Still not a step change in civilisational capacity.

severity_tiers.label: O'Neill high scenario / post-antibiotic transition
severity_tiers.description: The O'Neill Review's headline: '10 million lives a year and a cumulative 100 trillion USD of economic output are at risk' by 2050 if resistance is not slowed — about five times the GRAM forecast for the same year. The distinguishing feature is not the death count but the withdrawal of procedures: O'Neill notes that if antibiotics lose effectiveness, 'key medical procedures, such as gut surgery, caesarean sections, joint replacements, and treatments that depress the immune system, such as chemotherapy for cancer, could become too dangerous to perform'. Modern surgical and oncological medicine partially unwinds.

severity_tiers.label: Pan-resistant tail
severity_tiers.description: Simultaneous loss of last-line agents (carbapenems, then colistin — O'Neill flags 'the highly disturbing discovery of transferable colistin resistance, reported in late 2015') across the major Gram-negative pathogens, with no replacement class. Author-estimate: no published projection covers this scenario quantitatively. Mortality is dominated by hospital-acquired infection, obstetric sepsis and the withdrawal of immunosuppressive therapy. Recovery requires a new antimicrobial class or a mature phage/monoclonal alternative, not a return to the status quo.

key_parameters.label: Deaths per year directly attributable to bacterial AMR
key_parameters.effect: GRAM: 1.06 million (1990) -> 1.27 million (2019) -> 1.14 million (2021) -> 1.91 million forecast (2050), a 67.5% rise on 2021. Roughly flat historically and driven forward almost entirely by population ageing, so a first-order model can write attributable_deaths(t) proportional to the over-70 population share. The O'Neill 10-million figure sits at the far end of this range and is a scenario, not a burden estimate.

key_parameters.label: Deaths per year associated with bacterial AMR
key_parameters.effect: GRAM: 4.95 million (95% UI 3.62-6.57) in 2019; 4.71 million in 2021; 8.22 million forecast for 2050. The associated/attributable ratio is ~4.1 and is the right multiplier for converting a counterfactual-free burden into a total-burden figure. Use associated, not attributable, when the model's death accounting is by syndrome rather than by counterfactual.

key_parameters.label: Share of medically important antibiotics sold for use in animals
key_parameters.effect: O'Neill: 'In the US, for example, of the antibiotics defined as medically important for humans by the US Food and Drug Administration (FDA), over 70 percent (by weight) are sold for use in animals.' This is the largest single reducible selection pressure and the review's recommendation is 10-year national reduction targets from 2018. No published elasticity links a percentage cut here to a percentage change in human resistance prevalence, so treat it as a monotone driver with an assumed coefficient rather than a calibrated one.

key_parameters.label: Change in AMR deaths among people aged 70+, 1990-2021
key_parameters.effect: GRAM 2024: over-70 AMR deaths rose by more than 80% while under-five AMR deaths fell by ~50% over the same period, and over-70 deaths are projected to more than double again by 2050. This is the dominant term in the forecast: AMR burden is tracking the demographic transition, not resistance prevalence alone. A model that scales AMR mortality by resistance rates without an age structure will get the 2050 number badly wrong.

key_parameters.label: Market-entry reward per successful new antibiotic
key_parameters.effect: O'Neill proposes 'market entry rewards, of around one billion USD each' to break the broken-market problem (new antibiotics are held in reserve, so revenue is inversely related to good stewardship), against a stated 100 trillion USD cost of inaction by 2050 — a ratio the review argues makes the interventions 'extremely good value for money on a relative basis'. Also in the package: a global awareness campaign at 40-100 million USD/year, and the UK Fleming Fund at 375 million USD.

citations.claim: Global deaths attributable to and associated with bacterial antimicrobial resistance in 2019.
citations.authors: Antimicrobial Resistance Collaborators (Christopher J. L. Murray et al., 140 investigators)
citations.exact_figure: 'On the basis of our predictive statistical models, there were an estimated 4.95 million (3.62-6.57) deaths associated with bacterial AMR in 2019, including 1.27 million (95% UI 0.911-1.71) deaths attributable to bacterial AMR.' Six leading pathogens (E. coli, S. aureus, K. pneumoniae, S. pneumoniae, A. baumannii, P. aeruginosa) caused 929,000 attributable and 3.57 million associated deaths. 'Lower respiratory infections accounted for more than 1.5 million deaths associated with resistance in 2019, making it the most burdensome infectious syndrome.' 'One pathogen-drug combination, meticillin-resistant S aureus, caused more than 100,000 deaths attributable to AMR in 2019.' Regional attributable rates per 100,000: Australasia 6.5 (4.3-9.4), western sub-Saharan Africa 27.3 (20.9-35.3). Built from 471 million individual records or isolates, 23 pathogens, 88 pathogen-drug combinations.

citations.claim: AMR burden 1990-2021 and forecasts to 2050, including the divergent age trend.
citations.authors: GBD 2021 Antimicrobial Resistance Collaborators (reported via The Lancet's press release)
citations.venue: The Lancet 404(10459):1199-1226; figures retrieved this session from the journal's EurekAlert! press release 1057804
citations.exact_figure: 1.14 million deaths directly due to AMR in 2021, associated with a broader 4.71 million deaths; 1.06 million direct in 1990. Projected 1.91 million annual deaths directly due to AMR by 2050, with a role in a broader 8.22 million. 'Between 2025 and 2050 it is estimated AMR will lead directly to more than 39 million deaths and be associated with a broader 169 million deaths.' AMR deaths among children under five declined by 50%; those among people aged 70 or older increased by more than 80%. NOTE: the press release does not carry the 95% uncertainty intervals; the paper itself was behind a 403 and the UIs are therefore NOT reported here.

citations.claim: The O'Neill Review's 2050 projection and its economic figure — the high scenario in the tier table.
citations.authors: Jim O'Neill (chair), Review on Antimicrobial Resistance, commissioned by the UK Government and the Wellcome Trust
citations.venue: Tackling Drug-Resistant Infections Globally: Final Report and Recommendations, May 2016
citations.exact_figure: 'We estimate that by 2050, 10 million lives a year and a cumulative 100 trillion USD of economic output are at risk due to the rise of drug-resistant infections if we do not find proactive solutions now to slow down the rise of drug resistance. Even today, 700,000 people die of resistant infections every year.' Also, from the foreword: 'today's already large 700,000 deaths every year would become an extremely disturbing 10 million every year, more people than currently die from cancer'; 'The cost in terms of lost global production between now and 2050 would be an enormous 100 trillion USD if we do not take action.' Agriculture: 'in the US, for example, of the antibiotics defined as medically important for humans by the US Food and Drug Administration (FDA), over 70 percent (by weight) are sold for use in animals.' Proposed market entry rewards 'of around one billion USD each'.

hazards.uncertainty_notes:
THE FACTOR-OF-FIVE DISAGREEMENT IS THE MAIN FINDING. O'Neill (2016) projects 10 million AMR deaths per year by 2050; GRAM/GBD (2024) projects 1.91 million directly attributable and 8.22 million associated for the same year. These are not the same quantity and conflating them is the standard error in this literature. O'Neill's 10 million is a KPMG/RAND scenario extrapolation commissioned for advocacy, is not a burden estimate, and has been criticised for extrapolating resistance-rate growth without an age or syndrome structure; O'Neill himself writes in the foreword 'it is of course possible that our estimates may turn out to be too large'. GRAM's figures are systematic-analysis estimates with explicit counterfactuals. If a simulator wants one number, use GRAM's 8.22 million associated for 2050 and treat O'Neill's 10 million as the upper scenario — which is roughly what I have done in the tier table. Also note O'Neill's 'today's 700,000 deaths' figure predates GRAM entirely and is inconsistent with GRAM's own 1990 and 2019 back-estimates; it should not be used as a baseline.

ATTRIBUTABLE VERSUS ASSOCIATED. GRAM's two figures answer two different counterfactual questions — 'if the infection had been drug-susceptible' (attributable) versus 'if there had been no infection at all' (associated) — and the ratio is ~4.1. Reporting the associated figure as 'deaths from AMR' overstates by that factor; reporting the attributable figure as the total burden understates the health-system load. A simulator should carry both.

MISSING UNCERTAINTY INTERVALS. I have the 2019 GRAM figures with their full 95% UIs (4.95 million, 3.62-6.57; 1.27 million, 0.911-1.71) because PubMed Central served the paper. I do NOT have UIs for the 2021 figures or the 2050 forecasts: thelancet.com returned 403 and I fell back to the journal's own press release. Those forecast numbers should be treated as point estimates with unquantified spread, and a serious critic would attack any model that propagates them without one. The 39-million and 169-million cumulative figures in particular compound 25 years of an unstated-variance forecast.

WHAT A CRITIC WOULD ATTACK. (a) AMR is not an event, so the annual_probability field is set to 1.0 by construction; anyone summing this packet's annual probabilities across hazards will produce nonsense unless AMR is handled as a separate rate-of-loss term. (b) None of the tiers is terminal and none should be: AMR removes a therapeutic capability, it does not remove the reproductive base of the species, and pre-1940 humanity lived and grew with no antibiotics at all. Any model that produces an AMR extinction branch has a bug. (c) The pan-resistant tail tier's deaths_fraction of 0.03 is an author-estimate with no published projection behind it — I found none — and is the weakest number in this hazard. (d) The indirect burden (surgery, obstetrics, chemotherapy, transplantation withdrawn as prophylaxis fails) is the mechanism everyone cites and nobody has quantified globally; it is entirely absent from the GRAM death counts, which means the GRAM figures are a floor on total health impact, not a total. (e) Agricultural use: the '70 percent by weight' figure is US-specific and from 2016; I did not find a current global figure this session and it should not be applied worldwide without one.
cascades_into: natural-pandemic: loss of effective antibiotics raises the case-fatality ratio of any respiratory pandemic through untreatable secondary bacterial pneumonia — the mechanism that did most of the killing in 1918
systemic-healthcare-capacity-loss: withdrawal of surgery, obstetrics and chemotherapy that depend on working prophylaxis, a burden invisible in the AMR death counts

hazards.name: False-vacuum decay (electroweak vacuum metastability)
hazards.one_line: The measured Higgs and top masses place the Standard Model vacuum in a metastable state whose calculated decay lifetime is about 10^139 years, so spontaneous decay before the Sun dies is negligible and no collider can trigger it.
hazards.mechanism: The Standard Model Higgs quartic coupling lambda runs negative above an instability scale of roughly 10^10-10^11 GeV, so the electroweak vacuum we inhabit is not the global minimum of the Higgs potential but a metastable local one. Decay proceeds by quantum tunnelling: a bubble of true vacuum nucleates somewhere in spacetime and its wall then expands outward at essentially the speed of light. Inside the bubble the Higgs vacuum expectation value, and hence every particle mass and every nuclear binding energy, takes different values; atoms, nuclei and chemistry do not exist there. There is no precursor, no warning and no defence: the wall arrives at the same moment as the light announcing it. Nothing dies of famine here, which makes this the one hazard on this list whose kill mechanism is not starvation. Critically, the rate is set by fundamental parameters and is not raised by human activity — the empirical cosmic-ray bound (below) closes the accelerator route completely.

annual_probability.event_definition: spontaneous nucleation of a true-vacuum bubble inside our past light-cone, given Standard Model metastability; reciprocal of the Andreassen-Frost-Schwartz (2018) computed universe lifetime of 10^139 yr
annual_probability.trend: Flat in rate per unit four-volume. The nucleation rate depends only on the Higgs quartic coupling's running, which does not change. Human activity does not move it: the LSAG cosmic-ray argument shows Nature has already run ~10^31 LHC-equivalent programmes without producing a bubble. The one thing that could move the estimate is a shift in the measured top-quark pole mass, which is the dominant uncertainty.

severity_tiers.label: Bubble within causal reach
severity_tiers.description: A true-vacuum bubble nucleates inside the region from which light can still reach Earth. The wall sweeps through at ~c. All structure inside — atoms, nuclei, the Earth, any observers — ceases to exist in the transition. No survivors, no recovery, no possibility of preparation.

severity_tiers.label: Bubble beyond the cosmological event horizon
severity_tiers.description: In a dark-energy-dominated universe, regions beyond our cosmological event horizon are receding faster than a light-speed bubble wall can close on us. A nucleation event there never reaches Earth. This is the only branch in which a vacuum-decay event occurs and nobody dies.

key_parameters.label: Top quark pole mass
key_parameters.effect: The single dominant knob. Buttazzo et al. (2013) Eq. 64: absolute stability requires M_h > 129.6 GeV + 2.0*(M_t - 173.34 GeV) - 0.5 GeV*(alpha_3(M_Z)-0.1184)/0.0007, +/- 0.3 GeV. With M_h = 125.15 GeV, stability needs M_t below about 171.2 GeV. Lower M_t by ~2 GeV and the vacuum becomes absolutely stable and the hazard rate goes to exactly zero; raise it and the lifetime falls steeply (roughly exponentially in the bounce action S = 8*pi^2/(3*|lambda(Lambda_B)|)).

key_parameters.label: Higgs boson pole mass
key_parameters.effect: Measured to 125.15 +/- 0.24 GeV. Enters the stability condition linearly on the left-hand side of Eq. 64. The measured value sits about 4 GeV below the stability boundary — near-critical, which is why metastability is preferred at 99.3% CL rather than being decisively established.

key_parameters.label: Strong coupling at the Z pole
key_parameters.effect: Shifts the stability boundary by -0.5 GeV per 0.0007 in alpha_3(M_Z) (Buttazzo Eq. 64). Sub-dominant to M_t. Andreassen et al. note that ruling out absolute stability at 3 sigma would require reducing the alpha_s uncertainty below 0.00025.

key_parameters.label: Collider centre-of-mass energy
key_parameters.effect: ZERO effect on the rate, and this is the packet's most important null result. Cosmic-ray protons above 10^17 eV striking a fixed target exceed LHC centre-of-mass energy; over 3 x 10^22 such rays have hit Earth's surface since its formation. Nature has therefore already conducted ~10^5 LHC programmes on Earth, ~10^9 on the Sun, and ~10^31 in the visible Universe, and continues at ~3 x 10^13 complete LHC experiments per second. Any bubble producible at a collider would have been produced billions of years ago and would already have consumed large parts of the visible Universe. The continued existence of the Universe is the measurement. In a simulator this slider must be wired to nothing.

citations.claim: Absolute stability of the Standard Model Higgs potential is excluded at high confidence for the measured Higgs mass; the vacuum is metastable.
citations.authors: G. Degrassi, S. Di Vita, J. Elias-Miro, J. R. Espinosa, G. F. Giudice, G. Isidori, A. Strumia
citations.venue: Journal of High Energy Physics (arXiv:1205.6497)
citations.exact_figure: "absolute stability of the Higgs potential is excluded at 98% C.L. for Mh < 126 GeV"; theoretical uncertainty on the critical Mh for vacuum stability reduced to 1 GeV

citations.claim: The stability condition in terms of Higgs and top pole masses, and the confidence level for metastability.
citations.authors: D. Buttazzo, G. Degrassi, P. P. Giardino, G. F. Giudice, F. Sala, A. Salvio, A. Strumia
citations.venue: Journal of High Energy Physics (arXiv:1307.3536), 'Investigating the near-criticality of the Higgs boson'
citations.exact_figure: Eq. (64): "M_h > 129.6 GeV + 2.0(M_t - 173.34 GeV) - 0.5 GeV * (alpha_3(M_Z) - 0.1184)/0.0007 +/- 0.3 GeV"; measured "M_h = 125.15 +/- 0.24 GeV"; "metastability is now preferred at 99.3% CL"; "the SM vacuum is likely to survive for times that are enormously longer than any significant astrophysical age"

citations.claim: The complete computed lifetime of the metastable Standard Model vacuum.
citations.authors: A. Andreassen, W. Frost, M. D. Schwartz
citations.venue: Physical Review D 97, 056006 (arXiv:1707.08124), 'Scale-invariant instantons and the complete lifetime of the standard model'
citations.exact_figure: "the first complete calculation of the lifetime of our universe: 10^139 years"; "With 95% confidence, we expect our universe to last more than 10^58 years"

citations.claim: Cosmic-ray collisions empirically exclude collider-triggered vacuum-bubble production.
citations.authors: J. Ellis, G. Giudice, M. Mangano, I. Tkachev, U. Wiedemann (LHC Safety Assessment Group)
citations.venue: Journal of Physics G: Nuclear and Particle Physics 35 (2008) 115004, 'Review of the safety of LHC collisions'
citations.exact_figure: "These bubbles of new vacuum would already have expanded to consume large parts of the visible Universe several billion years ago. The continued existence of the Universe means that such vacuum bubbles are not produced in cosmic-ray collisions, and hence the LHC will also not produce any vacuum bubbles." Also: "Nature has already completed about 10^31 LHC experimental programmes since the beginning of the Universe" and "each second, the Universe continues to repeat about 3 x 10^13 complete LHC experiments"

hazards.uncertainty_notes: Three separate things are routinely conflated here and must be kept apart. (a) P(the vacuum is metastable at all): metastability is preferred at 99.3% CL (Buttazzo 2013), absolute stability excluded at 98% CL (Degrassi 2012) — so there is roughly a 0.7-2% chance the whole hazard has probability exactly zero. That is why the 'low' bound is 0, not a small number. (b) P(spontaneous decay per year): 10^-139, with a 95% floor on the lifetime of 10^58 yr giving the 'high' bound of 10^-58. (c) P(a human experiment triggers it): empirically zero, and the cosmic-ray argument is genuinely strong, not a reassurance — it is a measurement over 3 x 10^22 super-LHC-energy events on Earth alone. A serious critic would attack on three fronts. First, the dominant uncertainty is the top-quark pole mass, and the relation between the Monte-Carlo top mass reported by experiments and the pole mass entering these calculations carries an irreducible ~0.5 GeV ambiguity; Andreassen et al. note that 3-sigma exclusion of stability needs the pole-mass uncertainty below 250 MeV, which we do not have. Second, the entire calculation assumes no new physics between the electroweak and Planck scales; almost any beyond-SM sector changes the running of lambda and can render the vacuum stable or catastrophically unstable. Third, the cosmic-ray argument bounds bubble nucleation in collisions of a fast projectile on a stationary target; it does not by itself bound scenarios where the relevant variable is the low velocity of the produced object rather than the collision energy — LSAG addresses this explicitly for black holes but the general form of the objection (Kent 2004, 'A Critical Look at Risk Assessments for Global Catastrophes') is not fully closed. I did not retrieve a primary statement of the instability scale Lambda_I; the ~10^10-10^11 GeV figure is read off the contour lines of Buttazzo et al. Fig. 3, not quoted from text.

hazards.name: Strangelet catalysis of ordinary matter
hazards.one_line: A hypothetical stable negatively-charged lump of strange quark matter could in principle convert ordinary nuclei into strange matter, but the survival of the Moon under 4.5 Gyr of cosmic-ray heavy-ion bombardment excludes the scenario empirically.
hazards.mechanism: Strange quark matter is a hypothetical phase of roughly equal numbers of up, down and strange quarks that some models predict is more stable than ordinary nuclear matter above about mass number 10. A small lump — a strangelet — that were both stable and negatively charged would not be electrostatically repelled by ordinary nuclei; on contact it could absorb a nucleus, convert it to strange matter, grow, and repeat. Growth would be exponential in the absorbed mass, and the released binding energy would appear as heat. The end state is the conversion of the Earth into a body of strange matter a few hundred metres across, releasing energy comparable to a stellar event. Death here is instantaneous over hours to days, not by famine. Every link in the chain is speculative: it requires strange matter to be the true ground state of baryonic matter, requires stable strangelets to be negatively rather than positively charged (models say positive), and requires them to be produced in the first place — and the empirical bounds close the last link.

annual_probability.event_definition: initiation of runaway conversion of terrestrial matter to strange quark matter by a strangelet produced in a human heavy-ion collision, per year of collider operation at LHC-class energies
annual_probability.trend: Falling with collider energy, counter-intuitively. LSAG establishes that strangelet formation becomes LESS likely as the collision system gets hotter and the net baryon density at mid-rapidity falls, so LHC Pb-Pb is less dangerous than RHIC Au-Au, which was less dangerous than the 1980s-90s AGS/SPS programmes. Future higher-energy heavy-ion machines are therefore safer on this axis, not more dangerous.

severity_tiers.label: Strangelet produced but decays
severity_tiers.description: A strangelet forms and decays on the characteristic weak-interaction timescale of roughly a nanosecond, as most theoretical models predict. No macroscopic consequence whatsoever. This is overwhelmingly the most likely outcome even conditional on production.

severity_tiers.label: Stable positively-charged strangelet
severity_tiers.description: A stable strangelet forms but carries positive charge, as most model studies find. It is Coulomb-repelled by ordinary nuclei and cannot convert them. It stops in matter and sits inert as an exotic heavy isotope.

severity_tiers.label: Runaway conversion of the Earth
severity_tiers.description: A stable negatively-charged strangelet stops in terrestrial matter and begins exponential conversion. The Earth is converted to strange matter over hours to days with release of nuclear binding energy. This is the branch excluded by the survival of the Moon, and it is why the headline probability is set at author-estimate 10^-15 rather than anything a survey would assign.

key_parameters.label: Heavy-ion collision energy per nucleon pair
key_parameters.effect: Inverse. LSAG: "the probability for strangelet production decreases with increasing centre-of-mass energy", because the produced fireball is hotter (strangelets melt) and the net baryon density at mid-rapidity falls (strangelets need baryon number). LHC Pb-Pb at ~2.8 TeV/nucleon per beam is strictly safer than RHIC Au-Au at 200 GeV/nucleon-pair. The rate should be modelled as monotonically DECREASING in this knob.

key_parameters.label: Effective fireball temperature
key_parameters.effect: Strangelet binding is of order one to a few MeV per constituent, corresponding to a heat bath of tens of billions of degrees. RHIC fireballs measured at around 1.6 trillion degrees are two orders of magnitude hotter, so strangelet survival in the fireball is, in LSAG's own analogy, as likely as "producing an icecube in a furnace". Increasing this parameter suppresses the rate; it would have to fall by ~100x to be permissive.

key_parameters.label: Cosmic-ray heavy-ion exposure of the unshielded lunar surface
key_parameters.effect: The empirical bound. Cosmic rays include a large iron-nucleus component and the Moon has no atmosphere, so iron-on-iron collisions comparable to laboratory gold-gold and lead-lead have been running on the lunar surface for the age of the solar system. The Moon is still there. Setting this parameter to zero is the only way to unlock the hazard; at its real value the branch is empirically closed.

key_parameters.label: Sign of the charge of a stable strangelet
key_parameters.effect: A hard gate, not a dial. LSAG: "It is generally expected that any stable strangelet would have a positive charge, in which case it would be repelled by ordinary nuclear matter, and hence unable to convert it into strange matter." Only the -1 branch is dangerous, and LSAG notes there is "no rigorous proof" that the charge must be positive, which is exactly why the hazard is not formally zero.

citations.claim: Strangelet production at the LHC is less likely than at RHIC, and RHIC data support a thermal production model that places tight upper bounds.
citations.authors: J. Ellis, G. Giudice, M. Mangano, I. Tkachev, U. Wiedemann (LHC Safety Assessment Group)
citations.venue: Journal of Physics G: Nuclear and Particle Physics 35 (2008) 115004

citations.claim: Peer-reviewed publication venue and date of the LSAG review.
citations.authors: John Ellis, Gian Giudice, Michelangelo Mangano, Igor Tkachev, Urs Wiedemann
citations.venue: J. Phys. G: Nucl. Part. Phys. 35 (2008) 115004 (18pp), doi:10.1088/0954-3899/35/11/115004, received 26 August 2008, published 5 September 2008; preprint CERN-PH-TH/2008-136
