hazards.uncertainty_notes: The annual probability is an AUTHOR-ESTIMATE and must be labelled as such in any output. No peer-reviewed source states a per-year probability for strangelet catastrophe; the published literature states qualitative exclusions ('no basis for any conceivable threat') and empirical bounds, not rates. Secondary risk-assessment literature does quote numbers — Kent (2004, Risk Analysis) reports that Dar, De Rujula & Heinz's main bound gives p_catastrophe < 2 x 10^-8 and that the Busza-Jaffe-Sandweiss-Wilczek most conservative bound implies an expected death toll bounded by 60,000 — but I did NOT retrieve Kent or the primary DDH/BJSW papers this session, only a search-engine summary of them, so I have not used those figures as the basis. The 10^-9 'high' bound is my ceiling, chosen to be safely above any bound I saw quoted; the 10^-15 'best' reflects the Moon argument. A serious critic would attack in two places. First, the Moon argument requires an assumption about the velocity distribution of any strangelets produced in cosmic-ray collisions: those are made in a centre-of-mass frame moving at high speed relative to the lunar surface and might be broken up before they could slow enough to coalesce. LSAG addresses this and argues RHIC copper-ion data support the assumption, but it is an assumption. Second, the interstellar-accretion argument assumes strangelets do not decay on timescales much shorter than that of star formation. Both objections are honest and both are answered rather than dismissed in the primary literature, which is why I present the cosmic-ray/Moon bound as a genuinely strong safety result rather than a reassurance.

hazards.name: Self-replicating nanotechnology (grey goo) and molecular-manufacturing abuse
hazards.one_line: Runaway self-replicating nanomachines are physically possible but unnecessary for molecular manufacturing and can be prohibited; expert elicitation puts far more extinction weight on deliberate nanotech weapons than on accidental ecophagy.
hazards.mechanism: The original concern, framed by Drexler in the 1980s, was that molecular assemblers capable of building copies of themselves from ambient matter could escape control and consume the biosphere as feedstock — exponential replication with a doubling time of minutes to hours converting biomass and crustal material into more replicators. The kill mechanism is ecophagy: not the machines attacking people but the destruction of the substrate that agriculture and every food web depend on, followed by famine, plus the waste heat of a planetary-scale exothermic conversion. Phoenix and Drexler's 2004 retraction of the emphasis is the decisive design insight: productive nanosystems need not move about, use natural resources, or undergo incremental mutation; a fixed nanofactory is an assembly line, not a swarm, and self-replication is simply not on the development path. That reroutes the mechanism entirely. The realistic chain to mass death runs through deliberately engineered nanoscale weapons in a military-competition dynamic, where the kill mechanism is conventional — targeted destruction, infrastructure collapse, and then famine — rather than accidental runaway.

annual_probability.event_definition: human extinction caused by the single biggest nanotech accident, annualised from the Sandberg & Bostrom (2008) median of 0.5% before 2100 over the 92 years 2008-2100; the 'high' bound annualises their molecular-nanotech-weapons extinction median of 5%
annual_probability.trend: Currently far below the elicited value and rising conditionally. Atomically precise molecular manufacturing does not exist in 2026, so the accident rate is presently near zero; the elicited numbers are effectively conditional on the technology arriving this century. If nanofactory-style APM arrives, the accident branch stays suppressed by Phoenix & Drexler's design argument while the WEAPONS branch — which the same survey rates ten times higher for extinction — rises with military competition. The trend is therefore towards the deliberate-abuse pole, not the accidental one.

severity_tiers.label: Contained incident
severity_tiers.description: An escaped or misused nanosystem kills at least one million people before being contained — through localised ecophagy, infrastructure destruction, or a weapons release that is not global. Industrial civilisation continues. Derived from the survey's >1 million dead threshold for the single biggest nanotech accident.

severity_tiers.label: Global ecophagy or nanotech war
severity_tiers.description: At least one billion dead. Either a replicator escapes containment on a continental scale and destroys the agricultural substrate over a growing region, or a nanotech-weapons exchange collapses global food and energy distribution. Death is overwhelmingly by famine and the failure of supply chains, not by the machines themselves. Conditional probability derived as 1%/5% from the survey's paired medians.

severity_tiers.label: Extinction
severity_tiers.description: Complete conversion of the accessible biosphere, or a weapons campaign carried to completion. No self-sufficient human population survives. Conditional probability derived as 0.5%/5% from the survey's paired medians for the same risk.

key_parameters.label: Atomically precise molecular manufacturing exists
key_parameters.effect: A hard gate on the whole hazard. At 0 the annual probability is effectively zero regardless of every other setting; the elicited 0.5%/5% figures are conditional on this becoming 1. This is the parameter that makes the hazard a forecast rather than a rate.

key_parameters.label: Free-ranging self-replicators built or permitted
key_parameters.effect: The accident branch only. Phoenix & Drexler: "self-replication is unnecessary" and "the construction of anything resembling a dangerous self-replicating nanomachine can and should be prohibited". Setting this to 0 does NOT reduce the weapons branch, which is the larger term — a simulator that lets the user switch off grey goo and watch total risk barely move is showing the correct thing.

key_parameters.label: Elicited extinction probability, single biggest nanotech accident, by 2100
key_parameters.effect: Linear on the accident-branch annual rate: annual_rate = value/100 divided by the years remaining to 2100. At the elicited 0.5% over 92 years this gives 5.4 x 10^-5 /yr.

key_parameters.label: Elicited extinction probability, molecular nanotech weapons, by 2100
key_parameters.effect: Linear on the weapons-branch annual rate, and TEN TIMES the accident figure in the same survey by the same respondents. This ratio is the packet's main quantitative finding for this hazard and it agrees with Phoenix & Drexler's qualitative argument: "Since weapon systems will be both easier to build and more likely to draw investment, the potential for dangerous systems is best considered in the context of military competition and arms control."

citations.claim: Self-replication is unnecessary for molecular manufacturing; deliberate abuse and weapons, not runaway replication, are the real concern.
citations.authors: Chris Phoenix and K. Eric Drexler
citations.venue: Nanotechnology 15(8):869, IOP Publishing, doi:10.1088/0957-4484/15/8/001
citations.exact_figure: "Nanotechnology-based fabrication can be thoroughly non-biological and inherently safe: such systems need have no ability to move about, use natural resources, or undergo incremental mutation. Moreover, self-replication is unnecessary: the development and use of highly productive systems of nanomachinery (nanofactories) need not involve the construction of autonomous self-replicating nanomachines. Accordingly, the construction of anything resembling a dangerous self-replicating nanomachine can and should be prohibited... Since weapon systems will be both easier to build and more likely to draw investment, the potential for dangerous systems is best considered in the context of military competition and arms control."

citations.claim: Expert median estimates for nanotech accident versus nanotech weapons, at three severity thresholds, before 2100.
citations.authors: Anders Sandberg and Nick Bostrom
citations.venue: Global Catastrophic Risks Survey, Technical Report 2008/1, Future of Humanity Institute, Oxford University (informal survey at the Global Catastrophic Risk Conference, Oxford, 17-20 July 2008)
citations.exact_figure: "Number killed in the single biggest nanotech accident": at least 1 million dead 5%, at least 1 billion dead 1%, human extinction 0.5%. "Number killed by molecular nanotech weapons": at least 1 million dead 25%, at least 1 billion dead 10%, human extinction 5%. Overall risk of extinction prior to 2100: 19% (median).

citations.claim: The survey's own caveats about the reliability of these medians.
citations.authors: Anders Sandberg and Nick Bostrom
citations.venue: Global Catastrophic Risks Survey, Technical Report 2008/1, Future of Humanity Institute, Oxford University
citations.exact_figure: "These results should be taken with a grain of salt. Non-responses have been omitted, although some might represent a statement of zero probability rather than no opinion... There are likely to be many cognitive biases that affect the result, such as unpacking bias and the availability heuristic—as well as old-fashioned optimism and pessimism."

citations.claim: Drexler's own public retraction of the grey-goo emphasis at the time of the 2004 paper.
citations.authors: Institute of Physics / Foresight Institute press coverage of Phoenix & Drexler 2004
citations.venue: EurekAlert! / ScienceDaily press release for Nanotechnology 15(8):869, 9 June 2004
citations.exact_figure: Drexler quoted: "Runaway replicators, while theoretically possible according to the laws of physics, cannot be built with today's nanotechnology toolset" and "Self-replicating machines aren't necessary for molecular nanotechnology, and aren't part of current development plans."

hazards.uncertainty_notes: The three quantities must not be conflated. (a) P(the event happens): not directly elicited; the survey elicits P(deaths exceed a threshold), which bundles occurrence and severity. (b) P(mass death | event): I derived the conditional tier probabilities by dividing the survey's own paired medians (1%/5% and 0.5%/5%), which is arithmetically valid only if respondents' medians are internally coherent across thresholds — medians of a population are not guaranteed to be, and this is the weakest step in the hazard. (c) P(permanent extinction): 0.5% by 2100 for the accident, 5% for weapons. The deeper problem is that a 2008 elicitation of a technology that did not then and does not now exist is measuring beliefs about a timeline, not a physical rate; eighteen years have elapsed with no molecular manufacturing, which should shift the estimate down substantially, and I have not applied that correction because doing so would be inventing a number. A serious critic would say the survey suffers unpacking bias (asking separately about 'accident' and 'weapons' inflates the total), had a small and self-selected respondent pool at a conference explicitly about catastrophic risk, and that Sandberg & Bostrom themselves disclaim it. A second critic would say the opposite: that Phoenix & Drexler's 2004 argument is a statement about what responsible developers WOULD do, not a physical impossibility proof, and that a design argument is not a safety bound in the way the cosmic-ray argument for vacuum decay genuinely is. Both criticisms are correct. The honest summary is that this is the one exotic hazard in the packet with no empirical bound at all.

hazards.name: Microscopic black hole produced at a collider
hazards.one_line: Microscopic black holes require large extra dimensions to be producible at all, are expected to evaporate in about 10^-27 seconds, and the observed survival of white dwarfs and neutron stars under cosmic-ray bombardment excludes any stable accreting variety.
hazards.mechanism: In theories with large extra spatial dimensions, gravity becomes strong at TeV energies and colliding partons could form microscopic black holes. Hawking radiation is expected to evaporate them essentially instantly. The catastrophic branch requires simultaneously that Hawking radiation is suppressed (violating well-established quantum field theory in curved space), that the object is electrically neutral (otherwise it is stopped and would have accumulated in Earth and the Sun over billions of years with visible effect), and that it accretes fast enough to matter. Were all three true, a stopped black hole would slowly accrete the Earth over a timescale set by the extra-dimensional gravitational coupling; the population would die of the resulting geophysical collapse, not the hole itself. The chain is closed empirically at its far end: ultra-high-energy cosmic rays striking white dwarfs and neutron stars would have produced such objects copiously, and the dense stellar material would have stopped even neutral ones, leading to rapid accretion and explosive destruction of those stars on timescales far shorter than their observed lifetimes. White dwarfs and neutron stars are observed. Therefore cosmic rays do not produce such black holes, and neither will a collider.

annual_probability.event_definition: initiation of runaway accretion of the Earth by a stable microscopic black hole produced in a human collider, per year of collider operation
annual_probability.trend: Flat at zero. The bound is set by the observed population of white dwarfs and neutron stars, which does not change with collider energy or luminosity. Higher-energy machines are covered by the same argument because cosmic rays already exceed them.

severity_tiers.label: Evaporation (the physical expectation)
severity_tiers.description: The black hole decays by Hawking radiation with an expected lifetime of order 10^-27 seconds, or equivalently decays back into the partons that produced it because it carries no conserved quantum number they did not. It never reaches the detector walls. No consequence.

severity_tiers.label: Stable but harmless
severity_tiers.description: A stable microscopic black hole is produced but is either neutral and unstopped (passes through the Earth), or is stopped but accretes so slowly that in seven or more spacetime dimensions the Earth survives for billions of years before any harm. LSAG treats this as the residual case and shows it is still safe.

severity_tiers.label: Runaway accretion of the Earth
severity_tiers.description: A stable, charge-neutral, rapidly accreting black hole is stopped inside the Earth and consumes it. This requires violating quantum mechanics or general relativity and is excluded by the observed survival of white dwarfs and neutron stars. Included for completeness only.

key_parameters.label: Number of spacetime dimensions relevant at the TeV scale
key_parameters.effect: A gate with a non-monotonic interior. At 4 (no evidence for anything else) microscopic black holes cannot be produced at all: "there is no chance that any black holes could be produced at the LHC, since the conventional gravitational forces between fundamental particles are too weak". At 7 or more, production is possible but accretion is so slow that "Earth would survive for billions of years before any harm befell it". At 5 or 6, accretion would be fast enough that "the gravitational interactions of black holes, should they exist, would be detectable in the Universe" — and they are not.

key_parameters.label: Microscopic black hole lifetime
key_parameters.effect: LSAG: "the expected lifetime would be very short, O(10^-27 s)". This is the whole hazard. Suppressing Hawking radiation to make the lifetime long requires "a violation of some of the basic principles of quantum mechanics... and/or of general relativity". No dial in a simulator should be able to raise this without also flagging that the user has switched off known physics.

key_parameters.label: LHC-equivalent programmes already run by cosmic rays in the Universe
key_parameters.effect: The empirical bound, and the one number that should be visible on any page like this. LSAG: "over the history of the Universe, Nature has carried out the equivalent of 10^31 LHC projects (defined by the integrated luminosity for cosmic-ray collisions at a centre-of-mass energy of 14 TeV or more) and continues to do so at the rate of over 10^13 per second". The residual risk from one more human programme scales as 1/this number.

citations.claim: Microscopic black holes decay by Hawking radiation on a timescale of order 10^-27 seconds, and suppressing this requires violating basic physics.
citations.authors: J. Ellis, G. Giudice, M. Mangano, I. Tkachev, U. Wiedemann (LHC Safety Assessment Group)
citations.venue: Journal of Physics G: Nuclear and Particle Physics 35 (2008) 115004, section 4
citations.exact_figure: "a microscopic black hole cannot be completely black. In standard quantum physics, the decay rate would be directly related to the production rate, and the expected lifetime would be very short, O(10^-27 s)." And: suppression "would require a violation of some of the basic principles of quantum mechanics—which is a cornerstone of the laws of Nature—in order for the black hole decay rate to be suppressed relative to its production rate, and/or of general relativity, in order to suppress Hawking radiation."

citations.claim: The observed survival of white dwarfs and neutron stars excludes cosmic-ray production of dangerous stable black holes, and hence excludes collider production.
citations.authors: J. Ellis, G. Giudice, M. Mangano, I. Tkachev, U. Wiedemann (LHC Safety Assessment Group)
citations.venue: Journal of Physics G: Nuclear and Particle Physics 35 (2008) 115004, section 4
citations.exact_figure: "ultra-high-energy cosmic rays hitting dense stars such as white dwarfs and neutron stars would have produced black holes copiously during their lifetimes... would have led to the destruction of white dwarfs and neutron stars on time scales that are much shorter than their observed lifetimes. The final stages of their destruction would have released explosively large amounts of energy, which would have been highly visible. The observation of white dwarfs and neutron stars that would have been destroyed in this way tells us that cosmic rays do not produce such black holes, and hence neither will the LHC."

citations.claim: The scale of the natural experiment already performed, on Earth, on the Sun, and in the Universe.
citations.authors: J. Ellis, G. Giudice, M. Mangano, I. Tkachev, U. Wiedemann (LHC Safety Assessment Group)
citations.venue: Journal of Physics G: Nuclear and Particle Physics 35 (2008) 115004, section 2
citations.exact_figure: "over 3 x 10^22 cosmic rays with energies of 10^17 eV or more, equal to or greater than the LHC energy, have struck the Earth's surface since its formation. This means that Nature has already conducted the equivalent of about a hundred thousand LHC experimental programmes on Earth, and the planet still exists... Nature has therefore already conducted the LHC experimental programme about one billion times via the collisions of cosmic rays with the Sun, and the Sun still exists... Nature has already completed about 10^31 LHC experimental programmes since the beginning of the Universe. Moreover, each second, the Universe continues to repeat about 3 x 10^13 complete LHC experiments."

citations.claim: The number of extra dimensions determines whether accretion could ever be dangerous, and the intermediate cases are excluded observationally.
citations.authors: J. Ellis, G. Giudice, M. Mangano, I. Tkachev, U. Wiedemann (LHC Safety Assessment Group)
citations.venue: Journal of Physics G: Nuclear and Particle Physics 35 (2008) 115004, section 4
citations.exact_figure: "the rate at which absorption would take place would be so slow, if there are seven or more dimensions, that Earth would survive for billions of years before any harm befell it... If there are only five or six dimensions of spacetime relevant at the LHC scale, then the gravitational interactions of black holes, should they exist, would be strong enough such that their impact, should they exist, would be detectable in the Universe."

hazards.uncertainty_notes: I report a best-estimate annual probability of exactly 0 and I stand behind it, but a simulator should distinguish why: this is not a small number rounded down, it is a chain of conjunctions each of which requires overturning established physics, terminated by a direct astrophysical observation. The three quantities: (a) P(a microscopic black hole is produced at all) is not zero — it is small and depends entirely on whether large extra dimensions exist, for which there is no evidence; (b) P(it is stable AND neutral AND accretes) requires simultaneous violation of Hawking radiation, of the Schwinger charge-neutralisation mechanism, and of the observed integrity of degenerate stars; (c) P(permanent human extinction | runaway accretion) is 1. A serious critic makes one real objection: the general form of Kent's (2004) argument that risk assessments for very-low-probability, very-high-stakes events are dominated not by the physics but by the probability that the assessment itself is wrong — i.e. the probability of an error in the LSAG reasoning may exceed the probability of the catastrophe it bounds. That objection is methodologically sound and cannot be answered from within the physics. It applies with equal force to the vacuum-decay entry. The upper bound of 10^-20 is my own placeholder for that meta-uncertainty, not a published figure, and should be marked author-estimate wherever it is displayed.

hazards.name: End of vascular land plants (CO2 starvation / thermal limit)
hazards.one_line: The Sun's brightening drives the carbon-silicate weathering cycle to strip CO2 below the minimum for land plants, ending macroscopic land life somewhere between about 1.0 and 1.86 billion years from now.
hazards.mechanism: Solar luminosity rises as helium accumulates in the core, raising mean molecular weight so the core contracts and heats. Warmer surface temperatures accelerate silicate weathering, which consumes atmospheric CO2 and buries it as carbonate. The carbon-silicate thermostat that has stabilised Earth's climate for four billion years therefore runs the CO2 reservoir down. Below roughly 150 ppm C3 photosynthesis fails; C4 plants can work down to about 10 ppm and buy hundreds of millions of extra years. When CO2 crosses the floor, primary production on land collapses, and everything above it starves — this is a famine, exactly like the terrestrial catastrophes, just on a stellar clock. Graham, Halevy & Abbot (2024) revise the mechanism: if silicate weathering is only weakly temperature-dependent, the CO2 decline slows and temporarily reverses, averting starvation, and land plants instead die of heat when surface temperature reaches about 338 K. Either way the land biosphere ends; only the cause of death and the date change.

annual_probability.event_definition: CERTAINTY, NOT RISK. Atmospheric CO2 falls below the minimum for vascular land plants (or surface temperature reaches 338 K), ending macroscopic land life. Date: approximately 1.0 Gyr from now on the classical Caldeira-Kasting picture, extended to 1.6-1.86 Gyr by Graham, Halevy & Abbot (2024). Probability expressed as 1 divided by the years remaining.
annual_probability.trend: Rising monotonically and irreversibly. Solar luminosity increases on the Gough (1981) law L(t)/L_sun = 1/(1 + (2/5)(1 - t/t_sun)) with t_sun = 4.57 Gyr, which gives a present brightening of about 0.4/4.57 = 8.8% per Gyr, i.e. roughly 1% per 115 Myr. Nothing in the Standard Model of stellar evolution can slow it.

severity_tiers.label: C3 collapse
severity_tiers.description: CO2 drops below about 150 ppm and C3 photosynthesis — which is most trees, most crops, and the great majority of plant biomass — ceases. C4 grasses and any engineered analogues persist. Terrestrial food webs above the primary producers collapse over decades. Conditional on a technologically static biosphere still present at that date.

severity_tiers.label: Total loss of land macrobiota
severity_tiers.description: CO2 crosses the C4 floor at about 10 ppm, or global mean surface temperature reaches 338 K, and all vascular land plants die. Macroscopic land life ends. Marine and microbial life continue. Recovery of an industrial civilisation is impossible without artificial primary production.

key_parameters.label: Rate of solar luminosity increase
key_parameters.effect: Sets the clock for every hazard in this deep-time block. Derived from the Gough (1981) formula L(t)/L_sun = 1/(1 + (2/5)(1 - t/t_sun)) with t_sun = 4.57 Gyr: dL/dt at present = 0.4/4.57 per Gyr = 8.8% per Gyr, equivalently about 1% per 114 Myr. The date of every milestone scales inversely with this value.

key_parameters.label: Minimum CO2 for photosynthesis
key_parameters.effect: A step, not a slope. At 150 ppmv (the conventional C3 threshold) the biosphere ends in roughly 100 Myr on the pre-1992 models; at 10 ppmv (the C4 threshold that Caldeira & Kasting adopted) it lasts 0.9-1.5 Gyr. This single parameter change is what produced a tenfold extension of the estimated biosphere lifetime in 1992 — the largest revision in the field.

key_parameters.label: Temperature dependence of silicate weathering (Te)
key_parameters.effect: The current frontier. Caldeira & Kasting used Te = 13.7 K with beta = 0.25. Graham, Halevy & Abbot (2024) show that if weathering is weakly temperature-dependent (as recent data suggest) and/or strongly CO2-dependent, the luminosity-driven CO2 decrease slows and temporarily reverses, averting CO2 starvation entirely and extending plant survival from about 1 Gyr to 1.6-1.86 Gyr. Their range runs "from 0.55 Gyr at Te x beta = 0.6 to a maximum lifespan of 1.86 Gyr" — a factor of three in the answer from one poorly-constrained geochemical parameter.

key_parameters.label: Photosynthesis thermal shutdown temperature
key_parameters.effect: The revised kill mechanism. Under weak-temperature-dependence weathering "the biosphere overheats at 338 K after 1.66-1.86 Gyr", replacing CO2 starvation as the cause of death. Lowering this brings the date forward roughly linearly in the luminosity ramp.

citations.claim: C4 photosynthesis extends the biosphere's life span far beyond the C3 limit, giving 0.9-1.5 Gyr.
citations.authors: Ken Caldeira and James F. Kasting
citations.venue: Nature 360, 721-723, 'The life span of the biosphere revisited'
citations.exact_figure: a C4-plant-based biosphere "could survive for at least another 0.9 Gyr to 1.5 Gyr after the present time, depending respectively on whether CO2 or temperature is the limiting factor"; in previous models "atmospheric CO2 falls below the critical level for C3 photosynthesis (150 parts per million), in only 100 Myr"; C4 photosynthesis "can persist to much lower concentrations of atmospheric CO2 (less than 10 p.p.m.)"

citations.claim: The classical 1 Gyr result and its substantial revision upward, with a changed kill mechanism.
citations.authors: R. J. Graham, Itay Halevy, Dorian Abbot
citations.venue: The Planetary Science Journal (accepted; arXiv:2409.10714), 'Substantial extension of the lifetime of the terrestrial biosphere'
citations.exact_figure: "Approximately one billion years (Gyr) in the future, as the Sun brightens, Earth's carbonate-silicate cycle is expected to drive CO2 below the minimum level required by vascular land plants, eliminating most macroscopic land life... This dramatically lengthens plant survival from 1 Gyr up to ~1.6-1.86 Gyr, until extreme temperatures halt photosynthesis, suggesting a revised kill mechanism for land plants and potential doubling of the future lifespan of Earth's land macrobiota." Range: "from 0.55 Gyr at Te x beta = 0.6 to a maximum lifespan of 1.86 Gyr". CK92 parameters: "Te=13.7 K and beta=0.25", minimum CO2 for land plants "10 ppmv".

citations.claim: The standard parametrisation of solar luminosity evolution, from which the brightening rate is derived.
citations.authors: Georg Feulner, quoting D. O. Gough (1981)
citations.venue: Reviews of Geophysics 50, RG2006, 'The faint young Sun problem'
citations.exact_figure: Eq. (1): "L(t)/L_sun = 1 / (1 + (2/5)(1 - t/t_sun))", "where L_sun = 3.85 x 10^26 W is the present-day solar luminosity and t_sun = 4.57 Gyr (1 Ga = 10^9 years) is the age of the Sun"; at zero-age main sequence 4.57 Ga the bolometric luminosity "was about 30% lower as compared to the present epoch"; present solar constant "S0 = 1361 W m^-2 [Kopp and Lean, 2011]", Earth's albedo "A = 0.3"

cascades_into: deep-time-ocean-loss-end-of-surface-life: the same luminosity ramp that starves the plants continues and later boils the oceans
deep-time-moon-recession-obliquity: the obliquity chaos arrives on the same ~1.5 Gyr timescale and compounds the climate stress
hazards.uncertainty_notes: This is a schedule, not a risk: the annual probability of 10^-9 is 1/(years remaining) and should be read as 'this is certain, and it is this far away', not as a hazard rate. The dominant uncertainty is not solar physics — the luminosity ramp is one of the most robust predictions in astrophysics, agreeing between Gough's 1981 analytic formula and Bahcall et al.'s 2001 standard solar model to within the line width of a plot — but geochemistry. The temperature and CO2 dependence of silicate weathering is poorly constrained, and Graham, Halevy & Abbot (2024) show it moves the answer by a factor of three (0.55 to 1.86 Gyr). A serious critic would also point out that the entire framing assumes no biological or technological intervention over a billion years, which is the least defensible assumption in the packet. I was NOT able to retrieve the Caldeira & Kasting 1992 Nature paper itself this session — nature.com and PubMed both refused the fetch — so the 0.9-1.5 Gyr, 150 ppm and 10 ppm figures are taken from Graham, Halevy & Abbot's (2024) direct characterisation of CK92 plus the published Nature abstract as returned by search indexing. That is a second-hand chain and should be verified against the original before this number is used in anything load-bearing. Finally: 'end of land plants' is NOT 'end of life' and the two are constantly conflated in popular treatments — see the next hazard for the difference, which is 1.9 billion years wide.

hazards.name: Loss of the oceans and the end of surface life
hazards.one_line: Rising insolation drives a moist then runaway greenhouse that strips Earth of its oceans; microbial life in high-latitude refugia is modelled to persist until about 2.8 billion years from now.
hazards.mechanism: As insolation rises, surface warming increases water evaporation, which raises the greenhouse effect, which warms further. Two escape routes end the oceans. In the moist greenhouse, the stratosphere becomes humid enough that water is photodissociated and hydrogen escapes to space over hundreds of millions of years. In the runaway greenhouse, the destabilising feedback becomes unbounded and the entire ocean vaporises into a steam atmosphere; Leconte et al.'s 3D GCM puts that threshold at about 375 W/m2 absorbed, significantly higher than the older 1D estimates because unsaturated subsident regions created by the Hadley circulation stabilise the climate. Once the oceans are gone, surface temperature runs to several hundred kelvin and no known biochemistry functions. Before that, O'Malley-James et al. model the sequential retreat of the biosphere: complex life gives way to unicellular life, which retreats to high-latitude mountains and cold-trap ice caves, and persists there for up to 2.8 Gyr from present. This is the true end of Earth's biosphere, roughly 1.9 Gyr after the end of land plants.

annual_probability.event_definition: CERTAINTY, NOT RISK. Final extinction of all life on Earth's surface, following ocean loss to a moist or runaway greenhouse. Date: up to approximately 2.8 Gyr from now for unicellular life in high-latitude refugia (O'Malley-James et al. 2013); ocean loss itself falls between roughly 1 and 2 Gyr from now. Probability expressed as 1 divided by the years remaining.
annual_probability.trend: Rising monotonically with solar luminosity at 8.8% per Gyr (Gough 1981). Not affected by anything Earth or its inhabitants do; anthropogenic greenhouse forcing of a few W/m2 is negligible against the ~100 W/m2 increase required.

severity_tiers.label: Moist greenhouse / ocean escape
severity_tiers.description: Stratospheric humidity rises enough for water to be photodissociated and hydrogen lost to space. Oceans drain over hundreds of millions of years. Multicellular life is long gone; unicellular life retreats to residual water. Leconte et al. find that wavelength-dependent radiative effects keep the stratosphere cold and dry enough to hamper this escape route "even at large fluxes", which pushes the loss later than 1D models predicted.

severity_tiers.label: Runaway greenhouse
severity_tiers.description: Absorbed insolation crosses about 375 W/m2 and the destabilising water-vapour feedback runs away. The entire ocean vaporises into a dense steam atmosphere; surface temperatures reach many hundreds of kelvin. Earth becomes Venus-like. No refugium survives.

severity_tiers.label: Final microbial extinction in high-latitude refugia
severity_tiers.description: The last habitat. O'Malley-James et al.'s latitude-based climate model with eccentricity and obliquity variations finds unicellular life could persist in high-latitude mountains and cold-trap ice caves for up to 2.8 Gyr from present. After this, Earth carries no life at all. This is the honest date for 'the end of life on Earth' and it is 2.8 Gyr, not the 1 Gyr usually quoted.

key_parameters.label: Absorbed insolation threshold for runaway greenhouse
key_parameters.effect: Leconte et al. (2013): "the threshold for the runaway greenhouse is about 375 W/m2, significantly higher than previously thought". Earth today absorbs S0(1-A)/4 = 1361 x 0.7 / 4 = 238 W/m2. The date of ocean loss is set by when the solar ramp closes that gap, and moving this threshold by 25 W/m2 moves the date by hundreds of Myr.

key_parameters.label: Total solar irradiance at 1 AU
key_parameters.effect: Kopp & Lean (2011) value as used by Feulner (2012). Scales linearly with luminosity through the Gough law. Together with Earth's albedo A = 0.3 it sets the present absorbed flux against which the 375 W/m2 threshold is measured.

key_parameters.label: Maximum persistence of unicellular life in high-latitude refugia
key_parameters.effect: O'Malley-James et al. (2013): "Results suggest that in high latitude regions, unicellular life could persist for up to 2.8 Gyr from present." This is the outer envelope of the habitable lifetime and the number a scale-bar should use for 'end of life on Earth'. It exceeds the end of complex life by roughly 1.9 Gyr — the biosphere dies in sequence, not at once.

key_parameters.label: Earth's Bond albedo
key_parameters.effect: Directly scales absorbed flux as S0(1-A)/4. Leconte et al.'s central and counter-intuitive finding is that "clouds have a destabilizing feedback on the long term warming" — i.e. warming reduces the effective albedo rather than raising it — so this parameter cannot be treated as a self-correcting safety margin.

citations.claim: The runaway greenhouse threshold from a 3D global climate model, and why it is higher than 1D estimates.
citations.authors: Jeremy Leconte, Francois Forget, Benjamin Charnay, Robin Wordsworth, Alizee Pottier
citations.venue: Nature 504, 268-271 (arXiv:1312.3337), 'Increased insolation threshold for runaway greenhouse processes on Earth-like planets'
citations.exact_figure: "Here we use a 3D global climate model to show that the threshold for the runaway greenhouse is about 375 W/m2, significantly higher than previously thought... In contrast with previous studies, we find that clouds have a destabilizing feedback on the long term warming. However, subsident, unsaturated regions created by the Hadley circulation have a stabilizing effect that is strong enough to defer the runaway greenhouse limit to higher insolation than inferred from 1D models. Furthermore, because of wavelength-dependent radiative effects, the stratosphere remains cold and dry enough to hamper atmospheric water escape, even at large fluxes."

citations.claim: The sequential extinction of the biosphere and the maximum persistence of unicellular life in refugia.
citations.authors: J. T. O'Malley-James, J. S. Greaves, J. A. Raven, C. S. Cockell
citations.venue: International Journal of Astrobiology 12(2), 99-112 (arXiv:1210.5721), 'Swansong biospheres: refuges for life and novel microbial biospheres on terrestrial planets near the end of their habitable lifetimes'
citations.exact_figure: "A simple, latitude-based climate model incorporating eccentricity and obliquity variations is used as a guide to the temperature evolution of the Earth over the next 3 Gyr. This allows inferences to be made about potential refuges for life, particularly in mountains and cold-trap (ice) caves and what forms of life could live in these environments. Results suggest that in high latitude regions, unicellular life could persist for up to 2.8 Gyr from present." Also: "Unicellular life was probably present for at least 2.5 Gyr before multicellular life appeared and will likely be the only form of life capable of surviving on the planet in the far future."

citations.claim: Present solar irradiance and albedo, and the solar luminosity ramp that closes the gap to the runaway threshold.
citations.authors: Georg Feulner, quoting Kopp & Lean (2011) and Gough (1981)
citations.venue: Reviews of Geophysics 50, RG2006, 'The faint young Sun problem'
citations.exact_figure: "the present-day solar constant S0 = 1361 W m^-2 [Kopp and Lean, 2011] and Earth's current albedo A = 0.3"; radiative forcing formula "Delta F = Delta S0 (1 - A)/4"; Gough (1981) luminosity law L(t)/L_sun = 1/(1 + (2/5)(1 - t/t_sun)), t_sun = 4.57 Gyr

citations.claim: The revised land-plant kill mechanism that pushes the preceding milestone later and narrows the gap to ocean loss.
citations.authors: R. J. Graham, Itay Halevy, Dorian Abbot
citations.venue: The Planetary Science Journal (accepted; arXiv:2409.10714)
citations.exact_figure: "This dramatically lengthens plant survival from 1 Gyr up to ~1.6-1.86 Gyr, until extreme temperatures halt photosynthesis"; "the biosphere overheats at 338 K after 1.66-1.86 Gyr"

cascades_into: deep-time-sun-red-giant: the same stellar evolution continues to the red-giant phase 7.59 Gyr from now, by which time Earth has been sterile for ~4.8 Gyr
hazards.uncertainty_notes: Schedule, not risk. The date is the weakest part: neither Leconte et al. nor O'Malley-James et al. state, in the text I retrieved, a calendar date for ocean loss — Leconte gives a flux threshold (375 W/m2) and O'Malley-James gives a habitability envelope (2.8 Gyr). Converting the 375 W/m2 threshold into a date requires combining it with the Gough luminosity law, which is MY derivation, not either paper's, and the derivation is not clean because Earth's albedo changes as the climate warms and Leconte's own result is that clouds destabilise rather than stabilise. I have therefore anchored the headline date on O'Malley-James's directly-quoted 2.8 Gyr rather than on a number I computed. A serious critic would attack on three fronts: (1) the 3D GCM result rests on the fidelity of cloud and Hadley-circulation parametrisations in an atmosphere far outside any validated regime; (2) the moist-greenhouse and runaway-greenhouse routes give materially different dates and Leconte's finding that the stratosphere stays dry pushes against the moist route, which is a significant unresolved disagreement in the field; (3) O'Malley-James's refugia model is a simple latitude-based energy balance model, not a GCM, and 2.8 Gyr is an optimistic outer envelope for what a cold-trap ice cave can do. Distinguish carefully: the event (ocean loss) is certain; the fraction killed given the event is 1.0 for any surface biology; permanence is total — this branch has no recovery under any circumstance.

hazards.name: Lunar recession and the destabilisation of Earth's obliquity
hazards.one_line: Tidal transfer of angular momentum moves the Moon away at 38.30 millimetres per year, and in about 1.5 billion years Earth's spin axis enters a large chaotic zone in which obliquity can wander from 0 to more than 85 degrees.
hazards.mechanism: Ocean tides on a rotating Earth lag behind the Moon, so the tidal bulge exerts a forward torque on the Moon and a retarding torque on Earth's spin. Angular momentum flows from Earth's rotation to the lunar orbit: the day lengthens and the Moon recedes, currently at 38.30 plus or minus 0.09 millimetres per year measured directly by lunar laser ranging off the Apollo retroreflectors. As the Moon recedes, the lunar torque on Earth's equatorial bulge weakens and the precession period of Earth's spin axis lengthens. After about 1.5 Gyr that precession period becomes comparable to the precession periods of Earth's own orbital plane, driven by planetary perturbations, and the system enters a secular spin-orbit resonance overlap — a large chaotic zone. The obliquity, today a placid 23.25 degrees oscillating with 1.3 degrees amplitude on a 40 kyr period, can then wander chaotically between 0 and more than 85 degrees. At high obliquity the poles receive more annual insolation than the equator, seasonal extremes become violent, and continental climate becomes unsurvivable for large organisms over much of the planet. Death is by the collapse of agriculture and of stable ecosystems: famine again.

annual_probability.event_definition: CERTAINTY (of the dynamical transition), NOT RISK. Earth's spin axis enters the large chaotic zone created by secular spin-orbit resonance overlap as the Moon recedes. Date: approximately 1.5 Gyr from now (Neron de Surgy & Laskar 1997); the wider literature range for entering the chaotic zone is 1.5-4.5 Gyr. Probability expressed as 1 divided by the years remaining.
annual_probability.trend: Rising, and coupled to Earth's own geography. The recession rate is not constant: it depends on ocean tidal dissipation, which depends on continental configuration and on the proximity of ocean basins to tidal resonance. The present rate of 38.30 mm/yr is anomalously high relative to the geological-average rate, so extrapolating it linearly backwards or forwards is wrong. The direction, however, is monotonic.

severity_tiers.label: Entry into the chaotic zone
severity_tiers.description: The precession period of Earth's spin becomes comparable to the orbital-plane precession periods driven by planetary perturbations. Obliquity ceases to be quasi-periodic and becomes chaotic. Large excursions are now possible but not immediate; the diffusion timescale is tens of millions of years.

severity_tiers.label: Large obliquity excursion
severity_tiers.description: Obliquity wanders to values above about 50 degrees. Poles receive more annual insolation than the tropics; seasonal temperature swings of tens of degrees make continental interiors uninhabitable for large multicellular organisms and destroy any stable agricultural regime. Laskar's models give "a high probability to reach obliquities as high as 90 degrees within a few billion years".

severity_tiers.label: Compounded with the luminosity ramp
severity_tiers.description: The chaotic-obliquity transition at ~1.5 Gyr arrives at almost exactly the same epoch as the CO2/thermal collapse of the land biosphere (1.0-1.86 Gyr). The two are not independent: violent obliquity-driven climate swings on an already CO2-starved, overheating planet remove the high-latitude refugia that O'Malley-James et al. identify as the last habitat. This coincidence is the single most important structural fact in the deep-time block.

key_parameters.label: Lunar recession rate
key_parameters.effect: Directly measured: 38.30 plus or minus 0.09 mm/yr from lunar laser ranging (Williams et al. 2016, as reported by Maeder & Gueorguiev 2021). Sets the clock for the whole hazard. Reducing it delays the chaotic-zone entry roughly proportionally. Note the rate is NOT constant: it is set by ocean tidal dissipation, which is strongly dependent on continental configuration and on how near the ocean basins are to tidal resonance — the present value is high compared with the long-term geological average, so a simulator that extrapolates it linearly will get the date wrong.

key_parameters.label: Earth's obliquity
key_parameters.effect: Laskar: "At present, the average obliquity of the Earth is 23.25 degrees, and the obliquity oscillates around this value with 40 kyr periods and 1.3 degrees amplitude." Inside the chaotic zone the accessible range becomes 0 to more than 85 degrees. The climate consequence is highly non-linear: below about 54 degrees the equator receives more annual insolation than the poles; above it the ordering inverts and the planet's climate zones turn inside out.

key_parameters.label: Time until spin enters the chaotic zone
key_parameters.effect: Neron de Surgy & Laskar (1997): "After about 1.5 Gyr, the precession period of the Earth becomes comparable to the precession periods of the orbital plane of the Earth, due to planetary perturbations. The Earth then enters a large chaotic zone and the spin axis wanders chaotically between 0 and more than 85 degrees." The 1.5-4.5 Gyr spread in the derived literature reflects uncertainty in the tidal-dissipation history, not in the celestial mechanics.

key_parameters.label: Rate of increase of length of day
key_parameters.effect: The other side of the same angular-momentum ledger. Maeder & Gueorguiev report 1.78 ms/cy as the mean rate derived by Stephenson et al. (2016) from ancient eclipse records, against 1.09 ms/cy from lunar occultations and IERS data over 1680-2020. That the two do not agree — "the observed lunar recession appears too large when compared to the tidal slowing down of the Earth determined from eclipses" — is an open problem and the main reason the recession rate cannot simply be extrapolated.

cascades_into: deep-time-co2-starvation-land-plants: the ~1.5 Gyr chaos onset coincides with the 1.0-1.86 Gyr land-plant collapse and removes the climatic stability that any surviving refugium depends on

hazards.uncertainty_notes: Schedule, not risk — but with genuine dynamical uncertainty on top, which is unusual for this block. Three separable quantities: (a) P(the Moon keeps receding) = 1, this is angular-momentum bookkeeping; (b) P(the spin enters the chaotic zone) is essentially 1, but the DATE has a factor-three spread (1.5 to 4.5 Gyr) because it depends on the integrated tidal-dissipation history, which depends on plate tectonics and ocean-basin resonance over billions of years and is not predictable; (c) P(a large obliquity excursion actually occurs, and when) is genuinely probabilistic, because inside a chaotic zone only a diffusion rate can be quoted, not a trajectory. Laskar's own framing is "a high probability to reach obliquities as high as 90 degrees within a few billion years", which is a statement about a distribution, not a schedule. A serious critic would make two attacks. First, the present recession rate of 38.30 mm/yr is anomalously high relative to the geological average — if it were the long-term rate the Moon would have been at Earth's surface only ~1.5 Gyr ago, which contradicts the geological record — because the current ocean basins happen to sit near a tidal resonance. Any extrapolation using the present rate is therefore wrong in a known direction, and I have not corrected for it. Second, Maeder & Gueorguiev document an unresolved inconsistency between the LLR-derived recession and the eclipse-derived length-of-day change (1.09 vs 1.78 ms/cy), which they explicitly leave open. My 'low' bound of 2.2 x 10^-10 corresponds to the 4.5 Gyr end of the literature range; the 'best' uses Laskar's own 1.5 Gyr.

hazards.name: Milky Way - Andromeda collision and merger
hazards.one_line: HST proper motions show M31 is on a nearly radial orbit toward the Milky Way; first pericentre in 3.87 billion years and merger in 5.86 billion years, with essentially no direct threat to Earth.
hazards.mechanism: M31's transverse velocity, measured directly for the first time by comparing HST ACS/WFC and WFC3/UVIS images over five to seven year baselines, is consistent with zero — the orbit is nearly radial. The galaxies fall together, pass at a first pericentre of about 31 kiloparsecs, and merge into a single elliptical remnant. This is the one entry in the deep-time block with almost no mechanism for mass death: interstellar distances are so large relative to stellar diameters that direct stellar collisions are negligible. The real effects are dynamical — the Sun's galactocentric radius changes, with an 85% probability of ending up further out and a 10% probability of ending beyond 50 kpc, potentially in a tidal tail. Second-order consequences are a burst of star formation from compressed gas, hence more nearby supernovae and a raised cosmic-ray background, and a possible reactivation of the central black holes as active galactic nuclei. By the merger epoch Earth's surface has been sterile for roughly 3 Gyr, so for a biosphere this event arrives long after the funeral.

annual_probability.event_definition: CERTAINTY, NOT RISK. Merger of the Milky Way and M31 into a single remnant. Date: 5.86 (+1.61 / -0.72) Gyr from now, with first pericentre at 3.87 (+0.42 / -0.32) Gyr and pericentre distance 31.0 (+38.0 / -19.8) kpc. Probability expressed as 1 divided by the years remaining to merger.
annual_probability.trend: Fixed by measured kinematics. The uncertainty is dominated by the Local Group mass and by the M31 transverse velocity measurement, both of which will tighten with Gaia and further HST/JWST astrometry — indeed later Gaia eDR3 work has confirmed the nearly radial orbit. The date will move by hundreds of Myr as the mass estimate refines, not by Gyr.

severity_tiers.label: Merger occurs, Earth unaffected directly
severity_tiers.description: The galaxies merge. Stellar densities are so low that direct stellar collisions are negligible. The Sun most likely (p = 85%) ends up at larger galactocentric radius than today, possibly beyond 50 kpc (p = 10%), potentially in a tidal tail. No direct kill mechanism. This is the overwhelmingly likely outcome and the reason this hazard belongs on a scale bar rather than a risk register.

severity_tiers.label: Elevated supernova and AGN environment
severity_tiers.description: Gas compression during the merger triggers a starburst; the increased local supernova rate and the possible reactivation of the merged central black hole as an AGN raise the ionising radiation and cosmic-ray flux at the Sun's location. On a planet with an atmosphere and a biosphere this would strip ozone and elevate mutation rates. Earth by then has neither. Included because a simulator that carries humanity forward artificially needs the branch.

key_parameters.label: Time to merger
key_parameters.effect: Directly from van der Marel et al. (2012): "the MW and M31 will merge t = 5.86 (+1.61 -0.72) Gyr from now". The asymmetric error is the honest one; a simulator should not symmetrise it. Note this is AFTER the Sun's tip-RGB phase at 7.59 Gyr? No — it is before it, by 1.7 Gyr, which is a useful ordering fact: the galaxies merge while the Sun is still on the main sequence.

key_parameters.label: Time to first pericentre passage
key_parameters.effect: "a first pericenter at t = 3.87 (+0.42 -0.32) Gyr". This is the first observable event and the point at which the two disks first distort each other visibly. Tighter constrained than the merger time because it depends less on the poorly-known Local Group mass.

key_parameters.label: First pericentre distance
key_parameters.effect: "at a pericenter distance of r = 31.0 (+38.0 -19.8) kpc". The huge fractional uncertainty is the direct consequence of the M31 transverse velocity being consistent with zero. Van der Marel et al. give a 41% probability of a first-pericentre distance less than 25 kpc, which they define as a direct hit; the merger happens either way, only the number of pericentre passages changes.

key_parameters.label: Probability the Sun ends at larger galactocentric radius
key_parameters.effect: "The Sun will most likely (p=85%) end up at larger radius from the center of the MW-M31 merger remnant than its current distance from the MW center", and "possibly further than 50 kpc (p=10%)". A larger radius means lower ambient stellar density and a lower supernova rate — i.e. the most likely dynamical outcome for the Sun is marginally SAFER, not more dangerous.

cascades_into: deep-time-end-of-star-formation: the merger consumes the Local Group's cold gas in a starburst and accelerates the local approach to the end of the stelliferous era
hazards.uncertainty_notes: Schedule, not risk, and unusually the least dangerous entry in the whole packet — this is the item people find most frightening and it is the one with the smallest kill mechanism, which is exactly why a scale-bar page needs it. Distinguish carefully: P(the merger happens) is essentially 1 on the measured nearly-radial orbit; P(it kills anyone) is close to 0 because interstellar distances make direct stellar collisions negligible; P(permanent extinction) is 0. The uncertainties are honest and large: the transverse velocity of M31 is consistent with ZERO, which is why the pericentre distance carries a +38/-20 kpc error, and the merger time depends on the total Local Group mass, which is itself derived from the same measurement. The asymmetric error bars are physical (a more radial orbit merges sooner) and must not be symmetrised. A serious critic would note that these are 2012 numbers and that Gaia eDR3 astrometry has since revisited the M31 proper motion — the later work confirms the nearly radial orbit, so the conclusion is robust, but the specific timings will shift by hundreds of Myr as the Local Group mass estimate refines. I did not retrieve the Gaia eDR3 result in full this session, only its title and the confirmation of a nearly radial orbit, so I have not used its numbers.

hazards.name: The Sun's red-giant phase and the engulfment of Earth
hazards.one_line: The Sun reaches the tip of the red giant branch 7.59 billion years from now, shedding 0.332 solar masses, and Earth does not escape engulfment despite the orbital expansion that mass loss produces.
hazards.mechanism: After core hydrogen exhaustion the Sun ascends the red giant branch, its radius growing by two orders of magnitude while it sheds mass in a strong wind. Mass loss weakens the Sun's gravitational hold and Earth's orbit expands — the naive expectation is therefore that Earth escapes. Schroeder and Connon Smith's coupled calculation shows it does not: tidal interaction with the giant's envelope, plus dynamical drag in the lower chromosphere, removes orbital angular momentum faster than the mass loss adds it, and Earth spirals in. Their result is that a planet needs a present-day orbital radius of about 1.15 AU to survive the tip-RGB phase; Earth at 1.00 AU falls short. Nothing dies of famine here because nothing is alive: the surface has been sterile for roughly 4.8 Gyr by this date, since the end of life at ~2.8 Gyr. The planet itself is destroyed, evaporating in the giant's envelope. This is the terminal event for Earth as a physical object, distinct from the terminal event for Earth as a habitat, and the two are separated by nearly five billion years.

annual_probability.event_definition: CERTAINTY, NOT RISK. The Sun reaches the tip of the red giant branch and engulfs the Earth. Date: 7.59 Gyr from now (Schroeder & Connon Smith 2008). Probability expressed as 1 divided by the years remaining.
annual_probability.trend: Fixed by stellar structure. Standard solar models agree on the main-sequence lifetime to within a few percent; the tip-RGB timing is one of the better-determined numbers in this packet. The uncertain part is not WHEN but WHETHER Earth survives, and that hinges on the tidal and drag prescriptions.

severity_tiers.label: Habitable zone leaves Earth (long prior)
severity_tiers.description: Long before the red giant phase, rising luminosity has already ended the biosphere. By tip-RGB Earth has been lifeless for roughly 4.8 Gyr. This tier exists to mark that the famous 'the Sun will swallow the Earth' event is not the end of life on Earth and is not even close to it.

severity_tiers.label: Engulfment and destruction of the planet
severity_tiers.description: Earth spirals into the giant's chromosphere under tidal drag and is evaporated. The planet ceases to exist as a body. Schroeder & Connon Smith: "planet Earth will not be able to escape engulfment, despite the positive effect of solar mass-loss".

severity_tiers.label: Marginal survival
severity_tiers.description: If tidal dissipation in the giant envelope is weaker than modelled, or if mass loss is stronger than the assumed rate, Earth's orbit could expand past the engulfment radius and the planet survives as a charred rock orbiting a white dwarf. Schroeder & Connon Smith's own criterion — a present orbital radius of about 1.15 AU to survive — places Earth 15% inside the boundary, close enough that the modelling assumptions matter.

key_parameters.label: Time to tip of the red giant branch
key_parameters.effect: Schroeder & Connon Smith (2008): the mass lost as an RGB giant "will be 0.332 M_Sun, occurring 7.59 Gyr from now". Sets the outer clock for the solar system. Scales roughly with the main-sequence lifetime, which goes as M^-2.5 in stellar mass — but the Sun's mass is known to far better precision than any other input here.

key_parameters.label: Solar mass lost on the red giant branch
key_parameters.effect: The parameter that decides Earth's fate, and it pulls both ways. More mass loss means a weaker gravitational hold and a wider Earth orbit (helps survival), but also a denser and more extended envelope for the Earth to drag through (hurts). Schroeder & Connon Smith's coupled treatment finds the drag wins at 0.332 M_Sun.

key_parameters.label: Minimum present orbital radius to survive tip-RGB
key_parameters.effect: The decision boundary. Schroeder & Connon Smith: "about 1.15 AU" is needed for a hypothetical planet to survive the tip-RGB phase. Earth is at 1.00 AU, i.e. 15% inside. Any simulator should expose this as the single knob that flips Earth's fate, and should show how narrow the margin is: a 15% error in the drag prescription reverses the answer.

key_parameters.label: Time until the Sun exhausts core hydrogen
key_parameters.effect: Buttazzo et al. use this as their yardstick for 'a significant astrophysical age': "the sun will exhaust its fuel in about five billion years". Useful in a simulator as the reference against which every exotic-physics lifetime is compared — the vacuum's 10^139 yr exceeds it by 129 orders of magnitude.

cascades_into: deep-time-end-of-star-formation: the Sun's death is one instance of the process that, repeated across all stars, defines the end of the stelliferous era
hazards.uncertainty_notes: Schedule, not risk. Three separable quantities and they differ enormously: P(the Sun becomes a red giant at 7.59 Gyr) is essentially 1 and the date is good to a few percent; P(Earth is engulfed given the red-giant phase) is the genuinely uncertain one — Schroeder & Connon Smith say yes, but earlier work using mass loss alone said Earth escapes, and the difference is entirely in the tidal-dissipation and chromospheric-drag prescriptions, which are calibrated on very little data; P(this ends humanity) is not meaningful because the surface has been sterile for ~4.8 Gyr by then. A serious critic would attack the tidal prescription: the drag calculation depends on the density structure of the giant's extended envelope and on a tidal quality factor for a convective envelope that is uncertain by more than an order of magnitude, and Earth sits only 15% inside the survival boundary of 1.15 AU. That is well within the modelling uncertainty, so 'Earth is destroyed' should be reported as the current best answer, not as settled. I was only able to retrieve the abstract of Schroeder & Connon Smith, not the full text, so I have no figure for the Sun's radius at tip-RGB and none for the fates of Venus and Mars — those are absent rather than estimated. Finally, note the ordering fact that popular accounts get wrong: the Andromeda merger (5.86 Gyr) happens BEFORE the red-giant phase (7.59 Gyr), and the end of life on Earth (~2.8 Gyr) happens before both.

hazards.name: End of star formation and the close of the Stelliferous Era
hazards.one_line: Conventional star formation and stellar evolution both end around 10^14 years from now, when the supply of interstellar gas is exhausted and the longest-lived low-mass stars finally fade.
hazards.mechanism: Galaxies convert gas to stars, and stars lock most of their mass permanently into degenerate remnants. The gas reservoir is therefore drawn down and not fully returned. Adams and Laughlin's calculations follow the very low-mass M-type stars that dominate the stellar mass function: stars near 0.1 solar masses never experience a red giant phase at all, instead growing steadily brighter and bluer, reaching a maximum luminosity and then a maximum temperature before fading as helium white dwarfs. Their main-sequence lifetimes reach roughly 10^13 years. At times exceeding one to ten trillion years the interstellar gas supply is exhausted, though star formation continues at a highly attenuated level through collisions between brown dwarfs. Both conventional star formation and the last conventional stars terminate together at cosmological decade eta = 14, i.e. 10^14 years. There is no kill mechanism to describe: any life at this epoch has long since had to survive on something other than starlight, and the event marks the closing of the only large-scale free-energy source the universe has offered so far.

annual_probability.event_definition: CERTAINTY, NOT RISK. Conventional star formation and conventional stellar evolution both end. Date: cosmological decade eta = 14, i.e. 10^14 years from now (Adams & Laughlin 1997), where eta is defined as log10 of the time in years and the present epoch is eta = 10. Probability expressed as 1 divided by the years remaining.
annual_probability.trend: Falling in absolute terms and already far past its peak. The cosmic star-formation rate density peaked around redshift 2 and has been declining ever since; the trend over the next 10^14 years is monotonic exhaustion. Galaxy mergers such as Milky Way-Andromeda cause brief starbursts that consume the remaining cold gas faster, bringing the end marginally forward rather than delaying it.

severity_tiers.label: Gas exhaustion, attenuated star formation
severity_tiers.description: "At times exceeding ~1-10 trillion years, the supply of interstellar gas will be exhausted, yet star formation will continue at a highly attenuated level via collisions between brown dwarfs." The night sky empties over trillions of years. Any surviving civilisation must already be running on stellar remnants, black-hole accretion, or proton decay rather than fusion.

severity_tiers.label: End of the Stelliferous Era
severity_tiers.description: At eta = 14 the last conventional stars leave the main sequence and no new ones form by conventional means. Adams & Laughlin: "The era of conventional stars in the universe is confined to the range 6 < eta < 14." Energy generation shifts to proton decay and particle annihilation in the Degenerate Era, 15 < eta < 37.

key_parameters.label: Cosmological decade at which star formation ends
key_parameters.effect: Adams & Laughlin: "Both stellar evolution and conventional star formation come to an end at the cosmological decade eta ~ 14. This time scale only slightly exceeds the longest evolution time for a low mass star. It also corresponds to the time at which the galaxy runs out of raw material (gas) for producing new stars." The present epoch is eta = 10, so this is 10,000 times the current age of the universe. Note the logarithmic axis: a simulator that plots deep time linearly cannot show this block at all.

key_parameters.label: Current cosmological decade
key_parameters.effect: "the current age of the universe corresponds to eta ~ 10". This is the anchor for the whole logarithmic scale bar: everything from the Planck time (eta = -50) to the Dark Era (eta > 100) fits on one axis 150 decades wide, and Adams & Laughlin note "the ebb and flow of events is dispersed quite evenly across a hundred and fifty orders of magnitude in time".

key_parameters.label: Cosmological decades of brown-dwarf-collision star formation
key_parameters.effect: "this mode of star formation will be the leading source of new stars for cosmological decades in the range 15 < eta < 23". A residual trickle of stars persists a billion times longer than conventional star formation, but at a rate too low to matter energetically. Also at eta ~ 19: "most of the stars will leave the system" through stellar evaporation from the galaxy.

key_parameters.label: Fraction of the galaxy left in its central black hole
key_parameters.effect: "Some fraction (we roughly estimate ~0.01-0.10) of the galaxy is left behind in its central black hole." This is the mass that survives into the Black Hole Era; the other 90-99% is evaporated into intergalactic space as isolated remnants. It sets the mass, and hence the evaporation time, of the last objects in the universe.

cascades_into: deep-time-black-hole-evaporation: the remnants left when star formation ends are the objects that go on to decay through proton decay and Hawking radiation
hazards.uncertainty_notes: Schedule, not risk, and the units are the point: eta = 14 means 10^14 years, which is ten thousand times the present age of the universe. The 'deaths fraction' of 1.0 is formally correct but semantically odd — there is no population to kill; the tier exists to place the event on a common axis, and any page displaying it must say so. This is a 1997 paper and it predates the discovery of dark energy's dominance, which is its main weakness: an accelerating universe strips galaxy clusters of their surroundings, freezes structure formation, and isolates the Local Group, which changes the gas-supply history in ways Adams & Laughlin only treat speculatively in section V.E. A serious critic would say the eta = 14 figure is robust because it is set by low-mass stellar lifetimes (which are pure stellar physics), while the gas-exhaustion argument is much softer because it depends on galactic recycling efficiency and on whether accreted intergalactic gas continues to arrive. Adams & Laughlin themselves say so: "the stated time scales must therefore be viewed as approximate" and "parts of our current time line will undergo dramatic revision as physical understanding improves". My low/high bounds of eta = 13 to 15 are one decade either side, which is my own bracket and should be marked as such; the paper quotes no error bar.

hazards.name: Proton decay, black hole evaporation, and the Dark Era
hazards.one_line: Degenerate remnants decay through proton decay around 10^37 years, stellar-mass black holes evaporate by Hawking radiation around 10^65 years, and beyond 10^100 years nothing is left but photons, neutrinos, electrons and positrons.
hazards.mechanism: After the last stars fade, the universe's baryonic mass is locked in brown dwarfs, white dwarfs and neutron stars. If protons decay — the expected first-order lifetime corresponds to eta_P around 37, i.e. 10^37 years — these objects are slowly consumed from within: proton decay powers white dwarfs at luminosities of order 10^-12 solar, and the star gradually sublimates. Once the degenerate objects are gone, only black holes remain. Hawking radiation causes them to lose mass at a rate inversely proportional to the square of the mass, so evaporation time scales as M cubed: a stellar-mass hole takes about 10^65 years, and the supermassive holes at galactic centres, holding the 1-10% of galaxy mass that was not evaporated away, last until the close of the Black Hole Era at eta = 100. After that comes the Dark Era: "protons have decayed and black holes have evaporated. Only the waste products from these processes remain: mostly photons of colossal wavelength, neutrinos, electrons, and positrons." There is no kill mechanism; there is nothing left that could be killed.

annual_probability.event_definition: CERTAINTY, NOT RISK. Evaporation of stellar-mass black holes by Hawking radiation. Date: cosmological decade eta_BH ~ 65, i.e. 10^65 years from now. The 'high' bound is first-order proton decay at eta_P ~ 37 (10^37 yr, the earlier milestone); the 'low' bound is the close of the Black Hole Era at eta = 100 (10^100 yr), when the largest black holes are gone. Probability expressed as 1 divided by the years remaining.
annual_probability.trend: Flat. These are decay constants, not rates that respond to anything. The only live question is empirical: whether the proton decays at all. Current experimental searches set a firm lower bound and no definitive upper limit exists.

severity_tiers.label: Proton decay era
severity_tiers.description: At eta_P ~ 37 first-order proton decay destroys the degenerate remnants. White dwarfs powered by proton decay shine at luminosities around 10^-12 solar; their mass falls, they expand, and once below about 10^-3 solar masses they are lifted out of degeneracy. Adams & Laughlin: "if the proton does decay, a large fraction of the universe will be in the form of proton decay products (neutrinos, photons, positrons, etc.) for times eta > 35."

severity_tiers.label: Black hole evaporation
severity_tiers.description: At eta_BH ~ 65 a stellar-mass black hole has evaporated entirely by Hawking radiation. Adams & Laughlin give the ordering eta_P << eta_BH << eta_P2, with eta_P ~ 37 for first-order proton decay, eta_BH ~ 65 for a stellar-sized black hole to evaporate, and eta_P2 ~ 100-200 for proton decay through higher-order processes. Black holes dominate energy and entropy production over 36 < eta < 100.

severity_tiers.label: The Dark Era
severity_tiers.description: Beyond eta = 100. "At this late time, protons have decayed and black holes have evaporated. Only the waste products from these processes remain: mostly photons of colossal wavelength, neutrinos, electrons, and positrons." This is the terminal state on the standard picture, and it is the far end of the axis this packet is built to display.

key_parameters.label: Cosmological decade of first-order proton decay
key_parameters.effect: Adams & Laughlin Eq. (6.1): "32 < eta_P < 49 + 76(N - 1)", where N is the order of the process, giving eta_P < 201 for the third-order case. "Quantum gravity effects also lead to proton decay with time scales in the range 46 < eta_P < 169. Finally, sphalerons imply eta_P ~ 140." The firm lower bound comes from current experimental searches; there is no definitive upper limit. Whether the proton decays at all is the single largest open question in this block: "If the proton is stable to first order decay processes, then stellar objects in general and white dwarfs in particular can live in the range of cosmological decades eta < 100."

key_parameters.label: Cosmological decade for a stellar-mass black hole to evaporate
key_parameters.effect: Adams & Laughlin Eq. (6.2): eta_P << eta_BH << eta_P2 with "eta_BH ~ 65 is the time scale for a stellar-sized black hole to evaporate". Hawking evaporation time scales as the cube of the mass, so a black hole 10^8 times more massive lasts 10^24 times longer — which is exactly why the Black Hole Era extends to eta = 100 rather than stopping at 65. In a simulator, mass is the only knob and it enters cubed.

key_parameters.label: Cosmological decade at which the Dark Era begins
key_parameters.effect: "The Black Hole Era. 38 < eta < 100... The Dark Era. eta > 100." This is the end of the axis. Adams & Laughlin add the important caveat that this apparent poverty "is perhaps more due to the difficulties inherent in extrapolating far enough into the future, rather than an actual dearth of physical processes" — i.e. eta = 100 is where the model stops, not necessarily where events stop.

key_parameters.label: Cosmological decade of halo WIMP annihilation
key_parameters.effect: An intermediate energy source between the stars and the black holes. "the WIMPs in the halo annihilate on the time scale eta ~ 23. On the other hand, white dwarfs can capture WIMPs and thereby deplete the halo on the somewhat longer time scale eta ~ 25. The phenomenon of WIMP capture indicates that white dwarf cooling will be arrested rather shortly at a luminosity L ~ 10^-12 L_sun." Depends entirely on dark matter being a WIMP, which is far from established.
