cascades_into: deep-time-heat-death-vs-big-rip: whether the Dark Era is the true end state depends entirely on the dark-energy equation of state
hazards.uncertainty_notes: Schedule, not risk, and the deepest extrapolation in the packet — Adams & Laughlin themselves flag it: "The article of faith inherent in our discussion is that the laws of physics are constant in time, at least over the range of time scales 10 < eta < 100 under consideration. There is no general guarantee that this assumption holds." Three things must be kept separate. (a) P(protons decay at all): unknown. Experimental searches give a firm lower bound on the lifetime and no definitive upper limit; if the proton is absolutely stable, the Degenerate Era extends to eta < 100 and the whole ordering shifts. This is not a small uncertainty, it is a live experimental question, and Adams & Laughlin list it first among their open issues. (b) P(black holes evaporate): high confidence theoretically — LSAG note "broad consensus among physicists on the reality of Hawking radiation" — but they also note "no experiment has had the sensitivity required to find direct evidence for it". Hawking radiation has never been observed. The two most important numbers in this hazard both rest on unobserved physics. (c) P(the Dark Era is terminal): depends on the black-hole information question and on the dark-energy equation of state; Adams & Laughlin explicitly leave open whether "interesting things can continue to happen at the increasingly low levels of energy and entropy available in the universe of the future". A serious critic would also note that this is a 1997 paper written before dark-energy domination was established, and that an accelerating universe changes both the horizon structure and the entropy accounting substantially. My min/max brackets on the eta values are my own one-to-few-decade brackets around Adams & Laughlin's central figures; the paper quotes ranges only for proton decay.

hazards.name: Heat death versus Big Rip: the dark-energy end state
hazards.one_line: Whether the universe ends in cold dilution or is torn apart in a Big Rip depends on the dark-energy equation of state, and DESI DR2 gives a 2.8 to 4.2 sigma preference for evolving dark energy that was phantom in the past but is not phantom now.
hazards.mechanism: The dark-energy equation of state w = P/rho decides the terminal geometry. For w >= -1 the dark-energy density is constant or dilutes, the universe expands forever, structures already gravitationally bound remain bound, and the end state is cold and empty — heat death, reached asymptotically. For w < -1 (phantom energy) the dark-energy density grows with time; the quantity -(rho + 3P) increases without bound, and at a finite time every gravitationally bound system is torn apart in order of decreasing binding energy: clusters, then galaxies, then planetary orbits, then planets, then molecules, then atoms, then nuclei. The kill mechanism for a Big Rip is unusually literal and unusually fast — Caldwell, Kamionkowski & Weinberg's timeline for w = -3/2 has the Earth ripped from the Sun three months before the end, the Earth itself falling apart thirty minutes before, and atoms dissociating in the last 10^-19 seconds. Nobody starves. The current data disfavour this branch: DESI DR2 finds w0 > -1 and wa < 0, meaning the equation of state was phantom-like in the distant past and has since crossed to w > -1, which points to heat death rather than a rip.

annual_probability.event_definition: CERTAINTY OF SOME END STATE, uncertain which. Big Rip, conditional on a constant phantom equation of state w = -3/2 with H0 = 70 km/s/Mpc: 22 Gyr from now (35 Gyr from the Big Bang), giving 1/2.2e10 = 4.5e-11 per year. If w >= -1, or if w evolves as DESI DR2 indicates, there is no rip and the probability is exactly 0 — hence the 'low' bound.
annual_probability.trend: Under active revision, and this is the most volatile number in the packet. DESI DR2 (2025) reports a 3.1 sigma preference for evolving dark energy from BAO+CMB, rising to 2.8-4.2 sigma with supernovae, favouring the quadrant w0 > -1 and wa < 0 — i.e. AWAY from the phantom branch at the present epoch. If that holds, the Big Rip probability falls toward zero. The result is contested (see uncertainty notes).

severity_tiers.label: Heat death / cosmological dilution
severity_tiers.description: If w >= -1 at all times, the expansion continues, galaxies beyond the Local Group cross the cosmological event horizon and disappear, and the universe becomes cold, dark and empty. Adams & Laughlin note that a continually expanding universe never reaches true thermodynamic equilibrium, so classical heat death is avoided; what is reached is 'cosmological heat death', a state with constant entropy in a comoving volume and no ability to do physical work. This is the branch the DESI data currently favour.

severity_tiers.label: Big Rip
severity_tiers.description: If w < -1 persists, phantom-energy density grows without bound and everything is dissociated at a finite time. Caldwell, Kamionkowski & Weinberg's Table I for w = -3/2 gives the full sequence: galaxy clusters erased at t_rip - 1 Gyr; the Milky Way destroyed at t_rip - 60 Myr; the solar system unbound at t_rip - 3 months; Earth explodes at t_rip - 30 minutes; atoms dissociated at t_rip - 10^-19 s; Big Rip at t_rip = 35 Gyr from the Big Bang, i.e. 22 Gyr from now.

severity_tiers.label: Phantom crossing without a rip
severity_tiers.description: DESI DR2's actual best fit: the equation of state was phantom (w < -1) in the past, crossed the phantom divide at redshift z_c around 0.45, and is now w > -1. A past phantom phase does not produce a rip; only a persistent future one does. This branch has the universe expanding forever without dissociation, and is the current front-runner.

key_parameters.label: Present-day dark-energy equation of state
key_parameters.effect: The master switch for the universe's end state. w0 < -1 opens the Big Rip branch; w0 >= -1 closes it. The min/max are DESI's own flat prior, U[-3, 1] (their Table I). DESI DR2's combined data "favor the region w0 > -1 and wa < 0, away from a cosmological constant" — i.e. the Big Rip branch is disfavoured by current data, which is the single most important recent change to this hazard.

key_parameters.label: Evolution parameter of the equation of state (CPL)
key_parameters.effect: In the CPL parametrisation w(a) = w0 + wa(1 - a). wa = 0 recovers a constant w. DESI's prior is U[-3, 2] with the additional physical requirement w0 + wa < 0 to enforce a period of high-redshift matter domination. DESI DR2 favours wa < 0, meaning w rises with time — a universe becoming LESS phantom, which moves it away from a rip. This parameter is what turns a static question about the end state into a dynamic one.

key_parameters.label: Time remaining to the Big Rip for w = -3/2
key_parameters.effect: Caldwell, Kamionkowski & Weinberg: "for w = -3/2 and H0 = 70 km sec^-1 Mpc^-1, the time remaining before the Universe ends in this 'Big Rip' is 22 Gyr." The general formula they give is t_rip - t0 = (2/3)|1 + w|^-1 H0^-1 (1 - Omega_m)^-1/2, so the rip time diverges as w approaches -1 from below and shrinks as w becomes more negative. This is the one place in the packet where the equation is simple enough for a simulator to compute the date live from the slider.

key_parameters.label: Redshift at which w crosses the phantom divide
key_parameters.effect: DESI DR2: "before reaching its maximum (at z_c ~ 0.45, in our case), when the equation of state crosses the phantom line (w(z_c) = -1)". A crossing in the past with w > -1 today is the no-rip scenario. DESI caution that "the exact redshift at which this crossing happens depends on the dataset combination under consideration", and that a single-field dark energy component with w < -1 "would necessarily violate the null energy condition", so if the crossing is real it implies a substantially more complex dark sector.

citations.claim: Cosmological heat death is postponed until after the Dark Era, and is distinct from classical heat death.
citations.authors: Fred C. Adams and Gregory Laughlin
citations.venue: Reviews of Modern Physics 69, 337-372 (arXiv:astro-ph/9701131), section VI.D
citations.exact_figure: "A continually expanding universe never reaches true thermodynamic equilibrium and hence never reaches a constant temperature. Classical heat death is thus manifestly avoided. However, the expansion can, in principle, become purely adiabatic so that the entropy in a given comoving volume of the universe approaches (or attains) a constant value. In this case, the universe can still become a dull and lifeless place with no ability to do physical work. We denote this latter possibility as cosmological heat death."

cascades_into: deep-time-black-hole-evaporation-dark-era: the heat-death branch hands off to the Dark Era at eta > 100; the Big Rip branch truncates the timeline at 22 Gyr and the Dark Era never happens
hazards.uncertainty_notes: This is the least settled entry in the packet and the one most likely to be wrong within five years. Three distinct quantities, routinely conflated in popular coverage: (a) P(dark energy is dynamical rather than a cosmological constant): DESI DR2 says 3.1 sigma from BAO+CMB and 2.8-4.2 sigma with supernovae — evidence, not discovery, and the claim is contested; (b) P(w < -1 TODAY, which is what a Big Rip requires): currently disfavoured, since DESI's preferred quadrant is w0 > -1; a phantom PAST does not produce a rip; (c) P(the universe ends in a rip at a specific date): only meaningful conditional on a constant w < -1, which is precisely the model DESI's data disfavour. Conflating (a) with (c) — reading 'evidence for evolving dark energy' as 'evidence for a Big Rip' — is the single most common error in reporting on this result, and it points the wrong way. I could NOT retrieve the point estimates of w0 and wa with uncertainties from a primary source this session: I fetched the DESI DR2 key paper abstract, its HTML, and the extended dark-energy analysis in full, and none of the sections I reached carried the constraint table. I have therefore reported no w0/wa central values and no error bars, rather than repeat figures I saw only in a search-engine summary. That is a real gap in this packet and should be filled from the DESI DR2 key paper's dark energy section before the numbers are used. A serious critic would attack on several fronts: the significance depends on which supernova compilation is used (2.8 sigma with Pantheon+ vs 4.2 sigma with DES Y5, a spread that is itself suspicious); arXiv:2504.15222 argues there are "clear tensions among the CMB, BAO and SN datasets" making the combination invalid; the CPL parametrisation w0 + wa(1-a) may fail to capture the true w(z) and DESI themselves warn it "may fail to accurately approximate the true behavior of w(z) itself, potentially leading to a spurious indication of phantom crossing"; and a phantom crossing would violate the null energy condition for any single-field dark energy, which is a strong theoretical prior against it. The 0.15 probability I assign to the Big Rip branch is an AUTHOR-ESTIMATE reflecting these tensions, not a published posterior.

hazards.name: Extreme geomagnetic storm (Carrington-class) and grid collapse via geomagnetically induced currents
hazards.one_line: A coronal mass ejection drives a geomagnetic storm whose induced ground currents destroy extra-high-voltage transformers faster than they can be manufactured.
hazards.mechanism: A fast coronal mass ejection with a strongly southward magnetic field reconnects with Earth's magnetosphere, driving a large ring current (measured as a deeply negative Dst) and violent ionospheric electrojets. The rapidly changing magnetic field induces a horizontal geoelectric field at the ground; long conductors — transmission lines, pipelines, cables — integrate that field into quasi-DC geomagnetically induced currents (GIC) that flow into transformer neutrals. GIC drives the transformer core into half-cycle saturation, so magnetic flux leaks out of the core and heats structural steel and windings that were never designed to carry current; Lloyd's/AER model winding hot spots exceeding the IEEE 180 degC guideline, and also model cumulative insulation loss-of-life in units that stay below it. The saturation simultaneously injects harmonics and draws enormous reactive power, which is what actually tripped Hydro-Quebec in under two minutes in March 1989. Nobody dies of the current. Death, if it comes, comes from the replacement queue: destroyed extra-high-voltage transformers are bespoke 150-400 tonne objects, and the DOE reported in July 2024 that 36-month acquisition lead times are commonly quoted with maxima reaching 60 months, so a region that loses a concentrated cluster of them loses refrigeration, water pumping, fuel distribution, sewage and medical care for months to years, and the killer is famine, thirst, cold and untreated disease.

annual_probability.event_definition: A geomagnetic storm striking Earth with minimum hourly Dst at or below about -850 nT — the Siscoe et al. (2006) benchmark value for the 2 September 1859 Carrington storm, and the threshold Riley (2012) used explicitly. NOT the probability of grid collapse, which is carried by the severity tiers below.
annual_probability.trend: The occurrence rate itself is flat to falling: Riley and Love (2017) note that 'if the current trends persist, suggesting that we are entering a period of lower activity, our forecasts may represent upper limits rather than best estimates.' Consequence severity is rising sharply, and that is where the century-scale trend lives. Transformer lead times have lengthened from the 5-12 months (domestic) / 6-16 months (international) that Lloyd's/AER used in 2013 to the 36-month typical / 60-month maximum DOE reported in 2024; the US large-power-transformer fleet averages 38-40 years against a ~40-year design life; and 82% of US large power transformer units were imported in 2019 — so a globally correlated event finds a globally correlated supply chain.

severity_tiers.label: Regional trip, hours to days
severity_tiers.description: Voltage collapse and protective-relay cascades take down one or more control areas; a handful of transformers are damaged but restoration is by reswitching, not replacement. The March 1989 Quebec storm (Dst -589 nT) is the calibration point: the grid collapsed in under two minutes, six million people lost power for nine hours, two transformers were damaged, and the economic cost was about C$13.2 billion.

severity_tiers.label: Multi-region transformer loss, weeks to months
severity_tiers.description: Order 10-20 extra-high-voltage transformers destroyed, but concentrated: Lloyd's/AER stress that concentration matters far more than count, because a few units serving a dense population produce a prolonged outage. Outage of weeks to months across parts of one continent; excess mortality from loss of heating and cooling, water treatment, dialysis and refrigerated medicine.

severity_tiers.label: Continental grid loss, 1-2 years
severity_tiers.description: The Lloyd's/AER extreme scenario: 20-40 million people in the United States alone at risk of extended outage, with durations of 16 days up to 1-2 years, and a modelled total economic cost of $0.6-2.6 trillion. The 2008 US National Research Council workshop report estimated '$1 trillion to $2 trillion during the first year alone ... with recovery times of 4-10 years'. At this tier, industrial food production, ammonia synthesis and fuel logistics fail across an industrialised region and famine becomes the dominant killer.

severity_tiers.label: Multi-continental industrial collapse
severity_tiers.description: Simultaneous concentrated transformer destruction across North America, Europe and East Asia, so the surviving manufacturing base cannot cross-supply. With ~343 large power transformers per year as the maximum US domestic capacity, replacing a multi-thousand-unit loss is a decade-scale project undertaken without reliable electricity. This tier is an extrapolation, not a modelled scenario — no published study models a globally correlated grid loss.

key_parameters.label: Storm intensity (minimum hourly Dst magnitude)
key_parameters.effect: Sets the driving geoelectric field, and hence GIC amplitude, roughly monotonically (though dB/dt, not Dst, is the direct driver — see uncertainty notes). Frequency falls very steeply with intensity: Cliver et al. (2022) report waiting times of 25-60 years (median 55) for Dst about -600 nT but 49-333 years (median 93) for Dst -850 nT. Observed and inferred extremes: -589 nT (March 1989, largest instrumented), -949 +/- 30 nT (September 1859), -907 +/- 132 nT (May 1921), about -1000 nT (February 1872); -1182 nT modelled for the July 2012 near-miss had it been Earth-directed; theoretical ceiling about -2000 to -2500 nT.

key_parameters.label: Replacement lead time for a large power transformer
key_parameters.effect: This single number converts a one-day event into a multi-year catastrophe, and outage duration is roughly linear in it once spares are exhausted. Lloyd's/AER (2013) assumed a minimum of five months and modelled 16 days to 1-2 years of outage; DOE (2024) reports '36-month lead times being commonly quoted and maximum lead times reaching as much as 60 months.' Moving this knob from 36 to 5 months moves the modal outcome from severity tier 3 to tier 2.

key_parameters.label: Maximum domestic large-power-transformer manufacturing capacity (US)
key_parameters.effect: Recovery time is approximately (transformers destroyed) divided by (usable capacity). The US Department of Commerce estimated a total maximum capacity of about 343 LPTs per year for domestic manufacturers at about 40 percent utilisation. In a globally correlated event, imports cannot be assumed, so this is the binding constraint for tiers 3 and 4.

key_parameters.label: Fraction of large power transformers sourced abroad
key_parameters.effect: In 2019, 137 LPTs (18 percent) were produced domestically for domestic use while 617 units (82 percent) were imported. A geomagnetic storm is a hemisphere-scale event, so the exporting countries are damaged too; the effective replacement rate in a correlated event collapses toward the domestic figure, and expected outage duration scales roughly as 1/(1 - import_share) relative to a nominal-market assumption.

key_parameters.label: Average age of the installed large-power-transformer fleet
key_parameters.effect: DOE (2024) reports the average age of LPTs in the North American grid at 38-40 years against a typical ~40-year design lifetime. Lloyd's/AER model pre-1972 and post-1972 populations separately because 1972 marks a change in GIC robustness of manufacture and design; the damaged fraction at a given GIC rises with pre-existing insulation degradation, so this knob multiplies the number of units lost at fixed storm size.

cascades_into: extreme-solar-particle-event: not a causal cascade but a shared cause — the same eruptions that drive extreme Dst also accelerate protons, so an extreme storm raises the conditional odds of a co-occurring particle event and the two should not be sampled independently

global-famine-and-infrastructure-collapse: identifier outside this packet — the actual killing pathway is loss of refrigeration, water pumping, fuel distribution and ammonia synthesis, not the storm itself
nuclear-reactor-station-blackout: identifier outside this packet — simultaneous loss of offsite power at many sites, with diesel resupply itself dependent on the grid
hazards.uncertainty_notes: (1) The single largest uncertainty is the tail distribution, not the data. Riley and Love (2017) get 10.3% per decade from a power law and 3.0% from a lognormal on the SAME data; a modeller who picks one without saying so is hiding a factor of 3.4. My 'best' of 8e-3/yr is a judgement between them, the Lloyd's/AER 150-year mid-point (6.7e-3/yr) and Cliver's 93-year median for Dst -850 nT (1.1e-2/yr); it is not itself a published figure. The low and high are the Riley and Love power-law 95% CI bounds converted to annual rates. (2) Dst is the wrong variable for the damage. GIC is driven by dB/dt and local ground conductivity, not by ring-current strength: the 1989 Quebec collapse happened at only -589 nT, and the 2003 Halloween storms destroyed twelve transformers in South Africa at about 40 degrees corrected geomagnetic latitude, a region normally assumed immune. A simulator keyed only to Dst will systematically mis-rank exposure. (3) The NRC (2008) figures of $1-2 trillion in the first year and 4-10 year recovery are quoted here from Cliver et al. (2022), because the primary NRC text could not be retrieved this session (nap.nationalacademies.org serves page images, not text). The underlying Metatech/Kappenman scenario of ~350 destroyed EHV transformers has been contested in the literature and I did not verify it. The widely-circulated '130 million people affected' figure I could NOT source primarily and have deliberately excluded from this packet. (4) There is NO peer-reviewed global mortality estimate for a grid-collapse scenario. Every deaths_fraction in the severity tiers is my own estimate, basis author-estimate, built by combining Lloyd's population-at-risk and outage-duration figures with a judgement about excess mortality; a serious critic would attack these first and would be right to. (5) Lloyd's/AER model only North America and only transformer damage, and their $0.6-2.6 trillion is a lost-load calculation ($2.00/kW residential, $19.38/kW commercial, $8.40/kW industrial in 2001 dollars scaled by 1.31), not a general-equilibrium loss. (6) I could not retrieve the NERC TPL-007 benchmark geoelectric field value (widely cited as 8 V/km at 60 degrees geomagnetic latitude) from a primary source this session, so it is deliberately absent from the parameters rather than asserted. (7) Probability of permanent human extinction from this hazard: I assign zero and mark no tier terminal. Nothing in the retrieved literature supports an extinction pathway from a geomagnetic storm.

hazards.name: Extreme solar particle event (Miyake-class)
hazards.one_line: A solar eruption accelerates protons to a fluence roughly ten times anything in the instrumental record, as recorded by the AD 774-775 and AD 993-994 radiocarbon spikes.
hazards.mechanism: An eruptive flare and its CME-driven shock accelerate protons to hundreds of MeV with a hard spectrum. The particles reach Earth in minutes to hours, are funnelled toward the poles, and produce a nuclear cascade in the atmosphere that makes cosmogenic radionuclides (14C, 10Be, 36Cl) — the archive that lets us see events predating instruments. The population-level radiation dose at the surface is not the killer: Earth's atmosphere is about 10 tonnes per square metre of shielding, and Thomas et al. (2013) found only moderate ozone depletion for the hard-spectrum cases consistent with AD 774, concluding explicitly that 'no mass extinction is implied'. What such an event destroys is everything outside the atmosphere and everything that depends on it: single-event upsets and hard failures across the satellite fleet (>200 MeV protons penetrate practical shielding), loss of GNSS timing and positioning, ionospheric absorption blacking out HF and polar aviation communications, and crew dose in orbit and on polar flights. Because timing, navigation and communication are load-bearing for electricity, finance and logistics, the plausible mass-casualty path is the same one as for a geomagnetic superstorm — cascading infrastructure failure ending in famine — and it is worse because the eruptions capable of a Miyake-class fluence are the same eruptions capable of an extreme geomagnetic storm.

annual_probability.event_definition: A solar energetic particle event with >30 MeV omnidirectional proton fluence F30 of at least 5x10^10 cm^-2 — the class containing the five Holocene events confirmed in cosmogenic radionuclide archives (7176 BC, 5259 BC, 660 BC, AD 774, AD 993). NOT the probability of any resulting catastrophe.
annual_probability.trend: Flat over the coming century on the available evidence. The five confirmed Holocene events show no clear clustering and the rate is estimated over an ~11,700-year archive, so a one-century trend is not resolvable. The consequence trend is steeply rising: exposure scales with satellites in orbit, with GNSS dependence of timing-critical infrastructure, and with polar aviation traffic — none of which existed in AD 774. Cliver et al. (2022) also warn the rate estimate itself may rise as the search continues: 'additional similar events may be found as the search continues.'

severity_tiers.label: Radiation-and-technology event, no ecological damage
severity_tiers.description: Hard-spectrum event as inferred for AD 774. A substantial fraction of the operational satellite fleet degraded or lost; GNSS unusable for hours to days and degraded for longer; HF and polar aviation communication blackout; measurable crew dose on polar flights and to anyone outside the magnetosphere. Moderate ozone depletion with elevated erythema and plant UV damage, but no extinction pressure. Ground infrastructure survives.

severity_tiers.label: Compound event: particles plus an extreme geomagnetic storm
severity_tiers.description: The same eruption sequence that delivers the particle fluence also delivers a fast, strongly southward ICME, so satellite and GNSS loss coincides with transformer damage on the ground. Loss of timing and navigation removes exactly the tools grid operators would use to manage a GIC event. This is the compound scenario the risk literature is worst at pricing.

severity_tiers.label: Soft-spectrum variant with severe ozone depletion
severity_tiers.description: Thomas et al. (2013) explicitly ruled out a very soft spectrum for AD 774 because it would have caused severe ozone depletion and biological impacts inconsistent with the record — but ruling it out for that event does not rule it out as a future possibility. A soft-spectrum event of comparable total fluence deposits energy lower in the stratosphere and drives much larger ozone loss, with multi-year agricultural and marine-productivity damage on top of the technological damage.

key_parameters.label: >30 MeV integral proton fluence
key_parameters.effect: The primary severity axis, and the rate falls far faster than a power law would suggest. Cliver et al. (2022): 'events with the F30 fluences of 10^10, 5 x 10^10 and 10^11 cm^-2 are expected to occur once per roughly a century, a millennium and 10^4 years, respectively' — a factor 10 in fluence costs roughly a factor 100 in rate. The current value is the largest DIRECTLY OBSERVED fluence, the composite 2, 4 and 7 August 1972 event at 8.4 x 10^9 cm^-2; the maximum is the AD 774 inferred value of about 10^11 cm^-2, i.e. the record event is roughly ten times anything instrumented.

key_parameters.label: Spectral hardness SI = log(F30/F200)
key_parameters.effect: Decides WHICH severity tier is reached at a given total fluence. AD 774 had SI of about 0.8 (Mekhaldi et al., via Cliver et al. 2022), comparable to the hardest known ground level enhancements (23 February 1956, SI = 1.0; 20 January 2005, about 1.2). Hard spectra put the energy high, penetrating deep into the atmosphere and into spacecraft, but produce only moderate ozone loss. Soft spectra deposit in the mid-stratosphere and drive severe ozone depletion — the case Thomas et al. (2013) rule out for AD 774 and which defines severity tier 3 here.

key_parameters.label: Number of confirmed Holocene events with F30 > 5x10^10 cm^-2
key_parameters.effect: The rate lower limit is this count divided by the Holocene interval: Cliver et al. (2022) set 'a lower limit of P(> 5 x 10^10 (cm2 year)^-1) >= 1.2 x 10^-4 year^-1' from the five confirmed events (7176 BC, 5259 BC, 660 BC, AD 774, AD 993). The rate scales linearly in this count, and the count is a lower bound because the search is incomplete. The complementary upper constraint comes from non-detection at the next tier: 'The fact that no events with F30 > 10^11 (cm2 year)^-1 have been found ... poses an upper 90% confidence interval limit P(> 10^11 (cm2 year)^-1) <= 1.9 x 10^-4 year^-1.'

key_parameters.label: Global radiocarbon production attributed to the AD 774 event
key_parameters.effect: The measured quantity from which fluence is inferred, and the source of a systematic ~2x model spread. Published estimates of 14Q774 across carbon-cycle models are (1.1-1.5) [6-box], 1.7 [6-box], 2.2 [11-box], 2.16 [box-diffusion] and 2.18 [11-box], all in units of 10^8 cm^-2. That spread propagates directly into the inferred F30 and therefore into the assumed rate, so a simulator that treats the fluence as sharply known overstates what the archive supports.

cascades_into: carrington-class-geomagnetic-superstorm: shared driver — the eruptions capable of Miyake-class fluences are the same class capable of extreme Dst, so the two are positively correlated within a single eruption sequence and must not be sampled independently

satellite-and-gnss-infrastructure-loss: identifier outside this packet — >200 MeV protons penetrate practical spacecraft shielding and can degrade the whole orbiting fleet at once, taking timing and navigation with it
hazards.uncertainty_notes: (1) The three probabilities are genuinely different here and are routinely conflated. P(event) is reasonably constrained at order 10^-3 to 10^-4 per year by the cosmogenic archive. P(mass death given event) is NOT constrained by anything published — Thomas et al. (2013) say explicitly that no mass extinction is implied by an AD 774-class event — so my severity tiers rest on a technological-cascade argument, not on a published casualty model, and every deaths_fraction is an author-estimate. P(permanent extinction) I take as zero; nothing retrieved supports otherwise. (2) The AD 774 fluence is inferred, not measured, through two chained models: a carbon-cycle model to get 14C production (a ~2x spread across published models) and a spectral assumption to convert production to fluence. Cliver et al. give both '~8 x 10^10 cm^-2' (from the 45x-1956-GLE scaling) and '~10^11 cm^-2' (summary table) for the same event; I have used 10^11 as the headline and flagged the discrepancy rather than averaging it away. (3) The rate is a LOWER limit by construction: the Holocene archive is searched incompletely. My 'high' of 2e-3/yr is my own allowance for that incompleteness, basis author-estimate, not a published bound. (4) The strongest attack a critic can make is on the solar attribution itself: Miyake et al. (2012) originally concluded that neither a solar flare nor a local supernova was a likely cause, and the solar interpretation was established only afterwards by multi-isotope work; a minority position that some spikes have non-solar or partly climatic origins still exists. (5) I did NOT retrieve the AD 993-994 discovery paper (Miyake et al. 2013, Nature Communications) directly. The 993 event enters this packet only through Cliver et al. (2022)'s list of five confirmed Holocene events, which I did retrieve. Likewise the ~660 BC event's F30 of 2.09 (+/-0.75) x 10^10 cm^-2 appeared only in search-result text I could not verify against the primary O'Hare et al. (2019) PNAS paper, so I have excluded it.

hazards.name: Nearby gamma-ray burst
hazards.one_line: A long gamma-ray burst inside the Galaxy, beamed at Earth, strips a third of the ozone layer for years and is a leading hypothesis for the end-Ordovician extinction.
hazards.mechanism: A collapsing massive star launches a relativistic jet that radiates gamma rays into a narrow cone for about ten seconds. If the cone contains Earth, the gamma rays are absorbed in the stratosphere, dissociating N2 and O2 and producing nitric oxide, which then destroys ozone in catalytic cycles that regenerate the NO — so a ten-second input produces years of depletion. Thomas et al. (2005) model a 100 kJ/m^2 burst as giving 35% globally averaged ozone depletion, reaching 55% at some latitudes, with significant global depletion persisting for over 5 years. The killing agent is then solar, not the burst: unshielded UVB reaches the surface and the ocean's upper metres, destroying phytoplankton and damaging DNA in exposed organisms. Melott et al. note a second pathway — NO2 is a strong absorber, so the same chemistry can trigger global cooling, and the end-Ordovician extinction is associated with exactly such a rapid glaciation. For a human population the proximate killer is again famine: collapse of marine primary productivity and multi-year damage to unprotected agriculture.

annual_probability.event_definition: A long gamma-ray burst beamed at Earth from close enough within the Galaxy to deliver of order 100 kJ/m^2, i.e. the 'dangerously near' class Melott et al. (2004) place at roughly 2-3 kpc. NOT the rate of Galactic GRBs, which is far higher; this is the rate of ones that both point at us and are close enough to matter.
annual_probability.trend: Flat over the coming century — utterly flat, on a stellar-evolution timescale of hundreds of Myr. The only defensible non-flat statement is downward over cosmic time: Piran and Jimenez (2014) note the GRB rate was higher in the past and that 'life as it exists on Earth could not take place at z > 0.5', so the present epoch is comparatively safe. There is no mechanism by which anything humans do changes this rate, and no observational warning: the burst arrives with its own light.

severity_tiers.label: Partial ozone loss, ecological stress
severity_tiers.description: An off-axis or more distant burst delivering well under the 100 kJ/m^2 fiducial. Ozone depletion of order 10-20% for a few years, elevated UVB, damage to phytoplankton and unprotected crops, regional harvest failures. Industrial civilisation survives; agriculture adapts with shading and cultivar change.

severity_tiers.label: Ordovician-class: 35% global ozone depletion for over 5 years
severity_tiers.description: The Thomas et al. (2005) fiducial: 100 kJ/m^2 in ten seconds, 35% globally averaged ozone depletion and 55% at some latitudes, persisting over 5 years, plus possible NO2-driven cooling. Marine primary productivity collapses. The end-Ordovician extinction that Melott et al. attribute in part to this mechanism eliminated a large fraction of marine invertebrate genera. Multi-year global famine for a population that cannot grow food under cover.

severity_tiers.label: Close burst, deep and prolonged depletion
severity_tiers.description: A burst inside about 1 kpc, or unusually energetic, driving depletion well beyond the fiducial and for longer, combined with glaciation. Loss of most open-field agriculture for a decade or more. Survival is plausible only for populations that can grow food under cover or live from stores.

severity_tiers.label: Terminal
severity_tiers.description: Included for completeness and given a deliberately small probability. No retrieved source proposes a GRB as a human-extinction mechanism; life survived the end-Ordovician event, and a species that can build enclosed food production has a survival route trilobites did not. This tier represents the residual case where depletion is deep enough and long enough that no viable population persists.

key_parameters.label: Distance to the burst
key_parameters.effect: Fluence scales as 1/d^2, so this is the dominant severity knob. Melott et al. (2004) take 3 kpc as the threshold for a serious biospheric threat and derive 'a dangerous event rate of 6 x 10^-9 y^-1, in other words about 170 My between events within 3 kpc'; their cleaner blue-luminosity scaling gives a typical nearest-burst distance of 1.9 kpc t_G^-1/2 with t_G in Gyr, hence 'the nearest burst irradiating the Earth to have been at a distance of about 2 kpc over the last Gy'. The current value is that expected nearest distance over the ozone-shield era.

key_parameters.label: Gamma-ray fluence at Earth
key_parameters.effect: The direct input to atmospheric chemistry. At the 100 kJ/m^2 fiducial delivered in ten seconds, Thomas et al. (2005) obtain 35% globally averaged ozone depletion, 55% at some latitudes, persisting over 5 years. Depletion rises strongly but sub-linearly with fluence because the NO catalytic cycles saturate; a simulator should not extrapolate linearly to 1000 kJ/m^2.

key_parameters.label: Jet beaming correction factor
key_parameters.effect: A trap. The intuition that beaming makes GRBs safe by a factor of hundreds is wrong, and Melott et al. state why: 'For most purposes, beaming is irrelevant, as the actual GRB rate inferred from data varies inversely with the beaming angle, leaving the observed rate constant.' The observed rate already folds in the beaming; applying a beaming discount on top would understate the hazard by orders of magnitude. The current value is set to 1 to encode 'do not apply an extra beaming discount'.

key_parameters.label: Distance of the Sun from the Galactic centre
key_parameters.effect: Sets the local GRB rate through the stellar and star-formation density gradient. Piran and Jimenez (2014): 'the probability of a lethal GRB is much larger in the inner Milky Way (95% within a radius of 4 kpc from the galactic center) ... Only at the outskirts of the Milky Way, at more than 10 kpc from the galactic center, this probability drops below 50%.' At the Sun's radius the probability of at least one lethal burst in 500 Myr is about 50%. NOTE: the value 8 kpc is textbook astronomy, not a figure retrieved this session.

Only at the outskirts of the Milky Way, at more than 10 kpc from the galactic center, this probability drops below 50%."

cascades_into: global-famine-and-uv-driven-ecosystem-collapse: identifier outside this packet — ozone loss kills by removing marine primary productivity and open-field agriculture, not by direct radiation dose at the surface
hazards.uncertainty_notes: (1) The Ordovician attribution is a hypothesis and its own authors say so: Melott et al. call the GRB role 'only a credible working hypothesis'. It is not established that a GRB has ever caused a mass extinction, and there is no isotopic or geochemical signature for it comparable to the iridium layer for Chicxulub. (2) The rate is model-derived, not observed, and the two methods within Melott et al. disagree by a factor of three: a crude luminosity-density scaling gives 6 x 10^-9 yr^-1 within 3 kpc, while the blue-luminosity scaling gives a nearest-burst distance of about 2 kpc over 1 Gyr; the abstract's headline is 'two or more times per billion years'. Piran and Jimenez's 50%-in-500-Myr implies about 1.4 x 10^-9 yr^-1. My range spans these; the best of 2e-9 follows the Melott abstract. (3) Small-number statistics dominate. Melott et al.: 'Due to small number statistics, lack of knowledge of the recent GRB rate is a serious source of uncertainty in estimating the role they may have played in mass extinctions.' The papers cited date from 2004-2014; a modern Swift/Fermi-era re-derivation could move this by a factor of a few either way. (4) The severity tiers are mine. There is no published estimate of human deaths from a GRB. In particular the 0.5% terminal tier is an author-estimate placed to keep an extinction branch in the model without pretending it is measured; the honest statement is that P(human extinction | nearby GRB) is small and unquantified, so P(extinction from GRB per year) is of order 10^-11 or less. (5) Melott et al. also propose glaciation via NO2 absorption as a second, possibly dominant pathway for the Ordovician event; I have not given cooling its own tier, which understates that branch.

hazards.name: Nearby supernova
hazards.one_line: A core-collapse supernova within about 8 parsecs strips roughly half the ozone column — though a 2024 Earth-system model argues the atmosphere shields far better than that.
hazards.mechanism: A massive star within a few parsecs explodes, delivering first a prompt gamma-ray flash and then, over subsequent centuries, a large enhancement of the local cosmic-ray flux as the remnant's shock accelerates particles that reach the solar system. Both dissociate atmospheric nitrogen, producing NO and NO2 that catalytically destroy stratospheric ozone. Gehrels et al. (2003) computed that the combined gamma-ray and cosmic-ray contribution reaches about 47% ozone depletion — enough to roughly double biologically active UV at the surface — when the supernova is within about 8 pc. The killing agent is again solar UVB on an unprotected biosphere: DNA damage, loss of phytoplankton, damage to unshielded crops. A 2024 Earth-system-model study reaches a much weaker conclusion: with full three-dimensional chemistry, compensating catalytic cycles limit the net ozone loss for a 50 pc supernova with a hundredfold cosmic-ray enhancement to around 10% globally, comparable to observed anthropogenic depletion, while the associated ion-induced aerosol and cloud forcing is comparable in magnitude but opposite in sign to current anthropogenic climate forcing. Which of these two pictures is right is the central open question for this hazard.

annual_probability.event_definition: A core-collapse supernova occurring within 8 pc of the Sun — the Gehrels et al. (2003) critical distance for roughly doubling biologically active surface UV. NOT the rate of supernovae generally: within 100 pc one occurs roughly once per million years, a thousand times more often, with far smaller effect.
annual_probability.trend: Flat. The rate is set by the local density of massive stars and by the Sun's motion through the Galaxy, both of which change on timescales of tens of Myr, so over the coming century it is constant to many decimal places. There is also, uniquely among the hazards here, an element of advance certainty: any progenitor of a supernova within 8 pc would be a conspicuous massive star, and none is known that close — consistent with Gehrels et al.'s note that no signature of such a close supernova has been found in the geological record.

severity_tiers.label: Atmospheric shielding holds
severity_tiers.description: The Christoudias et al. (2024) result: net ozone depletion of around 10% globally, with polar depletion less than the present-day Antarctic ozone hole (60-70% column loss), most of the loss occurring at high latitudes, plus a cloud and aerosol radiative forcing comparable in magnitude but opposite in sign to current anthropogenic forcing. Measurable ecological stress and a modest climate perturbation; no mass casualty event.

severity_tiers.label: Gehrels-class: ~47% ozone depletion, doubled biologically active UV
severity_tiers.description: The classical two-dimensional-model result for a supernova at the 8 pc critical distance. Biologically active UV at the surface roughly doubles, sustained by the cosmic-ray enhancement over centuries rather than the years of a GRB. Sustained damage to marine primary productivity and to open-field agriculture; regional to global harvest shortfalls over decades.

severity_tiers.label: Very close event, centuries of elevated cosmic rays
severity_tiers.description: A supernova well inside 8 pc. Ozone depletion beyond the 47% fiducial, maintained for centuries by the continuing cosmic-ray bath rather than decaying in years, so there is no adaptation window of the kind a single-shot GRB allows. Multi-century loss of open-field agriculture; survival depends on covered cultivation at scale.

key_parameters.label: Distance to the supernova
key_parameters.effect: Sets both severity and rate, and they trade off very steeply. Gehrels et al. (2003) find 'the supernova must occur at < 8 pc' to roughly double biologically active surface UV, and that 'the time-averaged galactic rate of core-collapse supernovae occurring within 8 pc is ~ 1.5 Gyr^-1'; they also quote about 3 Gyr^-1 for distances under 10 pc. Christoudias et al. (2024) state 'a supernova within 100 parsecs of Earth occurs around once per million years'. The rate therefore scales roughly as d^2 in the thin Galactic disc, while fluence falls as 1/d^2 — so expected damage per unit time is roughly flat in distance, and the answer hinges entirely on where the biological threshold sits.

key_parameters.label: Global ozone column depletion
key_parameters.effect: The disputed variable, and the one a simulator should expose as a slider rather than fix. Gehrels et al. (2003) compute 'a combined ozone depletion from both gamma-rays and cosmic rays of ~47%' at 8 pc, sufficient to double biologically active UV. Christoudias et al. (2024), with a full Earth-system model including ion-induced aerosol chemistry, get 'around 10% globally' for a 50 pc supernova with 100x cosmic rays, and note the maximum polar depletion is less than the present-day Antarctic ozone hole 'which amounts to an ozone column loss of 60-70%'. The current value follows the newer 3-D result; the maximum is set by the anthropogenic ozone-hole benchmark.

key_parameters.label: Enhancement of the galactic cosmic ray flux
key_parameters.effect: The distinguishing feature of a supernova versus a GRB: the gamma flash is brief and, per Christoudias et al., largely attenuated before reaching the lower stratosphere, but 'a 100-fold increase of cosmic rays, lasting several centuries' is not. This drives both the NO chemistry that depletes ozone and, via ion-induced nucleation of cloud condensation nuclei, a radiative forcing the same authors find 'comparable in magnitude but opposite in sign to current anthropogenic climate forcing'. The factor 100 is the peak flux estimated for a supernova at 50 pc with a turbulent Galactic magnetic field.

citations.claim: A recent three-dimensional Earth-system-model revision arguing the atmosphere shields the biosphere far better than earlier two-dimensional models implied.
citations.authors: T. Christoudias, J. Kirkby, D. Stolzenburg, A. Pozzer, E. Sommer, G. P. Brasseur, M. Kulmala, J. Lelieveld
citations.venue: Communications Earth & Environment, doi:10.1038/s43247-024-01490-9
citations.exact_figure: "Geological evidence indicates that a supernova within 100 parsecs of Earth occurs around once per million years. Such nearby supernovas can produce an intense gamma-ray burst and a 100-fold increase of cosmic rays, lasting several centuries. We find that the effect of a short burst of gamma rays is small since they are strongly attenuated before reaching the lower stratosphere. Intense cosmic radiation affects stratospheric ozone but, due to compensating effects in catalytic chemical cycles, ozone depletion is moderate and comparable to that from current anthropogenic emissions. ... We conclude that Earth's atmosphere is effective at shielding the biosphere from nearby supernovae." Ozone loss is "around 10% globally"; "The maximum ozone depletion over the poles is less than the present-day anthropogenic ozone hole over Antarctica, which amounts to an ozone column loss of 60-70%". They also record the earlier consensus being revised: "They concluded that a supernova must occur within 8 pc to have a catastrophic effect on the biosphere. A signature of such a close supernova, however, has not been found in the geological record."

cascades_into: global-famine-and-uv-driven-ecosystem-collapse: identifier outside this packet — as with a GRB, deaths come from loss of primary productivity and open-field agriculture over decades to centuries
hazards.uncertainty_notes: (1) This hazard is in active revision and the literature disagrees by roughly a factor of five on the key severity number. Gehrels et al. (2003) get about 47% ozone depletion at 8 pc from a 2-D chemistry-transport model; Christoudias et al. (2024) get about 10% from a 3-D Earth-system model with ion-induced aerosol chemistry, and title their paper 'Earth's atmosphere protects the biosphere from nearby supernovae'. A modeller must choose, and should expose the choice. My tiers give the newer, weaker result the largest probability mass, but that is a judgement, not a measurement. (2) The rate of ~1.5 Gyr^-1 within 8 pc is itself derived from an OB-star census and a scale-height assumption, not from any direct count of nearby supernovae; Gehrels et al. quote competing values from about 0.3 to about 10 Gyr^-1 for 10 pc depending on the input catalogue, which is where my low and high come from. (3) There is a live third position not represented in my tiers: Christoudias et al. note that 'Fields et al. suggested that a nearby (~20 pc) supernova could intensify ionising radiation to such an extent that species extinctions can be expected'. I did not retrieve that paper and so did not build a tier on it, which may understate the hazard. (4) Only two distinct primary sources underlie this entry; the second citation object is a distinct figure from the same Gehrels paper. That is thinner sourcing than the solar entries and a reviewer should treat this hazard's numbers as the least well triangulated in the packet. (5) All deaths_fraction values are author-estimates. No published work estimates human mortality from a nearby supernova, and I mark no tier terminal: nothing retrieved supports human extinction from this cause.

hazards.name: Rogue star / stellar encounter perturbing the Oort cloud
hazards.one_line: A passing star deflects Oort-cloud comets onto Sun-crossing orbits, multiplying the km-class impact rate for a few million years — but the shower takes ~0.18 Myr to arrive and none is inbound.
hazards.mechanism: Roughly twenty stars pass within one parsec of the Sun per million years. A star passing close enough — of order 10,000 AU, i.e. inside the Oort cloud rather than merely near it — gives an impulse to comet orbits large enough to drop a population of them to perihelia inside the planetary region. Those comets do not arrive with the star: they must fall in from 10^4 to 10^5 AU, so the shower reaches the inner solar system about 0.18 Myr after the encounter and then persists for of order a Myr as successive cohorts arrive. During the shower the flux of km-class long-period comets crossing Earth's orbit rises by up to an order of magnitude over the steady state. The catastrophe is then an ordinary impact catastrophe — ejecta, thermal pulse, stratospheric dust and sulphate loading, and multi-year global cooling that ends agriculture — with the stellar encounter acting only as a rate multiplier. Nothing about the star itself touches Earth: the Sun's orbit and the planets are essentially unperturbed at these distances.

annual_probability.event_definition: A stellar passage within about 10^4 AU (0.048 pc) of the Sun — the distance Frogel and Gould (1998) take as sufficient to trigger a comet shower. This is the rate of the TRIGGER, not of an impact; impact probability is carried in the severity tiers. I computed it from the published rate of 19.7 +/- 2.2 encounters per Myr within 1 pc together with the published quadratic scaling law: 19.7 x (10^4/206265)^2 = 0.046 per Myr = 4.6 x 10^-8 per year. The arithmetic is mine; both inputs are published.
annual_probability.trend: Flat over the coming century, and — uniquely among the hazards in this packet — verifiably flat over the coming half-million years. Because a shower takes about 0.18 Myr to arrive, any shower that will hit Earth in that window was triggered by a star that has already passed and is now catalogued. Frogel and Gould searched Hipparcos and, in agreement with Garcia-Sanchez et al., found no such recent encounter, concluding 'it is highly unlikely that one will occur during the next 0.5 Myr'. Gaia has since catalogued encounters far more completely. This hazard is, for practical purposes, currently switched off.

severity_tiers.label: Shower arrives, no impact
severity_tiers.description: The overwhelmingly likely outcome. The comet flux through the inner solar system rises for of order a Myr — Cao, Loeb and MacLeod (2025) find that for a flyby at about 2,300 AU 'the terrestrial impact probability of 1 km comets increases by an order of magnitude compared to the steady state, slightly exceeding the asteroid impact probability at this size scale' — but no large body strikes Earth during the window in which any given civilisation exists. A spectacular sky, a research programme, and nothing else.

severity_tiers.label: Km-class cometary impact during the shower
severity_tiers.description: A body of roughly 1-2 km strikes Earth during the elevated-flux window. Regional devastation plus a global climate perturbation of a few years: stratospheric dust and sulphate loading, growing-season loss, and famine across the most food-insecure populations. Comets arrive faster than asteroids, so impact energy at a given diameter is several times higher than for an asteroid of the same size.

severity_tiers.label: Ten-km-class cometary impact
severity_tiers.description: A Chicxulub-class event delivered by the shower rather than by the background asteroid population. Global thermal pulse, months of darkness, collapse of photosynthesis, and decade-scale loss of agriculture worldwide. Recovery of an industrial civilisation, if any population survives, is a millennium-scale project.

key_parameters.label: Perihelion distance of the passing star
key_parameters.effect: The trigger threshold, and the rate is quadratic in it. Bailer-Jones et al. (2018) give 'the present rate of encounters within 1 pc to be 19.7 +/- 2.2 per Myr, a quantity expected to scale quadratically with the encounter distance out to at least several pc' — so the rate within distance b is 19.7 x (b/206265 AU)^2 per Myr. Frogel and Gould take about 10^4 AU as the shower-triggering distance. Halving the threshold quarters the trigger rate, while shower intensity at fixed distance rises steeply as b falls; Cao et al. give a logarithmic dependence of the critical impactor diameter on impact parameter.

key_parameters.label: Stellar encounter rate within 1 parsec
key_parameters.effect: The observationally anchored normalisation for the whole hazard, from Gaia DR2 after completeness correction (only 15% of encounters within 5 pc in a +/-5 Myr window had been identified before that correction). The trigger rate scales linearly in this number; the min and max are the published +/-2.2 (1 sigma) widened slightly.

key_parameters.label: Multiplier on the km-class comet impact rate during the shower
key_parameters.effect: Converts a trigger into a hazard. Cao, Loeb and MacLeod (2025), modelling the actual HD7977 encounter 2.47 Myr ago at an impact parameter possibly as small as 2,300 AU, find the terrestrial impact probability of 1 km comets 'increases by an order of magnitude compared to the steady state'. A separate 2025 analysis finds individual flybys enhance comet-shower rates 'by factors of about 2, producing a cumulative increase of roughly 40 over a Myr'. Expected deaths scale roughly linearly in this multiplier at fixed shower duration.

key_parameters.label: Delay between the stellar passage and arrival of the shower
key_parameters.effect: The reason this hazard cannot surprise us. Frogel and Gould: 'A star passing within ~10^4 AU of the Sun would trigger a comet shower that would reach the inner solar system about 0.18 Myr later.' Because the trigger is observable long before the consequence, a complete stellar census forward-dates the hazard: they 'calculate a prior probability of ~0.4% that a star has passed this close to the Sun but that the comet shower has not yet reached the Earth', searched for such stars, found none, and concluded 'it is highly unlikely that one will occur during the next 0.5 Myr'. In a simulator this parameter should gate the hazard OFF for the next ~0.5 Myr of simulated time.

citations.exact_figure: "A star passing within ~10^4 AU of the Sun would trigger a comet shower that would reach the inner solar system about 0.18 Myr later. We calculate a prior probability of ~0.4% that a star has passed this close to the Sun but that the comet shower has not yet reached the Earth. We search the HIPPARCOS catalog for such recent close-encounter candidates and, in agreement with Garcia-Sanchez et al. (1997), find none. ... we show that the search is sensitive to nearly all of the past encounters that would lead to a major shower in the future and conclude that it is highly unlikely that one will occur during the next 0.5 Myr."

citations.claim: The magnitude of the impact-rate enhancement a real close flyby produces.
citations.authors: Zhuoya Cao, Abraham Loeb, Morgan MacLeod
citations.venue: arXiv e-print 2511.11814 (PREPRINT, not peer-reviewed as of retrieval; submitted 14 November 2025)
citations.exact_figure: "For the closest approach (b ~ 2,300 AU), the terrestrial impact probability of 1 km comets increases by an order of magnitude compared to the steady state, slightly exceeding the asteroid impact probability at this size scale. ... We identify a threshold diameter D_0 = 2.25 km for which yields P = 1 in our model, with D_0 following a logarithmic dependence on b." Context: HD7977's encounter 2.47 Myr ago, 'with possible flyby distances ranging from 2,300 AU to ~13,000 AU'.

cascades_into: asteroid-comet-impact: identifier outside this packet — the stellar encounter is a rate multiplier on the impact hazard and has no independent killing mechanism of its own; a simulator should implement it as a time-varying multiplier on the impact rate, not as a separate death process
hazards.uncertainty_notes: (1) The headline annual probability is MY arithmetic, not a published figure, and is flagged basis 'author-estimate' for that reason. I combined two published inputs — the 19.7 +/- 2.2 per Myr rate within 1 pc and the published quadratic scaling — with Frogel and Gould's 10^4 AU threshold. If the true shower threshold is 5,000 AU rather than 10^4 AU the rate falls by a factor of four; if it is 20,000 AU it rises by four. Nothing I retrieved pins that threshold tightly. (2) The severity tiers are the weakest part of this entry. I had no retrieved source for the BACKGROUND km-class impact rate, so the impact probabilities within the shower window (2.8% and 0.2%) are author-estimates constructed from the order-of-magnitude enhancement figure and a rough shower duration. Do not treat 0.028 and 0.002 as literature values; replace them with a proper convolution against a sourced impact-frequency curve. (3) The enhancement magnitude rests on 2025 arXiv preprints that have not been peer reviewed. The Bailer-Jones encounter rate is solid; the impact multiplier is not. (4) This hazard has a property none of the others share and which a simulator must not lose: it is currently OFF and known to be off. Frogel and Gould's null search, now vastly strengthened by Gaia, means no shower can reach Earth for roughly the next 0.5 Myr. Sampling this as a memoryless Poisson process every year is wrong in a way that matters — the correct implementation gates on the observed stellar census. (5) A serious critic would also attack the premise that comet showers matter at all relative to the asteroid background: Cao et al. find the enhanced 1-km comet probability only 'slightly exceeding the asteroid impact probability at this size scale', i.e. even a strong shower roughly doubles the total km-class hazard rather than dominating it.

verdicts.citation_claim: NASEM 2019, 'Finding Hazardous Asteroids Using Infrared and Visible Wavelength Telescopes', Table 1.1 — 1 km every ~520,000 yr; 140 m every ~20,000 yr; ~24,000 NEOs >=140 m, one third catalogued; ~900 >=1 km exist
verdicts.note: Report, chapter and table all exist and the figures are verbatim. Retrieved https://www.nationalacademies.org/read/25476/chapter/3 : Table 1.1 gives 25-30 m = 80-180 yr, 50 m = 1,500 yr, 140 m = 20,000 yr, 1 km = 520,000 yr, and the text reads 'catalogued only about one-third of the estimated 24,000 NEOs that are at least 140 meters in diameter'. ONE CATEGORY SLIP: the packet's claim line says '~900 >=1 km exist' (a population estimate). The report's 897 figure is a count of the ALREADY-CATALOGUED population — 'Of these, 897 are estimated to be larger than 1 kilometer in diameter' out of 19,560 KNOWN asteroids as of January 2019. The estimated total >=1 km population is '1,000 or so' (2023 decadal, citation 3). Because ~95% of that population is found the two numbers nearly coincide, so nothing downstream breaks, but catalogued-count is being read as population-total.

verdicts.citation_claim: NRC 2010, 'Defending Planet Earth', Ch. 2 — 1.5 km global-catastrophe threshold; 25 m ~200 yr, 140 m ~30,000 yr, 1 km ~700,000 yr; decade-to-decades warning; comets <1% of risk
