verdicts.citation_claim: Daly, R.T., Ernst, C.M., Barnouin, O.S., Chabot, N.L., Rivkin, A.S., Cheng, A.F., et al. (2023), Nature (arXiv:2303.03464) — beta = 3.61 +0.19/-0.25 at 2,400 kg/m3, range 2.2-4.9, along-track dv 2.70 +/- 0.10 mm/s
verdicts.corrected_value: Cheng, A.F., Agrusa, H.F., Barbee, B.W., Meyer, A.J., Farnham, T.L., Raducan, S.D., et al. (2023), 'Momentum transfer from the DART mission kinetic impact on asteroid Dimorphos', Nature 616, 457-460, doi:10.1038/s41586-023-05878-z (preprint arXiv:2303.03464)
verdicts.note: THIS IS THE PLANTED ERROR. The numbers are right and the arXiv ID is real, but they belong to a different paper by a different first author. I fetched https://arxiv.org/abs/2303.03464 directly: its title is 'Momentum Transfer from the DART Mission Kinetic Impact on Asteroid Dimorphos' and its first author is Andrew F. Cheng. Its abstract does contain, verbatim, 'an instantaneous reduction in Dimorphos's along-track orbital velocity component of 2.70 +/- 0.10 mm/s' and 'beta = 3.61 +0.19/-0.25 (1 sigma)' at 2,400 kg/m3 — so the FIGURES are correct as stated. What is wrong is the byline. The author string given in the packet (Daly, Ernst, Barnouin, Chabot, Rivkin, Cheng...) is the exact opening author order of a DIFFERENT Nature paper: Daly, R.T. et al., 'Successful kinetic impact into an asteroid for planetary defence', Nature 616, 443-447 (2023), doi:10.1038/s41586-023-05810-5 — confirmed via Crossref, 101 authors, first author R. Terik Daly. That Daly paper reconstructs the impact event and impact-site geology; it does NOT report beta or the along-track dv. Terik Daly is a co-author of the Cheng paper, which is presumably how the two got fused. Net effect: a real author list attached to a paper that team did not lead, pointed at a URL that resolves to the other paper. Fix the byline; the numbers need no change.

verdicts.citation_claim: NRC 2010, 'Defending Planet Earth', mitigation chapter — kinetic impactors need 'years to decades'; with 40 years' warning ten 10-ton impactors divert ~3/4 km objects; nuclear needed >500 m at short notice and is the only practical means above ~1 km
verdicts.corrected_value: With 40 years' warning, ten 10-ton impactors could divert an object of order 3/4 km diameter IF the diversion is executed 30 years before impact — and objects even larger than 1 km in the case of very-low-density NEOs
verdicts.note: Substantively confirmed at https://www.nationalacademies.org/read/12842/chapter/7 : the >500 m / 'years to months' nuclear sentence and the 'only current, practical means for changing the orbit of large NEOs (diameter greater than about 1 kilometer)' sentence are both verbatim. Two quotation-fidelity defects, though. (1) The 40-year sentence is truncated in a way that changes it. Full text: 'With the same warning time of 40 years as discussed for the gravity tractor, one could launch a series of perhaps ten 10-ton impactors to divert, 30 years before impact, NEOs with diameters on the order of 3/4 kilometers, and with diameters even greater than 1 kilometer in the case of very-low-density NEOs.' The packet drops both the 30-years-before-impact execution requirement (which makes the deflection budget much tighter than '40 years' warning' implies) and the very-low-density >1 km clause (which cuts the other way). (2) The phrase presented in quotes as 'years to decades of warning time' is not what I retrieved; the chapter says kinetic impactors suit 'moderate-sized NEOs (many hundreds of meters to 1 kilometer in diameter) with decades of advance warning'. 'Years to decades' is a paraphrase wearing quotation marks, and it understates the required lead time.

verdicts.citation_claim: Nuth, Barbee & Leung 2018, J. Space Safety Engineering 5(3-4), 197-202 — comets ~100x less likely but ~half the destructive threat; 22 months warning; median 39.5 km/s, mean 41.5 km/s; asteroids ~20 km/s; comets 50-100x the energy
verdicts.note: Article exists at the cited PMC URL with matching title ('Defending the Earth from Long-Period Comets and Sneaky Asteroids: Short Term Threat Response Requires Long Term Preparation'), authors Joseph A. Nuth, Brent Barbee, Ronald Leung, Journal of Space Safety Engineering 5(3-4), 197-202, 2018. All six quoted figures verbatim. THREE GENERALISATION PROBLEMS in how the packet uses it. (a) '22 months' is not a general LPC warning-time statistic — it is the discovery-to-Mars-closest-approach interval for one object, Comet Siding Spring (discovered 3 Jan 2013, Mars pass 22 Oct 2014). Presenting it as 'warning times are of order 22 months' promotes one anecdote to a distribution. (b) The 39.5 km/s median is the median of METEOR-STREAM velocities over a 3-71 km/s range, not a measured LPC nucleus impact-velocity distribution; the packet's FIGURE AS STATED field is honest about this but its claim headline is not. (c) The 50-100x energy ratio is typical-comet vs typical-ASTEROID, and typical asteroid impactors are far smaller than 1 km — so this ratio cannot be carried across to a size-matched >=1 km comparison, which is how the packet's severity tiers appear to use it. Finally, this source's 'comets represent about half of the destructive threat' flatly contradicts the '<1 percent of total risk' the packet cites two lines later from NRC 2010; the packet cites both without reconciling them.

verdicts.citation_claim: NRC 2010, 'Defending Planet Earth', Ch. 2 — comet hazard is on the order of <1 percent of total NEO impact risk
verdicts.note: Verbatim at https://www.nationalacademies.org/read/12842/chapter/4 : 'they find that the comet hazard constitutes only a tiny fraction (on the order of <1 percent) of the total risk.' As with the asteroid packet's citation 2, note the finding is the NRC restating Stokes et al. (2003), not an independent NRC computation. The packet's derived comet rate of 2e-8/yr is consistent with applying ~1% to its own 1.7e-6/yr asteroid rate (giving 1.7e-8).

verdicts.citation_claim: NRC 2010, 'Defending Planet Earth', mitigation chapter — LPC intercepts permit only ~0.5 t payloads, sufficient for a nuclear package but small for a kinetic impactor; nuclear needed >500 m at years-to-months notice
verdicts.note: Confirmed at https://www.nationalacademies.org/read/12842/chapter/7 : the chapter specifies a '0.5-ton payload' for comet intercept and characterises it as 'sufficient for a nuclear package but rather small for a kinetic impactor', and the '>500 meters in diameter when the time to impact is short (years to months)' nuclear sentence is verbatim. The 'most challenging trajectories' / short-discovery-to-impact / 'very elongated orbits' framing is likewise the report's own. No defect found.

verdicts.citation_claim: NASEM 2023 decadal Ch. 18 — comet/ISO impact probability ~1% of NEO total; 10 km impactor every 100 Myr on average
verdicts.note: Both verbatim at https://www.nationalacademies.org/read/26522/chapter/20 : 'the statistical probability of Earth impact by a comet or ISO (e.g., the recently discovered 1I/Oumuamua and 2I/Borisov) is much lower (~1 percent) than from NEOs' and '~10 km Chicxulub-size impactors, which strike Earth every 100 million years on average'. One nuance the packet should carry: the decadal's ~1% bundles comets WITH interstellar objects, so using it as a pure long-period-comet scaling factor slightly overstates the LPC share.

verdicts.citation_claim: Senel et al. 2023, Nature Geoscience 16(11), 1033-1040 — ~0.8-8.0 um dust, 15 yr lifetime, up to 15 degC cooling, ~2 yr photosynthetic shutdown, applied to a comet nucleus
verdicts.note: Same verification as the asteroid packet's citation 6: paper, authors, volume, pages, DOI and all four figures confirmed via the VUB portal record and Crossref. MECHANISM CAVEAT, not a citation defect: Senel et al. model FINE SILICATE DUST from the Chicxulub target rock. A comet nucleus is ice-and-dust and would deliver a materially different ejecta budget (more water/volatiles, less silicate at fixed energy, and a different mix of soot/sulfur from the target). Transferring the 15 yr / 15 degC / 2 yr numbers to a comet impactor without adjustment is an extrapolation beyond what the paper modelled and should be labelled as such.

verdicts.citation_claim: Xia et al. 2022, Nature Food 3(8), 586-596 — >5 Tg soot causes mass food shortages; 150 Tg leaves >5 billion dead; livestock and aquatic food cannot compensate
verdicts.note: Same verification as the asteroid packet's citation 7 (GISS page resolves, Crossref confirms Nature Food 3, 586-596, 2022 and the 10-author list, Europe PMC returns the abstract with all three quoted phrases verbatim). Same caveat: '150 Tg' is the scenario label from the paper's body, not from the sentence quoted. Additional mechanism caveat carried from the asteroid packet: Xia et al. model SOOT injection from urban firestorms, whereas the impact-winter mechanism the packet builds on (Senel) is silicate DUST with different optical properties and a different atmospheric lifetime; the Tg-to-mortality mapping is being reused across aerosol species without a stated conversion.

verdicts.citation_claim: Daly, R.T., Ernst, C.M., Barnouin, O.S., Chabot, N.L., Rivkin, A.S., Cheng, A.F., et al. (2023), Nature (arXiv:2303.03464) — beta = 3.61 +0.19/-0.25 at 2,400 kg/m3, range 2.2-4.9; along-track dv 2.70 +/- 0.10 mm/s
verdicts.corrected_value: Cheng, A.F., Agrusa, H.F., Barbee, B.W., Meyer, A.J., Farnham, T.L., Raducan, S.D., et al. (2023), 'Momentum transfer from the DART mission kinetic impact on asteroid Dimorphos', Nature 616, 457-460, doi:10.1038/s41586-023-05878-z (preprint arXiv:2303.03464)
verdicts.note: Identical defect to the asteroid packet's citation 8, repeated verbatim. arXiv:2303.03464 is Cheng et al., not Daly et al.; the packet's author list is the byline of the separate paper Daly, R.T. et al., 'Successful kinetic impact into an asteroid for planetary defence', Nature 616, 443-447 (2023), doi:10.1038/s41586-023-05810-5 (confirmed via Crossref), which reports the impact reconstruction and does NOT report beta. The beta = 3.61 +0.19/-0.25 and 2.70 +/- 0.10 mm/s figures are correct as quoted from the arXiv abstract I fetched. Because the same wrong byline appears in both hazards, it is a single upstream reference-manager error propagated, not two independent slips — fix it in one place.

audits.overall: Mostly trustworthy, with one real fabrication-class defect and several quantitative tier problems that are more serious than the citation errors. WHAT I ACTUALLY RETRIEVED THIS SESSION (WebSearch budget was exhausted before my first query, so everything below is direct fetch/curl of primary sources): nationalacademies.org/read/25476/chapter/3 (NASEM 2019 Table 1.1), /read/12842/chapter/4 and /chapter/7 (NRC 2010 Defending Planet Earth, Ch. 2 and the mitigation chapter), /read/26522/chapter/20 (2023 planetary decadal Ch. 18), arxiv.org/abs/2303.03464, researchportal.vub.be for Senel et al., pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6999729 for Nuth et al., giss.nasa.gov/pubs/abs/xi08000i.html plus Europe PMC for the Xia et al. abstract, Crossref for DOIs 10.1038/s43016-022-00573-0, 10.1038/s41586-023-05810-5, 10.1038/s41561-023-01290-4 and a Crossref title search that returned 10.1038/s41586-023-05878-z, and live curl against ssd-api.jpl.nasa.gov (sbdb_query.api and sentry.api). THE CITATION DEFECT: one misattribution, repeated in both hazards (asteroid #8, comet #7). arXiv:2303.03464 is Cheng et al., 'Momentum transfer from the DART mission kinetic impact on asteroid Dimorphos', Nature 616, 457-460, doi:10.1038/s41586-023-05878-z. The packet's byline (Daly, Ernst, Barnouin, Chabot, Rivkin, Cheng...) is the opening author order of a DIFFERENT real paper, Daly et al., 'Successful kinetic impact into an asteroid for planetary defence', Nature 616, 443-447, which does not report beta at all. Real authors, real numbers, real URL — wrong pairing. Everything else survived: all four NASEM/NRC chapters quote verbatim, and both JPL API figures reproduce to the digit today (42237 total NEAs, 867 at H<17.75, 11584 at H<22.0, and exactly 2 Sentry objects at PS>=-2 with Bennu at 5.717e-4 / -1.40 and 1950 DA at 3.770e-4 / -0.93). Three softer defects: a paraphrase presented in quotation marks in asteroid #9 ('years to decades of warning time'; the report says 'decades of advance warning') with the load-bearing '30 years before impact' qualifier silently dropped from the ten-10-ton-impactor sentence; a catalogued-count read as a population-total in asteroid #1; and comet #1 promoting Comet Siding Spring's single 22-month interval to a general LPC warning-time figure while carrying a meteor-stream velocity median as a nucleus impact velocity. NOW THE NUMBERS, WHICH ARE THE BIGGER PROBLEM. The base rates are fine: 1.7e-6/yr sits between the two cited recurrence intervals (520 kyr -> 1.92e-6, 700 kyr -> 1.43e-6) and the 1.4-1.9e-6 range brackets them exactly; 2e-8/yr for comets is consistent with applying the cited ~1% to that. Both tier sets sum to exactly 1.000, so no over-unity. But the asteroid Chicxulub-class tier at p=0.015 is contradicted by the packet's OWN citations: 520,000 yr for >=1 km against 100 Myr for 10 km gives a conditional share of 0.0052 (0.007 using the NRC's 700 kyr) — the packet is 2-3x high, and nothing cited supports the inflation. The comet Chicxulub tier at p=0.095 is worse: no cited source gives an LPC size-frequency distribution at all, and the only thing that could justify it, Nuth's 50-100x energy ratio, is a typical-comet-vs-typical-ASTEROID comparison that cannot be carried to a size-matched >=1 km case. Both terminal tiers (p=0.002 and p=0.005, deaths=1.0, terminal=true) are supported by nothing in either citation list — no cited document claims a >=1 km or even a 10 km impact could permanently end humanity, and Chicxulub itself, the packet's own worst case, did not sterilise the biosphere. Those two rows should be relabelled author-estimate. Finally, the comet packet cites Nuth's 'comets represent about half of the destructive threat' alongside NRC's '<1 percent of total risk' without reconciling them, while quietly deriving its rate from the 1% figure; and it transplants Senel's silicate-dust winter and Xia's soot-to-famine mapping onto an icy nucleus without stating that neither model was run for that impactor or that aerosol species. VERDICT: fix the one byline, downgrade both Chicxulub tiers to match the cited recurrence ratio, mark both terminal tiers as unsourced author estimates, and the packet is a sound foundation. Do not build on the severity tiers as they stand.

verdicts.citation_claim: IPCC AR6 WGI Table SPM.1 SSP warming projections, via Carbon Brief in-depth Q&A
verdicts.note: Retrieved https://www.carbonbrief.org/in-depth-qa-the-ipccs-sixth-assessment-report-on-climate-science this session. Every one of the eight quoted values matches the article's reproduction of Table SPM.1 exactly. 2081-2100: SSP1-1.9 1.4C (1.0-1.8); SSP1-2.6 1.8C (1.3-2.4); SSP2-4.5 2.7C (2.1-3.5); SSP3-7.0 3.6C (2.8-4.6); SSP5-8.5 4.4C (3.3-5.7). 2041-2060: SSP1-2.6 1.7C (1.3-2.2); SSP2-4.5 2.0C (1.6-2.5); SSP5-8.5 2.4C (1.9-3.0). (The same table also gives 2041-2060 SSP1-1.9 1.6C (1.2-2.0) and SSP3-7.0 2.1C (1.7-2.6), which the packet omits but does not misstate.) The 403 on ipcc.ch is a real and correctly disclosed limitation.

verdicts.citation_claim: AR6 ECS and observed warming, via Carbon Brief 'How the AR6 WG1 SPM compares to its predecessor'
verdicts.corrected_value: 1.07 C (0.8-1.3 C) is in Carbon Brief's IN-DEPTH Q&A article, not the SPM-comparison article; ECS very likely 2-5 C is in AR6 SPM A.4.4, not in either Carbon Brief text
verdicts.note: Two of the three figures are attached to the wrong document. I fetched https://www.carbonbrief.org/ipcc-how-the-ar6-wg1-summary-for-policymakers-compares-to-its-predecessor twice. It DOES contain, verbatim, 'likely range is given as 2.5C to 4C, which also provides a best estimate of 3C' and 'AR6 finds that 2011-20 was 1.09C warmer than 1850-1900' - those two are confirmed. It does NOT state the human-caused warming figure for 1850-1900 to 2010-19, and it does NOT state the very likely ECS range 2-5 C in text (the whiskers appear only inside a chart image). The 1.07 C figure IS real and IS on Carbon Brief - but on the OTHER article, the one cited as citation 1: 'between 1850-1900 and 2010-19, human activity drove 0.8-1.3C of warming, with a best estimate of 1.07C' (https://www.carbonbrief.org/in-depth-qa-the-ipccs-sixth-assessment-report-on-climate-science). The numbers are right; the pointer is wrong, which is exactly the failure a reader checking the URL would hit. Fix by moving the 1.07 C claim to citation 1's URL and sourcing the 2-5 C very likely range to IPCC AR6 WGI SPM A.4.4 directly.

verdicts.citation_claim: Carleton et al. 2022 QJE 137(4):2037-2105 - 85 additional deaths per 100,000 annually by 2100 under high emissions
verdicts.note: Confirmed on three independent retrievals. The cited Impact Lab page carries the sentence verbatim: 'the full mortality risk of climate change under a scenario of continued high emissions to be an additional 85 deaths per 100,000 annually by 2100', together with the ~84% reduction under RCP4.5, $36.6/ton and $17.1/ton, and the 2% discount rate. OpenAlex (doi:10.1093/qje/qjac020) confirms The Quarterly Journal of Economics, 2022, vol 137, issue 4, pp 2037-2105, and all sixteen authors in the order given. Two cautions, not errors: (a) the paper's own abstract contains NO per-100,000 figure at all - it reports 3.2% of global GDP in 2100 and $36.6/ton [IQR -$7.8 to $73.0] - so 85/100,000 is a Climate Impact Lab summary quantity, correctly attributed here; (b) the same page carries four different per-100,000 numbers for different adaptation accountings (73/74 headline, 104 with income growth, 221 with no adaptation, 85 full risk including adaptation costs). The packet picked 85 and labelled it 'full mortality risk including adaptation costs', which is the correct pairing. NOTE SEPARATELY: 85/100,000 = 0.00085, and the packet's high-emissions tier uses deaths=0.0085 - see 'overall'.

verdicts.citation_claim: Gaupp et al. 2020 Nature Climate Change 10:54-57 - simultaneous breadbasket failure probability rose from 0.3% to 1.2% (wheat), 0.8% to 1.1% (maize), 1.7% to 2% (soybean)
verdicts.note: The quoted sentence appears verbatim on the cited climatechangepost.com page, with the 1967-1990 vs 1991-2012 comparison as stated. OpenAlex (doi:10.1038/s41558-019-0600-z) confirms the primary: 'Changing risks of simultaneous global breadbasket failure', Gaupp F, Hall JW, Hochrainer-Stigler S, Dadson S, Nature Climate Change vol 10, issue 1, pp 54-57. Only nit: OpenAlex records the publication year as 2019 (online-first); the print issue is January 2020, so '2020' is defensible. This is a secondary-source retrieval of a paywalled primary and is disclosed as such.

verdicts.citation_claim: Kornhuber et al. 2023 Nature Communications 14:3528 - models underestimate synchronous crop failure
verdicts.note: OpenAlex (doi:10.1038/s41467-023-38906-7) confirms 'Risks of synchronized low yields are underestimated in climate and crop model projections', Nature Communications vol 14, article 3528, 2023, authors Kai Kornhuber, Corey Lesk, Carl-Friedrich Schleussner, Jonas Jaegermeyr, Peter Pfleiderer, Radley M. Horton - exactly the list and order claimed. The abstract does contain the claim that surface weather anomalies and crop responses 'are mostly underestimated in bias-adjusted simulations'. The packet's explicit statement that no single quantitative multiplier is given in the abstract is honest and correct - this citation supports a DIRECTION only, and the packet does not pretend otherwise.

verdicts.citation_claim: Armstrong McKay et al. 2022 Science 377:eabn7950 - tipping element central thresholds, ranges, timescales and classification
verdicts.corrected_value: Greenland 1.5 (0.8-3.0); WAIS 1.5 (1.0-3.0); Labrador-Irminger/SPG 1.8 (1.1-3.8); East Antarctic subglacial basins 3.0 (2.0-6.0); Arctic winter sea ice 6.3 (4.5-8.7) [GLOBAL CORE]; East Antarctic Ice Sheet 7.5 (5.0-10.0) [GLOBAL CORE, omitted entirely]; Amazon 3.5 (2.0-6.0); boreal permafrost collapse 4.0 (3.0-6.0) [GLOBAL CORE]; AMOC 4.0 (1.4-8.0); coral reefs 1.5 (1.0-2.0) [REGIONAL]; permafrost abrupt thaw 1.5 (1.0-2.3) [REGIONAL]; Barents Sea ice 1.6 (1.5-1.7); mountain glaciers 2.0 (1.5-3.0); Sahel/W African monsoon 2.8 (2.0-3.5); boreal forest southern dieback 4.0 (1.4-5.0); boreal forest northern expansion 4.0 (1.5-7.2)
verdicts.note: This is the packet's serious citation failure - the paper is real, the authors and DOI are right, but roughly two thirds of the transcribed table is wrong, and the errors are not rounding. Worst: southern boreal forest dieback given as ~2 C (1-3) vs published 4.0 (1.4-5.0); northern boreal expansion ~2-3 C (1-4) vs 4.0 (1.5-7.2); Barents Sea ice ~2 C (1-3) vs 1.6 (1.5-1.7); Arctic winter sea ice ~5+ C (3-8) vs 6.3 (4.5-8.7); Yedoma/boreal permafrost collapse ~3-4 C (2-5) vs 4.0 (3.0-6.0). AMOC is given as a central BAND '~3-5 C' where the paper gives a point estimate 4.0 (1.4-8.0). Ranges are clipped throughout (Greenland low end 1 vs 0.8; Amazon high end 5 vs 6; Labrador-Irminger high end 3 vs 3.8; abrupt permafrost thaw high end 3 vs 2.3; mountain glaciers 1-4 vs 1.5-3.0; Sahel 1-4 vs 2.0-3.5). The global-core/regional classification is also scrambled: coral reefs, abrupt permafrost thaw and southern boreal dieback are listed as global core but are REGIONAL IMPACT elements in the paper, while Arctic winter sea ice and boreal permafrost collapse are listed as regional but are GLOBAL CORE - and the East Antarctic Ice Sheet, a global core element, is missing from the packet entirely. This matters directly to the hazard: the event is defined as 'three or more core tipping elements crossed', and the packet has miscounted which elements are core. Separately, the retrieval claim is not reproducible: I fetched https://climatetippingpoints.info/2022/09/09/climate-tipping-points-reassessment-explainer/ and Table 1 is present only as an IMAGE with no extractable numbers, so the stated provenance ('threshold table retrieved from the lead author's own paper explainer') cannot have produced these figures as text. Corrected values above cross-checked against the reproduction at https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tipping_points_in_the_climate_system, sourced to Armstrong McKay et al. 2022. Sea-level figures (Greenland 7+ m, WAIS 3-4 m, EASB 10+ m) I could not verify from any retrievable text; the 10+ m for the East Antarctic subglacial basins looks high and should be re-sourced before use.

verdicts.citation_claim: Kemp et al. 2022 PNAS 119(34):e2108146119 - GCR/decimation/extreme-climate-change definitions, Four Horsemen, heat exposure
verdicts.note: Retrieved https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9407216/. All three Table 1 definitions match verbatim: Global Catastrophic Risk = 'a loss of 25% of the global population and the severe disruption of global critical systems (such as food) within a given timeframe (years or decades)'; Global Decimation Risk = 'a loss of 10% (or more)'; Extreme Climate Change = 'Mean global surface temperature rise of 3 degrees C or more above preindustrial levels by 2100'. Four Horsemen (famine/undernutrition, extreme weather, conflict, vector-borne disease), the 30 million now / ~2 billion by 2070 under SSP3-7.0 heat-exposure figures, and the IPCC text-mining coverage-gap finding are all present. PNAS vol 119, article e2108146119, 2022, eleven authors in the order given. This is the packet's cleanest citation, and the two Kemp-keyed tiers (deaths 0.12 vs the 10% decimation threshold, 0.3 vs the 25% catastrophe threshold) are correctly matched to the definitions.

verdicts.citation_claim: Ditlevsen & Ditlevsen 2023 Nat Commun 14:4254 - AMOC collapse central estimate 2057, CI 2025-2095; 2025 Author Correction changes the estimate by 8 years
verdicts.corrected_value: Author Correction full reference: Nature Communications 16:7794 (2025), DOI 10.1038/s41467-025-63201-y, PMCID PMC12370995
verdicts.note: Both halves verified. The Conversation Q&A confirms the 2057 central estimate, the 2025-2095 confidence interval, the continued-current-emissions assumption, and both author caveats ('there's not the same probability across the entire interval'; 'we find it highly unlikely that a collapse could happen as early as 2025'). The Author Correction is real - I found it in Europe PMC and read the full text at PMC12370995 - and the quoted sentence is verbatim: 'In the last step of the Strang splitting in the pseudo maximum likelihood estimation, the flow should have been evaluated in the observation at time ti, but was wrongly partially evaluated at time ti-1', with 'When corrected, the tipping time estimate changes by 8 years.' Two things to tighten rather than fix: (a) the packet gives no volume/DOI for the correction - supplied above; (b) the correction does not state the DIRECTION of the 8-year shift, and the 2057 / 2025-2095 figures quoted here are the PRE-correction numbers, so the packet is quoting an estimate it simultaneously reports as superseded. A second coding error is also disclosed in the correction ('The code for calculating uniform residuals was wrong. It has no influence on estimates, only on model control').

verdicts.citation_claim: van Westen, Kliphuis & Dijkstra 2024 Science Advances 10(6):eadk1189 - physics-based AMOC early warning, no date and no probability
verdicts.note: OpenAlex (doi:10.1126/sciadv.adk1189) confirms 'Physics-based early warning signal shows that AMOC is on tipping course', Science Advances vol 10, issue 6, article eadk1189, 2024, authors Rene M. van Westen, Michael Kliphuis, Henk A. Dijkstra - exactly as claimed. The abstract does describe the freshwater-transport minimum indicator and the finding that the present-day AMOC is on route to tipping, and it does NOT give a collapse date or a probability. The packet's explicit statement of that absence is the correct handling and is what keeps this citation from being over-read.

verdicts.citation_claim: Sherwood & Huber 2010 PNAS 107:9552-9555 - 35 C wet-bulb limit, breached at ~7 C warming, majority of population at 11-12 C
verdicts.note: Abstract retrieved verbatim via Europe PMC (doi:10.1073/pnas.0913352107). Title 'An adaptability limit to climate change due to heat stress', Sherwood SC and Huber M, PNAS vol 107, pp 9552-9555, 2010. Every quoted clause matches the abstract word for word, including 'T(W) never exceeds 31 degrees C', 'it would begin to occur with global-mean warming of about 7 degrees C', and 'With 11-12 degrees C warming, such regions would spread to encompass the majority of the human population as currently distributed.' Correctly transcribed - but see 'overall' for whether it can carry the weight the tiers put on it.

verdicts.citation_claim: Vecellio et al. 2022 J Appl Physiol 132(2):340-345 - measured Twb,crit averaged 30.55 +/- 0.98 C, well below 35 C
verdicts.note: Abstract retrieved verbatim via Europe PMC (doi:10.1152/japplphysiol.00738.2021). Title 'Evaluating the 35 degrees C wet-bulb temperature adaptability threshold for young, healthy subjects (PSU HEAT Project)', Vecellio DJ, Wolf ST, Cottle RM, Kenney WL, Journal of Applied Physiology vol 132, issue 2, pp 340-345, 2022. Both quoted passages match the abstract exactly, including '30.55 +/- 0.98 degrees C' and the conclusion that where a wet-bulb threshold applies 'that threshold is well below 35 degrees C'. Correctly scoped as young healthy adults at modest metabolic rates.

verdicts.citation_claim: Ord 2020, The Precipice Table 6.1 - 1 in 1,000 existential risk from climate over 100 years, restated on tobyord.com
verdicts.note: Retrieved https://www.tobyord.com/writing/the-precipice-revisited. The quoted sentence is verbatim: '1 in 1,000 for Climate and for Nuclear, 1 in 30 for Pandemics and 1 in 10 for Unaligned AI.' The claim that Ord says climate risk has since decreased without giving a revised number is also correct - he writes 'Climate risk is down' and notes his estimates 'are all rounded off (usually to the nearest factor of 10)', offering no new point estimate. One clarification worth carrying into the packet: '1 in 30 for Pandemics' is Ord's own shorthand on that page for what Table 6.1 splits into engineered pandemics (~1 in 30) and naturally arising pandemics (~1 in 10,000); the packet quotes Ord accurately but should not be read as saying Table 6.1 has a single pandemic row. Critically, the packet uses this as an EXISTENTIAL anchor and labels it as such, which is the right distinction - Ord's 1/1,000 is P(permanent end of humanity), not P(catastrophe).

audits.overall: Roughly trustworthy at the bibliographic level, but not yet safe to build a model on - one citation is materially wrong and two derived numbers do not follow from their sources. Every paper cited exists, every author list I could check is correct and in the right order, no DOI or URL 404s, no invented journal, and ten of twelve citations reproduce their source verbatim. That is a good base rate, and the packet deserves credit for repeatedly disclosing what a source does NOT say (van Westen gives no date, Kornhuber gives no multiplier, Ord gives no revised climate number). The failures are these. (1) The Armstrong McKay et al. 2022 tipping table is substantially misreported: about two thirds of the rows have wrong central estimates, clipped ranges, or the wrong global-core/regional classification, with errors as large as ~2 C vs 4.0 C for southern boreal dieback and ~2 C (1-3) vs 1.6 C (1.5-1.7) for Barents Sea ice; the East Antarctic Ice Sheet is missing entirely. Because this hazard's event is defined as 'three or more CORE tipping elements crossed', a miscount of which elements are core propagates straight into the model. The stated provenance is also not reproducible - Table 1 on the cited explainer page exists only as an image with no extractable numbers. (2) Citation 2 of the mainline hazard attaches two real IPCC figures to a Carbon Brief article that does not contain them: the 1.07 C (0.8-1.3 C) human-caused warming figure is on the OTHER Carbon Brief article the packet already cites, and the very likely ECS range 2-5 C is in AR6 SPM A.4.4 and in neither Carbon Brief text. (3) A units problem the citations themselves expose: the mainline tiers appear to be exactly 10x Carleton's rate. Carleton's full mortality risk is 85 per 100,000 per year = 0.00085, but the high-emissions tier carries deaths=0.0085, and the current-policy tier's 0.0014 is 10x the 0.000136 that Carleton's own '84 percent lower under RCP4.5' implies - the ratio between those two tiers (0.165) reproduces the paper's 84% reduction to two digits, which proves the ladder was scaled from Carleton and then shifted a decimal place. At 8 billion people the high-emissions tier asserts 68 million climate deaths per year. That must be corrected, or the cumulative-vs-annual basis stated explicitly. (4) Two tiers outrun their cited mechanism: the wet-bulb pair (Sherwood 2010, Vecellio 2022) is correctly transcribed, but Sherwood's habitability breach requires ~7 C global warming and majority-population exposure requires 11-12 C, far above any tier in this packet, so those citations cannot support the 0.3 or 1.0 death fractions; and the terminal tier (deaths=1, p=0.005) has no supporting source at all - Kemp explicitly declines to quantify extinction, and the only existential anchor, Ord's 1/1,000 per century, is a number the author himself says has come down. On the arithmetic the packet is clean: tier probabilities sum to exactly 1.0 in both hazards; the mainline rate of 1/yr is the right treatment for a chronic non-stochastic hazard; and the tipping rate 0.0015/yr does compound to 13.9% over 100 years with the 0.0003-0.005 range giving 3.0%-39.4%, matching the stated 14% and 3%-40% - though that rate is an uncited author-estimate applied to an event defined by an END-OF-CENTURY temperature condition, which is a category mismatch (an annual onset hazard cannot cleanly represent 'reaches 3 C by 2100'), and the implied ~7.5e-4 per century for permanent extinction is at least in Ord's ballpark. Sources I actually retrieved this session: both Carbon Brief AR6 articles; the Climate Impact Lab Carleton summary (twice); OpenAlex records for doi:10.1093/qje/qjac020, 10.1038/s41558-019-0600-z, 10.1038/s41467-023-38906-7 and 10.1126/sciadv.adk1189; the NBER w27599 page; climatechangepost.com's Gaupp summary; climatetippingpoints.info's explainer (twice); the Wikipedia reproduction of Armstrong McKay Table 1 (twice); PMC9407216 (Kemp); The Conversation AMOC Q&A; Europe PMC searches for Ditlevsen/overturning and for DOI 10.1038/s41467-025-63201-y plus the full correction text at PMC12370995; Europe PMC abstracts for doi:10.1073/pnas.0913352107 and 10.1152/japplphysiol.00738.2021; and tobyord.com/writing/the-precipice-revisited. Caveat on my own coverage: WebSearch was unavailable (the session's 200-call budget was already exhausted at my first call), so all verification was done by direct WebFetch against cited URLs, DOI-keyed API records and independent reproductions. I could therefore check that what is cited is real, but I could not do open-ended searching to find better or contradicting literature the packet never mentions - and my Armstrong McKay corrections rest on a Wikipedia reproduction plus a garbled fetch of the author's explainer rather than on the paywalled Science table itself, so re-verify those numbers against the paper before editing the packet.

verdicts.note: The page is real, the author is real, and every quoted claim is accurate — but THE YEAR IS WRONG BY SIX YEARS. This matters more than a typo would in most packets: the packet is leaning on this source to overturn the Toba-bottleneck story, and dating a 2018 commentary to 2024 falsely implies it postdates and supersedes the 2021-2023 primary literature (Crick 2021, Caron 2023) that the packet cites alongside it. Content confirmed verbatim: 'Numerous genetic analyses have not detected a bottleneck that coincides with the Toba eruption'; the ~50 ka signal attributed to an out-of-Africa founder effect citing Lippold et al. 2014, Karmin et al. 2015, Malaspinas et al. 2016 (the page also cites Mallick et al. 2016, which the packet omits); a separate ~150-130 ka reduction coinciding with MIS 6 citing Li and Durbin 2011 and Kidd et al. 2012; and 'AMH populations were always relatively low, started to decline around 150 ka, and continued to decrease until ~30 ka'. I could not confirm the packet's claim that the page cites Henn et al. 2012. The packet is properly honest that this is expert commentary rather than peer-reviewed work. https://www.johnhawks.net/p/the-so-called-toba-bottleneck-didnt-happen

verdicts.citation_claim: Cassidy & Mani (2022), EA Forum, 'On the assessment of volcanic eruptions as global catastrophic or existential risks' — reporting Ord's 1 in 10,000 this century, '100 times that of asteroids and comets combined', Rougier's 17,000 (95% CI 5,200, 48,000), ice-core M8 of 15,000 yr, and '~1 in 6 this century' for M7+
verdicts.corrected_value: Year is 2021 (published 13 October 2021), not 2022
verdicts.note: Post is real, authors are right (Mike Cassidy and Lara Mani), every figure checks out — but THE YEAR IS WRONG. Published 13 October 2021, not 2022. Confirmed verbatim: 'Ord 2020, and others have suggested that the existential risk posed by volcanoes is the largest of the potential "natural" catastrophes - 100 times that of asteroids and comets combined'; "we won't provide a new estimate for probability of existential risk from volcanic eruptions from Ord's 1 in 10,000 chance this century estimate" — which confirms BOTH the Ord figure and the packet's statement that the authors offer no probability of their own. Their table reproduces Rougier's M7 as 1,200 years (95% CI 680-2,100) and M8 as 17,000 years (95% CI 5,200-48,000), and gives an ice-core M8 recurrence of 15,000 years. The '~1 in 6 this century' confirmed: 'If we use the recent ice age estimates this suggests that the combined probability of an eruption of magnitude 7 and above occurring is ~1 in 6 this century.' NOTE the attribution nuance the packet gets slightly wrong: the '100 times asteroids and comets' line is presented by Cassidy and Mani as 'Ord 2020, and others have suggested', not as Ord's claim alone. I did NOT retrieve The Precipice Table 6.1 directly this session, so Ord's 1-in-10,000 figure rests entirely on this second-hand report — which the packet correctly and explicitly discloses. https://forum.effectivealtruism.org/posts/jJDuEhLpF7tEThAHy/on-the-assessment-of-volcanic-eruptions-as-global

verdicts.citation_claim: 'Anna Pham', Juan B. Garcia Martinez, Vojtech Brynych, Ratheka Stormbjorne, Joshua M. Pearce, David C. Denkenberger (2022), Nutrients 14(3), 492, doi:10.3390/nu14030492 — ASRS framing; three response periods each 3-9 months; resilient-food diets achievable with residual vitamin D, E, K deficiency risk
verdicts.corrected_value: First author is Alix Pham, not Anna Pham
verdicts.note: Same defect as the vei7 instance of this citation, repeated verbatim — the first author is ALIX Pham, not Anna Pham. A wrong name propagated to both hazards is a sign the packet's citation records were copied rather than re-checked. Everything else confirms: Nutrients 14(3):492, 2022, doi:10.3390/nu14030492; ASRS definition verbatim; the three causes; 'The time following the catastrophe was divided into three periods, each expected to last between 3 and 9 months'; and the finding that nutritionally adequate resilient-food diets are achievable with preparation, with persistent vitamin D, E and K shortfalls (D and E reaching severe-risk levels in pessimistic scenarios). SUBSTANTIVE FLAG: the packet cites this as the 'mitigation lever' for a supereruption, but the paper's modelled case is a 150 Tg soot NUCLEAR winter, not a volcanic one, and it models diet composition rather than mortality. It cannot support the vei8 tier deaths_fractions of 0.12, 0.6 or 1. https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8839908/

audits.overall: Trustworthy on numbers, not on bylines — build on it only after correcting five attribution defects and re-deriving three tier figures. I retrieved and read all fifteen sources this session: the full Newhall/Self/Robock Geosphere PDF page by page (pages 1-24, including Tables 1-3 and the Concluding Remarks), the Lin et al. and Lohmann/Svensson and Crick et al. Climate of the Past HTML, the Rougier et al. EPSL record, the Wilson et al. and Caron et al. and Pham et al. PMC records, the Wieners/Halfdanarson NHESS HTML (including Sect. 6.1), the ScienceDaily/Illinois release, the John Hawks post, and the Cassidy/Mani EA Forum post. Every quantitative figure in the packet checked out — I found not one wrong number, and several quotes I expected to be spliced (Lin's 'three eruptions ... 0.07 per millennium', Newhall's '2 x 10-3 yr-1 ... demands our attention', Wieners' 11,500/8,200 England figures) are verbatim. The rate arithmetic is clean in both hazards: 1/1200 = 0.00083, Lin's 1.60/millennium = 0.0016, Newhall's 2/millennium = 0.002; and 1/17,000 = 0.000059 with 1/48,000 = 0.000021 and 1/5,200 = 0.00019. Tier probabilities sum to exactly 1.00 in both hazards. THE FAILURES ARE ALL IN THE ATTRIBUTION LAYER, and the worst is Wilson et al. 2023: the packet asserts 'author list as published' and then prints a list containing an invented author ('John Cassidy'), a misnamed real one ('Lauren Mani' for Lara Mani), and a real author silently deleted and replaced by a duplicate (Stefan Broennimann erased in favour of a second Cassidy). Four more: 'Anna Pham' for Alix Pham, repeated identically in both hazards; John Hawks dated 2024 when the post is from February 2018, which falsely implies it postdates the primary literature it is deployed against; and the Cassidy/Mani EA post dated 2022 when it is October 2021. Nothing is invented whole — no phantom paper, no dead DOI, no 404 — so the packet's sourcing discipline is real; but a byline is exactly what a downstream reader will re-use without re-checking, and a name that survives into a model's provenance record is a name that gets cited onward. SEPARATELY, THREE SEVERITY FIGURES ARE AUTHOR-ESTIMATES DRESSED IN CITED CLOTHING. vei7 tier 3 at deaths=0.06 implies roughly 490 million dead; the packet's own ceiling evidence is Newhall's 'could kill millions' (proximal) and Wilson's Tambora signal of a -1.9 degC land-temperature year with recovery by the mid-1820s — even tier 2 at 0.01 (~80 million) is an order of magnitude past 'millions', and 0.06 is unsupported by any source in the packet; the Laki one-sixth mortality is a national fluorosis-and-famine figure with no global analogue and cannot be scaled up. vei8 'decade without a summer' at deaths=0.6 (~4.9 billion) rests on Pham et al., which models diet composition under a 150 Tg NUCLEAR soot case and contains no mortality model at all. And vei8 terminal at p=0.015 is actively undercut by the packet's own citations 5 and 6: Timmreck's microphysical attenuation argument and Hawks' finding that no Toba-coincident bottleneck exists in the human genome — humanity passed through the largest eruption in two million years, at a small dispersed pre-agricultural population, without a detectable genetic signature. That p=0.015 multiplied by the 5.9e-5 rate happens to land at ~8.8e-5 per century, near Ord's 1-in-10,000 — but that is a coincidence of construction, not a derivation, and the packet does not say so. Two smaller framing issues worth fixing before modelling: the vei7 rate range mixes event definitions (Lin's low bound is forcing-based and would include Laki-type high-sulfur fissure eruptions, Rougier's M7 is geological and silicic-explosive only, so the interval is not a coherent uncertainty range on one quantity), and the Cabaniss 'months to years of warning' claim is about silicic caldera systems but is filed under the VEI-7 hazard, where Newhall says the runup was 'just hours to days'.

verdicts.citation_claim: Hellman 2012 Stanford STS152 Handout #6a — three initiating events in 1960-2010 gives 6%/yr; 1/3 conditional gives 2%/yr for a Cuban crisis; 10-50% threshold crossing gives 0.2-1%/yr; a further 10-50% gives 0.02-0.5%/yr for full-scale war; explicitly a lower bound
verdicts.note: Read the handout directly. Every quoted string is verbatim: 'A study of the first 50 years of the nuclear deterrence era (1960-2010)… Three events divided by 50 years produces an occurrence of 6% per year' (p.4); the empirical 1/3 and 'a 2% probability of having a Cuban crisis each year' (p.4); 'results in a range of 0.2% to 1% per year for the probability of crossing the nuclear threshold' (p.10); 'results in a range that runs from 0.02% per year to 0.5% per year for the risk of a full-scale nuclear war' (p.11). Lower-bound status confirmed by footnote 11 ('these estimates are lower bounds, so the true risk is higher') and by 'considering only crises involving Cuba as the cause of the war'. Header confirms Prof. Hellman, 'Nuclear Weapons, Risk and Hope,' Handout #6a, STS152, AUT 2012-13. RELEVANCE MISMATCH, not a citation error: this chain models a US-Russia Cuba-type crisis. It is filed under the India-Pakistan hazard, and its 0.5%/yr ceiling is what sets that hazard's 0.005/yr upper bound. Hellman himself notes a US-Russia first use 'carries a higher risk of producing a full-scale war than if the first use is by terrorists or India or Pakistan.' https://www-ee.stanford.edu/~hellman/sts152_03/handout06a.pdf

verdicts.note: Read the published PDF. Title, three authors, Science & Global Security 21:106-133, 2013, DOI 10.1080/08929882.2013.798984 all correct (paper prints 'Kelly Hostetler', no middle initial). Table 3 (p.121) and Table 4 (p.122) both give status quo 0.009 / 0.003 as claimed. The 90% CI sentence on p.120 is verbatim: 'ranges from 0.0002 to 0.07 in the base case, and from 0.00001 to 0.05 if excluding launch during low tensions.' The MAC-indication medians 0.01 / 0.0006 (Danger Calm) and 0.003 / 0.0000008 (Safe Calm) are Table 2 (p.121), exact. The n=37 / u=0.08 rejection argument is p.124, exact. The Hellman comparison is p.124, exact. DERIVATION FLAG: the packet's own rate range 0.0001-0.009 is NOT this source's interval. It puts Barrett's base-case MEDIAN (0.009) at its ceiling when Barrett's 95th percentile is 0.07, and its floor 0.0001 matches neither 0.0002 nor 0.00001. audits.overall: Mostly yes — this is an unusually clean packet, and I retrieved and read all thirteen sources rather than trusting a summarizer. Confirmed by direct reading: the Toon et al. 2019 Science Advances PDF (abstract and the pp.6-7 emission chain), the IPPNW Nuclear Famine 2022 PDF (Tables 1, 2 and 3, and the kcal page), the NASA GISS abstract page for Xia et al. 2022 Nature Food, the live FAS Status of World Nuclear Forces table, the EA Forum XPT post, Hellman's Stanford STS152 Handout #6a (pp.1-12), the Barrett/Baum/Hostetler 2013 Science & Global Security PDF (Tables 2-4 and pp.120-126), the Coupe et al. 2019 JGR PDF first page, the GCRI Working Paper 18-1 PDF, and Ord's The Precipice Revisited. Nothing is fabricated: every DOI, URL, journal, volume and page range resolves, and no author is attached to a paper out of thin air. TWO CITATION DEFECTS. (1) Figure error: the packet reports the worldwide calorie loss for the 250 x 100 kt scenario as 42%; the IPPNW report says 41% in its body text (p.13) and again in its own Table 3 (p.20), with 42% appearing only in a p.13 infographic circle — the packet copied the outlier. (2) Partial misattribution: citation 2 lists Nicole S. Lovenduski among the authors of Xia et al. 2022 Nature Food. She is not; she is an author of Toon et al. 2019. The packet's own citation 3 has the roster right, so this is a transcription slip, but it is exactly the failure mode that matters. THREE MODELLING PROBLEMS THAT ARE WORSE THAN THE CITATION ERRORS. (a) The full-scale rate range 0.0001-0.009/yr is presented as if it came from Barrett et al., but Barrett's stated 90% CI is 0.0002-0.07 (base case) — the packet's ceiling is Barrett's MEDIAN, understating the cited upper tail by roughly eightfold, and its basis label 'physical-model' is wrong for what is a fault-tree Monte Carlo with elicited parameters. (b) The counterforce-weighted tier assigns deaths_fraction 0.3 — about 2 billion people — but every cited death mechanism (Xia, IPPNW, Coupe) runs through soot from burning cities. A counterforce exchange by construction does not produce the ~37 Tg of urban soot that 30% mortality requires in the packet's own source table; that tier is unsupported by its cited mechanism. The adjacent 0.95-deaths / 200-year 'winter plus civilisational collapse' tier has no cited support at all and should be marked author-estimate. (c) The regional upper tier (37-47 Tg, p=0.35) requires 250-500 warheads at 100 kt, but the packet's own FAS citation gives India 190 and Pakistan 170 total inventory with tested yields of 12-45 kt, and IPPNW itself says those scenarios 'involve more nuclear weapons than India and Pakistan may now possess'. Weighting the physically-unavailable end of the ladder at 0.35 is an overweight. Two smaller notes: Hellman's chain is a US-Russia Cuba-type trigger but is used to set the India-Pakistan rate ceiling, and the 10/15/25-year recovery times sit below Mills et al. 2014 (quoted in the packet's own IPPNW Table 3), which puts surface temperatures reduced for more than 25 years for the 5 Tg case alone. To the packet's credit, the death fractions are all exactly reconstructible from IPPNW Table 2 plus direct fatalities (0.054 = (335.5+27)/6703; 0.21 = mean of (1122.4+52) and (1579.3+97) over 6703; 0.39 = mean of (2238.8+127) and (2675.3+164) over 6703; 0.808 = 5413/6703), both tier sets sum to exactly 1.00, and the terminal tier reconciles with Ord and XPT. Build on it, but fix the 42%, drop Lovenduski, re-derive the full-scale range from Barrett's actual percentiles, and rebuild or delete the counterforce and civilisational-collapse tiers.

verdicts.citation_claim: Cirillo & Taleb (2016), Physica A 452:29-45 / arXiv:1505.04722v2 — fat tails: GPD shape xi > 1, shadow mean >> sample mean
verdicts.note: Read the full arXiv:1505.04722v2 PDF this session. Every figure is exact. Abstract/§I: 565 armed conflicts with more than 3000 casualties over 1-2015 AD. §IV: 'the best threshold for the fitness of GPD is 25,000 casualties... A total of 331 armed conflicts lie above this threshold (58.6% of all our data)'; rescaled/dual threshold becomes 145k. Table III (p.9): Raw 25k xi=1.4985 (SE 0.1233), sigma=90620 (2016); Rescaled 145k xi=1.5868 (0.1265); Dual 145k xi=1.5915 (0.1268). §VII: restricted to 1500-2015, xi=1.4093 raw, 1.4653 rescaled. Table IV (p.10): at 145k, shadow 3.6885e7 vs sample 1.7710e7, ratio 2.08; ratios across thresholds 50k/100k/145k/300k/500k/1000k = 2.88/2.43/2.08/1.95/1.96/1.85, so the stated 1.85-2.88 range is right. Table V (p.11): at 145k shadow SD 3.0788e8 vs sample 1.0120e8, ratio 3.0422. Journal reference independently confirmed via Crossref (DOI 10.1016/j.physa.2016.01.050): Physica A vol 452, pp. 29-45, June 2016 — the packet's volume/pages are correct (the arXiv landing page's own journal-ref field is unreliable here). One nuance the packet gets right and most secondary citations get wrong: xi>1 makes the mean of the *unbounded/naive* fit non-existent, while the paper's whole point is that the bounded dual distribution has a finite but much larger 'shadow' mean. https://arxiv.org/pdf/1505.04722 ; https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1016/j.physa.2016.01.050

verdicts.citation_claim: Cirillo & Taleb (2016) — 'long peace' not distinguishable from chance; inter-arrival times table
verdicts.note: Table II (p.7 of the preprint) reproduced exactly, all 11 quoted numbers: Avg Raw / MAD Raw / Avg Rescaled / MAD Rescaled at thresholds 0.5M = 23.71/35.20/9.63/15.91; 1M = 34.08/47.73/13.28/20.53; 2M = 56.44/72.84/20.20/28.65; 5M = 93.03/113.57/34.88/46.85; 10M = 133.08/136.88/52.23/63.91; 20M = 247.14/261.31/73.12/86.19; 50M = 345.50/325.50/103.97/114.25. The quoted verbatim sentence is genuine (p.7): 'the absence of a conflict generating more than, say, 5 million casualties in the last sixty years is highly insufficient to state that their probability has decreased over time, given that the average inter-arrival time is 93.03 years, with a mean absolute deviation of 113.57 years!'. §VII confirms 504 events over 1500-2015 and that an equiprobable Multinomial cannot be rejected at a 10% confidence level. Caveat, not an error: this dataset is ALL armed conflicts including civil wars back to 1 AD, not interstate great-power war, so the raw 34.08 yr figure mixes epochs; the population-rescaled 13.28 yr is the like-for-like modern number. https://arxiv.org/pdf/1505.04722

audits.overall: Yes — with two bibliographic repairs and several severity-tier caveats, this packet is trustworthy enough to build on, which is an unusual verdict from me. I retrieved and read, in this session: the full arXiv:1505.04722v2 PDF (Cirillo & Taleb) including Tables II, III, IV and V and §VII; Crossref records for 10.1016/j.physa.2016.01.050, 10.1126/sciadv.aao3580 and 10.1093/isq/sqag046; Clauset's author preprint PDF at mn.uio.no including Table I; the OUP article page for ISQ 70(3) sqag046; the FHI Technical Report 2008/1 PDF (pp.1-5, the table and the 'Other Risks' paragraph); the EA Forum XPT announcement; the UNODA chemical weapons page; the HHS CHEMM Tokyo sarin case study; the NRC dirty-bombs backgrounder; Caplan's total4.doc at GMU; tobyord.com/writing/the-precipice-revisited; MichaelA's EA Forum post (twice, with different prompts); the Bostrom & Cirkovic Chapter 1 introduction PDF; and an Open Library full-text search that surfaced the book's own scanned table of contents. Every quantitative figure I could reach is exact to the last digit — the Cirillo-Taleb GPD shape parameters and inter-arrival table, Clauset's alpha=1.53+/-0.07, q=0.428+/-0.002, x_0.75=26,625 and all nine Table I probabilities, the full Sandberg-Bostrom matrix, the XPT medians, and all three chemical/radiological primary sources. The 2026 ISQ paper, which I expected to be the fabrication, is real (Spagat & Thompson, 'Great Power Warfare and the Decline of War Question') and its abstract carries the quoted 401-test, p=0.002 claim verbatim. Two citation defects: (1) Caplan's chapter is Chapter 22, not Chapter 25 — the book's own TOC and the editors' introduction both fix it, though p.504 is right and every probability he states is quoted correctly; (2) the EA Forum URL used to source Ord's Table 6.1 discusses that table but reproduces only five of the twelve claimed rows and contains none of the dystopia typology attributed to it — cite The Precipice, Table 6.1, p.167 directly instead. Beyond citations, four modelling problems the sources do not support. First, the war hazard's 'Civilisational' tier (deaths 0.24, ~2 billion) has no support in any cited mechanism: the event definition excludes nuclear use, yet Clauset's own billion-death discussion — the only place this scale appears in the packet's literature — explicitly conditions on 'current nuclear weapons... deployed widely'. Second, the tier labels are fraction-blind: 'World-war scale' at 0.004 is ~33M deaths, roughly an eighth of WWII's ~3% fractional toll, while 'Beyond any recorded war' at 0.037 is only just above it. Third, the chemical hazard's 'Maximum plausible use' at 3.7e-5 (~300,000 deaths in one calendar year) is triple the entire WWI chemical death toll accumulated over four years, and both attack-specific citations (Tokyo: 13 dead; NRC: an RDD 'would not release enough radiation to kill people') point an order of magnitude the other way — the packet honestly labels the rate author-estimate, but should label this tier the same way. Fourth, the dystopia rate's basis is labelled 'expert-elicitation' when the only quantitative anchor is one economist's own unconditional subjective probability; the packet's own fourth citation argues that the standard elicitation instruments cannot price this hazard at all, so the label contradicts the evidence beneath it — 'author-estimate' or 'single-expert judgement' is the honest tag. On the arithmetic: all three hazards' tier probabilities sum to exactly 1.000, none exceed 1, and the war rate is well-derived — 0.03/yr matches Cirillo-Taleb's raw 34.08-year inter-arrival for >=1M casualties, and the 0.075/yr upper bound matches their population-rescaled 13.28 years from the same table, so the range is anchored rather than decorative.

verdicts.citation_claim: Citation 1 — Marani, Katul, Pan & Parolari (2021) PNAS 118(35):e2105482118, post-correction: Py 0.11–0.89%; mean recurrence 879 y (95% CI 730–1081); T(5.7‰/y)=1/0.00114=877 y; GPD xi=1.40, sigma=0.0113 ‰/y, mu=0.001 ‰/y, P(i<=mu)=0.62; alpha=-0.71 for i>3e-2 ‰/y; 1600–1945, 395 events, 182 fully documented; tripled emergence -> 292 y (243–360); COVID i=2.63 ‰/y, T=523 y (450–622), P_Life=0.17, tripled 0.44.
verdicts.note: CONFIRMED VERBATIM, and unusually well done. I fetched the cited unipd PDF, which is the POST-correction version (it carries the 'SEE CORRECTION FOR THIS ARTICLE' banner and a 18 Oct 2023 download stamp) and read pages 1-4 directly. Every single element checks out word-for-word: abstract 'varies between 0.11 and 0.89% from 1600 to present, while its mean recurrence time today is 879 y (95% CI: 730 to 1081 y)'; body 'T(5.7 ‰/year) = 1/0.00114 = 877 y (95% CI is 730 to 1081 y)'; 'position parameter mu = 1.000 x 10^-3 ‰/year, scale parameter sigma = 0.0113 ‰/year, and shape parameter xi = 1.40'; 'p0 = P(i <= mu) = 0.62'; 'power-law exponent alpha = -0.71 approximately for i > 3 x 10^-2 ‰/year'; '182 epidemics with known occurrence, duration, and number of deaths, 108 ... and 105 ... for a total of 395 epidemics' (1600-1945); 'the mean recurrence interval of a Spanish flu-like event down to 292 y (95% CI 243 to 360 y)'; 'an intensity of 2.63 ‰/year, which corresponds to an average recurrence time of 523 y (95% CI 450 to 622 y)'; 'P_Life = 1 - (1 - 1/523)^100 = 0.17' and the tripled value 0.44. The two figures 877 vs 879 are the paper's own internal rounding, not a packet error. One residual oddity that is the PAPER's, not the packet's: the Significance box in the corrected PDF still carries the withdrawn '38%' lifetime figure. URL: https://www.research.unipd.it/bitstream/11577/3457653/2/marani-et-al-2021-intensity-and-frequency-of-extreme-novel-epidemics.pdf

verdicts.citation_claim: Citation 2 — Duke/EurekAlert release 926011 (23 Aug 2021) carrying the PRE-correction figures: '~2% in any year' for a COVID-impact pandemic; '0.3% to 1.9% per year'; '38% chance' for someone born in 2000. Superseded by correction 10.1073/pnas.2302169120 whose text blames code that summed events in two subsequent years.
verdicts.note: CONFIRMED on both halves. The EurekAlert release (https://www.eurekalert.org/news-releases/926011, Duke University, 23 August 2021, 'Statistics say large pandemics are more likely than we thought') returns all three quoted strings verbatim. The correction is real: Europe PMC returns 'Correction for Marani et al., Intensity and frequency of extreme novel epidemics', PNAS 120(12):e2302169120, 2023, DOI 10.1073/pnas.2302169120, PMID 36917675, PMCID PMC10041107. I read its full text via https://www.ebi.ac.uk/europepmc/webservices/rest/PMC10041107/fullTextXML and it does say 'the code erroneously computed the number of epidemics in one year by summing the number of events in two subsequent years', with the yearly probability revised from 0.27-1.9% to 0.11-0.89%, recurrence from ~400 y to 879 y, and the tripled-rate lifetime probability from 0.76 to 0.44. Recording the withdrawn numbers explicitly, as this packet does, is good practice — most secondary sources still quote the 2% / 38%.

verdicts.citation_claim: Citation 3 — Meadows, Stephenson, Madhav & Oppenheim (2023) BMJ Global Health 8(11):e012026: 75 spillover events, 24 countries, 1963-2019, 17,232 deaths; events +4.98%/y (95% CI 3.22-6.76); deaths +8.7%/y (95% CI 4.06-13.62); 4x events and 12x deaths by 2050; filoviruses 40/15,771, SARS-CoV-1 2/922, Machupo+Nipah 33/529. 'COVID-19, influenza and vector-borne pathogens excluded.'
verdicts.corrected_value: Exclusions are broader than stated: vector-borne pathogens (e.g. Zika, CCHF), influenza, ENDEMIC viruses (Lassa, hantavirus), AND any pathogen causing fewer than 50 deaths.
verdicts.note: Paper is real and every figure is verbatim correct — title 'Historical trends demonstrate a pattern of increasingly frequent and severe spillover events of high-consequence zoonotic viruses', authors and citation exactly as claimed (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10626885/). '4.98% (CI95% [3.22%; 6.76%])', '8.7% (CI 95% [4.06%; 13.62%])', 'four times the number of spillover events and 12 times the number of deaths in 2050', and the three pathogen rows all match. ONE UNDERSTATEMENT: the packet's exclusion list omits endemic viruses (Lassa, hantavirus) and the <50-deaths cut, which were applied specifically to minimise surveillance bias. That matters here, because the packet uses this 4.98%/y as support for the Marani 'tripling of emergence' scenario — and the exclusion of endemic and low-count outbreaks makes the trend a trend in HIGH-CONSEQUENCE spillover only, not in emergence generally.

verdicts.citation_claim: Citation 4 — Koch, Brierley, Maslin & Lewis (2019) Quaternary Science Reviews 207:13-36, doi:10.1016/j.quascirev.2018.12.004: 119 regional estimates, pre-1492 population 60.5 million (IQR 44.8-78.2), 1.04 ha/capita, epidemics removed 90% (IQR 87-92%), 55.8 Mha (IQR 39.0-78.4) abandoned, 7.4 Pg C (IQR 4.9-10.8), 3.5 ppm (IQR 2.3-5.1).

Title 'Earth system impacts of the European arrival and Great Dying in the Americas after 1492', Quaternary Science Reviews 207 (2019) 13-36, doi 10.1016/j.quascirev.2018.12.004, authors Alexander Koch, Chris Brierley, Mark M. Maslin, Simon L. Lewis. Every number matches to the digit including all four IQRs. Caveat on how it is USED rather than on the citation: Koch attributes the 90% to 'European epidemics' as a compound of disease with warfare, enslavement and famine in a first-contact, immunologically naive, isolated continental population — a configuration with no modern analogue. See my note on the 'Great-Dying-class' tier.

(2022) Nature Ecology & Evolution 6(3):297-306, doi:10.1038/s41559-021-01652-4: 261 radiocarbon-dated coring sites, 19 modern-day European countries, 21 historical regions; sharp decline in Scandinavia, France, western Germany, Greece, central Italy; continuity in central/eastern Europe, Ireland and Iberia.

verdicts.citation_claim: Citation 6 — Snyder-Beattie, Ord & Bonsall (2019) Scientific Reports 9:11054, doi:10.1038/s41598-019-47540-7: annual natural extinction probability 'almost guaranteed to be less than one in 14,000, and likely to be less than one in 87,000'; genus Homo 'below one in 870,000'; plus the caveat about risks our ancestors did not face.
verdicts.note: CONFIRMED VERBATIM (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6667434/; the nature.com URL 303-redirects to an IdP but the DOI is correct). Title 'An upper bound for the background rate of human extinction', Sci Rep 9:11054, 2019. All three one-in-X figures and the 'No similar guarantee can be made for risks that our ancestors did not face, such as anthropogenic climate change or nuclear/biological warfare' sentence are exact. verdicts.citation_claim: Citation 7 — Toby Ord, The Precipice (2020) Table 6.1, claimed 'retrieved this session via a third-party reproduction of the table' at an EA Forum post: natural pandemics ~1 in 10,000; engineered ~1 in 30; unaligned AI ~1 in 10; nuclear war ~1 in 1,000; asteroid ~1 in 1,000,000; supervolcano ~1 in 10,000; total ~1 in 6.
verdicts.corrected_value: Verified from Ord's own site (https://theprecipice.com/faq): total = 'humanity faces a one-in-six chance of existential catastrophe over the next century', and 'all natural risks TOGETHER amount to about a 1 in 10,000 chance of existential catastrophe per century'. The per-risk rows for pandemics, AI, nuclear, asteroid and supervolcano remain unverified.
verdicts.note: THE PACKET'S WEAKEST CITATION AND THE ONE I WOULD NOT BUILD ON. The cited URL does NOT reproduce Table 6.1. I fetched https://forum.effectivealtruism.org/posts/Z5KZ2cui8WDjyF6gJ/some-thoughts-on-toby-ord-s-existential-risk-estimates twice with different prompts; the page is a critique of Ord's methodology. The only numbers on it are scattered comment-thread references (1 in 6,000 and 1 in 1.5 million for asteroid size bands; 3% for engineered pandemics; 3% for unforeseen anthropogenic) — NOT the table. The 'right order of magnitude ... each could easily be a factor of 3 higher or lower' quote IS on that page, verbatim, so that half of the citation stands; the numeric table does not. I then tried five further reproductions and found none: Wikipedia 'Global catastrophic risk', 'Human extinction', 'The Precipice', 'Toby Ord', and 80000hours.org/problem-profiles all decline to reproduce the per-risk breakdown. SPECIFIC HAZARD FLAG: Ord's own FAQ states that ~1 in 10,000 per century is the figure for ALL NATURAL RISKS COMBINED. The packet attaches ~1 in 10,000 to 'naturally arising pandemics' AND separately ~1 in 10,000 to 'supervolcanic eruption', which would make the natural total ~1 in 5,000. That is exactly the total-vs-component conflation an auditor should expect, and I cannot rule it out from any source I retrieved. Until someone opens the book (or a scan of p. 167), treat every per-risk row here as unverified, and note that the terminal tier's calibration target (~1 in 8,800 per century) currently rests on it.

verdicts.citation_claim: Citation 8 — Spreeuwenberg, Kroneman & Paget (2018) AJE 187(12):2561-2567: best estimate 17.4 million (15 million 1918 + 2.5 million 1919), sample 402 million ~20% of a ~1.8 bn world population, no CI, 'simulations of total number of deaths being greater than 25 million are not realistic'.
verdicts.note: CONFIRMED (https://academic.oup.com/aje/article/187/12/2561/5092383, DOI 10.1093/aje/kwy191). Title 'Reassessing the Global Mortality Burden of the 1918 Influenza Pandemic'. Abstract: 'Total pandemic mortality was an estimated 15 million deaths worldwide in 1918 (n = 2.5 million in 1919) after including the rates for British India and controlling for wars and the underlying mortality trend.' Sample: 14 countries, combined 1918 population 402 million, ~20% of world population. The 25-million sentence is verbatim: 'According to our validity analysis, simulations of total number of deaths being greater than 25 million are not realistic based on the underlying mortality rates included in Human Mortality Database and in British India.' No CI is given, as the packet says. The 15 + 2.5 = 17.5 vs the headline 17.4 is the paper's own rounding, not a packet error.

verdicts.citation_claim: Citation 9 — Max Roser / Our World in Data (2020): world population in 1918 was 1.8 billion; Spreeuwenberg 17.4 m = 'almost 1% of the world population'; Johnson & Mueller 2002 'at least 50 million' = 2.7%, upper bound 100 million = 5.4%; Patterson & Pyle 1991 'between 24.7 and 39.3 million'.
verdicts.note: CONFIRMED (https://ourworldindata.org/spanish-flu-largest-influenza-pandemic-in-history, Max Roser, 2020). All four figures returned verbatim, including the 2.7% and 5.4% conversions and the Patterson & Pyle range. This is the citation that makes the tier-1 death fraction auditable — see my note on the 0.018 figure in 'overall'.

verdicts.citation_claim: Citation 10 — Jones, Patel, Levy, Storeygard, Balk, Gittleman & Daszak (2008) Nature 451(7181):990-993, doi:10.1038/nature06536: 335 EID events 1940-2004; zoonoses 60.3%; 71.8% of those from wildlife; 54.3% bacteria or rickettsia.
verdicts.note: CONFIRMED (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5960580/). Title 'Global trends in emerging infectious diseases', all seven authors in the stated order, Nature 451(7181):990-993, 2008, DOI 10.1038/nature06536. 'a database of 335 EID events (origins of EIDs) between 1940 and 2004', 'EID events are dominated by zoonoses (60.3% of EIDs): the majority of these (71.8%) originate in wildlife', '54.3% of EID events are caused by bacteria or rickettsia' — all exact. As with citation 6, the packet's URL is a Europe PMC REST query string rather than a human-readable page.

verdicts.citation_claim: Citation 11 — Bar-On, Phillips & Milo (2018) PNAS 115(25):6506-6511, doi:10.1073/pnas.1711842115: humans ~0.06 Gt C, livestock ~0.1 Gt C, wild mammals ~0.007 Gt C, domesticated poultry ~0.005 Gt C 'about threefold higher' than wild birds ~0.002 Gt C.
verdicts.note: CONFIRMED VERBATIM (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6016768/). 'The biomass distribution on Earth', PNAS 115(25):6506-6511, 2018, DOI as stated, all five biomass figures exact including the 'about threefold' phrasing (which is the paper's own rounding of 0.005/0.002 = 2.5x, not the packet's).

verdicts.citation_claim: Citation 12 — 'Miguel A. Acevedo, Forrest P. Dilleuth, Andrew J. Flick, Matthew J. Faldyn, Bret D. Elderd (2019), Evolution 73(4):636-647, doi:10.1111/evo.13692': meta-analysis of 29 empirical studies from over 6000 papers; abstract on partial support for the trade-off hypothesis; a quoted 'Mechanism' sentence.
verdicts.corrected_value: Second author is Forrest P. DILLEMUTH, not 'Dilleuth'.
verdicts.note: Paper is real and correctly identified — I read the PDF's title page directly (https://www.lsu.edu/faculty/elderd/ewExternalFiles/Acevedo_et_al-2019-Evolution.pdf): 'Virulence-driven trade-offs in disease transmission: A meta-analysis', Evolution 73-4: 636-647, doi 10.1111/evo.13692. '29 empirical studies, after reviewing over 6000 published papers' and the four core relationships are exact, and the long abstract quote ('We found strong support for an increasing relationship between replication and virulence... but more work remains to be done') is verbatim. TWO DEFECTS. (1) The second author's surname is misspelled: it is Forrest P. Dillemuth (Dept of Biological Sciences, LSU). 'Dilleuth' is not a person, and a name that does not exist is precisely the fingerprint of a fabricated citation even when — as here — the underlying paper is genuine. Fix it before this packet is read by anyone else. (2) The sentence the packet puts inside quotation marks as 'Mechanism:' ('increasing within-host replication rate increases mortality rates, which ultimately translates into a shorter infectious period at the population level, resulting in a deceleration in transmission rate') is NOT verbatim. The abstract's actual wording is 'This cost associated with replication ultimately results in a deceleration in transmission rate because increasing within-host replication increases host mortality.' Same substance, but it should not carry quotation marks.

verdicts.citation_claim: Citation 13 — Medievalists.net reporting Benedictow, The Complete History of the Black Death (2021): 65% mortality, ~52 million dead from ~80 million; Ziegler (1969) England 34-45% and 'one European in three'; 'John Aberth (2023)' approximately half.
verdicts.corrected_value: The '(2023)' attached to Aberth is the Medievalists.net article's own date (18 November 2023), not a date for Aberth. The page attributes the ~half estimate to Aberth's 'The Black Death: The Great Mortality of 1348-1350' and gives no year for it.
verdicts.note: CONFIRMED on substance (https://www.medievalists.net/2023/11/how-many-people-died-black-death/, published 18 November 2023). Benedictow: 'roughly around 80 million inhabitants' pre-plague and 'A mortality rate of 65% indicates that roughly 52 million died', from The Complete History of the Black Death (2021). Ziegler 1969: England 'between 34% and 45% died from the disease' and 'To maintain that one European in three died during the period of the Black Death'. Aberth: 'he believes that half the population died'. The only defect is the spurious year on Aberth. Also worth saying plainly: this is a popular-history website, not a peer-reviewed source, and the packet leans on it for the single largest mortality fraction in the tier table — the Benedictow 65% figure is contested, and the packet's own citation 5 (Izdebski, peer-reviewed) is the direct rebuttal.

verdicts.citation_claim: AMR citation 1 — Antimicrobial Resistance Collaborators / Murray et al. (2022) The Lancet 399(10325):629-655: 4.95 million (3.62-6.57) associated and 1.27 million (95% UI 0.911-1.71) attributable deaths in 2019; six pathogens 929,000 attributable / 3.57 million associated; LRI >1.5 million associated; MRSA >100,000 attributable; Australasia 6.5 (4.3-9.4) and western sub-Saharan Africa 27.3 (20.9-35.3) per 100,000; 471 million records, 23 pathogens, 88 pathogen-drug combinations.
verdicts.note: CONFIRMED VERBATIM, every element (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8841637/). 'Global burden of bacterial antimicrobial resistance in 2019: a systematic analysis', Lancet 399(10325):629-655, 2022. '4.95 million (3.62-6.57)' associated, '1.27 million (95% UI 0.911-1.71)' attributable, '929 000 (660 000-1 270 000)' and '3.57 million (2.62-4.78)' for the six pathogens, the LRI and MRSA sentences, both regional rates with their UIs, and 471 million / 23 / 88 all match. The packet is also careful to keep 'attributable' and 'associated' distinct in the citation text, which is correct — but see 'overall' for how the tier table then loses that distinction.

verdicts.citation_claim: AMR citation 2 — GBD 2021 AMR Collaborators (2024), Lancet 404(10459):1199-1226, figures taken from EurekAlert release 1057804: 1.14 m direct and 4.71 m associated in 2021, 1.06 m direct in 1990; 1.91 m direct and 8.22 m associated by 2050; 39 m direct / 169 m associated cumulative 2025-2050; under-fives 'declined by 50%', 70+ 'increased by more than 80%'. Packet states the 95% UIs are NOT reported because the paper was behind a 403.
verdicts.corrected_value: Under-five decline is 59.8% (488,000 in 1990 -> 193,000 in 2021), not 50%. And the missing UIs are recoverable: 2021 attributable 1.14 m (1.00-1.28), associated 4.71 m (4.23-5.19); 1990 attributable 1.06 m (0.841-1.27), associated 4.78 m (4.00-5.55); 2050 attributable 1.91 m (1.56-2.26), associated 8.22 m (6.85-9.65); cumulative 2025-2050 attributable 39.1 m (33.0-46.0), associated 169 m (145-196).
verdicts.note: Citation is real and the headline numbers are right. Volume/issue/pages confirmed independently: 'Global burden of bacterial antimicrobial resistance 1990-2021: a systematic analysis with forecasts to 2050', Lancet 404(10459):1199-1226, 2024, DOI 10.1016/S0140-6736(24)01867-1, PMID 39299261 (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11718157/). The press release (https://www.eurekalert.org/news-releases/1057804, 16 Sep 2024) returns all the quoted totals. TWO REPAIRS. (1) The under-five figure is understated: the release's own numbers are 488,000 (1990) to 193,000 (2021), a 59.8% decline; the 70+ rise is 89.7%, so 'more than 80%' is fine. (2) The packet's caveat that the uncertainty intervals could not be obtained is now void — the full abstract is open access at PMC11718157 and I have listed every UI above. A packet that reports point forecasts to 2050 without their intervals is understating its own uncertainty by a lot; 39.1 m cumulative has a range of 33.0-46.0 m.

verdicts.citation_claim: AMR citation 3 — Jim O'Neill, Review on Antimicrobial Resistance final report (May 2016): '10 million lives a year and a cumulative 100 trillion USD of economic output are at risk'; 700,000 deaths today; the cancer comparison; 'over 70 percent (by weight)' of US medically important antibiotics sold for animals; market entry rewards 'of around one billion USD each'.
verdicts.note: CONFIRMED VERBATIM against the actual report PDF, which I read (https://amr-review.org/sites/default/files/160518_Final%20paper_with%20cover.pdf; foreword pp. 1-3, executive summary pp. 4-5, signed 'May, 2016'). Executive summary: 'We estimate that by 2050, 10 million lives a year and a cumulative 100 trillion USD of economic output are at risk due to the rise of drug-resistant infections if we do not find proactive solutions now to slow down the rise of drug resistance. Even today, 700,000 people die of resistant infections every year.' Foreword: '...today's already large 700,000 deaths every year would become an extremely disturbing 10 million every year, more people than currently die from cancer' and 'The cost in terms of lost global production between now and 2050 would be an enormous 100 trillion USD if we do not take action.' Agriculture: 'In the US, for example, of the antibiotics defined as medically important for humans by the US Food and Drug Administration (FDA), over 70 percent (by weight) are sold for use in animals.' Market entry rewards: 'of around one billion USD each'. Commissioning bodies confirmed on p. 4: 'as commissioned by our sponsors, the UK Government and the Wellcome Trust.' Caveat on USE, not on the citation: O'Neill's 10 m is a widely criticised scenario projection, not an estimate, and O'Neill himself writes 'it is of course possible that our estimates may turn out to be too large'. The GRAM forecast for the same year is 1.91 m attributable / 8.22 m associated, so O'Neill's 10 m is roughly the GRAM ASSOCIATED figure — which is the sense in which the packet's 'high scenario' tier is defensible, but only if the associated/attributable distinction is stated.

audits.overall: Mostly trustworthy on citations, but NOT yet safe to build on, for two reasons — one bad citation and one arithmetic error that is worse than the citation. WHAT I ACTUALLY RETRIEVED (WebSearch was budget-exhausted, so every check below is a direct WebFetch of the source, several of them read as PDF page images): the Marani post-correction PDF at research.unipd.it (pp. 1-4, read directly — it carries the correction banner); EurekAlert 926011; the PNAS correction full text via Europe PMC PMC10041107 plus its bibliographic record; PMC10626885 (Meadows); the Koch PDF at White Rose (abstract page read directly); PMC8913360 (Izdebski); PMC6667434 (Snyder-Beattie); academic.oup.com AJE 187(12) (Spreeuwenberg); ourworldindata.org/spanish-flu; PMC5960580 (Jones 2008); PMC6016768 (Bar-On); the Acevedo PDF at lsu.edu (title page read directly); medievalists.net; PMC8841637 (GRAM 2019); EurekAlert 1057804 and PMC11718157 (GBD 2021 AMR); the O'Neill review PDF at amr-review.org (pp. 1-5 read directly); plus six failed attempts to find a reproduction of Ord's Table 6.1 (the cited EA Forum post twice, Wikipedia x3, 80000hours, and theprecipice.com/faq, which did yield the 1-in-6 total and the all-natural-risks-together figure). FINDING 1 — THE BAD CITATION. Ord Table 6.1 (natural-pandemic citation 7) is source-misattributed: the EA Forum URL does not reproduce the table, and the packet says so obliquely ('via a third-party reproduction') while presenting eleven per-risk figures as retrieved. Only the 'factor of 3' quote and the 1-in-6 total survive verification. Ord's own site says ~1 in 10,000 per century is the figure for ALL natural risks COMBINED, so the packet's ~1 in 10,000 for natural pandemics specifically may be a total-vs-component conflation. This matters because the terminal tier (p=0.001, implying ~1.14e-4 per century) is calibrated against it. FINDING 2 — THE ARITHMETIC, AND THIS IS THE ONE THAT WOULD BREAK A MODEL. Every AMR deaths_fraction is exactly 10x too large for an annual event. 4.71 m associated / ~8.0 bn = 0.00059, packet says 0.0059. 8.22 m / ~9.7 bn (2050) = 0.00085, packet says 0.0085. O'Neill's 10 m / ~9.7 bn = 0.00103, packet says 0.0103. Three independent tiers, the same factor of ten — this is a units slip (annual figures carrying a decadal denominator), not three coincidences. As written, tier 1 asserts that 0.59% of humanity, about 47 million people, die of AMR in a single year, which is 10x the cited associated figure and 41x the attributable one, and the hazard's own event definition is explicitly per-calendar-year. Fix the exponent or state the accumulation window. Compounding it: the event is defined on ATTRIBUTABLE deaths (1.14 m 'direct cause') while all four tiers are evidently built from ASSOCIATED deaths — the exact (a)/(b) conflation the brief warns about, in the one hazard where the packet had both numbers correctly quoted one paragraph earlier. THREE SMALLER DEFECTS: 'Forrest P. Dilleuth' should be Dillemuth (a nonexistent name is the fingerprint of fabrication even on a genuine paper); 'John Aberth (2023)' borrows the Medievalists.net article's date; and the packet's stated inability to obtain the GBD 2021 uncertainty intervals is now void — they are open access at PMC11718157 and I have supplied all eight. TIER PLAUSIBILITY (pandemic): probabilities sum to exactly 1.000 and 1.00, no overflow. Tier 1 at deaths=0.018 is internally consistent with i=5.7 per mil/yr over ~3.2 years, but sits 1.9x above the packet's own best-evidence citation (Spreeuwenberg 17.4 m / 1.8 bn = 0.0097) — justify the choice or move it toward 0.014.
