Tier 2 is the weakest: a 17% conditional chance that a 1918-intensity event kills 10% of humanity, ~7x the 1918 rate, leaning on Koch's 90% Americas figure — but that die-off was a first-contact, immunologically naive, isolated continental population, a configuration with no modern analogue, and the packet's own citation 5 (Izdebski) is the standing argument that even the Black Death was spatially heterogeneous. Tier 3 (deaths=0.35 globally) exceeds Ziegler's and Aberth's own European Black Death rates and applies them worldwide. The terminal tier survives the one hard constraint I could verify: 0.00114 x 0.001 = 1.14e-6/yr is comfortably under Snyder-Beattie's 1/14,000 bound, though it consumes ~10% of their 1/87,000 'likely' budget for all natural causes at once. The Marani rate itself (0.00114/yr, CI 0.000925-0.00137) is exactly 1/877 and 1/1081-1/730, verbatim from the corrected paper, and is the single best-executed piece of the packet.

verdicts.citation_claim: [1] FAO Cereal Supply and Demand Brief (04/09/2026): 2026/27 stocks-to-use 31.6% (down from 31.9%); stocks 947.2 Mt; utilization 2 965 Mt
verdicts.note: Retrieved https://www.fao.org/worldfoodsituation/csdb/en today (brief dated 04/09/2026). Verbatim: 'the resulting world stocks-to-use ratio for cereals at the end of seasons in 2026/27 is forecast at 31.6 percent, down from the previous season's level of 31.9 percent'; 'World cereal utilization in 2026/27 is forecast at 2 965 million tonnes'; stocks 947.2 Mt confirmed. Caveat for the packet, not the citation: this is a live page that is overwritten monthly, and a single current-year snapshot cannot support a basis=observed-frequency rate for a <=20% event — no time series is cited anywhere in the hazard.

verdicts.citation_claim: [2] FAO Crop Prospects and Food Situation No.1 Feb 2008: cereal stocks/trend-use 19.2%, 'lowest level of the past five years'; wheat 23.1% vs 34%; coarse grains 15%; rice 23.5%
verdicts.note: Retrieved https://www.fao.org/4/ah881e/ah881e05.htm. All four percentages and both qualifying clauses are verbatim, including 'the lowest level of the past five years' and 'well under 34 percent observed during the first half of the decade'. Note this ratio is ending stocks over TREND utilization of the FOLLOWING season — the same FAO measure as the 31.6% in citation 1, so the two are comparable. Good.

verdicts.citation_claim: [3] Adin Richards, IFP (12 Dec 2022): China 69% corn / 60% rice / 51% wheat; US share 40% (1980s) to just above 5%; 1973 stocks below 17%
verdicts.note: Retrieved https://ifp.org/food-reserves-global-food-security/. Author Adin Richards, 12 December 2022, title 'Food Reserves, Global Food Security, and International Stability'. All three figures verbatim ('China holds 69% of the corn, 60% of the rice, and 51% of the wheat stored worldwide'; 'declined from up to 40% in the 1980s to just above 5% today'; 'In 1973, stock levels fell below 17%'). The packet paraphrases 'holds' as 'currently possesses' — harmless. IFP is an advocacy think tank, not peer-reviewed; the China stock shares are USDA-derived and widely regarded as soft, which the packet does not flag.

verdicts.citation_claim: [4] Garcia Martinez, Behr, Pearce, Denkenberger (ALLFED EarthArXiv 08/2024): 'only enough food stocks to feed the global population for around 6 months (Denkenberger and Pearce 2014)'
verdicts.note: Downloaded the PDF from https://eartharxiv.org/repository/object/7688/download/14586/ and extracted the text. Title, four authors and 'This version: 08/2024' all correct. The sentence is verbatim at p.6, including the 'and little to no preparation to deploy interventions capable of offsetting a sudden food production loss' clause and the Denkenberger and Pearce 2014 attribution.

verdicts.citation_claim: [1] Puma, Bose, Chon, Cook (2015) ERL 10(2) 024007: 85%/83% low-or-marginal self-sufficiency; connections doubled, flows +42%/+90%; 6 of top 17 wheat and 4 of top 9 rice exporters restricted; >96% of wheat imports from France; 116->157 mmt wheat, 24.6->42.7 mmt rice
verdicts.note: Retrieved https://iopscience.iop.org/article/10.1088/1748-9326/10/2/024007. Title 'Assessing the evolving fragility of the global food system', authors/volume/year/article number all correct, and every numeric claim is verbatim. Two precision points: (a) the source says 'SSR is marginal or low in 83% of countries for 2005-2009, with an average of 85% over the entire period 1992-2009' — the packet lists both but does not say which is which; (b) the >96%-from-France claim is specifically 'Senegal and Haiti', not the packet's generic 'some least developed countries'. The quoted phrase 'an accelerating sensitivity' I could not isolate in the retrieved text and did not confirm.

verdicts.citation_claim: [2] IFPRI (2022): countries restricting food exports 'climbed from 3 to 16', 17% of traded calories; bans 16 countries/29 measures = 12.4%; licensing 7 countries/10 measures = 4.6%; 'across the whole of 2022, 32 countries imposed 77 export restrictions'
verdicts.note: The cited page is Glauber, Laborde & Mamun, 'From bad to worse: How Russia-Ukraine war-related export restrictions exacerbate global food insecurity' (IFPRI, early April 2022). Retrieved via reader proxy: '3 to 16', 'about 17% of total calories traded in the world', '12.4% of traded calories' and '4.6% of trade calories' are ALL verbatim and correct. But the fourth claim — 32 countries / 77 export restrictions across the whole of 2022 — cannot be on that page, which was written in early April 2022, and I did not find it on the Food and Fertilizer Export Restrictions Tracker either (https://www.foodsecurityportal.org/tools/COVID-19-food-trade-policy-tracker). Worse for the hazard: that tracker shows restricted traded calories FALLING through 2022 — 10.6% in May, 6.84% in July, 7.2% in September, 6.98% in October — so 17% is a one-month April peak, not a standing figure, and the packet uses it as if it characterised the episode. WebSearch was unavailable to me this session, so I can say the 32/77 figure is not at the cited URL, not that it exists nowhere.

verdicts.citation_claim: [3] FAO Crop Prospects Feb 2008: 19.2% stocks-to-use, 'lowest level of the past five years'
verdicts.note: Same retrieval as hazard-1 citation 2; verbatim at https://www.fao.org/4/ah881e/ah881e05.htm.

verdicts.citation_claim: [4] Adin Richards, IFP (2022): China 69%/60%/51% of world corn/rice/wheat stocks; '35 countries imposing agricultural export restrictions' after the invasion of Ukraine
verdicts.note: Both verbatim at https://ifp.org/food-reserves-global-food-security/ — including '35 countries imposing agricultural export restrictions in the wake of the disruptions caused by the Russian invasion of Ukraine'. Note this 35 is a different, looser count than IFPRI's 16-countries-with-bans, and the packet does not reconcile them.

verdicts.citation_claim: [1] Erisman, Sutton, Galloway, Klimont, Winiwarter (2008) Nature Geoscience 1:636-639: 44% (2000) / 48% (2008) fed by N fertilizer; ~100 Tg N/yr; ~80% of NH3 to fertilizer; 100 Tg N vs 17 Tg N consumed; NUE ~80% (1960) to ~30% (2000); >=32 MJ/kg N, ~1% of primary energy; 27% of population / ~4 billion births / 42%; 1.9 to 4.3 persons per hectare
verdicts.note: Downloaded the PDF from https://www.iai.int/.../2008.Erisman-et-al_NatureGeo.pdf and extracted full text. Title 'How a century of ammonia synthesis changed the world', five authors as listed, pages 636-639. EVERY ONE of the nine quoted figures is verbatim, including the exact sentences 'we estimate, that by 2000, nitrogen fertilizers were responsible for feeding 44% of the world's population. Our updated estimate for 2008 is 48% -- so the lives of around half of humanity are made possible by Haber-Bosch nitrogen' and 'equivalent to at least 32 MJ kg-1 N fixed, or about 1% of the global primary energy supply'. This is the cleanest citation in the packet. One conceptual caution the packet should carry: 48% is 'fed by', i.e. a dependence share, not a death fraction — it is not the (b)-type quantity the tiers need.

verdicts.citation_claim: [2] Hannah Ritchie / Our World in Data (2023): Smil — harvests ~half without N fertilizer, 40% of 2000 population dependent; Rosa & Gabrielli 2023 — about half of the global population fed by synthetic N in 2019
verdicts.corrected_value: Article is bylined 7 November 2017, not 2023
verdicts.note: Retrieved https://ourworldindata.org/how-many-people-does-synthetic-fertilizer-feed. All three figures confirmed: Smil's 'approximately half of current levels' and '40 percent of the global population in 2000', Erisman's 44%/48%, and Rosa & Gabrielli (2023) 'about half of the global population was fed by synthetic nitrogen fertilizers in 2019'. Defect: the year. OWID bylines the piece Hannah Ritchie, 7 November 2017; it evidently carries a later revision (that is how it can cite a 2023 paper), but the page shows no revision date, so '(2023)' in the packet is not what the source says.

verdicts.citation_claim: [3] ALLFED preprint reporting Moersdorf, Rivers, Denkenberger, Breuer & Jehn (2024, Global Challenges): yields -35% rice, -41% soybeans, -48% corn, -37% wheat without synthetic fertilizer, pesticides, irrigation and mechanization
verdicts.note: Verbatim in the extracted ALLFED PDF (p.5): 'Reductions in the agricultural yield of staple crops in the absence of synthetic fertilizer, pesticides, irrigation and mechanization have been estimated as -35% for rice, -41% for soybeans, -48% for corn, and -37% for wheat'. The Moersdorf author list, title ('The Fragile State of Industrial Agriculture: Estimating Crop Yield Reductions in a Global Catastrophic Infrastructure Loss Scenario'), journal (Global Challenges, Wiley) and year all match the preprint's reference list exactly. BUT the packet over-reads it: this hazard's event is a >=50% loss of Haber-Bosch ammonia ALONE, whereas the -35/-41/-48/-37% figures require removing fertilizer AND pesticides AND irrigation AND mechanization simultaneously. They do not license the tier-2 deaths=0.15 or tier-3 deaths=0.55 for a fertilizer-only shock.

verdicts.citation_claim: [1] Buldyrev, Parshani, Paul, Stanley, Havlin (2010) Nature 464:1025-1028 / arXiv:0907.1182: <k_c>=2.445 for two interdependent ER networks vs <k_c>=1 for a single ER network; broader degree distribution => more vulnerable
verdicts.note: Retrieved https://arxiv.org/abs/0907.1182. Title 'Catastrophic cascade of failures in interdependent networks', all five authors in the order given. Both quoted sentences are verbatim from the abstract, including the value 2.445 and the inversion of the broad-degree-distribution result. (The published Nature version states 2.4554; the packet quotes the arXiv figure and is consistent with the source it cites.) Note the paper is cited for a topological result about random ER graphs — it is not evidence about the real North American grid, and the packet does not use a number from it in the rate.

verdicts.citation_claim: [2] Hines, Apt, Talukdar (2009), CEIC 09-01 / Energy Policy: NERC 1984-2006, large-blackout frequency has not decreased, power-law size-frequency, 100-year North American blackout = 186,000 MW; 'large blackout' >= 50,000 customers or 300 MW
verdicts.note: Downloaded https://phines.w3.uvm.edu/publications/2009/hines_2009_blackouts.pdf and extracted full text. 'Large Blackouts in North America: Historical trends and policy implications', Paul Hines / Jay Apt / Sarosh Talukdar, CEIC Working Paper 09-01 (published version Energy Policy 37). Every quoted clause is verbatim from the abstract, including 'the size of the 100-year blackout, which for North America is 186,000 MW', and the definition 'service disruptions to at least 50,000 customers or 300 MW of demand'. The 0.01/yr rate is exactly 1/100 and is internally consistent with the cited recurrence. HOWEVER the same abstract states 'We do not find that blackout sizes and blackout durations are significantly correlated' — which directly undercuts the packet's tier structure: a 186,000 MW event is a size-of-load event, and Hines gives no basis for the tier-3 'months-scale continental grid loss' (deaths 0.1) being the 3% tail of it. The 2003 event was ~62,000 MW and was restored in days.

verdicts.citation_claim: [3] PNNL-32773 (April 2022), O'Brien et al.: blackstart mix hydro 37% / gas turbine 60% / fossil 1% / combined cycle 1% / diesel 1% / wind+solar 0%; nuclear cannot blackstart per NRC; coal cold start >48 h; nuclear offline for days after 14 Aug 2003
verdicts.note: Downloaded https://www.pnnl.gov/main/publications/external/technical_reports/PNNL-32773.pdf and extracted full text. Report number, April 2022 date, and all nine authors in the order given are correct; title is 'Electric Grid Blackstart: Trends, Challenges, and Opportunities'. Table 3 'Blackstart units registered with NERC' matches exactly (37/60/1/1/1/0). The NRC sentence is verbatim including the '(PJM 2019)' attribution; the coal 'cold start - not available to be synchronized to the grid for more than 48 hours' bullet is verbatim from section 2.1.3 (Coal Units); and 'multiple nuclear power facilities were offline for several days following the event (Eto 2004)' is verbatim.

verdicts.citation_claim: [4] Rinaldi, Peerenboom, Kelly (2001), IEEE Control Systems Magazine 21(6):11-25, DOI 10.1109/37.969131 — cited only for the interdependency taxonomy, no figure taken
verdicts.note: Verified the DOI against the Crossref record (https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1109/37.969131): title 'Identifying, understanding, and analyzing critical infrastructure interdependencies', IEEE Control Systems, volume 21, issue 6, pages 11-25, 2001. The DOI resolves and the metadata matches the packet exactly. The packet is honest that no number is taken and that it could not obtain the full text — that disclosure is the right behaviour. Minor: the supplied 'URL' is a Google Scholar lookup query string rather than a source document; https://doi.org/10.1109/37.969131 would be the proper locator.

verdicts.citation_claim: [1] NIST/RTI via Office of Space Commerce (2019): $1bn/day GPS outage impact; $45bn for a 30-day outage in planting season; $1.4tn US benefits since the 1980s; 'a 30-day maritime outage was put at almost $10 billion because there is currently no backup for GPS'
verdicts.corrected_value: $10.4 billion point estimate, range $7.8-14.6 billion
verdicts.note: I retrieved https://space.commerce.gov/doc-study-on-economic-benefits-of-gps/ and reproduced its full body text. The first three figures are verbatim and correct (RTI International for NIST, released 6 June 2019). The maritime claim is NOT on that page — the word 'maritime' does not appear on it at all, and no figure near $10 billion appears. I then downloaded the RTI final report itself (https://www.rti.org/sites/default/files/gps_finalreport.pdf) and found the real source, Section 9, Table 9-6: 'economic impacts associated with a 30-day loss of GPS range from $7.8 billion to $14.6 billion, with a point estimate of $10.4 billion', and the section summary 'because currently there is no backup for GPS, an unexpected outage of GPS today would have significant economic impacts'. So the quoted clause is real but comes from a different document, and 'almost $10 billion' understates a $10.4bn point estimate — it should be 'about $10.4 billion (range $7.8-14.6 billion)'. Cite the RTI final report, not the Commerce press page.

verdicts.citation_claim: [2] CLS Group (2016), 'Settlement Risk in the Global FX Market: How Much Remains?': CLS settles over 50% of global FX, roughly USD 1.5 trillion daily; netting cuts funding needs by an average of 96%; 18 eligible currencies
verdicts.corrected_value: CLS settled value: 'a little over $5.0 trillion per day in the first half of 2014' (gross, both legs; ~$2.5 trillion on a BIS-comparable basis), not $1.5 trillion
verdicts.note: Downloaded https://www.cls-group.com/media/mrgpmp2c/sringlobalfxoctober2016.pdf and extracted full text. TWO defects. (1) Authorship: this is a working paper by Dino Kos and Richard M. Levich, 'Draft: 26 October 2016' — not a corporate 'CLS Group (2016)' publication as the packet states; it is merely hosted on cls-group.com. (2) The daily figure is wrong by roughly a factor of three. The paper says CLS 'now settles roughly half of all FX turnover' (that part is right) but $1.5 trillion is the 1998 GLOBAL daily FX turnover in the paper's own opening comparison ('turnover from $1.5 trillion in 1998 to over $5.3 trillion in 2013'). CLS's own settled value is given as 'roughly $3.5 trillion per day in 2007', 'more than $4 trillion per day in mid-2008', and 'a little over $5.0 trillion per day in the first half of 2014' — and the paper explicitly warns that CLS counts both legs, so divide by two for BIS comparability (~$2.5tn). The other two claims ARE verbatim: 'CLS to settle all payment instructions is reduced by an average of 96%' and '18 CLS-eligible currencies'.

verdicts.citation_claim: [3] ALLFED preprint (2024): complex supply chains increase systemic vulnerability such that a disruption at one point could affect the entire system (Maynard 2015); COVID-19 highlighted the fragility of food systems
verdicts.note: Both sentences verbatim in the extracted ALLFED PDF (pp.3 and 6), with the '(Maynard 2015)' and '(Laborde et al. 2020; Liu, Lauta, and Maas 2020)' attributions intact. Note this citation carries no number at all — it supports narrative framing only, and cannot bear any weight in the 0.07/yr rate or the tier severities.

verdicts.citation_claim: [4] Puma et al. (2015): 85% of countries have low or marginal food self-sufficiency; 83% of countries for 2005-2009
verdicts.note: Confirmed at https://iopscience.iop.org/article/10.1088/1748-9326/10/2/024007: 'SSR is marginal (SSR ~1) or low (SSR < 1) in 83% of countries for 2005-2009, with an average of 85% over the entire period 1992-2009.' Both numbers are real; the packet presents them side by side without saying that 83% is the period-specific value and 85% the 1992-2009 average. Also worth noting: low self-sufficiency is not the same as exposure to a logistics failure, which is how the packet labels it — self-sufficiency ratio says nothing about buffer stocks or substitutability.

verdicts.citation_claim: [1] ALLFED preprint (2024): lignocellulosic sugar $0.43-0.91/person/day (Throup et al. 2022); natural-gas single cell protein ~3x global calorie need at $1.65-2.81 (Garcia Martinez et al. 2022); paraffin-derived fats 8-17% of calories at $0.74-2.71; ~6 months of food stocks; up to ~90% loss of staple crop production (Xia et al. 2022); vitamin C 140,000 t/yr and lysine 2.2 Mt/yr; Figure 10 Argentina ~32M -> ~305M people fed vs population ~46M
verdicts.note: All textual figures verified verbatim in the extracted PDF: the $0.43-0.91 and $1.65-2.81 and $0.74-2.71 cost ranges with their 'entire global production' framings and Throup/Garcia Martinez attributions; 'loss of up to ~90% of global staple crop production in the worst year of the catastrophe' with (Xia et al. 2022); 'produced industrially at 140,000 tonnes/year, and lysine at 2.2 million tonnes/year'; and the 6-months stocks sentence. ONE sub-claim I could not verify: the Figure 10 read-off (~32M -> ~305M against a ~46M population line) is the packet's own reading of a bar chart, and the figure caption states no numbers. The body text instead says Argentina's GROSS calorie production equals the requirements of '~600 million people -- 13 times the country's population' with net production '~110 million', and that under 150 Tg ASRS, dropping meat and biofuel use 'would enable feeding almost 4 times its population' (~184M, not 305M). Treat the 305M as unsourced until someone reads the actual axis.

verdicts.citation_claim: [2] Jehn et al. (2024), Earth's Future 12(3) e2023EF003710: seaweed scale-up to 45% of global human food demand in 9-14 months; substituting 15% of human food, 10% of animal feed, 50% of global biofuel; Gracilaria tikvahiae
verdicts.corrected_value: Earth's Future 12(1), e2023EF003710 (not 12(3))
verdicts.note: The paper is real and the headline figure is exactly right. Semantic Scholar returned the full abstract: 'Seaweed as a Resilient Food Solution After a Nuclear War', authors Florian Ulrich Jehn, Farrah Jasmine Dingal, Aron Mill, Cheryl Harrison, Ekaterina Ilin, Michael Y. Roleda, Scott C. James, David Denkenberger — verbatim: 'a scale up to an equivalent of 45% of the global human food demand (spread among food, animal feed, and biofuels) in around 9-14 months, while only using a small fraction of the global ocean area', and the Gracilaria tikvahiae model and the nutrient-mixing result are both confirmed. TWO defects. (1) The issue number is wrong: both Crossref (api.crossref.org/works/10.1029/2023EF003710) and OpenAlex give volume 12, ISSUE 1, article e2023EF003710, published January 2024 — not 12(3). (2) The 15%/10%/50% food/feed/biofuel breakdown is not in the abstract and I could not confirm it: Wiley returned 403 to every route I tried (direct, pdfdirect, reader proxy), Europe PMC has no record, and no preprint copy is on OSF/EarthArXiv. It may well be in the body, but as of this session it is an unverified number presented as a quotation.

verdicts.citation_claim: [3] FAO CSDB (2026): stocks 947.2 Mt against utilization 2 965 Mt, 'a stocks-to-use ratio of 31.6 percent -- approximately 115 days of cereal consumption'
verdicts.note: The two FAO numbers are verbatim and correct (retrieved today). The DERIVED ratio does not follow from the pair the packet puts it next to: 947.2/2965 = 31.9%. FAO's published 31.6% uses trend utilization of the FOLLOWING season as the denominator, which is a different number the packet never gives — so as written the citation invites the reader to check an arithmetic that fails. The days figure is 116.6, which 'approximately 115' rounds acceptably. Also note the days-of-consumption gloss double-counts against citation [1] of hazard 1: it is the same snapshot used twice for two different purposes.

verdicts.citation_claim: [4] Adin Richards, IFP (2022): China 69%/60%/51% of world corn/rice/wheat stocks; US share from up to 40% in the 1980s to just above 5% today
verdicts.note: Both figures verbatim at https://ifp.org/food-reserves-global-food-security/ (see hazard-1 citation 3). Same caveat: think-tank secondary source citing USDA stock estimates, and China's reported stocks are the least trustworthy line in the global balance sheet — a fact that matters more here than anywhere else in the packet, since this hazard's whole argument is that the buffer is not where it would be needed.

audits.overall: Better than the base rate for this failure mode, but not clean enough to build on unedited. I found no fabricated papers, no invented authors, and no dead DOIs: every one of the 15 citation entries points at a real document, and the two highest-load scientific citations — Erisman et al. 2008 (nine separate figures) and Hines/Apt/Talukdar 2009 (186,000 MW) — check out word for word against full texts I pulled and read this session. Three real defects. (1) CLS: the "roughly USD 1.5 trillion daily" is wrong by about a factor of three — $1.5tn is 1998 global FX turnover in the paper's own opening comparison, while CLS's settled value is "a little over $5.0 trillion per day in the first half of 2014" (~$2.5tn on a BIS-comparable basis) — and the document is a Kos & Levich working paper, not a "CLS Group" publication. (2) GPS: the maritime "almost $10 billion" clause is not on the Office of Space Commerce page it is attributed to; it comes from the RTI final report, Table 9-6, where the point estimate is $10.4bn (range $7.8-14.6bn). (3) IFPRI: the "32 countries imposed 77 export restrictions across the whole of 2022" cannot come from a blog written in early April 2022, and the tracker I retrieved shows restricted traded calories falling to 6.8-7.2% by autumn 2022 — so the 17% headline the hazard leans on is a one-month peak, not a standing level. Two metadata errors on top: Earth's Future 12(1) not 12(3), and the OWID piece is bylined 2017 not 2023. The structural problems are worse than the citation hygiene. Tier probabilities sum to exactly 1.00 in all six hazards (none exceed 1), but four of the six put their worst tier at "coincides with an abrupt sunlight reduction or infrastructure loss" — so a single ASRS is counted four times and each hazard silently borrows the ASRS's lethality rather than deriving deaths from its own mechanism; that is where deaths=0.35, 0.2, 0.55, 0.08 and 0.7 all come from, and none of them is supported by the cited source for that hazard. Specific unsupportable tiers: the infrastructure hazard's tier 3 (months-scale loss, deaths 0.1) is anchored to Hines's 100-year event, but Hines explicitly reports blackout size and duration are NOT significantly correlated, so a 186 GW size event licenses nothing about duration; the nitrogen hazard's tiers lean on Moersdorf's -35/-41/-48/-37% yields, which require removing fertilizer AND pesticides AND irrigation AND mechanization, not a fertilizer-only shock; and the resilient-food hazard defines its event as "deployed capacity below 1%" and then assigns p=0.05 to "shock met with full resilient-food deployment", which its own event definition rules out. On rates: the 0.01/yr blackout rate is exactly 1/100 and consistent with its citation; the 0.12/yr grain-buffer rate is roughly double what the packet's own evidence supports (the cited sub-20% episodes are 1973 and 2007/08, i.e. nearer 0.05-0.08/yr over the post-1960 record), and it is derived from a single live FAO snapshot with no time series cited. Sources I actually retrieved to reach these verdicts: the FAO CSDB page (twice, dated 04/09/2026), FAO Crop Prospects Feb 2008, the IFP article, the full ALLFED EarthArXiv PDF (text-extracted), Puma et al. via IOPscience (twice), the Erisman et al. PDF (text-extracted), the OWID page (twice, incl. via reader proxy), the Hines et al. CEIC PDF (text-extracted), the Buldyrev arXiv abstract, PNNL-32773 (text-extracted), the Crossref record for the Rinaldi DOI, the Office of Space Commerce GPS page (twice, incl. full body text), the RTI GPS final report PDF (text-extracted), the Kos & Levich CLS PDF (text-extracted), the Semantic Scholar / Crossref / OpenAlex records for the seaweed DOI, the IFPRI blog via reader proxy, and the foodsecurityportal export-restrictions tracker via reader proxy. Caveat on my own coverage: this session's WebSearch budget was already exhausted before I started, so everything above is direct fetching of the cited URLs plus DOI metadata APIs — I could not do independent discovery, which means for the two figures I could not locate (IFPRI 32/77, and the seaweed 15/10/50 split, both behind a Wiley 403) I can say they are not at the cited source, not that they exist nowhere.

verdicts.citation_claim: Cite 1 — Ord, The Precipice Table 6.1 as reproduced in Risk Frontiers Briefing Note 415: engineered pandemic 3 kyr (~1 in 30/century), 2nd after unaligned AI 1 kyr; nuclear/climate/env 100 kyr; natural pandemic & supervolcano 1 Myr; asteroid 100 Myr; supernova 100 Byr; total ~1 in 6.
verdicts.note: RETRIEVED AND EXTRACTED THE PDF. Briefing Note 415, 'Ranking of Potential Causes of Human Extinction', Paul Somerville, Risk Frontiers. Its Table 1 reads exactly: Unaligned AI 1 kyr; Engineered Pandemic 3 kyr; Unforeseen Anthropogenic 3 kyr; Other Anthropogenic 5 kyr; Nuclear War / Climate Change / Other Environmental Damage 100 kyr each; Natural Pandemic 1 Myr; Supervolcano Eruption 1 Myr; Flood Basalt 32 Myr (Snyder-Beattie et al. 2019, not Ord); Asteroid or Comet Impact 100 Myr; Supernova 100 Byr. Text confirms 'one-in-30 per century, constituting the second highest ranked risk', 'one-in-10 per century' for AI, and 'one-in-six risk this century'. TWO LABELLING CAVEATS: (a) the briefing note's table is 'Table 1', not 'Table 6.1' — Table 6.1 is the underlying table in the book, which the packet did not retrieve; (b) Ord's Table 6.1 quantifies EXISTENTIAL CATASTROPHE (extinction OR unrecoverable collapse), while both the briefing note and the packet call it 'extinction'. The packet also silently drops Unforeseen Anthropogenic (3 kyr, tied with engineered pandemics) and Other Anthropogenic (5 kyr) from its list. https://riskfrontiers.com/wp-content/uploads/2020/05/Briefing-Note_415-1.pdf

verdicts.citation_claim: Cite 2 — Ord (2023), 'The Precipice Revisited': 'These were 1 in 1,000 for Climate and for Nuclear, 1 in 30 for Pandemics and 1 in 10 for Unaligned AI'; update is directional only.
verdicts.note: Fetched tobyord.com/writing/the-precipice-revisited. The quoted sentence is verbatim. He also writes: 'these are all rounded off (usually to the nearest factor of 10) and none of them have moved that far' and 'Climate risk is down, Nuclear is up, and the story on Pandemics and AI is mixed — lots of changes, but no clear direction for the overall risk.' The packet's claim that he publishes no revised numerical estimate is correct.

verdicts.citation_claim: Cite 3 — XPT (Karger, Tetlock et al. 2023): GEP killing >1% in 5 years by 2100 — superforecaster median 4%, biorisk expert median 10.25%. Extinction from engineered pathogen by 2100 — superforecaster 0.01% (from 0.1%), expert 1% (from 0.7%).
verdicts.note: STRONGEST CITATION IN THE PACKET. Downloaded the 19.5 MB report PDF and read Tables 22 and 23 directly. Table 23: 'Genetically-engineered pathogen killing >1% population' — Superforecasters 0.25% (2030) / 1.5% (2050) / 4% (2100); Domain experts 1.22% / 8% / 10.25%. Table 22: 'Extinction risk by 2100, Engineered pathogens' — Superforecasters 0.1% pre-XPT → 0.01% post-XPT; Domain experts 0.7% → 1%. Question 1 wording confirms the 5-year window. Full author list: Ezra Karger, Josh Rosenberg, Zachary Jacobs, Molly Hickman, Rose Hadshar, Kayla Gamin, Taylor Smith, Bridget Williams, Tegan McCaslin, Stephen Thomas, Philip E. Tetlock; FRI Working Paper #1, 10 Jul 2023, rev. 8 Aug 2023. TWO SMALL FIXES: the packet calls these 'final-stage group medians' — the report labels them intake (Pre-XPT) and postmortem (Post-XPT) survey medians; and the report characterises the experts' 0.7%→1% move as having 'remained stable', not as an increase. SCOPE ERROR (see overall): the XPT question covers any genetically-engineered pathogen, accidental OR deliberate; the packet uses it as the rate for the deliberate-only branch and then adds a separate accidental hazard. https://forecastingresearch.org/pdf/existential-risk-persuasion-tournament.pdf

verdicts.citation_claim: Cite 4 — Esvelt (2022) GCSP 'Delay, Detect, Defend': tens of thousands of skilled individuals within a decade; US$1,500 pandemic-influenza construct, ~US$2,000 coronavirus; simultaneous release across travel hubs could threaten the stability of civilisation.
verdicts.note: Downloaded and text-extracted the Geneva Paper PDF. Masthead: 'Delay, Detect, Defend: Preparing for a Future in which Thousands Can Release New Pandemics', Geneva Paper 29/22, Kevin M. Esvelt, November 2022. Executive summary verbatim: 'The deliberate and simultaneous release of many pandemic viruses across travel hubs could threaten the stability of civilisation. Current trends suggest that within a decade, tens of thousands of skilled individuals will be able to access the information required for them to single-handedly cause new pandemics.' Body p.25 verbatim: 'DNA constructs of length sufficient to generate infectious 1918 influenza virus can now be obtained for US$1,500; coronaviruses cost approximately US$2,000, but typically must be enzymatically stitched together by hand prior to virus generation'. The packet's 'a historical pandemic influenza virus' is the 1918 virus specifically, and it omits the source's own hand-assembly caveat that currently limits who can use the coronavirus route.

verdicts.citation_claim: Cite 5 — IGSC (2017) press release: members 'represent approximately 80% of global commercial gene synthesis capacity'; consortium has represented ~80% since forming in 2009.
verdicts.corrected_value: Press release dated 3 January 2018 (not 2017); verbatim text is 'Since forming in 2009, IGSC has grown to represent approximately 80% of gene synthesis capacity worldwide.'
verdicts.note: Retrieved and text-extracted the PR Newswire page. THREE ERRORS. (1) YEAR: dateline is 'SAN DIEGO, Jan. 3, 2018 /PRNewswire/' — the packet dates it 2017. (2) MISQUOTE: the packet puts quotation marks around 'represent approximately 80% of global commercial gene synthesis capacity'; the source says 'approximately 80% of gene synthesis capacity worldwide' — the word 'commercial' is inserted by the packet, and it is load-bearing, because the 80% denominator is worldwide capacity, not commercial-only capacity. (3) MISREAD: 'has grown to represent approximately 80%' is a statement about growth to 2018; the packet converts it into 'has represented ~80% of worldwide capacity since forming in 2009', which the source does not say. The trailing inference 'leaving roughly one fifth of commercial production unscreened' is the packet's own arithmetic, not a source statement, and should be marked author-estimate. Also note this is an eight-year-old figure being used as a current screening-coverage parameter. https://www.prnewswire.com/news-releases/international-gene-synthesis-consortium-updates-screening-protocols-for-synthetic-dna-products-and-services-300576867.html

verdicts.citation_claim: Cite 6 — Wittmann et al. (2025) Science, DOI 10.1126/science.adu8578: three open-source generative protein models produced 76,080 synthetic sequences mimicking 72 'proteins of concern'; patches with four DNA synthesis companies greatly improved detection.
verdicts.note: BIBLIOGRAPHY FULLY CONFIRMED, HEADLINE NUMBERS NOT. Verified via Europe PMC (PMID 41037625), OpenAlex, the Microsoft Research publication page and an archived science.org record: 'Strengthening nucleic acid biosecurity screening against generative protein design tools', Science, 2 Oct 2025, Vol 390, Issue 6768, pp. 82-87, DOI 10.1126/science.adu8578. All twelve authors match the packet exactly (Wittmann, Alexanian, Bartling, Beal, Clore, Diggans, Flyangolts, Gemler, Mitchell, Murphy, Wheeler, Horvitz). The quoted patch outcome is verbatim in the abstract: 'we developed and deployed patches, greatly improving detection rates of synthetic homologs more likely to retain wild type-like function.' The Editor's summary confirms 'four commercial DNA synthesis companies'. BUT the three specific counts — 76,080 sequences, 72 proteins of concern, three open-source models — appear in neither the abstract nor the Editor's summary, and the full text is paywalled (OpenAlex oa_status: closed; science.org returns 403). I could not verify them from any source retrieved this session, so they should not be treated as checked. The Microsoft Research page, which the packet gives as the URL, does not contain them either.

verdicts.citation_claim: Cite 7 — Mouton, Lucas, Guest (2024) RAND RR-A2977-2: 'no statistically significant difference in the viability of plans generated with or without the assistance of the current generation of large language models'; problematic outputs 'generally mirror information readily available on the internet'.
verdicts.note: Retrieved via an archived rand.org record (rand.org itself 403s to this session). Title, report number RR-A2977-2, authors Christopher A. Mouton, Caleb Lucas, Ella Guest, and publication date 25 Jan 2024 all correct. Key Takeaways verbatim: 'The authors found no statistically significant difference in the viability of plans generated with or without LLM assistance' and 'these outputs generally mirror information readily available on the internet, suggesting that LLMs do not substantially increase the risks associated with biological weapon attack planning.' The packet's first quotation is a paraphrase presented inside quotation marks ('...with or without the assistance of the current generation of large language models' vs the source's '...with or without LLM assistance') — same meaning, but it is not verbatim. Worth carrying the report's own caveat, which the packet omits: it 'did not measure the distance between the existing LLM capability frontier and the knowledge needed'.

verdicts.citation_claim: Cite 8 — Anthropic (2025) 'Activating ASL3 protections': activated for Claude Opus 4 to limit misuse for CBRN weapons, precautionary because the threshold was not determined to be crossed; ASL-3 defined against systems that could 'substantially increase' capability of individuals with a basic STEM background.
verdicts.corrected_value: The page states the measures 'are focused exclusively on biological weapons', not CBRN generally; the 'basic STEM background' threshold definition is from Anthropic's Responsible Scaling Policy, not this page.
verdicts.note: Page exists and is dated 22 May 2025. Confirmed verbatim: 'we have not yet determined whether Claude Opus 4 has definitively passed the Capabilities Threshold that requires ASL-3 protections' — so the packet's precautionary framing is right. TWO ATTRIBUTION PROBLEMS. (1) The packet says ASL-3 was activated 'specifically to limit misuse for the development or acquisition of chemical, biological, radiological and nuclear weapons'; the page says the opposite about scope: 'Initially they are focused exclusively on biological weapons as we believe these account for the vast majority of the risk.' (2) The quoted definitional phrase about individuals with 'a basic STEM background' does not appear on this page; it is the CBRN-3 Capability Threshold wording in Anthropic's Responsible Scaling Policy, which the packet does not cite. Fix by citing the RSP for the definition and this page only for the activation.

verdicts.citation_claim: Cite 9 — Lancet Global Health 7-1-7 five-country study (2023), author list not retrieved: 41 outbreaks, 54% detection, 71% notification, 49% early response, ~1 in 4 met the full 7-1-7.
verdicts.corrected_value: Authors: Bochner AF, Makumbi I, Aderinola O, Abayneh A, Jetoh R, Yemanaberhan RL, Danjuma JS, Lazaro FT, Mahmoud HJ, Yeabah TO, Nakiire L, Yahaya AK, Teixeira RA, Lamorde M, Nabukenya I, Oladejo J, Adetifa IMO, Oliveira W, McClelland A, Lee CT. Lancet Glob Health 2023;11:e871-e879. DOI 10.1016/S2214-109X(23)00133-X. PMID 37060911.
verdicts.note: Every figure checks out against the abstract retrieved from Europe PMC. Verbatim Findings: 'Of 41 public health events assessed, 22 (54%) met a target of 7 days to detect (median 6 days [range 0-157]), 29 (71%) met a target of 1 day to notify (0 days [0-24]), and 20 (49%) met a target of 7 days to complete all early response actions (8 days [0-72]). 11 (27%) events met the complete 7-1-7 target'. The packet's 'about one in four' = 27%, correct. Countries: Brazil, Ethiopia, Liberia, Nigeria, Uganda; events from 1 Jan 2018 to 31 Dec 2022; funded by the Gates Foundation. The packet was honest about not having the author list — it is supplied above. Note the events are all naturally-occurring public-health events in five LMICs, so using this as the detection-latency knob for a deliberate release in any country is an extrapolation the source does not license.

verdicts.citation_claim: Cite 10 — OSTP 'Framework for Nucleic Acid Synthesis Screening' (released 29 April 2024) + EO 14292: federal life-science funding conditional on Framework-compliant providers; EO directed OSTP within 90 days to revise the Framework and to develop a non-federally-funded GOF strategy.
verdicts.corrected_value: The document at the cited URL is 'Revised: September 2024; Version 1: April 2024', a product of the NSTC Fast Track Action Committee on Synthetic Nucleic Acid Procurement Screening — not simply the 29 April 2024 release. The non-federally-funded gain-of-function strategy is a 180-day deliverable under EO 14292, not part of the 90-day Framework revision.
verdicts.note: DEAD LINK PLUS TWO DATE/SCOPE ERRORS. (1) The cited URL 404s: https://aspr.hhs.gov/S3/Documents/OSTP-Nucleic-Acid-Synthesis-Screening-Framework-Sep2024.pdf 301-redirects to www.aspr.gov and returns 404 there; the whole ASPR /S3/ area is gone. I recovered the document only from a Wayback snapshot (web.archive.org/web/20260601172725/...). A packet citation should not rest on a dead URL. (2) DATE: the recovered PDF's own title page reads 'Revised: September 2024 / Version 1: April 2024' — the packet's filename says Sep2024 while its prose dates it 29 April 2024. (3) SUBSTANCE IS OTHERWISE CORRECT: verbatim, 'federal funding agencies will, as appropriate and consistent with applicable law, require that procurement of synthetic nucleic acids and benchtop nucleic acid synthesis equipment using federal life sciences funding be conducted through Providers and Manufacturers that adhere to this framework', effective 'on or after April 26, 2025'. (4) SCOPE: EO 14292's 90-day clock covers only the Framework revision; the strategy for non-federally-funded dangerous gain-of-function research and non-federally-funded synthesis screening is a separate 180-day deliverable. (5) The citation header labels the whole thing '(2024)' while EO 14292 is 2025.

verdicts.citation_claim: Cite 11 — 2021 Global Health Security Index: average 38.9/100; 75% of countries scored low for biosecurity, dual-use oversight, emergency response, public-health/security linkage and MCM dispensing; only 11 countries with dual-use oversight legislation; 94% lacking oversight measures.
verdicts.corrected_value: The 75% figure is a 2019 GHS Index finding, not a 2021 one — the 2021 report states verbatim: 'In 2019, the GHS Index found that national capacity in those areas was generally weak, with 75% of countries receiving a low score for...'. The comparable 2021 statistic is 'On average, the world scores 29.6 out of a possible 100 in GCBR-relevant subindicators.'
verdicts.note: MOST OF THIS IS NOT AT THE CITED URL. The packet cites the NTI press release; I retrieved it in full. It contains only the 38.9/100 average (verbatim: 'The average overall 2021 GHS Index score is 38.9 out of a possible score of 100', and 'no country scored above 75.9'). It contains NONE of the 75%, 94% or 11-country claims. I then downloaded the 2021 GHS Index full report (ghsindex.org) and found: the '>94% of countries have no national-level oversight measures for dual-use research, which includes national laws or regulation on oversight, an agency responsible for the oversight, or evidence of a national assessment of dual-use research' — CONFIRMED (note it is '>94%', not '94%'); the 75% figure — CONFIRMED but explicitly attributed by the report to 2019, so the packet has aged a seven-year-old finding forward by two years. The 'only 11 countries had evidence of legislation requiring oversight of dual-use research' claim I could not find anywhere in the 2021 report; it is consistent with >94% of 195 (≤11 countries) but that is an inference, not a source statement, and should be marked author-estimate. Fix: cite https://www.ghsindex.org/wp-content/uploads/2021/12/2021_GHSindexFullReport_Final.pdf, not the press release.

verdicts.citation_claim: Cite 12 — Takahashi et al. (2004) EID 10(1): Aum Shinrikyo's 1993 Kameido anthrax release produced zero cases; Sterne 34F2 vaccine strain lacking pXO2; ~4 x 10^3 CFU/mL vs 10^9-10^10 for an effective preparation; failure from attenuated strain, low concentration, viscosity, clogged sprayer, solar inactivation.
verdicts.note: CLEANEST CITATION AFTER THE XPT. Verified via Europe PMC (PMID 15112666, DOI 10.3201/eid1001.030238, PMCID PMC3322761 — the packet's PMC URL resolves correctly) and by fetching the PMC full text. EID 2004;10(1):117-120. Authors Takahashi H, Keim P, Kaufmann AF, Keys C, Smith KL, Taniguchi K, Inouye S, Kurata T — 'Hiroshi Takahashi et al.' correct. Zero human cases confirmed ('none were found' after interviewing physicians at 39 medical facilities). Sterne 34F2 / missing pXO2 confirmed. Spore concentration verbatim: 'about 4 x 10³ colony-forming units (CFU) of the B. anthracis-like agent per milliliter', against 10⁹-10¹⁰ optimal. All five failure factors confirmed, including sunlight inactivation on an overcast day. Note: Europe PMC/PubMed render the title as 'Bacillus anthracis incident, Kameido, Tokyo, 1993'; the EID/PMC version carries the packet's longer title with 'Bioterrorism Incident' — both are correct, not an error.

verdicts.citation_claim: Cite 1 — Meselson et al. (1994) Science 266(5188):1202-1208, Sverdlovsk: 77 tabulated cases, at least 66 deaths, narrow downwind zone, aerosol escape from the military facility; ~59,000 eligible for prophylactic immunisation.
verdicts.note: BIBLIOGRAPHY EXACT, TWO SUB-FIGURES UNVERIFIED. Europe PMC record confirms: Meselson M, Guillemin J, Hugh-Jones M, Langmuir A, Popova I, Shelokov A, Yampolskaya O; Science 1994;266:1202-1208; PMID 7973702; the packet's PubMed URL resolves. The abstract confirms the packet's narrative claims almost word for word: 'most victims worked or lived in a narrow zone extending from the military facility to the southern city limit. Farther south, livestock died of anthrax along the zone's extended axis. The zone paralleled the northerly wind that prevailed shortly before the outbreak. It is concluded that the escape of an aerosol of anthrax pathogen at the military facility caused the outbreak.' HOWEVER the paper is closed-access (OpenAlex oa_status: closed; science.org 403) and I could not verify the '77 tabulated cases', 'at least 66 deaths' or '~59,000 eligible for immunisation' figures against the full text. Flagging one discrepancy worth resolving: a 2026 Europe PMC review (Dhawan et al., 'Epidemiological indicators of accidental laboratory-origin outbreaks', PMC12835948) reports for Sverdlovsk 'a total of 96 cases with 66 fatalities' from Soviet reports, with witness claims of ~105 deaths. 66 deaths is stable across sources; the case count is not, so the derived case-fatality ratio should not be treated as pinned.

verdicts.citation_claim: Cite 2 — Global BioLabs Report 2023 (Koblentz, Lentzos et al.): 69 BSL-4 labs across 27 countries; Europe 26, Asia 20, North America 15, Australia 3, Africa 3, South America 1; 12 high / 9 medium / 6 low on biosecurity; 7 of 27 above 70% on biorisk policies, Australia and UK each 83%; quote about the construction boom not being matched by oversight.
verdicts.corrected_value: Oceania has FOUR BSL-4 labs, all operational and all in Australia — not three. The packet's own regional figures then sum to 68, one short of the 69 it states.
verdicts.note: Downloaded and text-extracted the report PDF. ONE REAL NUMERIC ERROR, everything else confirmed. Verbatim: 'In 2021, we identified 59 BSL4 labs... By the beginning of 2023, that number had increased by ten to 69 labs. There are 51 BSL4 labs in operation, three under construction, and 15 planned, all spread over 27 countries.' Regional text verbatim: Europe 26; 'Asia has 20 BSL4 labs'; 'North America has 15'; 'Oceania has four BSL4 labs, all operational and located in Australia'; 'Africa has three'; 'South America has one planned BSL4 lab in Brazil'. 26+20+15+4+3+1 = 69, which is the internal check the packet's '3' fails. CONFIRMED: 'Only 12 out of the 27 countries with BSL4 labs score high on biosecurity governance... Nine countries score medium for biosecurity governance and six score low.' CONFIRMED: 'Among the seven countries that score high on biorisk management governance...' with Table 8 giving Canada 46/48, US 42, Australia 40, UK 40, France 38, Japan 38, Taiwan 35 — Australia and the UK are 40/48 = 83%, and the 7th (Taiwan, 35/48 = 73%) is indeed above 70%. The quoted sentence is very slightly repunctuated; verbatim it reads 'The boom in BSL4 lab construction appears so far not to have been accompanied by strengthened biorisk management oversight.' The 'most planned labs in countries with relatively low governance and stability scores' claim is also verbatim. https://www.kcl.ac.uk/warstudies/assets/global-biolabs-report-2023.pdf

verdicts.citation_claim: Cite 3 — Herfst, Schrauwen et al. (2012) Science 336(6088), DOI 10.1126/science.1213362: airborne-transmissible strain differed from the original by five mutations, ALL of which had been observed individually in wild viruses; NSABB autumn 2011 recommendation against publication, March 2012 reversal, Fouchier vote not unanimous.
verdicts.corrected_value: Only TWO of the five substitutions (T156A in HA and E627K in PB2) are common in natural H5N1 isolates — not all five. The five are four in haemagglutinin plus one in PB2; pages are 1534-1541.
verdicts.note: PAPER IS REAL AND CORRECTLY CITED — Europe PMC confirms Science 2012;336:1534-1541, DOI 10.1126/science.1213362, PMID 22723413, Herfst S, Schrauwen EJ, Linster M, Chutinimitkul S, de Wit E, Munster VJ, Sorrell EM, Bestebroer TM, Burke DF, Smith DJ, Rimmelzwaan GF, Osterhaus AD, Fouchier RA. The abstract confirms the five-substitution count: 'Four amino acid substitutions in the host receptor-binding protein hemagglutinin, and one in the polymerase complex protein basic polymerase 2, were consistently present in airborne-transmitted viruses' and 'None of the recipient ferrets died after airborne infection'. THE 'ALL OF WHICH HAD BEEN OBSERVED INDIVIDUALLY IN WILD VIRUSES' CLAIM IS WRONG. The packet's own companion source (CIDRAP, cite 4) says only that 'two of the mutations involved (T156A and E627K) are common in natural H5N1 isolates', with E627K in ~27% of avian and ~29% of human H5N1 sequences. This matters for the packet's model: the whole point of the H5N1 episode as an information hazard is that the specific COMBINATION, not each individual substitution, was the novel and hazardous result. Also, the NSABB's recommendation against full publication was announced in DECEMBER 2011, not 'autumn 2011'.

verdicts.citation_claim: Cite 4 — CIDRAP (2012) coverage of the NSABB reversal: five mutations all spotted individually in wild viruses; NSABB reviewed autumn 2011, recommended against full publication, reversed March 2012.
verdicts.corrected_value: CIDRAP says two of the five (T156A, E627K) are common in natural isolates, not all five. The NSABB redaction recommendation is dated December 2011 in the article, not 'autumn 2011'. Article: Robert Roos, CIDRAP News, 21 June 2012.
verdicts.note: THE ARTICLE EXISTS AT THE GIVEN URL and is correctly attributed to CIDRAP/University of Minnesota, but the packet has propagated the same overstatement as in cite 3 — and the packet is citing CIDRAP for a claim CIDRAP contradicts. Verbatim from the article: 'as few as five amino acid substitutions (four in HA and one in PB2) may be sufficient to confer airborne transmission'; 'two of the mutations involved (T156A and E627K) are common in natural H5N1 isolates'; 'E627K in PB2 has been found in about 27% of avian H5N1 sequences and about 29% of human H5N1 sequences'. Timeline verbatim: December 2011 the board 'recommended... both studies be stripped of key details before publication'; on 30 March 2012 it 'recommended... the full versions of both studies be published', with 'the NSABB voted unanimously in favor of publication for Kawaoka's paper, but it split 12-6 on Fouchier's' — so the packet's 'not unanimous' is right, and the 12-6 split is the specific figure it should have given. The severity qualifier in the packet's claim line is supported: 'all those infected via airborne viruses survived.' Author and date, which the packet omitted: Robert Roos, 21 June 2012.

verdicts.citation_claim: Cite 5 — Executive Order 14292 'Improving the Safety and Security of Biological Research' (signed 5 May 2025): 90-day revision of the 2024 Framework; funding-agency procurement requirement; strategy for non-federally-funded dangerous GOF including synthesis screening.
verdicts.note: Verified at the American Presidency Project. EO number 14292, title and 5 May 2025 signing date all correct. Verbatim: 'Within 90 days of the date of this order, the Director of OSTP... shall revise or replace the 2024 Framework'; agencies funding life-science research must 'ensure that synthetic nucleic acid procurement is conducted through providers or manufacturers that adhere to the updated Framework'; OSTP must 'develop and implement a strategy to govern, limit, and track dangerous gain-of-function research across the United States that occurs without Federal funding' including 'comprehensive, scalable, and verifiable nucleic acid synthesis screening in non-federally funded settings'. ONE SCOPE NOTE: the non-federally-funded strategy carries a 180-day clock, not the 90-day clock — this hazard's citation states it correctly by not attaching a deadline, but the same EO is misdescribed in hazard 1 cite 10, where the 90 days is applied to both.

verdicts.citation_claim: Cite 1 — Alibek (1999), Statement to the US Congress (Joint Economic Committee), FAS/IRP: Biopreparat ~32,000 employees and 40 facilities; overall programme 'over 60,000 people'; 'Hundreds of tons of anthrax weapon formulation'; 'dozens of tons' of smallpox and plague; 'many hundreds of tons of various agents annually'.
verdicts.corrected_value: Not the Joint Economic Committee. The document is 'Testimony of Dr. Kenneth Alibek, Chief Scientist at Hadron, Inc.', addressed to 'Congressman Hunter, Congressman Weldon, and members of the Subcommittees' — a joint House subcommittee hearing (Duncan Hunter and Curt Weldon chaired House Armed Services subcommittees), 20 October 1999, per the FAS file path /congress/1999_hr/.
verdicts.note: EVERY FIGURE IS VERBATIM CORRECT — I fetched and text-extracted the FAS page. 'I was responsible for approximately 32,000 employees and 40 facilities'; 'Biopreparat, the civilian arm of the biological weapons program, comprised over half of the entire program's personnel and facilities'; 'over 60,000 people were involved'; 'Hundreds of tons of anthrax weapon formulation were stockpiled, along with dozens of tons' [of smallpox and plague]; 'many hundreds of tons of various agents annually'. The ONLY error is the committee attribution — 'Joint Economic Committee' is wrong; Hunter and Weldon are House members and the FAS path marks it a House hearing. Alibek did also testify to the JEC (20 May 1998), which is probably the source of the confusion; the packet should either fix the committee or cite the JEC document. Separately, the packet's own claim label calls him 'former First Deputy Director of Biopreparat' — the testimony confirms 'I had been serving for four years as First Deputy Director of Biopreparat'. Note this is defector self-testimony with no independent verification of the tonnage figures.

verdicts.citation_claim: Cite 2 — Kent's Consortium for World Affairs (2023), 'Biopreparat: The Soviet biological weapons programme': INDEPENDENT account giving ~32,000 employees and 40 facilities, over half of programme personnel; Pasechnik/Alibekov smallpox revelations; Alibekov weaponised glanders and Marburg and built the first Soviet tularemia bomb.
verdicts.corrected_value: Published 16 March 2022 (not 2023), by Carmen Chas Bartolome, KCWA Politics and Society Mini-Series Part 1. The page contains NO employee/facility numbers and NO mention of glanders, Marburg or tularemia.
verdicts.note: WEAKEST CITATION IN THE PACKET. The page is real and I retrieved its full text. What it DOES support: 'Vladimir Pasechnik and Kanatian Alibekov revealed that the Soviet military had developed virulent strains of smallpox virus as a biological weapon and mass-produced it'; the Soviet Union became 'the sole possessor of stocks of this particularly lethal biological weapons agent'; 'one of the best-guarded secrets in the old Soviet Union' with the BWC violation emerging only in the 1990s. What it does NOT contain, contrary to the packet's 'FIGURE AS STATED': (a) '32,000 employees and 40 facilities' — that number appears nowhere on the page; it is Alibek's own testimony language from cite 1, transplanted; (b) 'over half of the entire programme's personnel and facilities' — same, verbatim from Alibek's testimony; (c) any mention of Alibekov weaponising glanders, Marburg haemorrhagic fever, or creating the first Soviet tularemia bomb — absent entirely. The citation's stated PURPOSE ('Independent account') therefore fails: the figures it is cited for come from Alibek himself, so cites 1 and 2 are not two independent anchors, they are one. The page also calls Alibekov 'the director (1988-1992) of the biological weapons programme', which conflicts with his own First-Deputy-Director-of-Biopreparat title. https://research.kent.ac.uk/kcwa/biopreparat-the-soviet-biological-weapons-programme/

verdicts.citation_claim: Cite 3 — Meselson et al. (1994), Sverdlovsk: 77 tabulated cases, at least 66 deaths, April-May 1979, downwind of a military microbiology facility; aerosol escape.
verdicts.note: Same source as hazard 2 cite 1 and the same verdict: bibliography exact (Science 1994;266:1202-1208, PMID 7973702, seven authors), narrative and conclusion verbatim in the abstract, but the 77/66 pair could not be checked against the paywalled full text and a 2026 Europe PMC review (PMC12835948) reports '96 cases with 66 fatalities' from Soviet reports. Note this is the same citation used in two hazards, so the two hazards are not independently evidenced on this point — worth stating explicitly in the packet, especially since the packet's own claim line rightly says the realised Soviet cost was an ACCIDENT and therefore evidence for the accident hazard, not for the state-use hazard whose rate it is placed under.

verdicts.citation_claim: Cite 4 — Ord (2020) via Risk Frontiers BN 415: engineered pandemic ~1 in 30 per century vs nuclear war ~1 in 1,000, i.e. ~33x, on the reasoning that even nuclear winter would probably not cause total extinction or unrecoverable collapse.
verdicts.note: Both ratio and reasoning confirmed in the extracted PDF. 1/30 ÷ 1/1000 = 33.3, and Briefing Note 415 states verbatim: 'Ord doubts that even nuclear winter would lead to total human extinction or the global unrecoverable collapse of civilisation.' Same 'Table 1 vs Table 6.1' and 'existential catastrophe vs extinction' labelling caveats as hazard 1 cite 1. Substantive caveat for the model, not the citation: Ord's ratio is about EXISTENTIAL risk from engineered pandemics generally, which is not the relevant comparison for a hazard defined as state BW use causing 100,000+ deaths in armed conflict — those are three different quantities.

audits.overall: Partially trustworthy, but not yet buildable without repairs — I found errors in 9 of the 21 citations, including one that inverts the meaning of a source and one that attributes an entire block of figures to a page that does not contain them. THE SOLID CORE (retrieved and checked line by line this session): the XPT report PDF, whose Tables 22 and 23 match the packet exactly (superforecaster 4% / expert 10.25% for >1% mortality by 2100; extinction 0.1%→0.01% and 0.7%→1%); Esvelt's Geneva Paper 29/22, quoted verbatim including the US$1,500 / US$2,000 construct prices; the Kameido EID paper, every figure including 4 x 10^3 CFU/mL; the Lancet 7-1-7 study, all four percentages; the RAND red-team report, both quotes; Risk Frontiers Briefing Note 415, whose table I extracted in full; 'The Precipice Revisited', quoted verbatim; and EO 14292. THE ERRORS, worst first: (1) the Kent KCWA page cited as an INDEPENDENT account of Biopreparat contains none of the figures attributed to it — the '32,000 employees and 40 facilities' and the glanders/Marburg/tularemia claims are Alibek's own testimony language transplanted onto it, so citations 1 and 2 of hazard 3 are one source, not two, and its date is 2022 not 2023; (2) the claim that all five H5N1 airborne-transmission substitutions 'had been observed individually in wild viruses' is contradicted by the packet's own CIDRAP source, which says only two (T156A, E627K) are common in natural isolates — this appears twice, in hazard 2 citations 3 and 4, and it understates the information hazard the packet is trying to model; (3) the Alibek testimony is not a Joint Economic Committee statement — it is addressed to Congressmen Hunter and Weldon at a House subcommittee hearing; (4) the GHS Index citation points at a press release that contains only the 38.9 figure, its '75% of countries' statistic is explicitly a 2019 finding restated in the 2021 report, and its 'only 11 countries' figure appears nowhere in the report; (5) the Global BioLabs regional breakdown says Australia 3 where the report says Oceania four, all in Australia — the packet's own regional numbers sum to 68 against its stated 69; (6) the IGSC press release is dated 3 January 2018 not 2017, the quotation has 'commercial' inserted into it, and 'has represented ~80% since 2009' misreads 'has grown to represent approximately 80%'; (7) the OSTP Framework URL is a hard 404 (recoverable only via Wayback), the document there is the September 2024 revision rather than the 29 April 2024 release, and the non-federally-funded gain-of-function strategy is a 180-day not a 90-day deliverable; (8) the Anthropic page says its ASL-3 measures are 'focused exclusively on biological weapons', not CBRN, and the 'basic STEM background' threshold language is from the Responsible Scaling Policy, not that page; (9) the Science/Wittmann paper is real and correctly cited down to the page numbers, but its three headline counts (76,080 sequences, 72 proteins of concern, three models) are paywalled and appear in neither the abstract nor the Editor's summary — I could not verify them. MODEL-LEVEL PROBLEMS BEYOND THE CITATIONS: the tier probabilities sum to exactly 1.000 in all three hazards, which is clean; hazard 1's rate range 0.0005-0.0014/yr converts correctly from the XPT medians (4% and 10.25% over ~78 years); but the XPT question covers engineered pathogens released ACCIDENTALLY OR DELIBERATELY, and the packet spends that whole probability on a deliberate-only event and then adds a separate accidental hazard on top — double counting. Hazard 1's implied terminal rate (0.0008 x 0.005 = 4e-6/yr, about 1 in 2,500 per century) is roughly 75x below Ord's 1-in-30, so citations 1, 2 and hazard 3's citation 4 are presented as anchors for a model that contradicts them by two orders of magnitude; it is defensible against the XPT superforecasters, not against Ord, and the packet should say so. Hazard 2's tier 1 is unsupportable as written: deaths_fraction 1.5e-8 is about 121 deaths from a 'contained local outbreak' seeded by a 50-plus-case event, which needs a case fatality ratio above 100% unless the outbreak is much larger than the event threshold. Its 0.02/yr rate is uncited and sits below a directly relevant XPT number the packet never used (Table 23: median 0.68 events of escaped biological agents killing 1,000 by 2050 for superforecasters, 0.5 for domain experts). Finally, every hazard's terminal tier pairs terminal=true with deaths_fraction of 0.95-0.97, leaving 240-400 million survivors — that is a civilisational-collapse tier, not extinction, and calling it terminal is the exact category confusion (permanent end of humanity vs killing a large fraction) that the brief warns against.

verdicts.citation_claim: Citation 1 — Karger, Rosenberg, Jacobs, Hickman, Hadshar, Gamin, Smith, Williams, McCaslin, Thomas, Tetlock (2023), FRI Working Paper #1, 'Forecasting Existential Risks' — XPT AI extinction/catastrophe medians by group with CIs, group sizes, tournament structure, extinction definition, Table 4 aggregations, AGI-2070 conditional.
verdicts.note: I downloaded the 19.5 MB PDF at the exact cited URL (it exceeds WebFetch's 10 MB cap) and extracted the text. EVERY figure checks out verbatim. Title page: 'Forecasting Existential Risks: Evidence from a Long-Run Forecasting Tournament', authors exactly as listed, 'First released on: July 10, 2023 / Current version: August 8, 2023 | FRI Working Paper #1'. Table 2: AI catastrophe 2.13% [1.83, 3.00]% / 12% [4.0, 18.5]% / 6.16% [5, 12]% / 10% [6.16, 16.12]% / 5% [5, 5]%; Total catastrophic risk 9.05% [6.13, 10.25]% vs 20% [15.44, 27.60]%. Table 3: AI extinction 0.38% [0.10, 0.75]% / 3% [0.49, 10.00]% / 2% [1.00, 4.03]% / 4.75% [1.9, 14.0]% / 2% [1, 2]%; Total extinction 1% [0.55, 1.23]% vs 6% [3.41, 10.00]%. Table 9 restates 2.13/12/6.16 and 0.38/3/2. Table 4: AI domain experts arithmetic mean 13.61% [6.46, 22.79]% vs median 3%; superforecasters 1.98% [0.86, 3.77]% vs median 0.38% — both exact, including the CI I initially suspected (22.79 is correct; 21.91 belongs to the adjacent trimmed-mean cell). Figure 4 does label 'AI Experts (n=29)' at a 3% median. Footnote 2 defines catastrophe as death of ≥10% of humans alive at the start of a five-year period and extinction as global population below 5,000. p.11: 'Nearly 200 participants signed up… and 169 submitted forecasts… 80 experts… with 111 [completing all four stages]'; 'expert sample (N=80) included 32 AI experts, 15 "general" experts…, 12 biorisk experts, 12 nuclear experts, and 9 climate experts'; ran June–October 2022. The AGI-2070 postmortem passage is verbatim ('0.38%… rose to 1%'). Footnote 70 confirms the public-survey elicitation-format effect (AI catastrophic risk 5% by textbox vs 1 in 50,000 by the alternative method). The IJF successor PII S0169207024001250 resolves via Crossref to a real paper: Karger, Rosenberg, Jacobs, Hickman & Tetlock, 'Subjective-probability forecasts of existential risk', Int. J. Forecasting 41(2):499–516, doi 10.1016/j.ijforecast.2024.11.008. ONE NUANCE THE PACKET INHERITS FROM THE SOURCE: 'N=88 superforecasters and N=59 domain experts' is verbatim the Table 2/3 caption, but the report's own AI appendix states the AI-catastrophe median was computed from N=30 domain experts and the AI-extinction median from N=29. The 12% median that drives the packet's high-end rate therefore rests on 30 people, not 59. Not the packet's error, but it overstates the precision of the load-bearing number. https://forecastingresearch.org/pdf/existential-risk-persuasion-tournament.pdf

verdicts.citation_claim: Citation 2 — Grace, Stewart, Sandkühler, Thomas, Weinstein-Raun, Brauner, Korzekwa (2024), arXiv:2401.02843 / JAIR 84 (2025), doi 10.1613/jair.1.19087 — response rates, Table 2 extinction questions, framing effects, HLMI timelines.
verdicts.note: Read the arXiv v3 PDF (pp. 1–22) directly. Every number verified. §6.3/6.4 verbatim: 'We found email addresses for 20,066 (92%) of collected names'; 'Out of the 20,066 emails we contacted, 1,607 (8%) bounced or failed, leaving 18,459 functioning email addresses. We received 2,778 responses, for a response rate of 15%.' Table 2 (p.15) matches every cell: Q1 2023 N=1321, mean 16.2% (23%), median 5% (IQR 19%); Q2 N=661, mean 19.4% (26%), median 10% (29%); Q3 N=655, mean 14.4% (22.2%), median 5% (19.9%); 2022 Q1 N=149 mean 15.7% median 5%, Q2 N=162 mean 20.5% median 10%. p.12 verbatim: 'The median prediction for extremely bad outcomes, such as human extinction, was 5% (mean 9%). Over a third of participants (38%)…'; 57.8%, 68.3%, 48.4%, 'one in ten… at least a 25% chance', and the 48%→38% / 14%→9.0% shift all present. p.14 verbatim: 'between 41.2% and 51.4% of respondents estimated a greater than 10% chance'. §3.3 framing-effect quote is exact, including '(34 years)' and '(17 years)'. Figure 14 / p.16: 70%, n=1329. Crossref confirms JAIR vol 84, doi 10.1613/jair.1.19087. TWO SMALL IMPRECISIONS, neither material: (a) 'Survey open 15–24 October 2023' — invitations to the 10% pilot groups went out 11 October 2023; 15 October is the date for the remainder. The close date of 24 October is exact. (b) The packet's 7-author list is the arXiv author list; the JAIR version of record carries 9 authors, adding Zach Stein-Perlman and John Salvatier. https://arxiv.org/pdf/2401.02843v3

verdicts.citation_claim: Citation 3 — 'Katja Grace, John Salvatier, Allan Dafoe, Baobao Zhang, Owain Evans (AI Impacts wiki compilation of surveys of experts on levels of AI risk) (2017), AI Impacts Wiki' — 2016 survey n=352/1,634 (21.5%), median 5%, 40% at ≥10%; Zhang et al. 2019 524/2,652 (19.7%), median 2%; Grace et al. 2022 N=738, median 5%, mean 14%, 48% at ≥10%.
verdicts.corrected_value: AI Impacts, 'Surveys of experts on levels of AI risk', AI Impacts Wiki (no named authors, undated wiki page), https://wiki.aiimpacts.org/uncategorized/ai_risk_surveys — for the underlying 2016 survey: Katja Grace, John Salvatier, Allan Dafoe, Baobao Zhang & Owain Evans, 'Viewpoint: When Will AI Exceed Human Performance? Evidence from AI Experts', Journal of Artificial Intelligence Research 62:729–754 (2018), doi 10.1613/jair.1.11222.
verdicts.note: THE NUMBERS ARE ALL CORRECT — I retrieved the wiki page and it states 352 of 1,634 (21.5%), median 5%, 40% at ≥10% for 2016; 524 of 2,652 (19.7%), median 2% for Zhang 2019; 738 of ~4,271 (17.3%), median 5%, 48% at ≥10% for 2022. The fault is citation hygiene, and it is exactly the pattern this audit is meant to catch: the cited artefact is an anonymous, undated AI Impacts wiki page, and the packet puts five named individuals in the author slot with a year (2017) that belongs to neither the wiki page nor the JAIR publication. Grace, Salvatier, Dafoe, Zhang and Evans did not write that wiki page. Crossref confirms the underlying paper is real and correctly described in the packet's own source field: JAIR 62:729–754 (2018), doi 10.1613/jair.1.11222, those five authors — so cite that (or arXiv:1705.08807) for the 2016 figures and cite the wiki page as an unattributed compilation. One further nit: the packet's question wording renders the paper's bracketed '[high-level machine intelligence]' as 'this'.

verdicts.citation_claim: Citation 4 — Toby Ord (2020), The Precipice, Table 6.1 (1 in 10 unaligned AI, 1 in 30 pandemics, 1 in 1,000 climate and nuclear, ~1 in 6 total, ~1 in 30 unforeseen anthropogenic, ~1 in 50 other anthropogenic), plus the 2024 'Precipice Revisited' refusal to restate.
verdicts.note: Fetched tobyord.com/writing/the-precipice-revisited: 'These were 1 in 1,000 for Climate and for Nuclear, 1 in 30 for Pandemics and 1 in 10 for Unaligned AI' — verbatim, as is 'these are all rounded off (usually to the nearest factor of 10) and none of them have moved that far.' (He adds, which the packet omits and which slightly strengthens its point: 'Climate risk is down, Nuclear is up, and the story on Pandemics and AI is mixed'.) The full Table 6.1 is reproduced at 80000hours.org/articles/existential-risks/ and confirms every row the packet cites, including Unforeseen anthropogenic risks ~1 in 30 and Other anthropogenic risks ~1 in 50, Total existential risk ~1 in 6. Independently corroborated inside the XPT report itself, which cites 'Ord, The Precipice, 167' for 16.7% total by 2120, 10% for AI, and 1 in 30 for engineered pandemics. The packet's caveat is not only correct but MORE careful than the XPT report: Ord's horizon is 2120 and his 'existential catastrophe' includes permanent curtailment, so it is not commensurable with the XPT's <5,000-population extinction criterion — the XPT's own Table 6 lists Ord's 10% under a heading about extinction, conflating exactly the (b)/(c) distinction. Credit where due.

verdicts.citation_claim: Citation 5 — Center for AI Safety (2023), the one-sentence extinction statement, its 30 May 2023 date, two-category signatory structure, named signatories, and the explicit refusal to assert a signatory total.
verdicts.note: Statement text verified verbatim at aistatement.com. The two headings 'AI Scientists' and 'Other Notable Figures' are correct, and I confirmed by direct retrieval that no total signatory count appears on the page — the packet's refusal to repeat the widely circulated '350+'/'700+' numbers is the correct call and is the single best piece of epistemic hygiene in this packet. All named signatories verified present: Hinton, Bengio, Hellman, Russell, Norvig, Goodfellow, Barto, Altman, Hassabis, Amodei, Gates, plus Chinese-university AI professors (Ya-Qin Zhang, Yi Zeng, Xianyuan Zhan). The 30 May 2023 date and Kersti Kaljulaid are NOT on aistatement.com; I found both on the CAIS press release ('For immediate release: May 30, 2023'; 'Kersti Kaljulaid (Former President of the Republic of Estonia)') at https://www.safe.ai/press-release — the packet's source field says 'safe.ai / aistatement.com', so this is covered, but the press-release URL should be given explicitly since aistatement.com alone does not support the date. The packet is also right that the statement carries no probability, horizon or mechanism and cannot be converted into a rate.

verdicts.citation_claim: Citation 6 — Rosenberg, Karger, Morris, Hickman, Hadshar, Jacobs, Tetlock (2024), FRI 'Roots of Disagreement on AI Risk', 11 March 2024 — n=22, group composition, 8 weeks, 80/31 median hours, 25%→20% and 0.10%→0.12%, the unrecoverable-collapse definition, and the XPT 'few minds were changed' quote.
verdicts.note: Downloaded and text-extracted the report PDF. Title page: 'Roots of Disagreement on AI Risk: Exploring the Potential and Pitfalls of Adversarial Collaboration', authors exactly as listed, 'First released on: March 11, 2024'. Verbatim: 'The skeptic group included nine superforecasters and two domain experts. The concerned group consisted of domain experts referred to us by staff members at Open Philanthropy' — so the packet's '11 participants, all domain experts' for the concerned group is right. 'Participants spent 8 weeks (skeptic median: 80 hours of work on the project; concerned median: 31 hours)'; 'The core activities of this project ran from April 1 to May 31, 2023' — matches 'April-May 2023'. 'the skeptic group's median moved from 0.10% to 0.12% and the concerned group's median fell from 25% to 20%.' Definition confirmed: extinction, or GDP below $1 trillion annually in 2022 dollars, or population below 1 million, for at least a million years. The XPT quote is verbatim at two places in the parent report: 'Few minds were changed during the XPT, even among the most active participants, and despite monetary incentives for persuading others.' The packet's inference — model the disagreement as a standing parameter, not as noise awaiting resolution — is well supported by the source.

verdicts.citation_claim: Citation 1 — Mouton, Lucas & Guest (2024), RAND RR-A2977-2, doi 10.7249/RRA2977-2, 25 January 2024, 24 pp. — 'did not measurably change the operational risk', 'beyond the capability frontier', 'no statistically significant difference', and the frontier-distance limitation.
verdicts.note: rand.org 403s WebFetch, so I retrieved the page with an explicit browser user-agent. Every element verified: title 'The Operational Risks of AI in Large-Scale Biological Attacks: Results of a Red-Team Study'; authors Christopher A. Mouton, Caleb Lucas, Ella Guest; 'Published Jan 25, 2024'; Document Details give Year 2024, Pages 24, DOI https://doi.org/10.7249/RRA2977-2, Document Number RR-A2977-2 (Crossref independently resolves that DOI to the same title). All three quoted passages are verbatim from the abstract and Key Takeaways, including the limitation 'This research did not measure the distance between the existing LLM capability frontier and the knowledge needed for biological weapon attack planning' and the sensitivity caveat about expanding the number of LLMs tested. The predecessor RR-A2977-1 ('A Red-Team Approach', 16 Oct 2023) is listed as related content, as the packet states. The packet's use of this as a downward anchor is legitimate — it is a null result on *planning uplift*, and the packet does not overclaim it as a null result on capability. https://www.rand.org/pubs/research_reports/RRA2977-2.html

verdicts.citation_claim: Citation 2 — Anthropic (2025), 'Activating AI Safety Level 3 Protections', 22 May 2025 — 'have not yet determined whether Claude Opus 4 has definitively passed the Capabilities Threshold'; precautionary and provisional; Sonnet 4 at ASL-2; CBRN focus on biological weapons.
verdicts.note: Retrieved anthropic.com/news/activating-asl3-protections. Title and date (22 May 2025) confirmed; the quoted sentence is verbatim; the deployment is described as 'a precautionary and provisional action'; Claude Sonnet 4 was ruled out as needing ASL-3 and remains under ASL-2; the focus is CBRN with initial emphasis on biological weapons, which the page says 'account for the vast majority of the risk'. The packet's own framing caveat — a first-party statement by an interested developer, published without the underlying evaluation data, an indicator of direction rather than a measurement of uplift — is accurate and should be kept.

verdicts.citation_claim: Citation 3 — Salvi, Horta Ribeiro, Gallotti & West, arXiv:2403.14380 / Nature Human Behaviour 9(8):1645-1653 (2025), doi 10.1038/s41562-025-02194-6 — 81.7% higher odds (p<0.01, N=820) with personalisation; non-significant without (p=0.31).
verdicts.note: Both figures are verbatim from the arXiv abstract I retrieved, including 'Without personalization, GPT-4 still outperforms humans, but the effect is lower and statistically non-significant (p=0.31)', and the pre-registered 2×2 factorial design is as described. Crossref resolves doi 10.1038/s41562-025-02194-6 to exactly 'On the conversational persuasiveness of GPT-4', Nature Human Behaviour, vol 9, issue 8, pages 1645-1653, 2025, same four authors — the packet's title/volume/issue/page claim is right down to the page range, which is the sort of detail that is usually fabricated when it is wrong. The packet's hedge that the NHB version is 'an expanded design and a slightly different N' is also exactly right and worth recording precisely: the published version is a 2×2×3 design with 12 conditions, N=900, reporting an 81.2% relative increase in odds (95% CI [+26.0%, +160.7%], P<0.01). Correctly labelled as sourced from the preprint.

verdicts.citation_claim: Citation 4 — UN Panel of Experts on Libya, S/2021/229, 8 March 2021 — para. 63 'fire, forget and find'; and 'Para. 64 records that retreating Haftar Affiliated Forces were subject to continual harassment… and suffered significant casualties.'
verdicts.corrected_value: Para. 64 actually reads: 'Once in retreat, they were subject to continual harassment from the unmanned combat aerial vehicles and lethal autonomous weapons systems, which were proving to be a highly effective combination in defeating the […] Pantsir S-1 surface-to-air missile systems. These suffered significant casualties, even when used in a passive electro-optical role to avoid GNA-AF jamming.' — 'These suffered significant casualties' refers to the Pantsir S-1 air-defence systems, not to HAF personnel.
verdicts.note: I retrieved the ICRC casebook page in full. The paragraph-63 quote is EXACT and correctly located: 'The lethal autonomous weapons systems were programmed to attack targets without requiring data connectivity between the operator and the munition: in effect, a true "fire, forget and find" capability.' The document number, date, the STM Kargu-2 identification, and the packet's central CRITICAL READING (the report attributes a capability, not an executed autonomous engagement, and supports no 'first autonomous kill' claim) are all correct and well made. But the second half of the paragraph-64 claim misreads the primary text. The subject of 'These suffered significant casualties' is the Pantsir S-1 surface-to-air missile systems named in the immediately preceding clause — the trailing qualifier 'even when used in a passive electro-optical role to avoid GNA-AF jamming' can only describe equipment, not retreating soldiers.
