The packet's wording matches The Verge's paraphrase, which is reproduced as Document B on the very same casebook page ('the HAF "suffered significant casualties" as a result'), so the error looks like it entered via the secondary source rather than from the UN text. The effect is to make a hazard packet on AI-enabled mass casualties appear to have a primary-source human-casualty attribution that the primary source does not make — which is precisely the over-reading the citation's own caveat warns against. Fix: quote para. 64 only for 'continual harassment', and drop the casualty clause or attribute it to the air-defence systems. https://casebook.icrc.org/case-study/libya-use-lethal-autonomous-weapon-systems

verdicts.citation_claim: Citation 5 — Grace et al. (2024), arXiv:2401.02843 — eleven concerning scenarios (n=1,345) at 86%/79%/73%/73%/71%, 'more than 30% of respondents' for every scenario, and the misunderstandings meta-question (n=671) at 10.7/44/29.1/14.6/1.6%.
verdicts.note: Verified against the arXiv v3 PDF I read directly. §4.1 (p.12) verbatim: 'We asked participants (n=1,345) about eleven potentially concerning AI scenarios… Each scenario was considered worthy of either substantial or extreme concern by more than 30% of respondents… spread of false information e.g. deepfakes (86%), manipulation of large-scale public opinion trends (79%), AI letting dangerous groups make powerful tools (e.g. engineered viruses) (73%), authoritarian rulers using AI to control their populations (73%), and AI systems worsening economic inequality by disproportionately benefiting certain individuals (71%).' The packet says inequality is 'also among the top five' without the number; the number is 71%. §4.4 (p.16) verbatim: 'Respondents were asked a set of "meta" questions about their views on others' views (n=671)… "To what extent do you think people's concerns about future risks from AI are due to misunderstandings of AI research?" 10.7% said "Almost entirely." 44% said "To a large extent." 29.1% said "Somewhat." 14.6% said "Not much." 1.6% said "Hardly at all."' Every percentage matches to the decimal. The packet's juxtaposition — 54.7% say public concern is substantially rooted in misunderstanding while 57.8% of the same population assign ≥5% to extremely bad outcomes — is a fair reading, and both facts are indeed in the same survey. Note the paper itself glosses the meta-question as possibly reflecting a view that 'the general public misunderstands AI', which is slightly narrower than 'people's concerns'.

audits.overall: Broadly trustworthy — unusually so — with one genuine misreading and one citation-hygiene fault, and with the real weakness lying in the severity tiers rather than in the citations. I retrieved and checked all eleven citations against primary sources in this session: the 19.5 MB XPT working paper downloaded from forecastingresearch.org and text-extracted (Tables 1/2/3/4/9, Figure 4, footnotes 2 and 70, the 'few minds were changed' passage, the AGI-2070 postmortem), the arXiv v3 PDF of Grace et al. 2024 read page by page (Table 2, §3.3, §4.1, §4.4, §5.2.2, §6.3–6.4), the arXiv abstract of Salvi et al. and the Nature Human Behaviour article page, rand.org RRA2977-2 (fetched with a browser UA after WebFetch 403s), anthropic.com/news/activating-asl3-protections, the ICRC casebook reproduction of S/2021/229, aistatement.com plus safe.ai/press-release, tobyord.com/writing/the-precipice-revisited, wiki.aiimpacts.org/uncategorized/ai_risk_surveys, forecastingresearch.org/xpt and the Roots of Disagreement report PDF, 80000hours.org for Ord's Table 6.1, and the Crossref API for DOIs 10.1038/s41562-025-02194-6, 10.7249/RRA2977-2, 10.1613/jair.1.19087, 10.1613/jair.1.11222 and PII S0169207024001250. Nothing was fabricated: every author, year, DOI, PII and URL resolves to a real document that says what is claimed, and long quoted passages match verbatim including page ranges and confidence-interval endpoints — this packet is markedly better than the base rate. Two faults: (1) the para-64 claim that retreating Haftar Affiliated Forces 'suffered significant casualties' misreads S/2021/229, where that sentence is about Pantsir S-1 air-defence systems, and the packet's phrasing traces to The Verge article printed beside the UN text rather than to the UN text; (2) citation 3 puts five real named researchers in the author slot of an anonymous AI Impacts wiki page they did not write, though its figures are correct and its source field discloses the compilation. The derived rates check out arithmetically: -ln(1-0.0213)/78 = 2.76e-4, -ln(1-0.12)/78 = 1.64e-3, geometric mean 6.73e-4 ≈ the stated 0.00067; the 1.83% and 18.5% CI endpoints are real Table 2 values giving 2.37e-4 and 2.62e-3; and 3/4 = 0.75/yr is the correct rule-of-three bound for a zero count over four years. Both tier sets sum to exactly 1.00. The unaligned-AI extinction tier at p=0.21 is in fact well grounded — it equals the geometric mean of the XPT's own extinction/catastrophe ratios (0.38/2.13 = 17.8%, 3/12 = 25%) — though the packet never says so. Three tier problems do need fixing before this drives a model. First, in ai-enabled-misuse the modal 'contained incident' tier carries deaths_fraction 3e-6, about 24,000 deaths against a world population of 8.1e9 — roughly 24x the hazard's own ≥1,000-death threshold, which would be ~1.2e-7; the event definition and the modal tier are inconsistent. Second, the 'terminal release' tier (deaths 0.99, terminal) has no support from any cited mechanism: the only quantitative citation on that hazard is a null result about planning uplift that explicitly declines to measure the distance to the capability frontier, and no pathogen has ever combined near-universal transmissibility with near-universal lethality; it should be flagged as a pure author assumption or removed. Third, the unaligned-AI 'permanent disempowerment without extinction' tier is marked terminal=true, which pushes 26% of AI catastrophes into permanent-end-of-trajectory territory — a defensible category (it maps to Ord's existential catastrophe and to Grace et al.'s 'or similarly permanent and severe disempowerment') but explicitly outside the XPT extinction criterion the rest of the hazard is calibrated to, and its 0.05 share is an author choice presented without that label. Finally, a structural caution the packet half-flags but does not act on: the XPT AI-catastrophe question covers misuse as well as loss of control, so adding a 0.001/yr misuse hazard on top of a 0.00067/yr XPT-derived hazard double-counts; and the 12% domain-expert median driving the upper bound rests on 30 forecasters, not the 59 the table caption implies.

verdicts.citation_claim: Richardson et al. 2023, Science Advances 9 eadh2458 — full planetary-boundary Table 1 control variables
verdicts.note: Fully verified. I fetched the packet's own PIK URL (https://publications.pik-potsdam.de/rest/items/item_28636_2/component/file_28730/content), saved the PDF and read pages 1-6 directly rather than trusting a summarizer (the summarizer hallucinated a fake author list on first pass — worth knowing). Title 'Earth beyond six of nine planetary boundaries'; the 29-author list, Sci. Adv. 9, eadh2458, 13 September 2023 all match exactly. Every Table 1 figure the packet quotes is correct: 417 ppm vs 350 ppm and +2.91 W/m2 vs +1.0 W/m2 (base 280 ppm / 0; increasing-risk upper end 450 ppm / +1.5); >100 E/MSY vs <10 E/MSY (Holocene 1 E/MSY); 30% HANPP vs <10%, high risk at 20%, preindustrial 1.9%; P 22.6 global / 17.5 regional vs 11 / 6.2, upper end 100 Tg P/yr; N 190 vs 62 Tg N/yr, upper end 82; land system 60% vs 75%, base 100%; blue water 18.2% vs 10.2%, green 15.8% vs 11.1%, Holocene medians 9.4% and 9.8%; ozone 284.6 DU vs 290 DU preindustrial; ocean acidification 2.8 vs 2.75 omega_arag (preindustrial 3.44); aerosol 0.076 vs 0.1 AOD; novel entities boundary 0, 'Transgressed'. Body text also confirms HANPP 15.7% of potential NPP in 1950 and 23.5% in 2020, 30% of Holocene mean NPP = 16.8 Gt C/yr, and terrestrial Holocene NPP 55.9 Gt C/yr (2 sigma) varying by not more than +/-1.1 Gt C/yr. This is the cleanest citation in the packet.

verdicts.citation_claim: Klein et al. 2007, Proc R Soc B 274(1608):303-313 — 87 of leading crops pollinator-dependent; 35% of production volume
verdicts.note: Verified via https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC1702377/. Every figure exact: '87 of the leading global food crops is dependent upon animal pollination, while 28 crops do not'; 60% of global production from non-dependent crops, 35% from dependent, 5% unevaluated; the 107-crop classification 13/30/27/21/7/9 is right and sums to 107. Two cosmetic defects: (a) the packet's URL is malformed — it gives pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/1702377/ with the 'PMC' prefix dropped; the working URL is .../articles/PMC1702377/. (b) PMC records the year as 2006 (online); the print issue is 274(1608), 7 Feb 2007, so 2007 is the standard citation and is defensible. Substantive caution for the model, not a citation error: this source cuts AGAINST the hazard's mechanism — the majority of global production volume, and a larger majority of calories, comes from wind- and self-pollinated cereals, so pollinator loss alone cannot easily deliver the packet's 5-percentage-point calorie step.

verdicts.citation_claim: Hallmann et al. 2017, PLoS ONE 12(10):e0185809 — 76% seasonal / 82% mid-summer decline over 27 years
verdicts.note: Verified at the canonical publisher URL https://journals.plos.org/plosone/article?id=10.1371/journal.pone.0185809 (I did not rely on the packet's third-party entomologica.org PDF mirror). All 12 authors, journal, article number and DOI correct. '76%' seasonal and '82%' mid-summer confirmed; 63 nature protection areas, 96 unique location-year combinations, 1989-2016 confirmed; and the crucial design caveat is verbatim: 'Most locations (59%, n = 37) were sampled in only one year, 20 locations in two years, five locations in three years, and one in four years.' Credit where due — the packet quotes the limitation rather than hiding it.

verdicts.citation_claim: van Klink et al. 2020, Science 368(6489):417-420 — -0.92%/yr terrestrial, +1.08%/yr freshwater; '2021 erratum' revising to -1.11%/yr and +1.16%/yr
verdicts.corrected_value: The erratum is 2020, not 2021: Science 370(6515), eabf1915, published 23 October 2020
verdicts.note: The MAIN figures are confirmed. I fetched the packet's own MLU Halle-Wittenberg press release (https://pressemitteilungen.pr.uni-halle.de/index.php?modus=pmanzeige&pm_id=3262): 166 long-term surveys, 1,676 sites, 1925-2018, -0.92%/yr terrestrial, +1.08%/yr freshwater, and van Klink's quote '24% fewer insects in 30 years' time and 50% fewer over 75 years', plus +38% over 30 years for freshwater. All exact. THE ERROR: the packet calls DOI 10.1126/science.abf1915 'a 2021 erratum'. It is not. Via NCBI E-utilities (esearch on the DOI returned PMID 33093114; efetch gave the full record) and Semantic Scholar, that DOI is 'Erratum for the Report...', Science 370(6515), eabf1915, publication date 2020-10-23 — six months after the original, not the following year. Separately, the erratum's revised rates (-1.11%/yr / -10.56% per decade; +1.16%/yr / +12.24% per decade) could NOT be verified from any source I retrieved: science.org 403s, the erratum has no abstract in PubMed or Semantic Scholar, and no repository copy exists. The packet itself flags these as taken from search-snippet text, which is the correct disclosure but means the numbers are unconfirmed and should not be leaned on.

verdicts.citation_claim: Montgomery 2007, PNAS 104(33):13268-13272 — agricultural erosion 1-2 orders of magnitude above soil production; ~1 mm/yr; T = 0.4-1.0 mm/yr
verdicts.note: Verified via https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC1948917/. Title 'Soil erosion and agricultural sustainability', sole author David R. Montgomery, PNAS 104(33):13268-13272, DOI 10.1073/pnas.0611508104 — all correct. Figures correct: 1-2 orders of magnitude; net erosion in conventionally plowed fields approximately 1 mm/yr; USDA T values 0.4-1.0 mm/yr. One quotation-integrity nit: the packet renders the abstract as 'Data drawn from a global compilation of studies confirm that erosion rates from conventionally plowed agricultural fields average 1-2 orders of magnitude greater than rates of soil production.' The actual sentence is 'Data drawn from a global compilation of studies quantitatively confirm the long-articulated contention that erosion rates from conventionally plowed agricultural fields average 1-2 orders of magnitude greater than rates of soil production, erosion under native vegetation, and long-term geological erosion.' The packet dropped 'quantitatively', the framing clause, and two of the three comparators while keeping the quotation marks. The number survives; the quote does not.

verdicts.citation_claim: Borrelli et al. 2017, Nature Communications 8:2013 — 35.9 Pg/yr eroded in 2012, +2.5%, 250 m resolution
verdicts.note: Verified via https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5722879/ (nature.com itself 303-redirects to an auth wall). Title 'An assessment of the global impact of 21st century land use change on soil erosion', all 14 authors, Nat Commun 8, article 2013, DOI 10.1038/s41467-017-02142-7 — all correct. 35.9 Pg yr-1 for 2012, 2.5% overall increase, 250 x 250 m model resolution, 'at least two times lower' than previous reference values (the ~75 Pg/yr 1990s figures), and greatest increases in Sub-Saharan Africa, South America and Southeast Asia — all confirmed.

verdicts.citation_claim: USGS MCS 2025 Morocco page — 50 billion t phosphate reserves, 68% of world; second-ranked producer, 15% of global production
verdicts.note: Verified verbatim at the packet's own URL https://www.usgs.gov/centers/national-minerals-information-center/morocco: 'The country was ranked first in phosphate rock reserves with 50 billion metric tons, which represented an estimated 68% of the world's reserves' and 'Morocco remained the world's second-ranked producer of phosphate rock after China and accounted for an estimated 15% of global production' in 2024. One small attribution slip: the page cites Jasinski 2025 AND Jasinski 2026 (Mineral Commodity Summaries 2025 and 2026), so pinning the whole entry to 'Mineral Commodity Summaries 2025' is imprecise. Note also the packet's own text says Morocco 'was ranked first in reserves' but then 'remained the world's second-ranked producer' — that is not a contradiction, it is the actual USGS finding (China out-produces Morocco despite far smaller reserves), and the packet reports it correctly.

verdicts.citation_claim: USGS SIR 2023-5143 — 16.5 ft area-weighted decline to 2019; 2.91 billion acre-ft in storage; 286.4 Maf decline
verdicts.note: The report EXISTS — DOI 10.3133/sir20235143 resolves (302) to https://pubs.usgs.gov/publication/sir20235143 — but every USGS pubs path returns HTTP 403 to me (landing page, /full, the PDF at /sir/2023/5143/, the pubs-services JSON API, and the pubs.er.usgs.gov mirror), so I could not read the abstract. The packet honestly discloses that it hit the same 403. What I COULD retrieve is the predecessor, SIR 2017-5040 (McGuire, predevelopment to 2015), via https://www.usgs.gov/centers/nebraska-water-science-center/science/high-plains-water-level-monitoring-study: area-weighted decline 15.8 ft; individual wells 'from a rise of 84 feet to a decline of 234 feet'; 'Recoverable water in storage in the aquifer in 2015 was about 2.91 billion acre-feet'; decline of 273.2 million acre-feet; '111.8 million acres (about 175,000 square miles) in parts of eight States'. The packet's 2019 numbers (16.5 ft, +86/-265 ft, 286.4 Maf, ~112 million acres / 175,000 sq mi / eight states) are plausible increments on those. BUT there is an internal arithmetic tell: if 2015 storage was 2.91 billion acre-ft after a 273.2 Maf decline, predevelopment was about 3,183 Maf; a 286.4 Maf decline then leaves about 2,897 Maf, which rounds to 2.90 billion acre-feet, not 2.91. The '2.91 billion' looks copied over from the 2015 report rather than read from the 2019 one. Do not use the storage figure without opening SIR 2023-5143 itself.

verdicts.citation_claim: FAO SOFIA 2026: 62.4% of stocks sustainable (2023), 'down from 64.5% reported for 2021 in SOFIA 2024'
verdicts.corrected_value: SOFIA 2024 reported 62.3 percent for 2021, not 64.5 percent
verdicts.note: This is the packet's clearest factual error. (a) The SOFIA 2024 figures the packet gives are correct — I confirmed at the FAO newsroom release of 07/06/2024 (https://www.fao.org/newsroom/detail/fao-report-global-fisheries-and-aquaculture-production-reaches-a-new-record-high/en): 'The proportion of marine stocks fished within biologically sustainable levels, however, decreased to 62.3 percent in 2021, 2.3 percent lower than in 2019' and 'an estimated 76.9 percent of the 2021 landings from stocks monitored by FAO were from biologically sustainable stocks.' (b) But the packet ALSO asserts SOFIA 2024 'reported 64.5% for 2021'. It did not — it reported 62.3%. The packet contradicts itself inside a single citation, then papers over the contradiction with a reconciliation note ('the same year on different stock sets') that is built on the misattribution. (c) The headline 62.4% (2023) figure is NOT on the cited URL. I fetched https://www.fao.org/newsroom/detail/sofia-2026--global-fisheries-and-aquaculture-production-reaches-new-highs/en and enumerated every number on the page: 89%, one-fifth, 3.1 billion, 600 million, 10%, 26.3 kg, 9.1 kg, twenty-threefold, sixfold, 53%, 59%, 72.6%, one-third, 21.1 kg, 21.3 kg. Only the landings figure the packet quotes — 'In 2023, 72.6 percent of all landings originated from biologically sustainable stocks' — is genuinely there, verbatim. 62.4% and 64.5% are both absent. I could not reach the full SOFIA 2026 report (openknowledge.fao.org and the digital edition both 403) to see whether 62.4% appears there. Treat the stock-share trend as unsupported until someone opens the report itself.

verdicts.citation_claim: USDA ERS Amber Waves Sept 2024 — fourfold output, 2.6x population, +53% per capita, +7.6% land, TFP 1.99%->1.12%
verdicts.note: Verified verbatim at the packet's own URL. Title 'Global Changes in Agricultural Production, Productivity, and Resource Use Over Six Decades', by Keith Fuglie, Stephen Morgan and Jeremy Jelliffe, published 9/30/2024 — the packet omits the authors entirely, which is sloppy but not an error. Figures all exact: 'Agricultural output increased nearly fourfold, and global population grew 2.6 times, resulting in a 53-percent increase in agricultural output per capita'; 'Agricultural land area expanded 7.6 percent between 1961 and 2020'; 'From 2011 to 2020, agricultural output grew 1.93 percent annually compared with 2.72 percent from 2001 to 2010'; TFP growth 'fell by nearly half, from 1.99 percent to 1.12 percent'. Quotation nit: the packet's 'Between 1961 and 2020, world agricultural output increased by nearly fourfold' is a paraphrase presented inside quotation marks; the source sentence is worded as above.

verdicts.citation_claim: Ord, The Precipice (2020) Table 6.1 — 'other environmental damage' existential risk approximately 1 in 1,000, as tabulated in an EA Forum review
verdicts.note: The cited page does not contain the table. I fetched https://forum.effectivealtruism.org/posts/Z5KZ2cui8WDjyF6gJ/... twice, the second time asking it to list EVERY numeric probability on the page. What is there: the 'factor of 3' quote, which IS verbatim — 'There is significant uncertainty remaining in these estimates and they should be treated as representing the right order of magnitude - each could easily be a factor of 3 higher or lower' — plus Ord's asteroid figures (1 in 6,000 for 1-10 km, 1 in 1.5 million for >10 km) and a commenter's '3%' for engineered pandemics and unforeseen anthropogenic risks (consistent with the packet's ~1 in 30). Table 6.1 itself is NOT reproduced. What I could independently confirm from other retrieved pages: total ~1 in 6 and unaligned AI ~1 in 10 (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Precipice... and /Human_extinction), and the qualitative ordering at Ord's own site (https://theprecipice.com/faq): 'nuclear weapons, climate change, and other environmental damage are each higher than all natural risks combined' and 'engineered pandemics and unaligned artificial intelligence are higher still'. That ordering is consistent with every number the packet lists, and I found nothing contradicting them — but the specific '~1 in 1,000 for other environmental damage', the load-bearing anchor for this hazard, was not retrieved from any source this session and is not on the URL cited. Cite a page of the book, or a source that actually prints the table.

verdicts.citation_claim: Gaupp et al. 2020, Nature Climate Change 10:54-57 — annual probability of simultaneous breadbasket climate risk rose 0.3%->1.2% wheat, 0.8%->1.1% maize, 1.7%->2% soybean; 25.9/18.8/0.5 Mt losses
verdicts.note: The citation SHELL is perfect — Crossref (api.crossref.org/works/10.1038/s41558-019-0600-z) and the Nature page both give 'Changing risks of simultaneous global breadbasket failure', Franziska Gaupp, Jim Hall, Stefan Hochrainer-Stigler, Simon Dadson, Nature Climate Change 10:54-57, online 9 Dec 2019 / print Jan 2020. But the packet attributes its numbers to the abstract, and the abstract contains NO NUMBERS AT ALL. I got through Nature's auth redirect chain and transcribed it word for word; it runs from 'The risk of extreme climatic conditions leading to unusually low global agricultural production is exacerbated if more than one global breadbasket is exposed at the same time' to '...enhance the resilience of the global food system', and it reports direction only: 'We show an increasing risk of simultaneous failure of wheat, maize and soybean crops across the breadbaskets analysed. For rice, risks of simultaneous adverse climate conditions have decreased in the recent past.' Neither the 0.3%/1.2%/0.8%/1.1%/1.7%/2% string nor the tonnage sentence is in it. They may well be in the paywalled body — I could not check: science-adjacent repositories all blocked (IIASA PURE serves an Anubis 403, Oxford ORA 403, ScienceDirect 403, core.ac.uk 403, and IA Scholar has zero hits). Two further tells inside the packet's own quote: it says 'Simultaneous maize, wheat and RICE climate risks... would lead to production losses of at least 25.9, 18.8 and 0.5 million tons' — rice, when the sentence before it is about wheat/maize/soybean and the real abstract says rice risks have DECREASED. A crop-set mismatch that a genuine transcription would not produce. This is the citation I would send back for re-sourcing first, because it is the only empirical per-year probability under the whole 0.005/yr rate.

verdicts.citation_claim: Gaupp et al. 2019, Agricultural Systems 175:34-45 — maize multiple-breadbasket-failure risk 6% -> 40% at 1.5 C -> 54% at 2 C; relative increases wheat 40%, maize 35%, soybean 23%
verdicts.note: Confirmed VERBATIM. ScienceDirect 403s, but OpenAlex gave alternate locations and the University of Bristol research portal (https://research-information.bris.ac.uk/en/publications/d5df7241-3564-43de-b9ef-31a103c7a46d) carries the full abstract. Both quoted sentences are exact, word for word: 'For maize, risks of multiple breadbasket failures increase the most, from 6% to 40% at 1.5 to 54% at 2 degrees C warming' and 'In relative terms, the highest simultaneous climate risk increase between the two warming scenarios was found for wheat (40%), followed by maize (35%) and soybean (23%).' Title, four authors (Gaupp, Hall, Mitchell, Dadson), volume 175, pages 34-45, DOI all correct — also independently cross-checked against Crossref. Useful context the packet omits: the same abstract says limiting warming to 1.5 C 'would avoid production losses of up to 2753 million (161,000, 265,000) tonnes maize (wheat, soybean)', and that the historical baseline corresponds to 0.85 C above pre-industrial — i.e. the '6%' is today, not zero warming.

verdicts.citation_claim: Martin & Anderson 2011, World Bank PRWP 5645 — 45% of the 2006-08 rice price rise and 30% of the wheat rise due to insulating behavior
verdicts.note: Confirmed verbatim from the PDF itself (fetched the packet's IMF-hosted URL, saved and read the cover and abstract pages). Cover: 'Policy Research Working Paper 5645 / Export Restrictions and Price Insulation during Commodity Price Booms / Will Martin, Kym Anderson / The World Bank, Development Research Group, Agriculture and Rural Development Team, May 2011' — every element of the packet's citation is right. Abstract, exact: 'The analysis suggests that 45 percent of the increase in rice prices in 2006-08, and 30 percent of the increase in wheat prices, was due to insulating behavior.' The awkward '...as developing account for only 3 percent of world rice consumption' and 'non-developing countries account for 27 percent' quotes are faithful excerpts of the source's own clumsy sentence, not packet errors. ONE uncited number: the packet's closing 'Contextual figure retrieved separately this session: export restrictions by India and Viet Nam combined with panic buying by importers such as the Philippines raised world rice prices 117-149% in Q1 2008' appears nowhere in this paper and carries no source of its own. It should be sourced or dropped.

verdicts.citation_claim: FAO Cereal Supply and Demand Brief, 4 Sept 2026 — production 2,980 Mt, utilization 2,965 Mt, stocks 947.2 Mt, stock-to-use 31.6%
verdicts.note: Confirmed at the packet's own URL https://www.fao.org/worldfoodsituation/csdb/en/, release date 04/09/2026. World cereal production 2026 forecast '2 980 million tonnes' (a decline of 61.1 Mt / 2.0 percent, 'the largest annual decline since 2018', still 'the second-largest harvest on record'); utilization 2026/27 '2 965 million tonnes'; ending stocks '947.2 million tonnes'; stocks-to-use '31.6 percent, down from the previous season's level of 31.9 percent'. All exact. Two minor items: the 2025/26 ending-stocks figure of 957.9 Mt was not visible on the page I retrieved (the 31.9% ratio was), and the packet's own derivation 31.6% x 365 = 115.3 days is arithmetically right but is the packet's construction, not FAO's. Worth flagging for the model: this same brief calls a 2.0% global decline the largest since 2018 — which makes the hazard's >=10% single-year global cereal decline an event with no analogue in the modern record.

verdicts.citation_claim: Khoury et al. 2014, PNAS 111(11):4001-4006 — homogeneity increased 16.7% 1961-2009 across 152 countries and 52 crop commodities
verdicts.note: Fully verified via https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3964121/. Title 'Increasing homogeneity in global food supplies and the implications for food security', all eight authors, PNAS 111(11):4001-4006, DOI 10.1073/pnas.1313490111 — correct. Verbatim: 'Between 1961 and 2009, homogeneity increased by 16.7%, as measured by the mean change in similarity between each country and the global standard composition'; 152 countries (representing 98% of world population); 52 measured crop commodities; '50 of the measured crop commodities currently contribute to the top 90% of calories, protein, fat, and weight around the world', composed of '94 crop species from 70 genera from 37 plant families'; and the abstract sentence about a 'global standard food supply, which is relatively species-rich in regard to measured crops at the national level, but species-poor globally'. No discrepancies.

verdicts.citation_claim: Erisman et al. 2008, Nature Geoscience 1:636-639 — Haber-Bosch supported 48% of global population; ~100 Tg N/yr, 80% for agriculture
verdicts.note: Citation shell confirmed, figures not retrieved. Via OpenAlex (api.openalex.org/works/doi:10.1038/ngeo325) and the NERC repository record (nora.nerc.ac.uk/id/eprint/5517/): 'How a century of ammonia synthesis changed the world', Jan Willem Erisman, Mark A. Sutton, James N. Galloway, Zbigniew Klimont, Wilfried Winiwarter, Nature Geoscience 1(10):636-639, 2008, DOI 10.1038/ngeo325 — every element of the packet's citation is right. But the article is paywalled and both repositories expose only the opening two sentences ('On 13 October 1908, Fritz Haber filed his patent...'), so I could NOT verify the 48% figure or the '~100 Tg N per year, with 80% used for agriculture' figure from any source this session. I am not asserting they are wrong — 48% is the number this paper is famous for — but the packet presents them without disclosing that they were not retrieved, unlike its honest disclosures elsewhere. Two cautions if the figure is kept: 48% is a 2008-vintage estimate and Erisman's own paper frames it as an estimate with wide uncertainty; and the ~100 Tg is Haber-Bosch production, which is a different quantity from the 190 Tg N/yr 'industrial and intentional fixation' control variable in this packet's own Richardson et al. citation. Do not let a reader net those two against each other.

verdicts.citation_claim: Cottrell et al. 2019, Nature Sustainability 2:130-137 — 226 shocks across 134 nations over 53 years; overfishing 45% of landing-data shocks
verdicts.note: Shell confirmed, key numbers not retrieved. OpenAlex and the Nature page confirm 'Food production shocks across land and sea', all 11 authors, Nature Sustainability 2(2):130-137, DOI 10.1038/s41893-018-0210-1. I transcribed the published abstract verbatim through Nature's auth redirect: it confirms 'production data from crop, livestock, aquaculture and fisheries sectors over 53 years', 'shock frequency has increased through time on land and sea at a global scale', and 'Geopolitical and extreme-weather events were the main shock drivers identified' — consistent with the packet. It does NOT contain '226 shocks', '134 nations', the '45%' overfishing figure, the sector ranking, or the South Asia claim; those live in the paywalled body or a press summary. Every open route to the body failed: both UTAS eprints preprint PDFs return 401, figshare and figshare.utas return 403, ecite redirects into the 403. The packet says these came from 'search-surfaced abstract and press summary' — the abstract half of that is demonstrably not the source. Numbers unconfirmed; 226/134/53 is a widely repeated triple and is probably right, but 'probably right' is not verification.

verdicts.citation_claim: Xia et al. 2022, Nature Food 3:586-596 — soot >5 Tg causes mass food shortages; >2 billion (India-Pakistan) and >5 billion (US-Russia) could die
verdicts.note: Confirmed at the packet's own URL https://www.giss.nasa.gov/pubs/abs/xi08000i.html. Title 'Global food insecurity and famine from reduced crop, marine fishery and livestock production due to climate disruption from nuclear war soot injection'; all ten authors (Xia, Robock, Scherrer, Harrison, Bodirsky, Weindl, Jagermeyr, Bardeen, Toon, Heneghan); Nature Food 3(8):586-596; DOI 10.1038/s43016-022-00573-0 — all correct. Figures correct: 'soot injections larger than 5 Tg would lead to mass food shortages', 'more than 2 billion people could die from nuclear war between India and Pakistan, and more than 5 billion could die from a war between the United States and Russia', and the limited benefit of food-waste reduction. The citation is clean. What is NOT clean is how the packet uses it — see the overall note: this hazard's event definition explicitly EXCLUDES nuclear-winter causes, yet the 0.25 deaths_fraction of its worst tier has no other source in the packet.

verdicts.citation_claim: Forecasting Research Institute XPT 2023 — expert median 20% catastrophe / 6% extinction; superforecaster 9% / 1%; 80 experts, 89 superforecasters
verdicts.note: Partially confirmed; the figures themselves were not retrieved. The packet's PDF URL (https://forecastingresearch.org/pdf/existential-risk-persuasion-tournament.pdf) exists but exceeds the 10 MB fetch limit, so I could not read it. The FRI landing page https://forecastingresearch.org/xpt confirms the report title 'Forecasting Existential Risks: Evidence from a Long-Run Forecasting Tournament' and that the tournament involved '169 forecasters' — which is exactly 80 + 89, a good corroboration of the packet's group sizes. But the 20%/6% and 9%/1% medians, the definition of catastrophe (>=10% of humans dead in a five-year period), the extinction threshold (fewer than 5,000), and the June-October 2022 dates were NOT visible on any page I retrieved. These match my prior understanding of the XPT and I found nothing contradicting them, but per the packet's own standard they should be marked as unretrieved. The packet's derived ratio claim does check out arithmetically against its own numbers: 20/6 = 3.3 and 9/1 = 9, hence 'roughly 3:1 to 9:1'.

verdicts.citation_claim: USDA ERS Amber Waves Sept 2024 counter-case, plus world cereal yields 1.4 t/ha (1961) to 4.2 t/ha (2022) from World Bank AG.YLD.CREL.KG
verdicts.note: The ERS half is confirmed verbatim — same verification as hazard 1 citation 10 (fourfold output, 2.6x population, +53% per capita, +7.6% land, 2.72%->1.93% output growth, 1.99%->1.12% TFP; Fuglie, Morgan and Jelliffe, 9/30/2024). The appended World Bank cereal-yield figures are a different matter: they carry no URL, are flagged only as 'separately retrieved', and I did not verify them. Note the series identifier AG.YLD.CREL.KG is reported in kilograms per hectare, so the packet's 't/ha' rendering is a unit conversion the packet performed silently (1.4 t/ha = ~1,400 kg/ha). The magnitudes are plausible; they are not verified. Also note the packet's framing claim that 'the 2007-08 spike produced no measurable global mortality signal' appears in the citation title but is supported by no source in the packet — it is an assertion, and it is doing real work in constraining the tiers.

audits.overall: Mixed, and not yet safe to build on without repairs — though it is a good deal better than the typical packet, and its self-disclosures are unusually honest. Thirteen of the twenty-one citations came back fully confirmed against sources I actually retrieved this session: Richardson et al. 2023 (I downloaded the PDF from the packet's own PIK link and read Table 1 page by page — every one of the two dozen control-variable numbers is exact), Klein et al. 2007 and Khoury et al. 2014 and Montgomery 2007 and Borrelli et al. 2017 via PMC, Hallmann et al. 2017 via PLOS, van Klink's main figures via the packet's Halle press release, USGS Morocco and USDA ERS and the FAO Cereal Supply and Demand Brief at their own URLs, Xia et al. via NASA GISS, Martin & Anderson from the working-paper PDF itself, and Gaupp et al. 2019 verbatim via the University of Bristol research portal. Nothing in the packet is wholly fabricated: every author list, journal, volume, page range and DOI I checked resolved to a real paper with the right people on it (verified independently through Crossref, OpenAlex, Semantic Scholar and NCBI E-utilities). Four defects matter. (1) The FAO fisheries entry is factually wrong: it claims SOFIA 2024 reported 64.5% of stocks sustainable for 2021, when SOFIA 2024 says 62.3% — the packet even quotes the correct 62.3% two sentences later and then reconciles the contradiction with a note built on its own error; and its headline 62.4% for 2023 is absent from the cited page, where I enumerated every number and found only the 72.6%-of-landings figure it also quotes. (2) The Gaupp 2020 Nature Climate Change numbers are attributed to an abstract that contains no numbers at all — I transcribed it verbatim, and it reports direction only; the packet's quoted sentence also mismatches its own crop set, naming rice in a wheat/maize/soybean result when the real abstract says rice risk has decreased. That matters more than the others because it is the only empirical per-year probability anywhere under the 0.005/yr rate. (3) The van Klink erratum is misdated a year (it is Science 370(6515), 23 October 2020, not 2021), and its revised rates are unretrieved. (4) The Ord anchor cites an EA Forum post that does not tabulate Table 6.1; the "factor of 3" quote there is verbatim and the ~1-in-6 total and ~1-in-10 AI figures check out elsewhere, but the load-bearing "~1 in 1,000 for other environmental damage" was not retrieved from anything. Erisman's 48%, Cottrell's 226/134/45%, the XPT medians and the USGS High Plains figures are all unverifiable behind paywalls or 403s — and the High Plains entry carries an arithmetic tell that its "2.91 billion acre-feet" was copied from the 2015 predecessor report rather than read from the 2019 one. On the numbers rather than the sources: both tier sets sum to exactly 1.00, so nothing exceeds unity, but two tiers are unsupportable as cited. The multi-breadbasket "compound collapse" tier (p=0.02, deaths_fraction=0.25, roughly two billion people) has exactly one source in the packet capable of producing that magnitude — Xia et al. — and that mechanism requires 5+ Tg of stratospheric soot, which this hazard's event definition explicitly excludes. The packet flags the tension in prose and then uses the number anyway. Likewise the "multi-year deficit" tier at 5% mortality sits uneasily against the packet's own counter-citations (31.6% stock-to-use, roughly 115 days of buffer; output per capita up 53% across the entire degradation period). Finally, the rate basis label on the food-shock hazard should be corrected from "physical-model" to author-estimate: no cited source outputs 0.005/yr, the two Gaupp papers are copula fits to a different quantity (simultaneous climate risk, not a 10% global production decline), and the packet's own FAO citation calls a 2.0% annual fall the largest since 2018, putting the defined event outside the observed record entirely. Fix the FAO figure, re-source Gaupp 2020 from the paywalled body, correct the erratum year, cite a page of The Precipice, and either re-derive the 0.25 tier from a non-nuclear mechanism or drop it — after that this is a usable foundation.

verdicts.citation_claim: Degrassi et al. 2012 (arXiv:1205.6497) — absolute stability excluded at 98% C.L. for Mh < 126 GeV; theory uncertainty on critical Mh reduced to 1 GeV
verdicts.note: Retrieved https://arxiv.org/abs/1205.6497. Title 'Higgs mass and vacuum stability in the Standard Model at NNLO'; all seven authors, year and JHEP venue correct. Abstract reads verbatim: 'reducing the theoretical uncertainty in the determination of the critical value of Mh for vacuum stability to 1 GeV' and 'absolute stability of the Higgs potential is excluded at 98% C.L. for Mh < 126 GeV'. Exact match.

verdicts.citation_claim: Buttazzo et al. 2013 (arXiv:1307.3536) — Eq. (64) stability condition; Mh = 125.15 +/- 0.24 GeV; 'metastability is now preferred at 99.3% CL'; SM vacuum survives longer than astrophysical ages
verdicts.note: Read the v4 PDF directly (an ar5iv HTML render truncated before section 6.3 and falsely reported these strings absent — I only caught this by paging the actual PDF). p.31: 'the SM vacuum is likely to survive for times that are enormously longer than any significant astrophysical age (e.g. the sun will exhaust its fuel in about five billion years).' Section 7: 'we cannot conclusively establish the fate of the EW vacuum, although metastability is now preferred at 99.3% CL.' Eq. (64) and Table 2 value Mh = 125.15 +/- 0.24 GeV both confirmed. Note for completeness that the paper ALSO states 'vacuum stability of the SM up to the Planck scale is excluded at 2.8 sigma (99.8% C.L. one-sided)' — a different, non-contradictory quantity. https://arxiv.org/pdf/1307.3536v4

verdicts.citation_claim: Andreassen, Frost & Schwartz 2018, PRD 97 056006 — universe lifetime 10^139 yr; >10^58 yr at 95% confidence
verdicts.note: Retrieved https://arxiv.org/abs/1707.08124. 'we produce the first complete calculation of the lifetime of our universe: 10^139 years. With 95% confidence, we expect our universe to last more than 10^58 years.' Verbatim match; PRD 97, 056006 (2018) correct. (Published title capitalisation is 'Scale Invariant Instantons and the Complete Lifetime of the Standard Model'.)

verdicts.citation_claim: Ellis, Giudice, Mangano, Tkachev & Wiedemann (LSAG) 2008, J.Phys.G 35 115004 — cosmic rays exclude collider-triggered vacuum bubbles; 10^31 LHC programmes; 3x10^13 per second
verdicts.note: Read the full published PDF at the cited URL (https://hep.ph.liv.ac.uk/~green/cern/LHCsafe.pdf), which is the genuine IOP typeset article. Section 3 p.5 verbatim: 'These bubbles of new vacuum would already have expanded to consume large parts of the visible Universe several billion years ago. The continued existence of the Universe means that such vacuum bubbles are not produced in cosmic-ray collisions, and hence the LHC will also not produce any vacuum bubbles.' p.4: 'Nature has already completed about 10^31 LHC experimental programmes since the beginning of the Universe. Moreover, each second, the Universe continues to repeat about 3 x 10^13 complete LHC experiments.' Exact.

verdicts.citation_claim: LSAG 2008 — 'icecube in a furnace'; production probability falls with sqrt(s); RHIC furnace ~1.6 trillion degrees; plasma falls apart within 10^-23 s
verdicts.note: All four figures verified verbatim in the PDF. p.10: 'the likelihood of strangelet production in relativistic heavy-ion collisions can be compared to the likelihood of producing an icecube in a furnace'; Figure 2 caption and p.10 text: 'a theoretical calculation assuming a furnace with a temperature around 1.6 trillion degrees'; p.9: 'the plasma produced in the collision is very short-lived, expanding rapidly at about half the velocity of light and falling apart within 10^-23 s'; Appendix A: 'the probability for strangelet production decreases with increasing centre-of-mass energy'.

verdicts.citation_claim: Moon-survival strangelet bound, LSAG 2008 'reporting and strengthening Dar, De Rujula & Heinz (2008)'
verdicts.corrected_value: Busza, Jaffe, Sandweiss & Wilczek (2000), Rev. Mod. Phys. 72, 1125
verdicts.note: The QUOTED TEXT is genuine (LSAG section 5, p.11, verbatim). The ATTRIBUTION is wrong. LSAG introduces the Moon argument as 'It has been shown that the continuing survival of the Moon under cosmic-ray bombardment ensures that heavy-ion collisions do not pose any conceivable threat via strangelet production [6]' — and reference [6] in the LSAG bibliography (p.18) is 'Busza W et al 2000 Rev. Mod. Phys. 72 1125', i.e. Jaffe, Busza, Sandweiss & Wilczek, 'Review of speculative disaster scenarios at RHIC' (2000). Not Dar, De Rujula & Heinz, and not 2008. The packet has swapped this attribution with the one in the next citation. https://hep.ph.liv.ac.uk/~green/cern/LHCsafe.pdf

verdicts.citation_claim: Interstellar cosmic-ray / absence-of-stellar-explosions argument, LSAG 2008 'citing Jaffe, Busza, Wilczek & Sandweiss (2008)'
verdicts.corrected_value: Dar, De Rujula & Heinz (1999), Phys. Lett. B 470, 142
verdicts.note: Again the quoted text is genuine (LSAG p.11: 'An independent safety argument, which does not require any assumption about the velocity distribution of any hypothetical strangelets, has been given in [17]. The rate of cosmic-ray heavy-ion collisions in interstellar space is known...'). But LSAG reference [17] is 'Dar A, De Rujula A and Heinz U 1999 Phys. Lett. B 470 142'. The packet has exactly transposed the two source attributions between this citation and the previous one, and dated both to 2008 when the true years are 2000 and 1999. This is the clearest fabrication-class error in the packet.

verdicts.citation_claim: LSAG publication metadata: J.Phys.G 35 (2008) 115004 (18pp), doi:10.1088/0954-3899/35/11/115004, received 26 Aug 2008, published 5 Sept 2008
verdicts.note: Title page of the published PDF confirms every element: 'J. Phys. G: Nucl. Part. Phys. 35 (2008) 115004 (18pp)', 'doi:10.1088/0954-3899/35/11/115004', 'Received 26 August 2008 / Published 5 September 2008', authors John Ellis, Gian Giudice, Michelangelo Mangano, Igor Tkachev, Urs Wiedemann (LHC Safety Assessment Group). Abstract quote is accurate (source word order is 'constrains severely'). arXiv:0806.3414 confirmed at https://arxiv.org/abs/0806.3414. Note the packet's tier structure is incoherent rather than mis-cited: the stated event rate (1e-15/yr) is defined as the runaway-initiation rate, yet a tier then applies a further p=1e-9 for runaway, implying 1e-24/yr; and LSAG itself supplies no probability, so 'author-estimate' is correctly labelled.

verdicts.citation_claim: Phoenix & Drexler 2004, Nanotechnology 15(8):869, doi:10.1088/0957-4484/15/8/001 — self-replication unnecessary; weapons are the real concern
verdicts.note: Bibliographic record verified via Semantic Scholar API on the DOI: 'Safe exponential manufacturing', Chris Phoenix and Eric Drexler, Nanotechnology vol. 15, pp. 869-872, 2004, DOI 10.1088/0957-4484/15/8/001. Caveat I must state plainly: the publisher elides the abstract and IOP blocked direct fetch (bot wall), so I could NOT verify the quoted abstract sentences verbatim against an open primary copy. The substance is corroborated by the IOP's own press release for this paper (see next verdict). Title/authors/venue/year/DOI/pages all correct as cited.

verdicts.citation_claim: Sandberg & Bostrom 2008 GCR Survey — nanotech accident 5%/1%/0.5%; nanotech weapons 25%/10%/5%; overall extinction 19%
verdicts.note: Retrieved and read the report PDF at the cited URL (https://global-catastrophic-risks.com/docs/2008-1.pdf). Page 1 table verbatim: 'Number killed in the single biggest nanotech accident' 5% / 1% / 0.5%; 'Number killed by molecular nanotech weapons' 25% / 10% / 5%; 'Overall risk of extinction prior to 2100' 19%. Conference date '(17-20 July, 2008)' and Technical Report 2008/1, FHI Oxford, all correct. Arithmetic check: 0.005/92 = 5.43e-5, matching the 'best' 5.4e-5; but the 'high' bound 5.6e-4 should be 0.05/92 = 5.4e-4.

verdicts.citation_claim: Sandberg & Bostrom 2008 — the 'grain of salt' / cognitive-bias caveat
verdicts.note: Verbatim on pages 1-2 of the same PDF: 'These results should be taken with a grain of salt. Non-responses have been omitted, although some might represent a statement of zero probability rather than no opinion.' and 'There are likely to be many cognitive biases that affect the result, such as unpacking bias and the availability heuristic—as well as old-fashioned optimism and pessimism.' Exact match.

verdicts.citation_claim: ScienceDaily / EurekAlert! press release 9 June 2004 — Drexler on runaway replicators
verdicts.note: Retrieved https://www.sciencedaily.com/releases/2004/06/040609072100.htm — headline 'Nanotechnology Pioneer Slays Grey Goo Myths', dated June 9 2004, source Institute Of Physics. Both Drexler quotes appear verbatim as cited. One correction to the citation's framing: the release is Institute of Physics coverage, not 'Institute of Physics / Foresight Institute'; Chris Phoenix is identified there as Director of Research of the Center for Responsible Nanotechnology, not Foresight.

verdicts.citation_claim: LSAG 2008 sec.4 — microscopic black hole lifetime O(10^-27 s); suppression requires violating quantum mechanics / general relativity
verdicts.note: LSAG p.6-7 verbatim: 'For this reason, a microscopic black hole cannot be completely black. In standard quantum physics, the decay rate would be directly related to the production rate, and the expected lifetime would be very short, O(10^-27 s).' and p.7: '...would require a violation of some of the basic principles of quantum mechanics—which is a cornerstone of the laws of Nature—in order for the black hole decay rate to be suppressed relative to its production rate, and/or of general relativity, in order to suppress Hawking radiation.' Exact.

verdicts.citation_claim: LSAG 2008 sec.4 — survival of white dwarfs and neutron stars excludes cosmic-ray production of dangerous stable black holes
verdicts.note: LSAG p.7 verbatim: 'ultra-high-energy cosmic rays hitting dense stars such as white dwarfs and neutron stars would have produced black holes copiously during their lifetimes... would have led to the destruction of white dwarfs and neutron stars on time scales that are much shorter than their observed lifetimes. The final stages of their destruction would have released explosively large amounts of energy, which would have been highly visible. The observation of white dwarfs and neutron stars that would have been destroyed in this way tells us that cosmic rays do not produce such black holes, and hence neither will the LHC.' Exact.

verdicts.citation_claim: LSAG 2008 sec.2 — 3x10^22 cosmic rays at >=10^17 eV; hundred thousand LHC programmes on Earth; one billion times on the Sun
verdicts.note: LSAG p.4 verbatim: 'over 3 x 10^22 cosmic rays with energies of 10^17 eV or more, equal to or greater than the LHC energy, have struck the Earth's surface since its formation. This means that Nature has already conducted the equivalent of about a hundred thousand LHC experimental programmes on Earth, and the planet still exists... Nature has therefore already conducted the LHC experimental programme about one billion times via the collisions of cosmic rays with the Sun, and the Sun still exists.' Exact.

verdicts.citation_claim: LSAG 2008 sec.4 — seven or more dimensions gives billions of years; five or six dimensions would be detectable
verdicts.note: LSAG p.7 verbatim: 'the rate at which absorption would take place would be so slow, if there are seven or more dimensions, that Earth would survive for billions of years before any harm befell it' and 'If there are only five or six dimensions of spacetime relevant at the LHC scale, then the gravitational interactions of black holes are strong enough such that their impact, should they exist, would be detectable in the Universe.' The packet's rendering duplicates the clause 'should they exist' — a transcription artefact only. Separately: the hazard's rate basis is mislabelled — 'observed-frequency' cannot yield an exact 0/yr; LSAG establishes an empirical upper bound, not a measured frequency.

verdicts.citation_claim: Caldeira & Kasting 1992, Nature 360, 721-723 — C4 biosphere survives 0.9-1.5 Gyr; C3 limit 150 ppm; 100 Myr; C4 persists below 10 ppm
verdicts.note: The record is real and correctly cited: Semantic Scholar on DOI 10.1038/360721a0 returns 'The life span of the biosphere revisited', K. Caldeira and J. Kasting, Nature, vol. 360, pp. 721-723, 1992. But the abstract is paywalled (Nature 303-redirects to an auth wall; the Caltech mirror fails TLS verification), so I could NOT retrieve the quoted sentences verbatim from the primary source. Partial independent corroboration: Graham et al. 2024 states 'the 0.9 Gyr calculated in the original study' and that CK92's C4 model used a '10 ppmv' compensation threshold. Separate defect: the URL attached to this citation is https://arxiv.org/html/2409.10714v1 — that is the Graham 2024 preprint, not the 1992 Nature paper. A reader following that URL does not reach the cited source.

verdicts.citation_claim: Graham, Halevy & Abbot 2024 (arXiv:2409.10714) — 1.6-1.86 Gyr; Te=13.7 K, beta=0.25; 0.55 Gyr at Te x beta = 0.6; 'minimum CO2 for land plants 10 ppmv'
verdicts.corrected_value: 2.9 ppmv (this paper's own C4 compensation point); 10 ppmv is the value CK92 and earlier studies assumed
verdicts.note: Most of this citation checks out verbatim against https://arxiv.org/abs/2409.10714 and its HTML full text: title, authors, PSJ acceptance, the abstract sentence 'This dramatically lengthens plant survival from 1 Gyr up to ~1.6-1.86 Gyr, until extreme temperatures halt photosynthesis', 'lifespans in the CO2 starvation regime range from 0.55 Gyr at Te x beta = 0.6 to a maximum lifespan', and CK92 parameters Te = 13.7 K, beta = 0.25. The one wrong number is the CO2 figure: the paper states 'our default parameter choices for the C4 plant productivity model utilized in this study produce a CO2 compensation point of 2.9 ppmv' and explicitly contrasts this with the 10 ppmv of prior work ('in our model C4 plants have a lower compensation threshold (2.9 ppmv, rather than 10 ppmv)'). Attributing 10 ppmv to Graham et al. imports someone else's parameter.

verdicts.citation_claim: Feulner 2012, Rev. Geophys. 50 RG2006 — Gough (1981) luminosity law, L_sun = 3.85e26 W, t_sun = 4.57 Gyr, 30% lower at ZAMS, S0 = 1361 W/m2, A = 0.3
verdicts.note: Read the PDF at the cited Harvard URL. Paragraph [6] p.2 gives Eq. (1) exactly as quoted, 'where L_sun = 3.85 x 10^26 W is the present-day solar luminosity and t_sun = 4.57 Gyr (1 Ga = 10^9 years) is the age of the Sun', and 'the bolometric luminosity of the Sun ... was about 30% lower as compared to the present epoch'. Paragraph [12] p.3: 'the present-day solar constant S0 = 1361 W m^-2 [Kopp and Lean, 2011] and Earth's current albedo A ~ 0.3'. Citation 'Feulner, G. (2012), The faint young Sun problem, Rev. Geophys., 50, RG2006, doi:10.1029/2011RG000375' matches.

verdicts.note: Retrieved https://arxiv.org/abs/1312.3337. Title, all five authors and Nature 504 correct. verdicts.citation_claim: Feulner 2012 — S0 = 1361 W/m2, A = 0.3, Delta F = Delta S0 (1-A)/4, Gough luminosity law

verdicts.citation_claim: Graham, Halevy & Abbot 2024 — 'the biosphere overheats at 338 K after 1.66-1.86 Gyr'

verdicts.citation_claim: Neron de Surgy & Laskar 1997, A&A 318, 975-989, as presented on Laskar's IMCCE page — chaotic zone after ~1.5 Gyr; axis wanders 0 to >85 degrees; present obliquity 23.25 deg, 40 kyr, 1.3 deg
verdicts.corrected_value: The 0-to->85-degree wandering is the Moonless-Earth result of Laskar, Joutel & Robutel (1993), not a consequence of the 1.5 Gyr transition described by Neron de Surgy & Laskar (1997)
verdicts.note: Retrieved https://perso.imcce.fr/jacques-laskar/en/general-audience/earth-without-the-moon/. The page does say 'After about 1.5 Gyr, the precession period of the Earth becomes comparable to the precession periods of the orbital plane', 'the spin axis wanders chaotically between 0 and more than 85 degrees', and 'At present, the average obliquity of the Earth is 23.25 degrees, and the obliquity oscillates around this value with 40 kyr periods and 1.3 degrees amplitude'. It lists 'O. Neron de Surgy and J. Laskar: On the long term evolution of the spin of the Earth, Astron. Astrophys. 318, 975-989', so the reference is real and correctly numbered. The defect is that the 0-85 degree range is the page's description of an Earth WITHOUT the Moon (Laskar/Joutel/Robutel 1993, Nature 361, 615), which the packet's own citation 3 attributes correctly — so the packet asserts the same figure under two different sources. I could not fetch the A&A abstract itself (ADS returned 405), so the excursion amplitude actually predicted by Neron de Surgy & Laskar 1997 is unverified. Note also that the tier 'Large obliquity excursion: deaths=0.9' has no support in any cited source; Laskar's work is purely dynamical and says nothing about mortality.

verdicts.note: Retrieved https://arxiv.org/abs/1205.6863. Title 'The M31 Velocity Vector. I. Hubble Space Telescope Proper Motion Measurements', authors and ApJ 753:7 correct. verdicts.note: Retrieved https://arxiv.org/abs/0801.4031. verdicts.citation_claim: Schroeder & Connon Smith 2008 — tidal interaction and chromospheric drag at the tip-RGB
verdicts.note: Same abstract: the authors 'consider the loss of orbital angular momentum suffered by planet Earth from tidal interaction with the giant Sun, as well as dynamical drag in the lower chromosphere', and identify the tip-RGB phase as the closest encounter. Correctly cited; MNRAS 386, 155-163 (2008) correct.

verdicts.citation_claim: Buttazzo et al. 2013 sec. 6.3 — 'the sun will exhaust its fuel in about five billion years'
verdicts.note: Verified on p.31 of the v4 PDF, in the paragraph closing section 6.3 (Lifetime of the SM vacuum): 'As shown, the SM vacuum is likely to survive for times that are enormously longer than any significant astrophysical age (e.g. the sun will exhaust its fuel in about five billion years).' Section number 6.3 is correct. Worth noting the yardstick is a parenthetical aside in a particle-physics paper, not a stellar-evolution result, and it disagrees by ~2.6 Gyr with the tip-RGB figure (7.59 Gyr) the same hazard uses as its date — they measure different milestones.

verdicts.citation_claim: Feulner 2012 quoting Gough (1981, p.28) and Bahcall et al. (2001) — luminosity increase an inevitable consequence of Newtonian physics; ZAMS 30% lower

Paragraph [6] gives the 30%-lower ZAMS figure at 4.57 Ga. Bahcall et al. (2001) is genuinely cited (Figure 1, solid line). Exact.

verdicts.citation_claim: Adams & Laughlin 1997, RMP 69, 337-372 — eta = log10(tau/yr); star formation ends at eta ~ 14; era of conventional stars 6 < eta < 14
verdicts.note: Read the full arXiv PDF (astro-ph/9701131). Section VI.A, Summary of Results item [2], verbatim: 'Both stellar evolution and conventional star formation come to an end at the cosmological decade eta ~ 14. This time scale only slightly exceeds the longest evolution time for a low mass star. It also corresponds to the time at which the galaxy runs out of raw material (gas) for producing new stars. The era of conventional stars in the universe is confined to the range 6 < eta < 14.' Word-for-word match. Title, authors, RMP 69, 337-372 all correct.

verdicts.citation_claim: Adams & Laughlin 1997 abstract — gas exhausted at ~1-10 trillion years; star formation continues via brown-dwarf collisions
verdicts.note: Abstract on p.1 of the PDF, verbatim: 'At times exceeding ~1-10 trillion years, the supply of interstellar gas will be exhausted, yet star formation will continue at a highly attenuated level via collisions between brown dwarfs. This process tails off as the galaxy gradually depletes its stars by ejecting the majority, and driving a minority toward eventual accretion onto massive black holes.' Exact. Note an internal tension in the packet, not the citation: gas exhaustion at 1-10 trillion years is eta ~ 12-13, whereas the hazard's date is eta = 14.

verdicts.citation_claim: Adams & Laughlin 1997 Summary item [1] — 0.1 M_sun stars skip red giant phases, fade as helium white dwarfs
verdicts.note: Section VI.A item [1], verbatim: 'Stars with very small mass (~ 0.1 M_sun) do not experience any red giant phases. verdicts.citation_claim: Adams & Laughlin 1997 sec. VI.B — the five eras and their eta ranges, first named 'The Radiation Dominated Era, -inf < eta < 4'
verdicts.note: I specifically suspected this one (many secondary sources call the first era 'Primordial') and it survives. Section VI.B p.46, verbatim: '[A] The Radiation Dominated Era. -infinity < eta < 4. [B] The Stelliferous Era. 6 < eta < 14. [C] The Degenerate Era. 15 < eta < 37. At this late time, protons have decayed and black holes have evaporated. Only the waste products from these processes remain: mostly photons of colossal wavelength, neutrinos, electrons, and positrons.' Exact.

As a result, cosmological heat death is postponed until after that epoch, i.e., until the Dark Era.' Eq. (6.3) is 'S <= 2 pi R E / (h-bar c)'. All three exact.

verdicts.citation_claim: LSAG 2008 sec.4 citing Hawking — all black holes ultimately unstable; broad consensus but no direct evidence
verdicts.note: LSAG p.6 verbatim: 'As was pointed out 30 years ago by Stephen Hawking [7], it is expected that all black holes are ultimately unstable. This is because of very basic features of quantum mechanics in curved spaces... There is broad consensus among physicists on the reality of Hawking radiation, but so far no experiment has had the sensitivity required to find direct evidence for it.' Reference [7] in LSAG is 'Hawking S W 1975 Commun. Math. Phys. 43 199', so the underlying attribution is to Hawking 1975, not 2008 (the packet's '(2008)' is the LSAG paper's own year, which is how it is framed, so this is acceptable as written).

verdicts.citation_claim: 'DESI Collaboration (A. G. Adame et al.) (2025)', DESI DR2 Results II (arXiv:2503.14738) — 3.1 sigma; 2.8-4.2 sigma with SNe; w0 > -1, wa < 0
verdicts.corrected_value: DESI Collaboration: M. Abdul-Karim et al. (2025)

Adame et al. is the DESI DR1 BAO author string (arXiv:2404.03002) — a real name pinned to a paper they did not lead. verdicts.citation_claim: '(authors of arXiv:2504.15222) (2025)' — 'Did DESI DR2 truly reveal dynamical dark energy?'; DESI's DDE claim not robust; fate likely matter-dominated
verdicts.corrected_value: Authors are Deng Wang and David F. Mota
verdicts.note: Retrieved https://arxiv.org/abs/2504.15222. The paper exists with that exact title and year; every quoted phrase is verbatim from its abstract. Two defects worth recording: (1) the packet leaves the authors as '(authors of arXiv:2504.15222)' — they are Deng Wang and David Mota, and a citation that declines to name its authors is a smell even when the paper is real; (2) the packet's ellipsis silently removes the paper's central positive finding, 'Through a statistical comparison for each dataset, on average, we find that DDE is strongly preferred over the LambdaCDM model. This suggests that DDE likely exists' — so the quotation as edited reverses the paper's stance on dynamical dark energy while accurately reproducing its stance on dataset tensions.

verdicts.citation_claim: Adams & Laughlin 1997 sec. VI.D — continually expanding universe never reaches equilibrium; cosmological heat death distinguished from classical
verdicts.note: Section VI.D p.47, verbatim: 'A continually expanding universe never reaches true thermodynamic equilibrium and hence never reaches a constant temperature. Classical heat death is thus manifestly avoided. However, the expansion can, in principle, become purely adiabatic so that the entropy in a given comoving volume of the universe approaches (or attains) a constant value. In this case, the universe can still become a dull and lifeless place with no ability to do physical work. We denote this latter possibility as cosmological heat death.' Exact match.

audits.overall: Partly. The bibliographic spine is unusually good — I pulled and read the actual PDFs or abstract pages for Degrassi 2012 (arXiv:1205.6497), Buttazzo 2013 (the full v4 PDF, pages 30-45), Andreassen 2018 (arXiv:1707.08124), the published LSAG review (all 18 pages, including its reference list), the Sandberg & Bostrom 2008 report PDF (all 5 pages), Adams & Laughlin 1997 (the full 49-page arXiv PDF, sections IV.F, V, VI.A-D and the abstract), Caldwell 2003, van der Marel 2012 (arXiv PDF), Sohn 2012, Schroeder & Smith 2008, Leconte 2013, O'Malley-James 2013, Graham 2024 (abstract + HTML full text), Feulner 2012 (the PDF at the cited Harvard URL), Maeder & Gueorguiev 2021 (PDF), Laskar's IMCCE page, the ScienceDaily release, DESI 2503.14738, 2503.14743 and Wang & Mota 2504.15222, plus Semantic Scholar records for Phoenix & Drexler and Caldeira & Kasting. Forty of forty-seven quotations reproduce their sources word-for-word, including several I actively expected to be wrong (the Adams & Laughlin era names, the Buttazzo 99.3% CL, the van der Marel pericentre distance). Four defects are real: (1) the strangelet hazard TRANSPOSES two attributions — LSAG ref [6], the Moon-survival argument, is Busza/Jaffe/Sandweiss/Wilczek 2000, and ref [17], the interstellar/stellar-explosion argument, is Dar/De Rujula/Heinz 1999; the packet swaps them and dates both to 2008; (2) DESI DR2 Results II is led by M. Abdul-Karim et al., not A. G. Adame et al. (that is the DR1 author string) — a real name on the wrong paper; (3) Graham et al.'s land-plant CO2 floor is 2.9 ppmv, not the 10 ppmv the packet attributes to them (10 ppmv is the older Caldeira-Kasting value); (4) the Neron de Surgy & Laskar citation borrows the 0-to->85-degree figure, which is the Moonless-Earth result of Laskar/Joutel/Robutel 1993 and is separately and correctly cited elsewhere in the same hazard. Two housekeeping faults: the Caldeira & Kasting 1992 citation carries the Graham 2024 arXiv URL rather than any route to the Nature paper (and I could not verify its abstract verbatim behind Nature's paywall), and the Wang & Mota quotation elides the sentence in which that paper says dynamical dark energy IS strongly preferred, inverting its conclusion. The more serious problem is not citation hygiene but the derived numbers, which no source vouches for. Tier probabilities exceed 1 in eight of the eleven hazards (grey goo 1.3, co2-starvation 1.9, ocean-loss 2.0, moon 2.4, red-giant 2.0, heat-death 1.6, collider-BH 1.000001), and in several cases the tiers are not a partition at all but three overlapping conditionals. Three tiers are affirmatively contradicted or unsupported by their own cited mechanism: red-giant 'Marginal survival p=0.15' against Schroeder & Smith's explicit 'planet Earth will not be able to escape engulfment'; Andromeda 'Elevated supernova and AGN environment p=0.3, deaths=0.1', which appears nowhere in van der Marel or Sohn; and moon-recession 'Large obliquity excursion deaths=0.9', which is pure author estimate dressed as a consequence of a dynamical result. Two rates do not follow from their stated derivation: the vacuum-decay 'best' of 7.2e-140/yr is not the reciprocal of 10^139 yr (that is 1e-139), and the grey-goo 'high' of 5.6e-4 should be 0.05/92 = 5.4e-4. The grey-goo hazard also conflates exactly the three quantities the brief warns about — it annualises the survey's EXTINCTION median to get the event rate, then multiplies by a further 0.1 extinction tier while attaching p=1 to a 'contained incident' drawn from a different survey row. Verdict: the citations are trustworthy enough to build on after the four attribution fixes; the tier layer is not, and should be rebuilt before any model consumes it.

verdicts.citation_claim: Riley (2012), Space Weather 10, doi:10.1029/2011SW000734 — 'probability of another Carrington event (based on Dst less than -850 nT) occurring within the next decade is approximately 12%'
verdicts.note: Retrieved the NTRS record (https://ntrs.nasa.gov/citations/20120003491). Title 'On the Probability of Occurrence of Extreme Space Weather Events', Riley, Pete (Predictive Science Inc.), Space Weather vol. 10 issue S02012, DOI 10.1029/2011SW000734 — all as claimed. The abstract sentence is word-for-word identical to the packet's quote, including the -850 nT Dst basis. URL live, not a 404.

verdicts.citation_claim: Riley & Love (2017), Space Weather 15, 53-64, doi:10.1002/2016SW001470 — 10.3% [0.9,18.7] power law vs 3.0% [0.6,9.0] lognormal per decade
verdicts.note: Retrieved the USGS Publications Warehouse entry (https://www.usgs.gov/publications/extreme-geomagnetic-storms-probabilistic-forecasts-and-their-uncertainties): both percentages and both 95% CIs match exactly, and each is attached to the correct distribution.
