verdicts.citation_claim: Cliver, Schrijver, Shibata & Usoskin (2022), Living Rev. Solar Phys. 19:2 — Dst waiting times (25-60 yr / median 55 yr at -600 nT; 49-333 yr / median 93 yr at -850 nT), reconstructed 1859/1921/1872 intensities, -1200/-1400 nT direct-observation extremes, ~-2000 to -2500 nT theoretical max, and the NRC 2008 cost quote
verdicts.note: Downloaded the full 143-page published article (https://arxiv.org/pdf/2205.09265, header reads 'Living Reviews in Solar Physics (2022)19:2') and text-searched it. Every figure is verbatim: waiting-time sentence in Sect. 8 ('range from 25 to 60 years with a median value of 55 years ... range from 49 to 333 years with a median of 93 years'); Table 10 summary '-949 (+/-~30) nT; -907 (+/-132) nT, May 1921; ~-1000 nT, February 1872 ... -1200 nT, July 2012, -1400 nT, August 1972 ... ~-2000 to -2500 nT'; and the NRC quote in Sect. 1 ('$1 trillion to $2 trillion during the first year alone ... with recovery times of 4-10 years'). The -850 nT / Siscoe et al. (2006) attribution in the packet's event definition is also Cliver's own wording. Note the Springer URL given in the packet 303-redirects to an IdP login; the article is genuinely open access via the arXiv/Springer PDF.

verdicts.citation_claim: Lloyd's of London (2013), research by N. Homeier and L. Wei (AER), 'Solar Storm Risk to the North American Electric Grid' — 20-40 million at risk, 16 days to 1-2 years, $0.6-2.6 trillion, 150 yr return period (100-250), 50 yr Quebec (35-70), 5-12/6-16 month lead times, 1989 and 2003 calibration details
verdicts.note: Downloaded the Lloyd's PDF from the exact URL given and extracted the text. Cover page credits 'research and analysis by scientists from Atmospheric and Environmental Research, Inc. (AER) Nicole Homeier, PhD ... Lisa Wei, PhD', (c) Lloyd's 2013. Every quoted figure is verbatim, including the ones most likely to be garbled: '-589 nT on the Dst scale', 'in less than two minutes', 'more than six million people for nine hours at an economic cost estimated to be around C$13.2Bn', 'Two transformers were damaged due to voltage overloads', 'twelve transformers in South Africa', 'around 50,000 customers', '$100k per blocking capacitor for a total of $100 million to protect the 1,000 most vulnerable transformers', and 'lead time of 15-30 minutes'. Return periods confirmed at p.189: 'mid-point estimate for the return period of a Carrington-level is 150 years, with a reasonable range of 100 - 250 years. For a Quebec-level event, the return period is 50 years, with a reasonable range of 35 - 70 years.'

verdicts.citation_claim: U.S. DOE (2024), 'Large Power Transformer Resilience' Report to Congress — 36/60-month lead times, 150-400 tons, 4,900-6,799 LPTs, 137 (18%) domestic / 617 (82%) imported, ~343 LPTs/year capacity, 38-40 year average age, NERC TPL-007
verdicts.note: Downloaded the PDF from the exact energy.gov URL and extracted the text. Title 'Large Power Transformer Resilience, Report to Congress July 2024', signed Jennifer Granholm; statutory basis confirmed as 'Infrastructure Investment and Jobs Act (Public Law 117-58), also known as the Bipartisan Infrastructure Law (BIL), section 40103(d)'. All seven figures are verbatim, including the easily-transposed ones: '137 LPTs (18 percent) were produced domestically for domestic use while 617 units (82 percent) were imported for domestic use, and only 4 units were exported' and 'the average age of LPTs in the North American grid was 38-40 years'. TPL-007 sentence verbatim.

verdicts.citation_claim: Miyake, Nagaya, Masuda & Nakamura (2012), Nature 486, 240-242, doi:10.1038/nature11123 — 'a rapid increase of about 12 per mil in the 14C content from ad 774 to 775, which is about 20 times larger than the change attributed to ordinary solar modulation'
verdicts.note: nature.com and Semantic Scholar both withhold the abstract, so I pulled the full record from Europe PMC (https://www.ebi.ac.uk/europepmc/webservices/rest/search?query=DOI:%2210.1038/nature11123%22&resultType=core). Title 'A signature of cosmic-ray increase in AD 774-775 from tree rings in Japan', Miyake F, Nagaya K, Masuda K, Nakamura T, Nature 486:240-242, 2012 — author list, order, volume, pages and DOI all correct. The abstract reads 'We find a rapid increase of about 12 per mil in the 14C content from ad 774 to 775, which is about 20 times larger than the change attributed to ordinary solar modulation' — identical to the packet.

verdicts.citation_claim: Cliver et al. (2022), Living Rev. Solar Phys. 19:2 — F30 fluences of 10^10 / 5x10^10 / 10^11 cm^-2 once per century / millennium / 10^4 yr; P(>5x10^10) >= 1.2x10^-4 yr^-1; five Holocene events; 8.4x10^9 cm^-2 Aug 1972 and 1.4x10^8 cm^-2 Feb 1956 direct maxima; 45-fold 1956 GLE implying ~8x10^10 cm^-2; Carrington flare X45 +/- 5; X44/X101 century/millennium flares
verdicts.note: All checked against the same locally extracted full text. Verbatim hits: 'Figure 52 indicates that, roughly, events with the F30 fluences of 10^10, 5 x 10^10 and 10^11 cm^-2 are expected to occur once per roughly a century, a millennium and 10^4 years, respectively'; 'Five historical events (7176 BC, 5259 BC, 660 BC, 774 AD, 993 AD) with F30 > 5 x 10^10 (cm2 year)^-1 ... a lower limit of P(> 5 x 10^10 (cm2 year)^-1) >= 1.2 x 10^-4 year^-1 has been set'; Table 10 '8.4x10^9 cm^-2, composite event in August 1972; at 200 MeV: 1.4x10^8 cm^-2, 23 February 1956'; Sect. 7.4 'would imply a F30 value of ~8 x 10^10 cm^-2, ~10 times larger than that of the strongest 3-month interval of SEP activity in the modern era'; Sect. 3.1 'Cliver and Dietrich (2013) obtained an estimate for the Carrington flare of X45 +/- 5 based on the magnetic crochet'; and 'The century- and millennium-level flares ... are X44 and X101, respectively'. One unit nuance the packet elides: Cliver's 5x10^10 threshold is an ANNUAL fluence, (cm^2 year)^-1, not a per-event fluence; the packet's event definition states it as a per-event cm^-2 threshold.

verdicts.citation_claim: Thomas, Melott, Arkenberg & Snyder II (2013), Geophys. Res. Lett. 40, 1237-1240 — one order of magnitude beyond the Oct 1989 SPE; hard spectra give moderate ozone depletion, no mass extinction; soft-spectrum case ruled out; 'modern technological implications of such an event may be extreme'
verdicts.note: Retrieved https://arxiv.org/abs/1302.1501. Title 'Terrestrial effects of possible astrophysical sources of an AD 774-775 increase in 14C production'; authors Brian C. Thomas, Adrian L. Melott, Keith R. Arkenberg, Brock R. Snyder II; journal-ref 'Geophysical Research Letters, vol. 40, 1237-1240, 2013'; DOI 10.1002/grl.50222. The packet's quoted string is a contiguous verbatim excerpt of the abstract. Caveat on how the packet USES it: Thomas et al. RULE OUT the very soft-spectrum severe-ozone-depletion case, yet the packet keeps it as a 1%-weight severity tier — defensible only as residual model uncertainty, and the packet does not say so.

verdicts.citation_claim: Melott et al. (2004), Int. J. Astrobiol. — 'two or more times per billion years'; 6x10^-9 y^-1 and ~170 My within 3 kpc; 1.9 kpc t_G^-1/2; beaming irrelevant; 'credible working hypothesis'
verdicts.note: Retrieved the abs page and the full PDF (https://arxiv.org/abs/astro-ph/0309415, journal-ref Int.J.Astrobiol.3:55,2004, DOI 10.1017/S1473550404001910; Semantic Scholar gives pages 55-61). Nine-author list matches the packet exactly. All four quotes are verbatim in the body: 'we would expect a dangerous event rate of 6 x 10-9 y-1, in other words about 170 [My]'; 'the typical distance to the nearest GRB irradiating a locale within our galaxy would be 1.9 kpc tG-1/2'; 'For most purposes, beaming is irrelevant...'; 'only a "credible working hypothesis"'. The packet's 100 kJ/m^2 at 2-3 kpc event definition is also supported: their GRB1 is 'at 2 kpc' delivering 'about 10 kW/m2' for 10 s, and they 'regard 3 kpc as a reasonable estimate of the proximity at which a GRB becomes disruptive'.

verdicts.citation_claim: Thomas et al. (2005), ApJ 622, L153-L156 — 10 s burst delivering 100 kJ/m^2 gives 35% global ozone depletion, 55% at some latitudes, persisting over 5 years
verdicts.note: Retrieved https://arxiv.org/abs/astro-ph/0411284. Title 'Terrestrial Ozone Depletion Due to a Milky Way Gamma-Ray Burst'; authors Brian C. Thomas, Charles H. Jackman, Adrian L. Melott, Claude M. Laird, Richard S. Stolarski, Neil Gehrels, John K. Cannizzo, Daniel P. Hogan — matches the packet's eight-author list in order; journal-ref 'Astrophys.J. 622 (2005) L153-L156', DOI 10.1086/429799. Every quoted number is verbatim from the abstract.

verdicts.citation_claim: Piran & Jimenez (2014), Phys. Rev. Lett. 113, 231102 — 50% chance of a lethal GRB in the last 500 Myr; 95% within 4 kpc of the galactic centre; below 50% beyond 10 kpc
verdicts.note: Retrieved https://arxiv.org/abs/1409.2506. Journal-ref 'Phys. Rev. Lett. 113, 231102 (2014)', DOI 10.1103/PhysRevLett.113.231102, authors Tsvi Piran and Raul Jimenez. The packet's long quotation is a verbatim contiguous excerpt of the abstract. (Paper title, not given in the packet, is 'On the role of GRBs on life extinction in the Universe'.) Useful cross-check the packet did not make: 50% in 500 Myr implies ~1.4x10^-9 yr^-1, consistent with the packet's 2x10^-9 best estimate. But note Piran & Jimenez's 'lethal' means significant damage to life generally, not human extinction — it does not support the packet's terminal tier.

verdicts.citation_claim: Gehrels et al. (2003), ApJ 585 — ~8 pc critical distance and ~47% combined ozone depletion roughly doubling biologically active UV
verdicts.note: Retrieved the abs page and full PDF (https://arxiv.org/abs/astro-ph/0211361; journal-ref Astrophys.J. 585 (2003) 1169-1176, DOI 10.1086/346127). Six-author list matches exactly. Conclusions section verbatim: 'a core-collapse SN would need to be situated approximately 8 pc away to produce a combined ozone depletion from both gamma-rays and cosmic rays of ~47%, which would roughly double the globally-averaged, biologically active UV reaching the ground.'

verdicts.citation_claim: Gehrels et al. (2003), ApJ 585 — time-averaged galactic rate of core-collapse SNe within 8 pc is ~1.5 Gyr^-1; ~3 Gyr^-1 for D<10 pc
verdicts.note: Same PDF. Abstract: 'the time-averaged galactic rate of core-collapse supernovae occurring within 8 pc is ~1.5/Gyr'. Sect. 5 verbatim: '~3 Gyr-1 for DSN < 10 pc, or ~1.5 Gyr-1 for DSN < Dcrit ~ 8 pc, where we used the fact that the rate varies as DSN^3'. The packet's 1.5e-9/yr best rate follows directly. Its stated range 5e-10 to 6e-9 also brackets the alternatives Gehrels discusses (van den Bergh ~0.3/Gyr within 10 pc at the low end; Clark et al. ~10/Gyr within 10 pc at the high end), though the packet does not say so.

verdicts.citation_claim: Christoudias et al. (2024), Commun. Earth Environ., doi:10.1038/s43247-024-01490-9 — abstract as quoted; ozone loss 'around 10% globally'; Antarctic hole 60-70%; no 8-pc supernova signature in the geological record
verdicts.note: Metadata confirmed via Semantic Scholar (title 'Earth's atmosphere protects the biosphere from nearby supernovae', Commun. Earth Environ. vol. 5, 2024, DOI as given, all eight authors in the packet's order); the packet's block quote is the published abstract verbatim. I then downloaded the full PDF from the packet's INSPIRE URL (live) and confirmed the three body quotes word-for-word: 'equivalent to around 10% globally'; 'The maximum ozone depletion over the poles is less than the present-day anthropogenic ozone hole over Antarctica, which amounts to an ozone column loss of 60-70%'; and 'A signature of such a close supernova, however, has not been found in the geological record.' The citation is clean; the packet's USE of it is not (see overall).

verdicts.citation_claim: Bailer-Jones, Rybizki, Andrae & Fouesneau (2018), A&A 616, A37 — 19.7 +/- 2.2 encounters per Myr within 1 pc, scaling quadratically; 26 with >50% chance inside 1 pc (7 within 0.5 pc); Gl 710 95% within 0.08 pc (17,000 AU); only 15% of encounters within 5 pc identified
verdicts.note: Retrieved https://arxiv.org/abs/1805.07581. Title 'New stellar encounters discovered in the second Gaia data release', journal-ref 'A&A 616, A37 (2018)', DOI 10.1051/0004-6361/201833456, four authors as listed. All four quoted claims are verbatim from the abstract, including the exact rate and the 'expected to scale quadratically with the encounter distance out to at least several pc' clause. Two caveats the packet omits: (i) that quadratic law is asserted OUTWARD to several pc, whereas the packet extrapolates it INWARD by a factor of ~20 to 0.048 pc, where gravitational focusing makes the true scaling shallower than quadratic (i.e. 4.6e-8/yr is likely a slight UNDER-estimate); (ii) the abstract's own warning that 'Spuriously large parallaxes in our sample from imperfect filtering would tend to inflate both the number of encounters found and this inferred rate.'

verdicts.citation_claim: Frogel & Gould (1998), arXiv astro-ph/9801052, 'no journal reference recorded in the arXiv metadata' — ~10^4 AU trigger distance, shower arrives ~0.18 Myr later, ~0.4% prior probability, none found in HIPPARCOS, unlikely in the next 0.5 Myr
verdicts.note: Retrieved the arXiv API record for astro-ph/9801052: title 'No Death Star -- For Now', authors Jay A. Frogel and Andrew Gould, submitted 7 January 1998. The packet's long quotation is the abstract VERBATIM, every clause. Correction to the citation's framing, not its figures: the packet's parenthetical is misleading. arXiv's journal_ref field is indeed empty, but the same metadata carries DOI 10.1086/311367 and a comment 'In press at The Astrophysical Journal Letters', and Semantic Scholar resolves that DOI to The Astrophysical Journal Letters 499, L219-L222 (1998). This is a peer-reviewed published Letter, not an unpublished e-print, and should be cited as such. Separately, a cross-check the packet missed: Frogel & Gould's own ~0.4% prior over a 0.18 Myr look-back implies ~2.2x10^-8/yr for the same trigger distance, about half the packet's Gaia-derived 4.6x10^-8/yr — both inside the stated range, and worth stating as independent corroboration.

verdicts.citation_claim: Cao, Loeb & MacLeod (2025), arXiv:2511.11814, described as a PREPRINT not peer-reviewed — order-of-magnitude rise in 1 km comet impact probability at b ~ 2,300 AU; threshold diameter D_0 = 2.25 km; HD7977 flyby 2.47 Myr ago at 2,300-13,000 AU
verdicts.corrected_value: Now published/accepted: Scientific Reports, doi:10.1038/s41598-025-29033-y
verdicts.note: Retrieved the arXiv API record for 2511.11814: 'On the coincidence between the close passage of HD7977 and the Pliocene-Pleistocene transition', Zhuoya Cao, Abraham Loeb, Morgan MacLeod, submitted 14 November 2025. The packet's quoted passages are verbatim from the abstract, and the 'submitted 14 November 2025' date is right. One correction: the arXiv metadata as of this session now carries journal_ref 'Scientific Reports (accepted)' and DOI 10.1038/s41598-025-29033-y, so the packet's 'PREPRINT, not peer-reviewed as of retrieval' descriptor is stale and should be updated. This does not change any figure. Note also that the packet's tier structure leans on this paper for a 10-km cometary impact tier (p=0.002) that the paper says nothing about — Cao et al. model 1 km comets and a 2.25 km P=1 threshold.

audits.overall: Unusually clean on citations, weak on the severity tiers. I could not find a single fabricated, misattributed or mis-transcribed citation: all 17 exist, all authors/years/volumes/DOIs are right, every URL resolves, and every "FIGURE AS STATED" string I checked was verbatim in the source, including the ones most likely to be corrupted by memory (Lloyd's C$13.2Bn / twelve South African transformers / 15-30 minute warning; DOE's 137-vs-617 transformer split; Cliver's 49-333 yr and 1.2x10^-4 yr^-1; Riley & Love's two CIs). Sources I actually retrieved this session (WebSearch was budget-exhausted, so everything was direct fetch of primary documents): NTRS record 20120003491; the USGS Publications Warehouse entry for Riley & Love 2017 plus its Semantic Scholar record; the full 143-page Cliver et al. 2022 Living Reviews PDF (text-extracted locally and grep-verified for every quoted string); the Lloyd's 2013 PDF from the packet's own assets.lloyds.com URL; the DOE July 2024 LPT Report to Congress PDF from energy.gov; the Europe PMC record for Miyake et al. 2012; arXiv abs pages and full PDFs for Melott et al. 2004 and Gehrels et al. 2003; arXiv abs pages for Thomas et al. 2005, Piran & Jimenez 2014, Thomas et al. 2013 and Bailer-Jones et al. 2018; the Christoudias et al. 2024 Semantic Scholar record plus the full PDF from the packet's INSPIRE URL; and arXiv API records for Frogel & Gould 1998 and Cao, Loeb & MacLeod 2025. Only two citation-level corrections exist and both are metadata, not numbers: Frogel & Gould is a published Letter (ApJL 499, L219-L222, doi:10.1086/311367), not the journal-less e-print the packet implies; and Cao et al. is no longer a bare preprint (Scientific Reports, doi:10.1038/s41598-025-29033-y). The derived rates also survive scrutiny — 0.008/yr sits between Riley's 12%/decade and Lloyd's 150-yr midpoint with a range that is exactly Riley & Love's power-law 95% CI in per-year units; 0.001/yr is Cliver's millennium figure with his own 1.2x10^-4 floor; 1.5e-9 and 2e-9 come straight from Gehrels and Melott; and the stellar-encounter arithmetic (19.7 x (10^4/206265)^2 = 4.6x10^-8/yr) is correct and honestly flagged as author-estimate. No tier set sums above 1.0 (all five sum to exactly 1.000). Where the packet is NOT trustworthy is everything to the right of the citations: not one deaths_fraction in any tier of any hazard is traceable to a cited source, and several contradict the sources cited beside them. The GRB terminal tier (p=0.005, deaths=1, terminal=true) has no mechanism in Melott, Thomas or Piran — the modelled worst case is 35-55% ozone depletion, and Piran's "lethal" means damage to life, not permanent human extinction; the 0.8 and 0.3 death fractions for the closer GRB tiers are equally unsourced. The supernova tiers are worse: they give 35% weight to a Gehrels-class 47%-depletion outcome killing 5% of humanity and 5% weight to a 40%-mortality outcome, when the packet's own newest citation (Christoudias et al. 2024) concludes the atmosphere shields the biosphere, puts global ozone loss near 10%, and says a close-supernova signature has never been found in the geological record — the weights invert the evidence they cite. The geomagnetic tiers assign up to 10% human mortality where the cited literature offers only dollars and outage-days (Lloyd's 20-40 million at risk of outage; NRC $1-2T). And the ESPE packet keeps a soft-spectrum severe-depletion tier that Thomas et al. 2013 explicitly rule out. Verdict: the citation layer is solid enough to build on and the event-frequency layer is defensible; the conditional-consequence layer is undocumented author judgement wearing the same footnotes, and should be relabelled as such before any of these death fractions are used in a model.
